5.1.11.
Relation with the anomaly condition of
[
BDF+22
]
.

Proposition
5.1.5
explicates the anomaly condition in terms of the symplectic representation
V
of the subgroup
H\subset G
(of the structure theorem). The paper
[
BDF+22
]
introduces a different “anomaly vanishing” condition for a symplectic
H
-representation
V
; without going into much detail, we reformulate their condition as follows:

Definition 5.1.12
.

M
satisfies the anomaly-vanishing condition of
[
BDF+22
]
if the pullback of
V
to the simply-connected cover
H_{sc}
of the derived group of
H
is anomaly-free in the sense of Proposition
5.1.5
, that is to say,

c_{2}(V)
vanishes mod
2
in the cohomology of
H_{sc}
.

It might as well be that this is the “correct” anomaly-vanishing condition; we presently do not know any examples of hyperspherical varieties where the two conditions differ.
In any case, we can directly confirm that the dual of a
tempered spherical variety is anomaly-free in the sense of (
5.1.12
):

Proposition 5.1.13
.

Assuming Conjecture
4.3.16
, if
P(X)=B
, the dual Hamiltonian space of the spherical variety
X
satisfies the anomaly-vanishing condition of Definition
5.1.12
.

Proof.

In the notation of Proposition (
5.1.5
), but with
\check{G}_{X}
in place of
H
, it is enough to show that the sum
\sum_{\chi\in\Xi/\{\pm 1\}}\chi
(mod 2) vanishes on the coroots of
\check{G}_{X}
. Indeed, its pullback to the simply connected cover of the derived group of
\check{G}_{X}
will then be trivial (mod 2).

Since we have assumed that
P(X)=B
, the symplectic representation
V
coincides with the representation
S_{X}
of Definition
4.4.3
. The only summand of (
4.15
) for which this could fail is the summand
S_{Y}
. In the notation of Conjecture
4.3.16
(but replacing
X
by
Y
), the sub-sum of
\Xi
that corresponds to
S_{Y}
can be written as
\chi_{Y}=\sum_{b\in\mathfrak{B}_{Y}^{+}}\textrm{wt}(b)
. Finally, we have, for every simple coroot
\gamma
of
\check{G}_{X}
, with
w_{\gamma}
the corresponding Weyl reflection, that

\chi_{Y}-w_{\gamma}\chi_{Y}=\langle\chi_{Y},\gamma\rangle\check{\gamma}.

By Conjecture
4.3.16
,
w_{\gamma}\chi_{Y}=\chi_{Y}
, unless
(Y,\gamma)
is of type
T
with associated valuations
\check{v}_{1},\check{v}_{2}
, in which case
w_{\gamma}\chi_{Y}=\chi_{Y}-2(\check{v}_{1}+\check{v}_{2})=\chi_{Y}-2\check{\gamma}
. In particular,

\langle\chi_{Y},\gamma\rangle\in 2\mathbb{Z}
.
∎

5.2.
Hyperspherical dual pairs over
\mathbb{C}

The most ideal form of hyperspherical duality would be:

Expectation 5.2.1
.

There exists a bijection

(G,M)\leftrightarrow(\check{G},\check{M}),

between isomorphism classes of anomaly-free hyperspherical
(G,M)
over
\mathbb{C}

with anomaly-free hyperspherical
(\check{G},\check{M})
over
\mathbb{C}
, with the following properties:

If
M
admits a distinguished polarization
M=T^{*}(X,\Psi)
, as in Definition
3.7.1
, then
\check{M}
arises from
(X,\Psi)
via the procedure of §
4
, and vice versa.

We must admit at the moment that this expectation remains somewhat tentative: we would not formulate it as a “conjecture,”
but we believe that something like it should be true, perhaps after slight modifications of the
definitions of “anomaly-free” or “hyperspherical.”

In the remainder of this paper, we will use the phrase
hyperspherical dual pair
(over
\mathbb{C}
)
to mean either a pair as
(G,M),(\check{G},\check{M})
which
arises via the construction of §
4
, or its reverse.
We anticipate, however, that
all the statements of the paper will apply to the
class of dual pairs of Expectation
5.2.1
.

5.2.2.
Some consequences of Expectation
5.2.1

We will explicitly note several consequences of the expectation. They are are valid in examples that we have checked, but we have no general proof:

(i)

The construction of §
4
is independent of distinguished polarization.
It is likely this is provable using ideas from the theory of spherical varieties.

(ii)

Any
(\check{G},\check{M})
arising via the procedure of §
4
from
(G,M=T^{*}(X,\Psi))
is non-anomalous.
For what we have proved in this direction, see Proposition
5.1.13
.

(iii)

If
(G,M)
and
(\check{G},\check{M})

are a distinguished hyperspherical pair, where
both sides admit distinguished polarizations, and
(\check{G},\check{M})

arises from
(G,M)
via the procedure of §
4
, then
the reverse is also true:
(G,M)
arises from
(\check{G},\check{M})

from the procedure of §
4
.

(iv)

In the setting of
M=T^{*}(X,\Psi)
and
\check{M}
as in §
4
, we have proved in Proposition
4.6.1

(5.7)

\mbox{parity: }e^{2\check{\rho}}\eta(-1)\in\check{G}\mbox{ acts trivially on $\check{M}$.}

where
\eta:G\rightarrow{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
is the character of a
G
-eigenmeasure on
X
, identified with a dual central cocharacter in
{\check{G}}
.

Expectation
5.2.1
implies that the parity condition (
5.7
)
also holds “in reverse” for a hyperspherical dual pair if
\check{M}
also admits a distinguished polarization:

(5.8)

\mbox{dual parity: }e^{2\check{\rho}}\check{\eta}(-1)\in G\mbox{ acts trivially on $M$.}

where
\check{\eta}:\check{G}\rightarrow{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
is the character of a
\check{G}
-eigenmeasure on
\check{X}
, again identified to a cocharacter for
G
.
38
38

38

This statement
doesn’t depend on the choice of eigenmeasure, cf. §
3.8.2
.

Remark 5.2.3
.

Although
we have often used them as a crutch, no special role in the duality should be played by the existence
of eigenforms as in §
3.8
.
A typical example of a dual pair, where one side has no eigenmeasure, is given by

(G,(X,\Psi))=(\mathrm{PGL}_{3},{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\cdot({\mathbb{G}_{a}}^{2},\psi)\backslash\mathrm{PGL}_{3})\mbox{and }(\check{G},\check{X})=(\mathrm{SL}_{3},\mathbb{A}^{3}).

This is related to the Example
4.3.11
.
One can, in such cases, still apply the local and global conjectures
by reducing them to a case with an eigenform, as described earlier in
§
3.8.2
; but it would be
good, in a further elaboration of this work, to do this in a more intrinsic way. See e.g. Remark
12.6.5
.

Remark 5.2.4
.

(a)

The putative duality requires some kind of anomaly vanishing condition, unless one modifies the nature of the duality;
in the classical theory of automorphic forms the
appearance of metaplectic groups necessitates a modification
even for the duality on reductive groups, cf.
[
Wei14
]
. It is an
important problem to study anomalous examples –there are many in the automorphic literature, that is to say period integrals involving covering groups; let us point only to Shimura’s integral
[
Shi75
]
– and extend the proposals
here to that context.

(b)

We do not know of examples of dual
(M,\check{M})
where neither
side admits a twisted polarization, but there seems to be no reason for such examples not to exist. It would
interesting to exhibit one.

5.3.
Hyperspherical dual pairs over arithmetic fields.

We have already seen in our previous discussions of §
3.9
and §
4.8

that it is important to consider
models for
(G,M)

over other fields.
We propose
that in the non-anomalous
case, at least, there is a best one:

There exists a distinguished “split” form of each hyperspherical
(G,M)
, defined over
\mathbb{Z}
.

In this subsection, after discussing this
proposal, we will use it to give a working
definition of a class of dual pairs

(G,M)_{/\mathbb{F}}\leftrightarrow(\check{G},\check{M})_{/k}

where

\mathbb{F}
is either a finite field or
\mathbb{C}
, and
k
is either
\mathbb{C}
or the closure of an
\ell
-adic field.

Our primary motivation to understand the theory over general
\mathbb{F}
arises
from automorphic forms.
We will discuss this motivation later, in
§
5.3.7
. Perhaps the main takeaway is that,
for
\mathbb{F}
not algebraically closed, the hyperspherical
datum over
\mathbb{F}

best adapted to automorphic phenomena is not always the most obvious one.

At this point, we should remind the reader what was done in §
3.9
and
4.8
: In the former,
we used the structure theorem to define a notion of “hyperspherical datum/scheme” over (more) general rings, and to describe, in some cases, a “distinguished split form” of those. In the latter, we used the structure theorem to describe a split form of the dual Hamiltonian space of a spherical variety, depending on some mild choices. Here, we will combine these discussions into a wishlist for the “distinguished split form of
M
,” that will also make some forward references to our local conjecture.
We fix a pinning in order to rigidify
G
(thus, the notion of a distinguished split form of
M
is really to be understood with reference to a pinned group
G
).

Expectation 5.3.1
.

Each nonanomalous hyperspherical pair
(G,M)
over
\mathbb{C}

admits a distinguished
\mathbb{Z}
-form
(G,M)_{\mathbb{Z}}

with the following properties.

(a)

Write
\mathbb{Z}^{\prime}
for the ring obtained from
\mathbb{Z}

by inverting
N_{G}
, as in (
3.41
). Then

(G,M)_{\mathbb{Z}^{\prime}}
corresponds to a split
\mathbb{Z}^{\prime}
-form of the linear algebra datum
\mathcal{D}(G,M)

(see Definition
3.9.3
).

(b)

Suppose that
(G,M),(\check{G},\check{M})
form
a hyperspherical dual pair over
\mathbb{C}
, with
\check{M}=T^{*}X
polarized.
Then, for any field
k
not of characteristic
2
, the base change
(G,M)_{k}
to
k
of the distinguished
\mathbb{Z}
-form
belongs to the distinguished class of forms constructed in
§
4.8
, switching
(G,M)
and
(\check{G},\check{M})
in that discussion.
(cf. also Proposition
4.8.10
).

(c)

Suppose that
M,\check{M}
form
a hyperspherical dual pair, with
\check{M}=T^{*}X
polarized;
then
\mathbb{Z}[\check{M}]
is the local Plancherel algebra,
see Remark
8.1.10
.

Remark 5.3.2
.

•

Points (a) and (b) are suggested by the study of examples known to us.
The word “split” in (a) is suggested by the work
[
GN10
]
wherein a maximal torus of
H
– the reductive subgroup
of
G
appearing in the structural data for
M
, as in (
3.1
) –
appears from degenerating to a horospherical variety.

•

We are perhaps being overly cautious
in (a) and (b); perhaps it is unnecessary to invert all primes dividing
N_{G}
.
An example illustrating the difficulties at
p=2
is the case
G=\mathrm{Sp}_{4}

when
M
is defined by the datum
(H=\mathrm{SL}_{2},S=\mathbb{A}^{2})

and the auxiliary
\mathrm{SL}_{2}
is the centralizer of
H
in
G
.

•

The strongest reason to believe in this expectation
is the one of point (c), namely, the local conjecture that we are about to formulate in
§
7
. In favorable circumstances,
it gives rise to an explicit ring with Poisson bracket
which should be the coordinate ring of the distinguished split form of
M
over
\mathbb{Z}
.

Indeed, recall that one way of constructing the split form of a group is provided by the geometric Satake correspondence:
the split form of
G
over
\mathbb{Q}
and even over
\mathbb{Z}
, can be reconstructed from the category of sheaves
of the affine Grassmannian of
\check{G}
. Point (c) is
an analogous proposal –
we will see in §
8.5
that
M
can be conjecturally reconstructed as a
G\times\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-space
given access to a polarized dual space
\check{M}=T^{*}(\check{X},\check{\Psi})

by considering a suitable category of constructible sheaves.
This category of constructible sheaves
can be defined with
\mathbb{Z}
coefficients when
\Psi
is trivial (simply by considering sheaves of abelian groups), in particular giving
a
\mathbb{Z}
-structure to
M
.
39
39

39

In fact, a similar argument
applies when
\Psi
is nontrivial. However, it does not give rise to models over
\mathbb{Z}
, but
rather over completions of various cyclotomic integer rings.

Remark 5.3.3
.

For the purposes of applications to automorphic forms,
the very best situation would not be
to try to cherry-pick our favorite form,
but rather find an enhanced
version of the duality

(5.9)

(G,M)\leftrightarrow(\check{G},\check{M})

that took into account rational structures and Galois actions on both sides.
In the case of
G\leftrightarrow\check{G}
, a form of

G
over a non-separably closed field
\mathbb{F}
provides an action of the absolute Galois group of
\mathbb{F}

on the dual group
\check{G}
; this datum is used to define the
L
-group.
An analogous Galois action in the case of the duality (
5.9
)
is provided, in part, by the analysis of §
4.8.1
, see Definition
4.8.9
.
Such an action of the Galois group should naturally arise from the construction of the duality (
5.9
) in the general case.

5.3.4.
Some consequences of Expectation
5.3.1

Expectation
5.3.1

has various explicit consequences which, again, we do not know how to prove in general,
but are valid in those cases we have examined.

(i)

The existence of a
\mathbb{Z}
-form proposed in Expectation
5.3.1
implies that the isomorphism class of
(G,M)
is stable by any field automorphism of
\mathbb{C}
,
and in particular
(G,M)
can be unambiguously transferred to any algebraically closed field of characteristic zero
by the Lefschetz principle.

(ii)

Point (c) also has very strong implications (perhaps too strong?) The local conjecture relates the ring of regular functions on
M
to certain constructible cohomology groups;
thus, for
\mathbb{Z}[\check{M}]
to be flat over
\mathbb{Z}
, these particular cohomology groups should have no torsion. See
Remark
8.1.10
for further discussion.

5.3.5.
Characteristic
2
subtleties, quadratic refinements

Let us consider the case when
M=V
is a vector space
and look at what we expect about the integral model of
M
; in this case, we expect, of course,
this to be simply a
\mathbb{Z}
-lattice
V_{\mathbb{Z}}

equipped with its standard symplectic form,
equipped with an action of the Chevalley form
G_{\mathbb{Z}}
.

However, we expect (hope?) this to have a further property, namely:

(*)
the associated representation of
\mathbb{F}_{2}
-algebraic groups

G_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}(V_{\mathbb{F}_{2}})
should preserve a quadratic refinement
of the symplectic form,

i.e.,
G_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}
preserves a quadratic
function
Q
on
V_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}
such that
Q(x+y)-Q(x)-Q(y)
gives the symplectic form.

There are two reasons to expect this.
Firstly, this allows one to construct a moment
action for the action of
G_{\mathbb{Z}}
on
V_{\mathbb{Z}}
.
The second is topological, arising
from the existence of extra mod
2
operations
on the the cohomology of
E_{3}
-spaces (cf. §
17
).

Not all hyperspherical
G
-representations
will admit a
\mathbb{Z}
-lattice with this property.
For example, the standard representation of
G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}

on
M=\mathbb{A}^{2}
does not have this property.
However, it is plausible that all anomaly-free
examples have property (*), and in some cases
it helps distinguish the appropriate form.

For example, take
G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}

acting on
M=\mathbb{A}^{2}\times\mathbb{A}^{2}
,
there are two possible
\mathbb{Z}
forms.
Namely take

M_{\mathbb{Z}}=(\mathbb{Z}^{2},\omega)\otimes(\mathbb{Z}^{2},B)

with
\omega
the standard symplectic structure, and
for some symmetric bilinear unimodular form
B
.
The only possibilities for
B
are, up to equivalence,
represented by the matrices
\left[{\small\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\
1&0\end{array}}\right]
and the identity matrix; the first possibility satisfies (*) and the second does not.

5.3.6.
Working definition of hyperspherical dual pairs over
(\mathbb{F},k)

Although it is not clear that the different desiderata in Expectation
5.3.1

are compatible with one another, they are quite restrictive when they apply.
We will focus here on (a) of that expectation. The “distinguished split form” introduced in Definition
3.9.9
, whenever it applies, is necessarily the reduction of the conjectural distinguished split form to an appropriate finite field, and this permits us to transpose the notion of hyperspherical dual pairs, as in §
5.2
,
to pairs over arithmetic fields, suitable for our applications to the Langlands program.

Suppose that
(G\times\mathbb{G}_{gr},M)
and
(\check{G}\times\mathbb{G}_{gr},\check{M})
is a hyperspherical dual pair over
\mathbb{C}
, in the sense of §
5.2
.
Let
\mathbb{F}
be either
\mathbb{F}_{q},\overline{\mathbb{F}_{q}}
or
\mathbb{C}
, and let
k
be either
\mathbb{C}
or the closure of an
\ell
-adic field.
Then, by a

distinguished split form
of the above pair over
(\mathbb{F},k)
, we shall mean

(G\times\mathbb{G}_{gr},M)_{/\mathbb{F}}\mbox{ and }(\check{G}\times\mathbb{G}_{gr},\check{M})_{/k}

where, if
\mathbb{F}\neq\mathbb{C}
, the left hand side is a split form as defined in (a) above,
and the right hand side is obtained from
(\check{G}\times\mathbb{G}_{gr},\check{M})
by means of an isomorphism
k\simeq\mathbb{C}
.
40
40

40

It would follow
from §
5.3.4
(i) that this is independent of choice of isomorphism.

In the case that
M
or
\check{M}
come with distinguished polarizations, we can similarly define a split form of the pair equipped with their polarizations.

5.3.7.
Some automorphic examples and motivation

The following discussion presupposes
some familiarity with the conjectures in the remainder of the paper;
it is motivational and can be skipped. The main takeaway from the section is that
the “best” form of
(G,M)
may not be the most obvious one.
A related discussion, but on the spectral side, is given in §
4.8
.

In the Langlands program
we are concerned with reductive groups
G
over arithmetic fields
F
of several types –
for example,

F
could be the function field of a projective curve
\Sigma
over a finite field,
or a number field, or a local field. Correspondingly, we want to be able
to work with
(G,M)
over the same types of fields.
Now,
the automorphic data corresponding to
M
is sensitive to the form of
M

over
F
, and not only to its isomorphism class over
\bar{F}
.
Here is an example:

Example 5.3.8
.

Let
F
be a local field. The space
X_{d}
of
2\times 2
-matrices of determinant
d\in F^{\times}
, under the action of
G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}
, is isomorphic to the space
X=X_{1}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}
over the algebraic closure, but not necessarily over
F
. The set of
X
-distinguished irreducible representations
\pi\hookrightarrow C^{\infty}(X(F))
consists of those of the form
\pi=\tilde{\tau}\otimes\tau
, while for
X_{d}
they are of the form
\tilde{\tau}^{d}\otimes\tau
, where
\tilde{\tau}^{d}
is the twist of
\tilde{\tau}
(= the contragredient of
\tau
) by the automorphism given by conjugation by
\text{diag}(d,1)
. For the purposes of the Langlands parametrization, this automorphism does not change the
L
-parameter, but can act nontrivially on the elements of an
L
-packet.

In the language just introduced, both
X,X_{d}
are defined by polarized hyperspherical data, with trivial
\mathrm{SL}_{2}
;
what differs is the
F
-form of the embedding
H\rightarrow G
.

A point of crucial interest to us is that the form of
M
or
X
that interacts
in the cleanest way with the local Langlands conjecture may not be the obvious one.
The following example can be considered a generalization of the
d=-1
case of the previous one:

Example 5.3.9
.

Consider the group
G=H\times H
, where
H
is a quasisplit reductive group, and both copies of
H
are assumed to carry the same pinning
f_{H}\in\mathfrak{h}^{*}
. Let
X
be the
G
-space
H
, i.e.,

X
is the quotient
\Delta H\backslash H\times H

and let
X^{\prime}
be the following form of
X
:

X^{\prime}=\Delta^{\prime}H\backslash(H\times H),

where

\Delta^{\prime}H=\ \text{graph of the inner automorphism}(-1)^{\check{\rho}_{H}}:H\rightarrow H.

(The half sum of positive coroots
\check{\rho}_{H}
is considered as a cocharacter into the group of inner automorphisms of
H
via the pinning fixed.)
Note that this inner automorphism (let us denote it by
\iota
) is the one connecting the Chevalley and duality involutions (see §
2.3.2
):

h^{d}=(h^{c})^{\iota}.

As we now explain, it is functions on
X^{\prime}
, rather than functions on
X
,
which look more natural on the spectral side of the Langlands correspondence:

Consider a tempered local
L
-parameter
\phi
for
H
; according to the local Langlands conjectures as refined by Vogan
[
Vog93
]
, the choice of a Whittaker model for
H
(which is afforded by a combination of the pinning with a character of the additive group of the field) is supposed to be fixing a basepoint in the Vogan
L
-packet associated to
\phi
, and a parametrization of the elements
\tau
of this
L
-packet by the irreducible representations
\eta
of the component group of the stabilizer
\check{H}_{\phi}
of
\phi
in
\check{H}
. The pair
(\phi,\eta)
can be called the Langlands–Vogan parameter of
\tau
. The (pinned) Chevalley involution
c
of the dual group acts on the set of Langlands–Vogan parameters, and a naive hypothesis would be that
(\phi^{c},\eta^{c})
is the Langlands–Vogan parameter of the contragredient representation
\tilde{\tau}
. This is wrong, however, and in
[
Pra19
, Conjecture 2]
Prasad corrected this naive hypothesis by postulating that this is the Langlands–Vogan parameter of
\tilde{\tau}^{\iota}
, the twist of
\tilde{\tau}
by the involution
\iota
. But the set of tempered representations
\tau\otimes\tilde{\tau}^{\iota}
is precisely the set of representations appearing in the Plancherel formula for the space
L^{2}(X^{\prime})
, where
T^{*}X^{\prime}
is the pinned hyperspherical space as above!

In terms of the language just introduced, both
X
and
X^{\prime}
are defined by polarized hyperspherical data, with trivial
\mathrm{SL}_{2}
and
\rho
, and with
H=G
; what
differs is the embedding
\iota:H_{/F}\hookrightarrow G_{/F}
. As we just saw,
X^{\prime}
is in some respects more natural, although the associated
embedding
\iota^{\prime}
involves a “strange” conjugation by an involution.

To conclude discussion of this example, let us observe that
X
and
X^{\prime}
are distinguished from one another in the following abstract way:

(f_{H},-f_{H})
lies in the
F
-points of the image of the moment map for
T^{*}X
, but the point
f=(f_{H},f_{H})
may not be in the image; on the other hand
M^{\prime}=T^{*}X^{\prime}
contains
f
in the (
F
-point) image of the moment map.
This notion will be formalized later in §
4.8
: we will say that
M^{\prime}
is a pinned hyperspherical space.

Part II
Local theory

In Part 2 of this work we formulate and study the local form of our conjecture in the unramified setting.
For an overview of this part, see
page
1.4
.

6.
Shearing and geometric Satake.

In this section we discuss the operation of
shearing
with respect to
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-actions, in which the weights of the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action are paired with cohomological shifts.
This concept will arise throughout the paper; it already arises in the geometric Satake isomorphism,
as we will recall in §
6.6
.
Shearing is implicitly present throughout the Koszul duality literature. It is studied explicitly in the work of Arinkin and Gaitsgory – see
[
AG15
, Section A.2]
, but note that
[
AG15
]
shear by 2, while we shear by 1, hence the appearance of super-signs.

The contents of the section are as follows:

•

§
6.1
discusses shearing of vector spaces.

•

§
6.2
discusses shearing of algebras.

•

§
6.3
discusses shearing of categories.

•

§
6.4
discusses various examples of shearing
on categories of geometric or representation-theoretic origin.

•

§
6.5
discusses abelian geometric Satake by way of example. Although
shearing does not appear in the usual formulations of this, we take
the opportunity, by way of illustration, to explain how some of the subtle features there can be expressed in terms of shearing.
We will separately discuss an “analytic” and an “arithmetic” form, cf. §
2.7
.

•

§
6.6
discusses derived geometric Satake,
again, presented as an example of the shearing language.

•

§
6.7
discusses both abelian and derived Satake when
the base field is replaced by a finite field.

•

§
6.8
discusses the example of shearing the coordinate ring
of a hyperspherical variety. This could be subsumed in the previous section, but we isolate
it because of its later use in the paper.

6.1.
Shearing of vector spaces

There is an autoequivalence of the category
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})

of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant complexes of
k
-vector spaces (i.e., complexes of graded vector spaces),
called
shearing

defined by

M=\bigoplus_{i}M_{i}\mapsto M^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}:=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}M_{i}[i]

where
M_{i}
is the
i
-isotypical space,
upon which
\lambda\in{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
acts by
\lambda^{i}
;
this has inverse (unshearing)

N=\bigoplus N_{i}\mapsto N^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatbslash}}:=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}N_{i}[-i]

Note that
{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatbslash}}
has the property that it takes an ordinary graded vector space (i.e., a graded dg-vector space concentrated in cohomological degree
0
) to a dg-vector space for which the weight on the cohomology agrees with the cohomological degree.

The equivalence
M\mapsto M^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
is a
monoidal
autoequivalence, i.e., there is a natural identification

(M\otimes N)^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\simeq M^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\otimes N^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

using the corresponding property of translation (§
2.5.5
). We moreover have

\mathrm{Hom}(M,N)^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\simeq\mathrm{Hom}(M^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}},N^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}),

if we impose e.g.
N
finite-dimensional (the
\mathrm{Hom}
s here are not
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant, hence carry a natural
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action, besides the cohomological grading).

The even iterates
M\mapsto M^{2n{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
of the shearing have the natural structure of symmetric monoidal autoequivalences.
The shearing operation itself
M\mapsto M^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
is not symmetric monoidal (nor are its odd iterates), because of the Koszul rule of signs.
Thus we “correct” the shearing functor as in §
2.5.7
by replacing the shift
[i]
with the parity-corrected shift
\Pi^{i}[i]
, giving an endofunctor of
\text{Rep}^{\mathrm{super}}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
,

M=\bigoplus_{i}M_{i}\mapsto M^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}:=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}M_{i}\langle i\rangle

which does admit a natural symmetric monoidal structure. Restricting to even complexes
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})\subset\text{Rep}^{\mathrm{super}}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
(applying “Galois descent”, see Remark
2.5.4
) we find a symmetric monoidal equivalence

(-)^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}:\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})\longrightarrow\text{Rep}_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{super}}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})\subset\text{Rep}^{\mathrm{super}}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})

with the full subcategory of those super graded chain complexes in which the parity is given by the action of
\epsilon=-1\in{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
(i.e., representations of odd
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-weight are odd vector spaces, and those of even
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-weight are even).

With this convention,
shearing preserves traces
: given an automorphism

\alpha:M\rightarrow M
of a bounded complex
M
, the
super-trace
\mathrm{tr}(M)
satisfies
\mathrm{tr}(M)=\mathrm{tr}(M^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}})
,
since, in shearing the
i
th graded piece by
i
, we get a factor of
(-1)^{i}
by the cohomological shift,
and another factor of
(-1)^{i}
from switching between even and odd vector spaces.
As usual, the trace of an automorphism on a super-vector space
is understood to be the even trace minus the odd trace.

Remark 6.1.1
.

In §
2.5.7
we introduced a convention that, in a Frobenius-equivariant context, the shift operation
\langle 1\rangle=\Pi[1](1/2)
also includes
a Tate twist, and hence so does shearing. In the current context we would formalize this as follows:
there is a monoidal autoequivalence of the category of representations
of
\mathbb{G}_{gr}\times\langle\mathrm{Frobenius}\rangle

where we additionally twist the action of Frobenius on the
n
-th graded piece by
q^{-\frac{n}{2}}
.
One can readily transpose the discussion in this chapter to that setting.

6.2.
Some motivation for shearing

By way of motivation for what follows, let us describe a situation where shearing of algebras naturally arises
(which indeed reflects the way it occurs in the main text), and also
why it is natural to shear categories too. The experienced reader can skip this section without loss.

We will often encounter situations where there is an equivalence of triangulated categories

(6.1)

\mbox{a suitable category of constructible sheaves on a variety $X$}=D(\mathsf{A}),

where we have, on the right, a derived category of modules for
some differential graded
k
-algebra

\mathsf{A}
– e.g.,
\mathsf{A}
may arise as endomorphisms of a suitable object.
Now, in a situation where
X
is over a finite field, one often
obtains a weight decomposition on the
\mathrm{Hom}
-spaces on the left, and in favorable cases,
this arises from a grading on
\mathsf{A}
itself, i.e.,
a decomposition

\mathsf{A}=\bigoplus\mathsf{A}^{i}_{w}

with differential increasing
i
but preserving
w
.
In this situation one often has “purity,” that is to say,

H^{i}(\mathsf{A})
has weight grading entirely in degree
w=i

In this case, the shear

\mathsf{B}:=\mathsf{A}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
by the weight grading is
entirely in degree zero
,
and therefore can be considered as a usual graded ring (“usual” means that there is no differential to worry about).
We may then seek to describe the category of sheaves on
X
in terms of the usual ring
\mathsf{B}
.

At the level of
graded
derived categories the answer is quite simple:
there is an equivalence
of the graded derived category of
\mathsf{A}
and
\mathsf{B}
:

(6.2)

D^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathsf{A})\simeq D^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathsf{B}),M\mapsto M^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}.

To be explicit, this takes
a graded
\mathsf{A}
-module
M=\bigoplus M^{i}_{w}
,
where
w
is the grading variable so that again the differential increases
i
and preserves
w
,
and then associating it to the graded
\mathsf{B}
-module
given by
M^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}=\bigoplus M^{i}_{w}[w]
, i.e.,
regrading
M^{i}_{w}
to be in degree
i-w
.

In the geometric situation described above,
D^{gr}(\mathsf{A})

will typically describe a category of mixed sheaves on
X
. Correspondingly,
this mixed category can be described as the category of graded modules for a (usual, underived) ring.

Note
\mathrm{Hom}_{D(\mathsf{A})}(M,N)
and
\mathrm{Hom}_{D(\mathsf{A}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}})}(M^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}},N^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}})
do not coincide – the latter
is the shear of the former.
Indeed the
ungraded
categories
D(\mathsf{A})
and
D(\mathsf{B})
need not be equivalent.
They can be recoved from each other by an abstract categorical process of “shearing,”
which will be described in the next section, and will be written like this:

D(\mathsf{B})=D(\mathsf{A})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}.

In other words, there is an operation
\mathcal{C}\mapsto\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
on dg categories (whose effect we’re describing on underlying triangulated categories) which reflects the shearing operation on rings,
informally obtained by

passing to graded objects, shearing all
\mathrm{Hom}
-spaces, and then passing
back to all objects,

and thus the category of constructible sheaves in (
6.1
) becomes, under the purity assumption above, the shear of the derived category of a usual ring.
We now turn to formally constructing this
shearing operation on categories; please fasten your seatbelts.

6.3.
Shearing of categories

In this section we discuss different variants of the shearing operation on the level of categories.

All categories in this section will be “large” (=presentable) dg categories §
B.2
.

This is essential for the frequent use of de-equivariantization and 1-affineness starting from §
6.3.5
(though in practice the categories we encounter are compactly generated so one can pass back to small categories).

6.3.1.
Shearing graded categories.

We can use the shearing autoequivalence of
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
to shear
graded categories
, i.e., module categories over the rigid symmetric monoidal tensor category
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
. Model example of such categories are:

(i)

{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant sheaves
QC(X/{\mathbb{G}_{m}})
on a variety
X

with
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
action;

(ii)

Graded modules
\mathsf{A}-\textsf{mod}^{gr}
for a graded ring
\mathsf{A}
.

Such categories
are automatically enriched in graded vector spaces, and the shearing
operation does not change the underlying category but shears the graded
\mathrm{Hom}
spaces
in the sense of §
6.1
.

Definition 6.3.2
.

We define an autoequivalence
41
41

41

As a model example for the definition that follows (and to normalize signs) that for
X
a complex of graded vector spaces, we have

X^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\otimes Y=(X\otimes Y^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatbslash}}})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
;
that is to say, the action of
Y\in\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
on
X^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
corresponds
to the action of
Y^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatbslash}}}
on
X
.

(-)^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\circlearrowright\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
of the category of graded categories by twisting the
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
-action on a given category by the monoidal autoequivalence
(-)^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatbslash}}
of
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
. Explicitly,
the new action of
M\in\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
corresponds to the old action of
M^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatbslash}}}
.

In other words,

D^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}=D\otimes_{\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})}\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}

where
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}

denotes
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
considered as a
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
-bimodule, with left
action of
Y
given by
Y^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\otimes
and right action given by
\otimes Y
.

For example, in our model example we have

(6.3)

\left(\mathsf{A}-\textsf{mod}^{gr}\right)^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\simeq{\mathsf{A}}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}-\textsf{mod}^{gr},

i.e., shearing of graded categories extends the notion of shearing of graded algebras.

In particular, for a graded category
D
as above,
there is a tautological equivalence of underlying categories
D\rightarrow D^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
,
which we will denote by
X\mapsto X^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
,
which has the property that

(6.4)

\mathrm{Hom}(X^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}},Y^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}})=\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

where the
\mathrm{Hom}
is the enriched hom into graded vector spaces.
We write out the argument for (
6.4
) to verify signs:
The enriched
\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)

has graded degree
n
component given by
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X(n),Y)
, with
(n)
denoting twisting
by the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-representation of weight
n
.
By definition,
X^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}(n)=(X(n))^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}[-n]
,
and the corresponding graded degree
n
component
of
\mathrm{Hom}(X^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}},Y^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}})
is therefore given by

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X(n),Y)[n]
.

6.3.3.
Monoidal structure of shearing.

Recall that modules over a commutative ring have a functorial symmetric monoidal structure. In our
\infty
-categorical setting
[
Lura
]
this provides the category
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
of graded categories with a natural symmetric monoidal structure.
Since we will have occasion to consider the interaction of tensor structures with shearing, we note the following:

Proposition 6.3.4
.

•

The autoequivalences
(-)^{2n{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\circlearrowright\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
given by even shears naturally lift to symmetric monoidal autoequivalences of
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
.

•

The autoequivalence
(-)^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
lifts to a symmetric monoidal autoequivalence of

\text{Rep}^{\mathrm{super}}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
.

•

The autoequivalence
(-)^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
and its odd iterates lift to symmetric monoidal equivalences

\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\longrightarrow\text{Rep}_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{super}}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}

(as do its odd iterates); see §
6.1
for the notation
\text{Rep}_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{super}}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
.

6.3.5.
Shearing categories with
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action.

Next, we want to carry out a corresponding shearing for categories with a
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
action.

We briefly recall the notion of categorical representation of an algebraic group
G
(sometimes called a “weak action” of
G
),
see
[
FG06
]
and
[
Gai15c
]
for a thorough study.
Morally, an action of
G
on a dg category
\mathcal{C}
is a family of autoequivalences of
\mathcal{C}
labelled by elements
g\in G
, satisying coherent associative composition laws and varying algebraically with
g
. Formally, this is captured by the notion of module category for the category
(QC(G),\ast)
of quasicoherent sheaves on
G
equipped with the monoidal structure given by convolution
42
42

42

Thanks to the self-duality of
QC(G)
, this is equivalent to the notion of
co
module category for
QC(G)
with the convolution coalgebra structure, which is more immediately parallel to the notion of algebraic representation of an affine group scheme.
, or (thanks to the general formalism of descent) to the notion of quasicoherent sheaf of categories on the stack
BG
. We denote the category of
G
-categories by
Cat^{G}
.
The main result in the subject is Gaitsgory’s 1-affineness theorem
[
Gai15c
]
, which (when applied to the stack
BG
) asserts that the notion of
G
-category (i.e.,
(QC(G),\ast)
-module) for
G
affine is equivalent to that of module category for the
symmetric
monoidal category
(Rep(G),\otimes)
.

Let us focus on
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-categories, i.e.,
module categories for the convolution monoidal category
(QC({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\ast)
.
Model examples of such categories are:

(i)

Sheaves
QC(X)
on variety
X

with
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
action;

(ii)

(All) modules
\mathsf{A}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
for a graded ring
\mathsf{A}
.

The relationship between this and our previous examples:

\mathsf{A}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\leftrightarrow\mathsf{A}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}^{gr},QC(X)\leftrightarrow QC(X/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}).

is a general one
relating

(6.5)

\mbox{categories with ${\mathbb{G}_{m}}$ actions}\leftrightarrow\mbox{graded categories}.

We detail this relationship in general; the discussion
that follows
is a categorical version of the passage
from a
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-space
X
to
\left(X/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to B{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\right)
and,
in the other direction the passage from a space
Z
over
B{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
to
the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-space
Z\times_{B{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}pt
.

Given a category
\mathcal{C}
with
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
action we can apply equivariantization, i.e., pass to the category of equivariant objects

\mathcal{C}\mapsto\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}=\mathrm{Hom}_{QC({\mathbb{G}_{m}})}(\mathrm{Vect},\mathcal{C})

using the “augmentation module”, i.e., the pushforward functor
QC({\mathbb{G}_{m}})\to\mathrm{Vect}
, which upgrades to a symmetric monoidal functor. The result has the natural structure of graded category, expressing the familiar fact that (nonequivariant) Hom spaces between equivariant sheaves carry representations of the group. Thus equivariantization defines a functor

Cat^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}\longrightarrow\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}.

Applying this construction to
\mathrm{Vect}
itself we find

\mathrm{Vect}^{\mathbb{G}_{m}}=\mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{QC}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})}(\mathrm{Vect})\simeq\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),

so that in particular we may consider
\mathrm{Vect}
as a
(\mathrm{QC}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}))
-bimodule category.
Equivariantization has a left adjoint construction of de-equivariantization

\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\longrightarrow Cat^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}},\hskip 21.68121pt\mathcal{D}\mapsto\underline{\mathcal{D}}=\mathcal{D}\otimes_{\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})}\mathrm{Vect}.

Gaitsgory’s 1-affineness theorem
[
Gai15c
]
(applied to the stack
B{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
) asserts that the bimodule
\mathrm{Vect}

produces a Morita equivalence between the monoidal categories
(QC({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\ast)
and
(\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\otimes)
, i.e., equivariantization and deequivariantization define inverse equivalences between
Cat^{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
and
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
. (Indeed this entire discussion holds with
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
replaced by any affine algebraic group
G
.)

We use this equivalence to transport the shearing operation from graded categories to
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-categories:

Definition 6.3.6
.

The shear of categories with
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action is the autoequivalence

(-)^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\circlearrowright Cat^{\mathbb{G}_{m}},\hskip 21.68121pt\mathcal{C}\mapsto\mathcal{C}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}=(\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}})^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\otimes_{\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})}\mathrm{Vect}.

It’s important to note that shearing
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-categories
does
change the underlying category. However, it does not change the category of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant objects: it induces an equivalence of categories

(6.6)

{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}:\mathcal{C}^{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to(\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}})^{\mathbb{G}_{m}}.

It is useful to think of the equivalence
{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
above – which arises out of the construction – as part of the data of a sheared category.

Example 6.3.7

(Model example)
.

If
\mathsf{A}
is a graded dg-ring, then
shearing carries
\mathsf{A}
-modules to
\mathsf{A}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
-modules,

\left(\mathsf{A}-\textsf{mod}\right)^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\simeq\mathsf{A}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}-\textsf{mod}.

The associated equivalence (
6.6
) is the equivalence
6.3
constructed
after (
6.2
) and is given simply by naive shearing.

Example 6.3.8

(Trivial action)
.

Any linear category
\mathcal{C}
can be regarded as carrying a trivial
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action.
Shearing of graded objects (defined just as in §
6.1
)
defines an equivalence

(6.7)

{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatbslash}}:(\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}},

which we will often denote later by the “unshear” symbol
{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatbslash}}
as it identifies the sheared with the usual category.

For
X
an object of
\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}
, this
equivalence sends the object
X^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
on the left to the object regrettably
43
43

43

It could be worse.
also denoted
X^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
on the right:
On the left, we use the notation described after (
6.4
), i.e.

X^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
is the image of
X
by the equivalence of underlying categories
which arises whenever we shear a graded category;
on the right,
X^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
means the shear of the graded object
X
defined in a way parallel to
§
6.1
, i.e., we cohomologically
regrade
X

using its
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action.

In any case, (
6.7
) induces

\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\simeq\mathcal{C}.

Remark 6.3.9

(Monoidal structure of shearing)
.

As in §
2.7.2
, the sheared category comes also in a super-version,
i.e., as a
\mathrm{Vect}^{{\mathrm{super}}}
-linear category, which we will allow ourselves to denote by the same notation:

(6.8)

\mathcal{C}\mapsto\mathcal{C}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}=(\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}})^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\otimes_{\text{Rep}_{\epsilon}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})}\mathrm{Vect}^{{\mathrm{super}}}.

It is better to use the super- version for considerations involving symmetric monoidal structure, and in particular
considerations involving traces.

Indeed, just as representations of a group have a tensor product lifting the tensor of underlying vector spaces,
Cat^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}
has a symmetric monoidal structure lifting the (Lurie) tensor product of categories, and the equivariantization equivalence
Cat^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}\simeq\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
is naturally symmetric monoidal.
Then (
6.8
) describes a symmetric monoidal equivalence of

\mathrm{Vect}^{{\mathrm{super}}}
-linear
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-categories.

Example 6.3.10

(Functoriality of shearing)
.

A formal feature of shearing that will be useful in our applications is that shearing objects commutes with equivariant morphisms.
Suppose
\pi_{*}:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
is a morphism of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-categories

\pi_{*}\in Hom_{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}-cat}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\simeq Hom_{\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})-mod}(\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}},\mathcal{D}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}).

Then we get a commuting square

\textstyle{\mathcal{C}^{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\pi_{*}}
\scriptstyle{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
\textstyle{(\mathcal{C}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}})^{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\pi_{*}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{D}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
\textstyle{(\mathcal{D}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}})^{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}

A case which will arise later is the situation when
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
acts trivially on
\mathcal{D}
. In this case
we can augment the square by means of the equivalence of Example
6.3.8
.

(6.9)

\textstyle{\mathcal{C}^{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\pi_{*}}
\scriptstyle{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
\textstyle{(\mathcal{C}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}})^{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\pi_{*}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{D}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
\textstyle{(\mathcal{D}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}})^{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\sim}
\textstyle{(\mathcal{D})^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}}

where
\sim
comes from (
6.7
).
The functor from
\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}
to the far right copy of
\mathcal{D}^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}

is, therefore, given by
X\mapsto(\pi_{*}X)^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
: usual pushforward,
followed by shearing of a graded object through the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
action.

Example 6.3.11

(Automorphic shearing)
.

We present another point of view on the foregoing discussion
which can be seen as “Cartier dual,” and which appears as an automorphic counterpart to shearing.
Here we replace the role of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
by that of its Cartier dual
\mathbb{Z}
.

We will apply the equivalences of symmetric monoidal categories

(\text{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}),\otimes)\simeq(\mathrm{QC}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\ast)\mbox{ and }(\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{Z}),\ast)\simeq(\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\otimes).

where
\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{Z})
means simply the category of
\mathbb{Z}
-graded vector spaces; e.g., the second equivalence
arises from the fact that a representation of
\mathbb{Z}

over the field
k
is equivalent to a
k[t,t^{-1}]
-module.
It follows from (
6.5
) that
(\text{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}),\otimes)
and
(\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{Z}),\ast)
are Morita equivalent.
Modules
\mathcal{D}
over
(\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{Z}),\ast)
, i.e., categories with
\mathbb{Z}
-action, are identified with local systems of categories over
S^{1}=B\mathbb{Z}
.
On the other hand, the global sections
\mathcal{C}=\mathrm{Hom}_{Cat^{\mathbb{Z}}}(\mathrm{Vect},\mathcal{D})
of such a local system of categories is a module for
End_{Cat^{\mathbb{Z}}}(Vect)=(Rep(\mathbb{Z})=\mathrm{Loc}(B\mathbb{Z}),\otimes)
. (Equivalently,
\mathcal{C}
carries a
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action where
\lambda\in{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
acts by
tensoring by a rank one local system on
S^{1}
with monodromy
\lambda
.) The Morita equivalence
\mathcal{C}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{D}
then establishes the 1-affineness of
B\mathbb{Z}
, i.e., that we can recover a local system of categories
\mathcal{D}
over the circle from its global sections
\mathcal{C}
as
\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{C}\otimes_{\text{Rep}(\mathbb{Z})}\mathrm{Vect}
.

As was the case for (de)equivariantization of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-actions (see (
6.5
))
this Morita equivalence is a categorical shadow of the equivalence

\mbox{spaces $X$ over $S^{1}$}\leftrightarrow\mbox{spaces $Y$ with $\mathbb{Z}$-action}

(where a space
X\to S^{1}
determines a homotopy fiber
Y=X\times_{B\mathbb{Z}}pt
with
\mathbb{Z}
-action, while
in the reverse direction, we pass from
Y
to
X
by taking homotopy quotient by
\mathbb{Z}
).
44
44

44

Note that these operations are opposite to those defining the Morita equivalence of
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
and
\mathrm{QC}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
, in that the role of
\otimes
and
\mathrm{Hom}
or equivariantization and de-equivariantization are exchanged. This is made possible by the fact that
\mathrm{Vect}
is canonically
self-dual
, allowing us to exchange tensors for Homs.

Finally we ask, how does shearing look from this viewpoint?
If we consider
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-categories as (global sections of) local systems of categories over
B\mathbb{Z}
,

shearing = composing the monodromy automorphism with the shift
\langle 1\rangle
.

Explicitly, for a sheaf of categories over
B\mathbb{Z}
with fiber
\mathcal{D}
with monodromy automorphism
M:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}
, we obtain a sheared automorphism
M^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}=M\circ\langle 1\rangle
of
\mathcal{D}
. This defines a sheared local system of categories
\mathcal{D}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
over
B\mathbb{Z}
, whose global sections
\mathcal{C}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
are the shear of the
(\text{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}),\otimes)\simeq(\mathrm{QC}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\ast)
-category
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{Z}}
.

Example 6.3.12

(Automorphic shearing of categorical representations)
.

We now explain a general pattern of shearing categorical representations as a categorical analog of twisting representations by characters:
Given a group
G
and a homomorphism
\iota:G\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}
, there is a way to shear a categorical representation
\mathcal{C}
of
G
,
which amounts to

\mathcal{C}^{\iota{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}=\mathcal{C}
with the action of
g\in G
sheared by
\langle\deg(g)\rangle

We
will apply it to loop groups (and Hecke categories) in defining the normalized action of
G_{F}
on
\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O})
in §
7.4
.
Because this will come up for us often it will be useful to have a couple of different ways to think about it:

Schematically, a categorical representation of
G
is a sheaf of categories over
BG
in a suitable sheaf theory. The category
SHVCAT(BG)
of
G
-categories is linear over
\mathrm{SHV}(BG)
. Tensoring by an invertible sheaf of categories defines an autoequivalence of the category of categorical representations. A natural source of such invertible categorical representations is homomorphisms
\iota:G\to\mathbb{Z}
: we pull back to
BG
the sheaf of categories on
B\mathbb{Z}
given by the categorical representation
\mathrm{Vect}\langle 1\rangle
of
\mathbb{Z}
–
this is the representation which,
under the identification
(\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{Z}),\ast)\simeq(\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\otimes)
. corresponds to the sheared fiber functor on
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
. This defines the operation
denoted
\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\iota}
on categorical representations of
G
.

Another way to describe this shearing operation (along the lines of
[
BZG17
]
) is as follows. Let’s describe categorial representations of
G
as modules for a monoidal category
(\mathrm{SHV}(G),\ast)
of sheaves on
G
under convolution in our fixed sheaf theory. Then the linearity of categorical representations over
\mathrm{SHV}(BG)
amounts to a (braided monoidal) central functor
(\mathrm{SHV}(BG),\otimes)\to\mathcal{Z}(\mathrm{SHV}(G)),
which lifts the trivial monoidal functor
(\mathrm{SHV}(BG),\otimes)\to(Vect,\otimes)\to(\mathrm{SHV}(G),\ast),
i.e., the action factors through the augmentation. This expresses the presentation
G\simeq pt\times_{BG}pt
of
G
as a groupoid over
BG
. Now given
\iota:G\to\mathbb{Z}
, we obtain a tensor functor

(\text{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}),\otimes)\simeq(\mathrm{QC}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\ast)\to(\mathrm{SHV}(BG),\otimes)\longrightarrow\mathcal{Z}(\mathrm{SHV}(G)),

which again is trivial (factors through the augmentation) as a plain monoidal functor. In other words,
G
-categories acquire functorial
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-actions, which are trivial as actions on the underlying categories. The operation
\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\iota}
above is given by shearing by this
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action.

6.4.
Shearing in geometry

We give several examples of shearing of categories of quasicoherent sheaves.

Remark 6.4.1

(Shearing and coaffine stacks)
.

For any stack
X
with
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action we obtain a
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action
\mathrm{QC}(X)\in Cat^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}
and consider the sheared category, which we denote
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(X)
.
We begin with a general warning about interpreting this category geometrically.

In general for
X=\mathrm{Spec}(A)
with
A
a non-negatively graded (discrete) algebra, we can think of the category
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(X)=A^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
as a variant of the category of sheaves on the “coaffine stack”

X^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}=\rm{Spec}(A^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}})
, the object of derived algebraic geometry represented by the coconnective commutative dga
A^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
.
The category of sheaves on the latter can be defined, following the general formalism of derived algebraic geometry, as a limit over maps from affines into
X^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
, i.e., in terms of connective cdgas.

To illustrate how the two differ, take
\mathbb{A}^{1}
with squaring
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
action and
A

the ring of functions on
\mathbb{A}^{1}
. We denote the coaffine stack represented by
A^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
as
\mathbb{A}^{1}[2]
.
The category of quasicoherent sheaves on this stack, which is equivalently described as
B^{2}{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
, does not coincide
with the category

{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathbb{A}^{1})=A^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}=\mathcal{O}((\mathbb{A}^{1})^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}.

In terms of the Koszul dual exterior algebra of functions on the derived affine scheme
\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1]
, we have
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathbb{A}^{1})\simeq QC^{!}(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])
while,
thinking of
\mathbb{A}^{1}[2]
as a coaffine stack, we have instead
QC(\mathbb{A}^{1}[2])\simeq QC(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])\simeq\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1]){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
.

Example 6.4.2

(Shearing of
G
-representations)
.

A cocharacter
\underline{\varpi}:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to Aut(G)
gives an action of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
on
BG
, hence on
QC(BG)=\text{Rep}(G)
;
it makes
k[G]
into a graded Hopf algebra,
\mathfrak{g}
into a graded Lie algebra and
G
into a “graded algebraic group” in the sense of §
3.4.7
.
We obtain a sheared category of representations
\mathsf{D}=\text{Rep}(G)^{\underline{\varpi}{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
which can be described as comodules for the sheared Hopf algebra
k(G)^{\underline{\varpi}{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
,

(6.10)

C\rightarrow C\otimes k[G]^{\underline{\varpi}{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}.

In particular, such a comodule inherits an action of the sheared Lie algebra
\mathfrak{g}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
, i.e.
a map

\mathfrak{g}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\otimes C\rightarrow C.

If we
grade the Lie algebra
\mathfrak{g}=\bigoplus\mathfrak{g}_{j}

via
\underline{\varpi}
, then
X\in\mathfrak{g}_{j}
decreases degree by
j

(for
X\in\mathfrak{g}_{j}
corresponds to an element of
\mathfrak{g}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
in cohomological degree
-j
).
That is to say,
we can think of
\mathrm{Rep}(G)^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
as being

“complexes with a non-degree-preserving action of
G
,”

(For a model example of such a complex, see Example
6.4.3
below.)

The graded category obtained by equivariantizing
\text{Rep}(G)
is the category
\text{Rep}(G\rtimes{\mathbb{G}_{m}})
, with its natural
\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
action: tensoring by representations inflated from
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
.

Example 6.4.3

(Inner shearing of
G
-representations.)
.

Continue with the prior example but now assume that
\underline{\varpi}
in fact lifts to
\varpi:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\rightarrow G
. Then we have in fact

(6.11)

\text{Rep}(G)\simeq\text{Rep}(G)^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\varpi}.

Indeed given
C\in\text{Rep}(G)

the shear
C^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
through
\varpi:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\rightarrow G
defines an object
of the category
\mathsf{D}
above. Note that in the presentation (
6.10
) of

\text{Rep}(G)^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
as comodules,
this category comes with a fiber functor; the resulting (pulled back) fiber functor
on
\text{Rep}(G)
via (
6.11
) is not the usual
fiber functor on
\text{Rep}(G)
under (
6.11
), but rather a shear of it.
45
45

45

To say a different way: for inner actions the resulting action of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
on
BG
can be trivialized;
but the trivialization of the action on
BG
doesn’t preserve basepoints.

Alternately we can see (
6.11
) as arising from
an equivalence of the associated graded categories, which in turn arises from the group isomorphism

(6.12)

(g,t)\in G\rtimes{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\mapsto(g\varpi(t),t)\in G\times{\mathbb{G}_{m}}.

compatible with projection to
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
.

Example 6.4.4
.

We generalize the foregoing example from the case of a point to a general
G
-space:
Suppose that
G
acts on a space
X

and
\lambda:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\rightarrow G
is a one-parameter subgroup,
which we regard as acting on
G
via the adjoint action,
and on
X
through
G
. Then

(6.13)

QC(X/G)^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\simeq QC(X/G).

This recovers
(
6.11
) when
X
is a point.
Again, it can be deduced from the equivalence of stacks

X/(G\rtimes{\mathbb{G}_{m}})\simeq X/(G\times{\mathbb{G}_{m}})

where
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
on the right is acting trivially;
this equivalence arises from (
6.12
) on the acting
groups and the identity on
X
.

We make the equivalence more explicit
when
X=\mathrm{Spec}(R)
is affine.

The category
QC(X/G)
is the category of
(G,R)
-modules, that is to say (complexes of)
R
-modules
with compatible
G
-action.
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
acts
on the pair
(G,R)
via

x:g\mapsto\lambda(x)g\lambda(x)^{-1},r\mapsto\lambda(x).r,

and correspondingly acts on the category of
(G,R)
-modules.
The category
QC(X/G)^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
is now the category of
(G^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}},R^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}})
-modules,
i.e., complexes with an
R^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
-action and an action of
G

that does not preserve degree (just as in (
6.4.2
)).
Just as discussed after (
6.11
), regrading
a
(G,R)
-complex by means of
\lambda

exhibits the equivalence with
(G^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}},R^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}})
-modules.

6.5.
Abelian geometric Satake

We will now discuss the geometric Satake equivalence,
both for reference in the rest of the paper, and
because it is a convenient example of shearing.

Let
G
be a reductive group over
\mathbb{F}
. For now, we assume that
\mathbb{F}
is algebraically closed.
We will discuss the case of
\mathbb{F}
a finite field in §
6.7
.
Attached to
G
is the
affine Grassmannian

\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
, an ind-variety over
\mathbb{F}
.
We call the
Satake category
of
G
the abelian category

\text{Sat}_{G}:=\mathrm{Perv}_{k}(G_{O}\backslash\mathrm{Gr}_{G})

of
G_{O}
-equivariant perverse sheaves on the Grassmannian with coefficients in
k
.
This is a full subcategory of the abelian category
\mathrm{Perv}_{k}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})
of all perverse sheaves on the Grassmannian, characterized by constructibility with respect to the stratification by
G_{O}
-orbits. (The entire derived category of
G_{O}
-equivariant sheaves on
\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
will be called the
Hecke category
in this paper, in order not to have to distinguish between “perverse” and “derived” Satake categories.)

This category has a monoidal structure defined by convolution, and a non-obvious
commutativity structure that can be defined by fusion.
These definitions can be found in
[
MV07
]
.
As usual, there are several choices for sheaf theory. For our current purposes,
we will follow
[
MV07
]
and use étale sheaf theory
(see
[
MV07
, §14]
).

6.5.1.
Abelian Satake

Roughly speaking, the abelian geometric Satake isomorphism identifies
\text{Sat}_{G}
, viewed as a Tannakian category with the fiber functor to
Vect_{k}
given by total (non-equivariant) cohomology over
\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
, with the category of representations of the dual group
\check{G}
. However, this is slightly imprecise due to a fundamental parity issue. Namely, the cohomology functor from
\text{Sat}_{G}
to vector spaces is a monoidal functor, but the
commutativity constraint on
\text{Sat}_{G}
is not compatible with that on vector spaces.
Rather, considering cohomology as a functor to
graded
vector spaces,
the commutativity constraint on
\text{Sat}_{G}
is intertwined
with the “Koszul” commutativity constraint on graded vector spaces
by
[
MV07
, Lemma 6.1]
.

This parity issue is handled in Proposition 6.3 of
op. cit.

by modifying the geometric commutativity constraint on the Satake category. One can instead modify the representation category in the following way, parallel to §
6.1
: let us
replace
\text{Rep}(\check{G})
with the symmetric monoidal category
\text{Rep}^{{\mathrm{super}}}({\check{G}})

of representations on super-vector spaces.
Concretly, objects are pairs
(V_{+},V_{-})

of representations of
\check{G}
, and when
one swaps the tensor product of two odd vector spaces, one incurs a
-
sign.
Then the abelian Satake correspondence gives a symmetric monoidal equivalence

(6.14)

\text{Sat}_{G}^{{\mathrm{super}}}\simeq\text{Rep}^{{\mathrm{super}}}({\check{G}})

between the super-version of the Satake category of perverse sheaves on the Grassmannian
and super-representations of
{\check{G}}
. Under this equivalence (applying descent, Remark
2.5.4
) even sheaves on the left correspond to representations whose parity
is given by the central element
(-1)^{2\rho}\in\check{G}
. We thus get a symmetric monoidal equivalence for the usual Satake category in the form

(6.15)

\text{Sat}_{G}\simeq\text{Rep}^{super}_{2\rho}({\check{G}}):=\mbox{super-representations of $\check{G}$ whose parity is given by $(-1)^{2\rho}$}.

(Compare with the appearance of
\text{Rep}^{super}_{\epsilon}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
in §
6.1
and §
6.3.3
.)
While this might seem overly elaborate, we have already discussed in §
2.5.3
and §
2.7.2

why it is essentially inevitable to consider
super-vector spaces if one wants to study numerical questions.

In the following sections, use the following notation:
For every representation
V
of
\check{G}
, define
\mathcal{T}_{V}
to be

(6.16)

\mathcal{T}_{V}=\mbox{ the correspondent to $V$ under \eqref{abSatakeequivalence}}

Hence,
\mathcal{T}_{V}

is ‘‘analytically normalized,’’ that is to say, it is Verdier self-dual,
where the notion of Verdier duality on the affine Grassmannian
is normalized to preserve the unit object.
46
46

46

We make a couple of normalization comments to avoid sign confusion later.
\mathcal{T}_{V}
is the IC sheaf of a certain stratum in
\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
. If that stratum is
k
-dimensional, then
\mathcal{T}_{V}
, restricted to the smooth locus, will be
the constant local system shifted by
\langle k\rangle
, i.e., in cohomological degree
-k
and with weight
-k/2
.
Moreover, as is relevant when computing trace functions,
\mathcal{T}_{V}
is regarded as a super-sheaf
whose parity is given by the action of
e^{2\rho}(-1)
on
V
.

Example 6.5.2
.

(a)

Take
\lambda\in X_{*}(T)
, a cocharacter of the maximal torus of
G
. Under this equivalence, the IC sheaf of the closure
\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}
of the
G_{O}
-orbit represented by
t^{\lambda}
(considered as a super-vector space with parity
\left<2\rho,\lambda\right>
), is mapped to the representation with highest weight
\lambda
.

(b)

Specializing further the example of (a), consider the case
G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}
, and take
the first nontrivial stratum
\mathcal{S}\subset\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
(the closed orbit on the “odd” or non-neutral component of the Grassmannian) is a copy of
\mathbb{P}^{1}
,
corresponding to an elementary modification of a rank
2
vector bundle.

The constant sheaf
k_{\mathcal{S}}\langle 1\rangle
, placed in degree
-1
,
defines an object of the Satake category, and under the above equivalence

k_{\mathcal{S}}\langle 1\rangle\mapsto\mbox{standard representation of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ in even parity},

that is to say,
\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{std}}
is simply
k_{\mathcal{S}}\langle 1\rangle
.
The associated trace function equals
q^{-1/2}1_{\mathcal{S}}
. Note there
is no minus sign despite the fact that the sheaf is in odd degree, for
the notation
\langle\dots\rangle
includes a shift of super parity, according to our conventions.

6.5.3.
Arithmetic shearing

There is another way of formulating the geometric Satake equivalence,
using shearing, rather than modifying the commutativity constraint
or using super-vector spaces.

To explicate, we introduce a(n even) cohomological grading on
k[\check{G}]
that is equal to the grading by the cocoharacter
\varpi=2\rho

, i.e., by the following action of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
:

(6.17)

(t\cdot f)(g)=\text{Inn}(t^{2\rho})(f)(g):=f\left(\text{Inn}(t^{-2\rho})(g)\right),

where
Inn
is the
left
action of
\check{G}
on itself by conjugation.
The resulting graded Hopf algebra, considered as a dg-algebra with trivial differentials, will be denoted by
k[\check{G}]^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
(as in §
6.4.2
); we will call this the “arithmetic shear” of
k[\check{G}]
(or of
\check{G}
, by abuse of language).
Explicitly, if
t\cdot f=t^{a}f
, then
f
defines an element of
k[\check{G}]^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
in cohomological degree
-a
.

Recall that the sheared category
\text{Rep}(\check{G})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

of §
6.3
from Example
6.4.2
, can be described as complexes of vector spaces
with a comodule structure for
k[\check{G}]^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
. The element
e\in\mathfrak{g}

has weight
-2
for the action
\text{Inn}(t^{-2\rho})
and therefore

raises degree by
2
.

Now, inside the dg-category
\text{Rep}(\check{G})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

we can consider the full abelian subcategory
\text{Rep}_{2\rho}(\check{G})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

which comes from transporting the
complexes supported in degree zero
under the equivalence
{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}:\text{Rep}(\check{G})\to\text{Rep}(\check{G})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
of (
6.11
).
Equivalently,
\text{Rep}_{2\rho}(\check{G})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
coincides with the category of

k[\check{G}]^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
-comodules on finite-dimensional graded vector spaces,
where grading and the action of
2\rho
coincide.
Then,
\text{Rep}_{2\rho}(\check{G})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
is an abelian tensor category,
with monoidal structure
and commutativity inherited from
\text{Rep}(\check{G})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
,
and there is an equivalence of abelian tensor categories

(6.18)

\text{Sat}_{G}\simeq\text{Rep}_{2\rho}(\check{G})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

compatible with tensor functors to graded vector spaces (cohomology over
Gr_{G}
on the left, forgetting the
\check{G}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
-action on the right).

In other words, the action of
\check{G}

on
V=
the cohomology of a perverse sheaf on
\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
is upgraded to a coaction

k[V]\to k[\check{G}]^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\otimes k[V]

respecting the cohomological grading. We will sometimes denote this coaction, by abuse of notation, as
\check{G}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\times V\to V
.

Example 6.5.4
.

We continue with Example
6.5.1
part (b).
In the same notation, the functor of (
6.18
)
sends
k_{\mathcal{S}}
to its total cohomology, i.e.
the complex
k\oplus k[-2]
with zero differential,
or equivalently the object of
\text{Rep}_{2\rho}(\mathrm{SL}_{2})

obtained by
starting with
\mathrm{std}[-1]\in\text{Rep}(\mathrm{SL}_{2})
, the standard representation in cohomological
degree one, and then shearing through
2\rho
.

6.6.
Derived Geometric Satake

We now turn to the derived setting and discuss the full dg spherical Hecke category

\mathcal{H}_{G}:=\mathrm{Shv}(G_{O}\backslash\mathrm{Gr}_{G}),\overline{\mathcal{H}_{G}}=\mathrm{SHV}(G_{O}\backslash\mathrm{Gr}_{G})

of sheaves with
k
-coefficients on the affine Grassmannian defined over an algebraically closed field
\mathbb{F}
.

As discussed in §
B
, this comes in two versions, a small version
\mathcal{H}_{G}

of constructible sheaves,
and a large version which we will denote by
\overline{\mathcal{H}_{G}}
.
We note only here that while the small version is almost certainly what you think it is (if you think about such matters);
the large version involves a choice about the order in which one takes certain limiting operations, and we use the ind-finite (i.e., renormalized) version, see
§
B.6
.

For
\mathbb{F}=k=\mathbb{C}
the different sheaf theories from §
B
– constructible sheaves,
D
-modules, Betti sheaves or all sheaves – give rise to equivalent small sheaf categories which we denote simply by
\mathrm{Shv}
(i.e.,
G_{O}
-equivariant coherent
D
-modules are forced to be regular holonomic,
G_{O}
-equivariant Betti sheaves are forced to be locally constant on the
G_{O}
-orbits and the compact objects constructible, and the two are identified by the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence compatibly with the various functors we consider).
We will also be interested in the case
\mathbb{F}=\overline{\mathbb{F}_{q}}
, with
k=\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}
where
l
is different from the characteristic of
\mathbb{F}
, in which case
\mathrm{Shv}
refers to
l
-adic étale constructible complexes.

We now state a mildly strengthened version of the derived geometric Satake theorem of
Bezrukavnikov and Finkelberg
[
BF08
, Theorem 5]
. First, the original theorem is stated in the setting of triangulated rather than dg categories. However the technique of the proof extends to prove the stronger dg statement, and it is stated as such in
[
AG15
, Theorem 11.3.3, Proposition 11.4.2]
.
Next, the original theorem
[
BF08
, Theorem 5]
was stated for
\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{C}
,
k=\mathbb{C}
, but it is observed in
[
BF08
, Proposition 5]
that it extends to the case
\mathbb{F}=\overline{\mathbb{F}_{q}}
, with
k=\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}
, where
l
is different from the characteristic of
\mathbb{F}
. We will outline below why the arguments of
[
BF08
]
work to establish it also with
k=\mathbb{Q}_{l}
, together with the action of Frobenius that follows (when
G
is defined over
\mathbb{F}_{q}
).

Theorem 6.6.1

(Derived Geometric Satake)
.

For the shearing in the following statements, we regard
\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}

as a
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-space via the squaring action,
and
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
is acting trivially on
\check{G}
.

•

Small version:
There is an equivalence of monoidal dg categories

(\mathcal{H}_{G},\ast)\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(k[\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}]^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}/{\check{G}}),

where the right hand side denotes dg derived category
of
{\check{G}}
-equivariant perfect
47
47

47

At the level of homotopy categories, this corresponds to
the smallest triangulated subcategory containing
\mathcal{O}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
.
dg-modules over
k[\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}]^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
and
with monoidal structure given by tensor product.

•

Large: There is an equivalence of monoidal large categories

(\overline{\mathcal{H}_{G}},*)\simeq\mathrm{QC}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})

where the right hand side denotes
the shearing of the category
\mathrm{QC}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})
of

{\check{G}}
-equivariant coherent sheaves on
\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}
.

Remark 6.6.2
.

•

Note that the theorem asserts an equivalence only of monoidal categories, even though the spectral side has an evident symmetric monoidal structure.
This accounts for the absence of any “parity” correction. The derived substitute for the symmetric monoidal structure on the abelian spherical category is an
E_{3}
- or factorization structure on
\mathcal{H}
, see §
17.1
.

•

(As discussed in §
2.7.2
): For issues involving symmetric monoidal structure or traces, it is preferable
to take the point of view – as in §

– that this is an equivalence

Remark 6.6.3

(Compatibility with Cartier duality of (co)characters)
.

Consider the data of a character
\eta:G\to{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
, dual to that of a central cocharacter
\eta^{\vee}:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to Z({\check{G}})
.

Working over a local field, one classically knows that twisting an unramified representation
by
\eta^{*}\lambda^{{\operatorname{val}}}
, for
\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}
, has
the effect of twisting its Satake parameter through
\eta^{\vee}(\lambda)\in\check{G}
(up to sign).
We now describe a corresponding compatibility of the geometric Satake correspondence with Cartier duality for the center of
{\check{G}}

(an “opposite” compatibility, for the center of
G
, is mentioned in Remark
C.3.8
).
This will take the form of corresponding actions of
(\mathrm{QC}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\ast)
on the two sides of the Satake isomorphism.

On the automorphic side the action of
(\mathrm{QC}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\ast)\simeq(\mathrm{Loc}(B\mathbb{Z}),\otimes)
comes from the map

\textstyle{G_{O}\backslash G_{F}/G_{O}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{BG_{F}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{B\eta}
\textstyle{B({\mathbb{G}_{m}})_{F}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{B\mathbb{Z}}

which provides the spherical Hecke category the structure of sheaf of monoidal categories over the circle.
This results in a central action of
(\mathrm{Loc}(B\mathbb{Z}),\otimes)\simeq(\mathrm{QC}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\ast)
on
\overline{\mathcal{H}_{G}}
. Compare
Examples
6.3.11
and
Example
6.3.12
.

On the spectral side,
the cocharacter
\eta^{\vee}
defines a braided monoidal functor from
(\mathrm{QC}({\mathbb{G}_{m}}),\ast)
to the Drinfeld center
\mathrm{QC}({\check{G}}/{\check{G}})
of
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
(coming from pushforward along the map
\eta^{\vee}:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to{\check{G}}/{\check{G}}
), or better to the Drinfeld center
QC(\mathcal{L}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}}))^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
of the Hecke category.

The fact these two actions correspond follows from the results of
[
BZG17
]
:
the automorphic action is part
of a larger central action, the Ngô action of
[
BZG17
]
, by all of
(\mathrm{Loc}(BG_{F}),\otimes)
. The results of
[
BZG17
]
identifying this categorical action with Ngô’s spectral action of the group scheme of regular centralizers imply in particular the compatibility above.

6.7.
Geometric Satake over a finite field

Let us now consider the analogous story when the group
G
is defined over a finite field.

We start by recalling the “standard” action of Frobenius on the dual group
\check{G}
, which we will term “analytic”
in terms of the general division of §
2.7
,
as well as an action that will be termed “arithmetic”:

Analytic Frobenius action on
\check{G}

When
G
is defined over
\mathbb{F}_{q}
, we have a Frobenius automorphism on the character group of its (universal) Cartan
A
, which gives rise to an action of Frobenius on the dual Cartan
\check{A}\subset\check{G}
. By construction (
A
is defined as the torus quotient of any Borel subgroup), this action preserves the set of positive coroots, which define the standard Borel
\check{B}\subset\check{G}
. The classical definition of the dual
group
\check{G}
(over
k
)
49
49

49

Note that, if
k
is not algebraically
closed,
\check{G}
will always be taken to be split over
k
, as is necessary for the
existence of the pinning.
requires it to be pinned, allowing for a unique extension of the Frobenius action to
\check{G}
, by pinned
automorphisms.

Definition 6.7.1
.

The analytic action of Frobenius on
\check{G}
is the pinned action dual to the Frobenius action on the root datum of
G
.

Now, we continue to denote by
\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
the affine Grassmannian over the algebraic closure

comes with an extra structure, which is the action of Frobenius by pullback of sheaves,
\mathcal{F}\mapsto\mathrm{Fr}^{*}\mathcal{F}
.
We then have the following:

Proposition 6.7.2
.

The equivalences (
6.15
)
and (
6.18
) of abelian tensor categories
are compatible with Frobenius actions,
using respectively analytic and arithmetic Frobenius actions on
\check{G}

(a)

In the equivalence (

to be the analytic action noted above.

(b)

In the equivalence (
6.18
)

\mathrm{Sat}_{G}\simeq\mathrm{Rep}_{2\rho}(\check{G})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}=k[{\check{G}}]^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{comod}_{fd}

Remark 6.7.3
.

(a)

Explicitly, the “arithmetic” Frobenius action of (b)
on
k[\check{G}]^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

into

Thus we have

k[{\check{G}}]^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}=\bigoplus k[{\check{G}}]_{i}\langle i\rangle,

. Note that, since the grading is even, this does not require choosing a square root of the Tate twist.

The resulting sheared Lie algebra

possesses an element “

which is in cohomological degree

Tensoring with any generator of

,

therefore defines a Frobenius-invariant element of
\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}(1)
,

(b)

In the current context, one motivation (see also §

) for introducing
an arithmetic action is that
the analytic action is not the action on
\check{G}
that arises from the canonical isomorphism
of fiber functors

H^{\bullet}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G},\mathcal{F})=H^{\bullet}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G},\mathrm{Fr}^{*}\mathcal{F}).

To see this, recall that, in the geometric Satake isomorphism, the pinning comes from cup product with the Chern class

of the determinant line bundle;
that is to say,

However, this Chern class lives in

.
This is the element noted in (a) above.

The natural action of Frobenius on

and the canonical isomorphism (

) via the Tannakian formalism and preserves this “twisted pinning,” has been described in
