\mathrm{SHV}_{u}(X_{F}/G_{O}):=\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O}\rtimes{\mathbb{G}_{m}})=\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O})^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}},

i.e., the strongly
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant objects in the
X
-spherical category. This is a
H^{*}_{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}(\mbox{pt},k)\simeq k[u]
-linear category, where
u
has cohomological degree two, which specializes at
u=0
to a full subcategory (the
equivariantizable objects
) of the original category,

\mathrm{SHV}_{u}(X_{F}/G_{O})\otimes_{k[u]}k\hookrightarrow\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O}).

(The fullness is a consequence of the Koszul duality of
[
GKM98
]
, see e.g.
[
BZCHN23
, Proposition A.6]
.) In other words, we have a canonical deformation of a full subcategory of the
X
-spherical category.

Lemma 7.5.13
.

Conjecture
7.5.1
implies that all of
\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O})
is equivariantizable,

\mathrm{SHV}_{u}(X_{F}/G_{O})\otimes_{k[u]}k\simeq\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O}).

Proof.

For the spherical Hecke category
\mathcal{H}_{G}
itself the full subcategory of equivariantizable objects is the entire category. Since the basic object is naturally
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant, it follows that the full subcategory it generates under the Hecke action is equivariantizable as well.
The Lemma follows from the observation (§
7.5.3
) that in the presence of the local conjecture, the entire automorphic category is generated in this way.
∎

We now require that under the local conjecture this
u
-deformation defines a deformation quantization of
{\check{M}}/{\check{G}}
with its (sheared) Poisson bracket. We formulate here a very weak form of this requirement:

\bullet

[Poisson structure]
The Hochschild cohomology class of
\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O})
defined by the first-order data of the
u
-deformation
\mathrm{SHV}_{u}(X_{F}/G_{O})
is matched with the Hochschild cohomology class of
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})
defined by the (sheared, 2-shifted) symplectic form.

Note that the Hochschild classes in question are in fact in degree 0. Automorphically, the
u
-deformation is a deformation over
k[u]
where
u
has cohomological degree 2. Spectrally, since the symplectic form on
{\check{M}}
has
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-weight 2, the sheared bracket on
\mathcal{O}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}({\check{M}})
has degree
-2
(i.e., defines a
P_{3}
-structure) whence again a degree 0 Hochschild class.

The structure theory of hyperspherical varieties can be used to prescribe a canonical global
k[u]
-deformation quantization of
{\check{M}}/{\check{G}}
.
A stronger form of this compatibility requires this entire deformation to match the
u
-deformation of the automorphic category. This is formulated (using the language of Plancherel algebras) as Conjecture
8.5.1
in the next section.

7.6.
Examples

Let us discuss several examples where at least some parts of Conjecture
7.5.1
are known.

Example 7.6.1
.

We return to our “easy” running example of
X=\mathbb{A}^{1}
(see Example
7.3.5
,
7.3.6
,
7.4.1
).
In this case one can verify the equivalence “by hand,”
as we will essentially do below; we will also see what happens to the “Dirac delta” and “Lebesgue” sheafs
from Example
7.4.1
.

Here
\check{M}=T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{1}
.
In the normalized action, the
G^{\vee}={\mathbb{G}_{m}}
action
on
\check{M}
scales the
\mathbb{A}^{1}
-direction and antiscales the
dual
T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{1}
-direction.
Let
x
be a coordinate on
\mathbb{A}^{1}
and
\xi
a dual coordinate on
T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{1}
, so that
the
G^{\vee}
action is given by
\lambda\cdot x=\lambda^{-1}x,\lambda\cdot\xi=\lambda\xi

and the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
action antiscales both; both
x,\xi
are in cohomological degree
1
.

We will write

[n]
for the representation
z\mapsto z^{n}
of
\check{G}
; the sheaf
\delta_{n}
introduced in Exanple
7.3.5

corresponds to
[n]\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\check{M}}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
.
We have computed
\mathrm{Hom}(\delta_{n},\delta_{m})
in (
7.9
);
on the spectral side the same computation yields

\mathrm{Hom}([n]\otimes\mathcal{O},[m]\otimes\mathcal{O})=\mathrm{Hom}_{G^{\vee}}([n-m],\mathcal{O}).

The invariants in question are spanned by monomials
x^{a}\xi^{b}
where
a,b\geq 0
and
b-a=n-m
.
This lies in cohomological degree
a+b
. That is to say, the
\mathrm{Hom}
-space
is one-dimensional in degrees
|n-m|,|n-m|+2,\dots
, which matches with (
7.9
).

Let us also discuss what happens in the limit, to see where
the objects
\delta_{0},\mu
of Example
7.3.6
go.
The unnormalized sheaf
k_{X^{l}}
corresponds, on the spectral side,
to
[l]\otimes\mathcal{O}\langle-l\rangle
,
which we can formally think of as
x^{-l}\mathcal{O}
.
The skyscraper at
0
corresponds
to taking a limit as
l\rightarrow-\infty
, which gives
a
\mathcal{O}
-module which can be identified
with
k[x,x^{-1},\xi]
. We can also take the limit of sheaves
k_{X^{l}}\langle 2l\rangle

as
l\rightarrow\infty
, corresponding to
[l]\otimes\mathcal{O}\langle l\rangle

or
\xi^{l}\mathcal{O}
, and get the object
k[x,\xi,\xi^{-1}]
. It might be quite interesting
to study the images of other natural distributions on
X
, under the local conjecture,
in more general instances.

7.6.2.
The group case

Here the space
X
is a reductive group
H
with a left and right action of
G=H\times H
;
and the dual symplectic variety is now
{\check{M}}=T^{\ast}{\check{H}}
as a Hamiltonian
{\check{H}}\times{\check{H}}
-space
where the action of one factor is twisted by the duality involution. In particular,
we have
\check{G}_{X}={\check{H}}
and the space
V_{X}
is
the dual Lie algebra
(\mathfrak{h}^{\vee})^{*}
, placed in
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
weight
2
;
thus, the conjecture
is precisely the derived Satake theorem of
[
BF08
]
,
in the case of
\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{C}
,
which was recalled as Theorem
6.6.1
.

Let us talk through the various desiderata:
the requirement on pointings (§
7.5.2
) follows from the construction.
The statement about the equivalence
and Hecke actions (§
7.5.3
)

almost
follows from the monoidal nature of derived Satake,
but there is a subtlety:
one needs to know that the action of the
inversion map
H\to H
is induced on the spectral side of
{\mathbb{L}}_{H}
by the
duality involution

\check{H}\rightarrow\check{H}
defined in §
2.3.2
,
for which we don’t know a reference. (This assertion has content
even in abelian Satake if we work over coefficient field
k=\mathbb{Q}
.)

The statement about Poisson structure
(§
7.5.11
but even the stronger statement discussed in §
8.5
) was also proven by Bezrukavnikov and Finkelberg
[
BF08
]
.
Finally, the
statement about Galois actions does not apparently
appear in the literature, but
we have sketched a proof after §
6.7.5
;
see also
[
Zhu17
]
,

[
RS21
]
, and
[
Bez06
]
.

7.6.3.
The trivial period

We now take
X
to be the point.
Thus
\mathcal{H}_{X}
is simply the category of constructible sheaves on
BG
. That is to say (see
[
BL94
]
),
taking into account the formality of the cohomology of
BG
,

\mathcal{H}_{X}
is simply the category of perfect modules under
H^{*}(BG)
.

In this case,
{\check{M}}
is the Whittaker model, that is to say,
the Hamiltonian
{\check{G}}
-space obtained by Whittaker indcution
of the point under the principal
\mathrm{SL}_{2}\rightarrow{\check{G}}
;
and

{\check{M}}/{\check{G}}\simeq\mathfrak{c}_{G}
is the Kostant slice.
The equivalence as abstract categories follows from the identification of the equivariant cohomology ring
H^{*}(BG)
with the shear of the ring of invariant polynomials
\mathcal{O}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star})^{{\check{G}}}
. The equivalence as module categories for the Hecke category is a theorem of Bezrukavnikov-Finkelberg
[
BF08
]
(the same paper also proves the compatibility of the Poisson bracket with loop rotation equivariance).

7.6.4.
The Whittaker period

Dually, we consider the Whittaker model on the automorphic side. In other words, we take
M=T^{\ast}G{/\!/}_{\psi}U
. In this case the Hecke category
\mathcal{H}_{M}
is the category
\mathrm{Shv}(G_{F}/G_{O})^{U(F),\psi}
of Whittaker sheaves on the Grassmannian. The dual period is
{\check{M}}=pt
, so that
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})\simeq Rep({\check{G}})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}.
The resulting equivalence of categories is due to Frenkel-Gaitsgory-Vilonen
[
FGV01
]
(see also
[
ABB+05
]
).

7.6.5.
Other examples

Several other instances of the local conjecture have been proved recently – verifying at least
the “Hecke” desideratum of the statement, although it is likely that the proofs give more.

Hilburn and Raskin
[
HR23
]
prove a fully ramified, de Rham version of the local conjecture for the Iwasawa–Tate period.

Braverman, Dhillon, Finkelberg, Raskin and Travkin
[
BDF+22
]
, and Teleman
[
Tel23
]
discuss geometric counterparts to the Weil representation and the construction of Coulomb branches (hence formulation of the local conjecture) in unpolarized settings.

Chen, Macerato, Nadler, and O’Brien
[
CMNO22
]
prove the local conjecture in the case
X=GL_{2n}/Sp_{2n}
and
{\check{M}}=T^{*}(GL_{2n}/GL_{n}\ltimes U,\psi)\simeq GL_{2n}\times^{GL_{n}}M_{n}

(in automorphic terminology, the “symplectic period” studied by Jacquet and Rallis
[
JR92
]
).

Chen and Nadler
[
CN24
]
construct an equivalence, in the case of
X
a symmetric variety, between the category
\mathcal{H}^{X}
and a category of sheaves
arising in global
real
Langlands: sheaves on the space of principal bundles for a certain real form of
G
over the real projective line. They show, among other results,
the formality of the category
\mathcal{H}^{X}
in this case, see
[
CN24
, Theorem 13.4]
.

The results of Macerato and Taylor
[
MT24
]
(when combined with
[
CN24
]
) imply that the local category for the symmetric variety
X=PSL_{2}/PO_{2}
(which is outside of our hyperspherical setting due to the presence of Type N roots) contains a block equivalent to representations of quantum
SL_{2}
at a fourth root of unity. This suggests that in this generality one should expect interesting braided (
E_{2}
) tensor categories to appear instead of the symmetric ones in our conjecture.

Devalapurkar
[
Dev24b
]
proves the local conjecture for the case of homogeneous affine spherical varieties of rank
1
, modulo
certain hypotheses relating to placidity and evenness.
Moreover, in
[
Dev24a
]
, under the same hypotheses, he proves the local conjecture in the case of the triple product
L
-function
(the diagonal inclusion of
\mathrm{PGL}_{2}
into
\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}
).

The papers
[
BFGT21
]
and
[
BFT22a
]
of Braverman, Finkelberg, Ginzburg and Travkin prove the local conjecture (in a Koszul dual formulation)
in cases corresponding to:

-

X=\mathrm{GL}_{n}
as
G=\mathrm{GL}_{n}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}
-space,

-

X=\mathrm{GL}_{n}\times\mathbb{A}^{n}
as
G=\mathrm{GL}_{n}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n}
-space

-

X=\mathrm{SO}_{n}
as
G=\mathrm{SO}_{n}\times\mathrm{SO}_{n-1}
-space.

In automorphic terminology, these correspond to the Rankin–Selberg
periods for
\mathrm{GL}_{n}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}
and
\mathrm{GL}_{n}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n}

[
JPSS83
]
and the Gross–Prasad period for
\mathrm{SO}_{n}\times\mathrm{SO}_{n-1}
. Travkin and Yang
[
TY23b
]
prove
the local conjecture in the case of the
the Rankin-Selberg period for
\mathrm{GL}_{m}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n}
when
m<n-1
; the dual is then

{\check{X}}=\mathrm{Mat}_{m\times n}
acted on by
{\check{G}}=\mathrm{GL}_{m}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n}
.

Remark 7.6.6

(The Gaiotto Conjecture)
.

The geometric Langlands correspondence, at least in de Rham and Betti forms, has a so-called quantum deformation introduced by Feigin, Frenkel and Stoyanovsky, in which the automorphic categories are replaced by categories of twisted sheaves on moduli of
G
-bundles, see
[
Gai16c
,
FG20
,
BZN18
]
and references therein. The spectral side has a description, in the Betti version, in terms of categories of representations of quantum groups. It is a natural question which forms of the relative Langlands conjectures admit quantum deformations – it is easy to see that many periods do not admit such deformations, and even in cases that do (such as the group case) the deformed local category becomes much smaller or trivial. The Gaiotto conjecture provides a quantum deformation of the local conjecture for a family of periods where (like the Whittaker case) the deformed category is of the same size. Remarkably, these cases correspond to quantum supergroups, with
{\check{G}}
as the even part and
{\check{M}}
as the odd part, and include all the Rankin-Selberg and Gross-Prasad type integrals in the previous paragraph.

The Gaiotto conjecture is formulated in
[
BFGT21
, §2]
, and the quantum analogs of the above cases have now been proven for generic level in
[
BFT22b
]
,
[
TY23b
]
and
[
TY23a
]
(the Whittaker case corresponds to the Fundamental Local Equivalence, proven for irrational level in
[
Gai08
]
and for rational level in
[
CDR21
]
). Crucially, these conjectural descriptions are equivalences of monoidal categories, with the monoidal structure coming from factorization corresponding to the braided tensor product coming from quantum groups.
It would be very interesting to compare these spectral models with ours, and to apply the techniques developed in these papers to construct monoidal (or even braided monoidal) structures on the categories
\mathcal{H}^{X}
in general, see §
16.2
and Problem
16.2.11
.

8.
The Plancherel algebra and the Coulomb branch

In §
7
(whose notations we follow), we studied the category of constructible sheaves on
X_{F}/G_{O}
as a module category for the spherical Hecke category, and formulated the local conjecture identifying this structure in terms of coherent sheaf theory on
{\check{M}}
and the moment map. In this section we will study a more concrete and less categorical manifestation of local geometric duality, connecting the local conjecture to the study of
Coulomb branches
, as pioneered in the mathematical literature by Braverman, Finkelberg and Nakajima
[
BFN18
,
BFN19
]
.
This concerns, roughly speaking, the
affine
aspects of the story, or
‘‘the part of the local conjecture that has to do with the basic object.’’
64
64

64

From the point of view of boundary conditions in topological field theory, we are passing from categories of line operators to vector spaces of local operators

The key object here is what we call the

Plancherel algebra
(or
relative Coulomb branch
):

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}=\mbox{``endomorphisms of the basic object inside the Hecke category'' }

The Plancherel algebra is an algebra object in the Hecke category – that is to say,
it is equipped with an associative multiplication
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}\star{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}\rightarrow{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
, where
\star

is convolution of sheaves on the affine Grassmannian.
The definition will be explicated and spelled out in §
8.3
– it can be viewed as a gadget encoding not just endomorphisms of the basic object, but all Hom spaces between Hecke functors applied to the basic object.
The local conjecture predicts that, under the geometric Satake equivalence,

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
corresponds to the ring of functions
\mathcal{O}_{{\check{M}}}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
, as a representation of
{\check{G}}
,
and compatibly with the moment map (i.e., as an algebra object in sheared
{\check{G}}
-equivariant sheaves on the coadjoint representation
\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}
). See
§
8.1
for more discussion of this point of view.

The Plancherel algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
is a more concrete object than the local category
\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O})
, and also enjoys an important technical advantage. As we saw, “constructible sheaf theory”
in the local conjecture involves serious subtleties related to the
fact that loop spaces are singular; this makes it extremely difficult to actually compute anything. However,
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
can
be computed solely in terms of computations on smooth arc spaces
and (therefore) its definition reduces entirely to computations on finite-dimensional varieties, as described in
Proposition

8.3.1
. As a result, it is possible to compute explicitly in examples, see e.g. §
8.4
.

We derive this essentially finite-dimensional description of the Plancherel algebra from the general sheaf theory formalism.
That sheaf theory formalism is subject to the caveat noted in §
7.2
, namely, it is not well-documented in the literature at the current time.
However, one could take the point of view that the
finite-dimensional explication
is the
definition
of the Plancherel algebra and bypass the categorical prerequisites. Moreover, thanks to the affineness of
{\check{M}}
, the local conjecture implies that one can recover the entire automorphic category from the Plancherel algebra (see Section
7.5.3
).

The name “Plancherel algebra” emphasizes the fact, to be further explained in §
9
,
that it categorifies an object with a long mathematical history: the
Plancherel measure
;
and the
known numerical evaluations of the Plancherel measure provide
supporting evidence for our categorical conjecture – this will be explained in §
9
.

In the case when
X
is a vector space,
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
is precisely the
relative Coulomb branch algebra
, the ring object
in the Hecke category introduced by Braverman, Finkelberg and Nakajima in
[
BFN19
]

in the course of their mathematical study of Coulomb branches of 3d supersymmetric gauge theories. This ring object (or rather, its spectrum
\mu:{\check{M}}\to\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}
) is a
relative
version of the Coulomb branch, corresponding physically not to a 3d field theory but to a boundary condition for 4d
\mathcal{N}=4
supersymmetric gauge theory.
From the point of view of
[
BFN19
]
, perhaps the most novel part of the present chapter
is to formulate a precise conjecture description of the relative Coulomb branch (and its noncommutative deformation) associated
to a spherical variety.

We have included a liberal sprinkling of examples.
Some of these examples correspond to already-proven cases of the local conjecture;
our purpose in putting them here is, rather, “for fun” – that is, to illustrate the pretty geometry
and invariant theory underlying the story.

•

§
8.1
motivates and defines the Plancherel algebra, and then formulates the “Plancherel algebra conjecture,” Conjecture

8.1.8
,
identifying it with the ring of functions on
{\check{M}}
.
As explained above this is a “reduced” version of the full local conjecture which avoids
the intricacies of sheaf theory on
X_{F}
.

•

§
8.2
introduces the “relative Grassmannian”
which will play a useful role;
in the case of
X=H\backslash G
it is essentially the affine Grassmannian for
H
.

•

§
8.3
presents an explicit description of the Plancherel algebra, which in particular reduces to finite-dimensional calculations.

•

§
8.4
discusses several examples of Plancherel algebras.

•

§
8.5
studies loop rotation and formulates a conjecture on the corresponding noncommutative deformation of the Plancherel algebra. This explains, in particular, how the symplectic structure on
{\check{M}}
is relevant to the local conjecture.

We follow general notations as in the last section
§
7
. In particular,
(G,X)
will be defined over
\mathbb{F}
,
either
\mathbb{C}
or the algebraic closure of a finite field,
and the dual
(\check{G},\check{M})
is defined
over a coefficient field
k
. In line
with our conventions in
§
2.1
,
k
will generally be taken to be algebraically closed of characteristic zero,
although we will comment on more general settings at points.

8.1.
The Plancherel algebra

8.1.1.
Motivation: the ring of functions on
{\check{M}}

As motivation, let us examine how to recover
{\check{M}}
from the coherent side of the local
Conjecture

7.5.1
,
that is to say, from the category of
{\check{G}}
-equivariant sheaves on
{\check{M}}
(for simplicity,
let us ignore the shearing).

Since

{\check{M}}
is affine it is determined by its ring
\mathcal{O}_{{\check{M}}}
of globally regular functions.
If we were not working with
{\check{G}}
-equivariant sheaves, this can be recovered by taking endomorphisms of the (coherent) structure sheaf
of
{\check{M}}
.
But, working instead in the category of sheaves on
{\check{M}}/{\check{G}}
,
the endomorphisms of the structure sheaf recovers not
\mathcal{O}_{{\check{M}}}

but rather only the
{\check{G}}
-invariant elements.
This can be remedied by computing
endomorphisms
as a
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
-enriched category
.
In other words,
the category of
{\check{G}}
-equivariant sheaves is a module category for the rigid tensor category
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
,
which permits us to compute “internal endomorphisms in
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
.”
(The phrase “internal endomorphisms” is most commonly used
in the case of a monoidal category acting
on itself
though it applies more generally.)
This is analogous to the discussion in Section
6.3
of
Rep({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
-categories as categories enriched in graded vector spaces (representations of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
).

Work, for a moment, with ordinary (underived) categories, and take an object
\mathcal{F}
in the category of coherent sheaves on
{\check{M}}/{\check{G}}
.
Its internal endomorphisms, relative to
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
, is the
{\check{G}}
-representation
\underline{\mathrm{End}}(\mathcal{F})
characterized
as such by the property

(8.1)

\mathrm{Hom}(V,W\otimes\underline{\mathrm{End}}(\mathcal{F}))=\mathrm{Hom}(V\otimes\mathcal{F},W\otimes\mathcal{F}),

for
V,W
finite-dimensional
{\check{G}}
-representations;
the evident composition law on the right hand side, if we work with three representations
V,W,S
, gives
on
\underline{\mathrm{End}}(\mathcal{F})
the structure of
{\check{G}}
-algebra.

Remark 8.1.2

(Categorical definition of inner endomorphisms)
.

A more formal and categorical point of view, well adapted to the
\infty
-categorical setting, is based on the theory of rigid tensor categories briefly reviewed in Appendix
B.9.5
(see also
[
GR17
, Section 1.9]
). Namely, given a module category
\mathcal{M}
for a rigid tensor category
\mathcal{C}
and a compact object
F
, let
act_{F}:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{M}
denote the
\mathcal{C}
-module functor given by action on
F
. Then rigidity implies that
act_{F}
admits a
\mathcal{C}
-linear right adjoint, which is by definition the inner hom from
F
,
act_{F}^{R}=\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(F,-)
. The algebra object
\underline{\mathrm{End}}(F)=\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(F,F)\in Alg(\mathcal{C})
represents the monad
act_{F}^{R}\circ act_{F}
on
\mathcal{C}
. Applying this to
\mathcal{M}=\mathrm{QC}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})
and
\mathcal{C}=\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
recovers the construction above.
In particular Equation
8.1
applies in this generality (as a combination of the
\mathcal{C}
-linearity of and adjunction between
act_{F},act_{F}^{R}
), i.e., the internal endomorphism object of
F
collects the data of all Hom spaces between the objects
V\otimes F
and
W\otimes F
for compact (hence dualizable) objects
V,W\in\mathcal{C}
.

Yet another formulation is that we can recover the category
\mathrm{QC}({\check{M}})
with its
{\check{G}}
-action by de-equivariantization of
\mathrm{QC}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})
with its
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
action thanks to 1-affineness (as discussed in Section
6.3
for
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
): i.e., we are computing endomorphisms of the
{\check{G}}
-equivariant structure sheaf in the de-equivariantized category
\mathrm{QC}({\check{M}})\simeq\mathrm{QC}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})\otimes_{\text{Rep}({\check{G}})}Vect
.

8.1.3.
The Plancherel algebra

We have just explained how to reconstruct
{\check{M}}
from the coherent sheaf category
of the local conjecture
7.5.1
– namely, by taking internal endomorphisms
of the structure sheaf of
{\check{M}}
relative to
\text{Rep}(\check{G})
. Since that conjecture predicts that this is the
same as the “automorphic” sheaf category
\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O})
,
it also predicts that we can reconstruct
{\check{M}}

by taking internal endomorphisms of the basic object in
\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O})
relative to the spherical Hecke category.

To spell out: we use that the
X
-spherical category is a module category under the (large) Hecke category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{G}\simeq{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})
, and just as above
we can compute internal endomorphisms of an object and produce an algebra object in the Hecke category. Spectrally, this corresponds (after shearing) to thinking of
\mu_{*}\mathcal{O}_{{\check{M}}}
as an algebra object in
\mathrm{QC}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})
, i.e., remembering both the moment map and
{\check{G}}
-action.

This motivates that we consider the following.

Definition 8.1.4
.

(Plancherel algebra):
The Plancherel algebra of the

G
-variety
X
is the algebra object in the Hecke category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{G}
defined as the inner endomorphism algebra of the basic object

\delta_{X}\in{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X}
in the
X
-Hecke module category
65
65

65

Recall that the superscripts over
\mathcal{H}
refer to the large versions of the categories.
:

(8.2)

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}:=\underline{End}_{{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{G}}(\delta_{X})\in Alg({\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{G})

Via the derived Satake equivalence,
Theorem
6.6.1
, this

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
defines (uniquely, up to homotopy)
a differential graded algebra over
\mathcal{O}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
equipped with a
\check{G}
-action,
and we will equally well use
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
to denote this algebra.
66
66

66

In the cases of interest,
the local conjecture predicts that this differential graded algebra is formal, i.e., equivalent
to its cohomology. Thus, at least in principle, no information would be lost by passing to cohomology here.

Here “internal endomorphisms” are defined as explained after
(
8.1
), now working relative to the Hecke category rather than
\text{Rep}(\check{G})
; in particular,
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
is a unital algebra object of the Hecke category for
G
.
As we have noted, the Plancherel algebra defined above
is
entirely reducible to finite-dimensional computations
, see
§
8.3
.

Remark 8.1.5
.

Just as with the previous section,
we should strictly speaking fix a choice of sheaf theory (de Rham or étale) and
include this in the notation, but, again since it matters very little, we don’t do it that way.
A formal expression of this irrelevance is Proposition
8.3.1
,
which computes
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
in terms of cohomology groups, which can be
compared in a standard way between étale and de Rham versions.

Remark 8.1.6
.

We have only defined the sheaf category in the case when there is no

\mathbb{A}^{1}
-bundle
\Psi\rightarrow X
.
However, once the foundational definitions
have been suitably extended (cf. §
7.2.11
)
the same definition should be adopted in both twisted and unpolarized cases
(indeed, the paper
[
BDF+22
]
already
amounts to a definition of
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
for
X
a symplectic vector space).

8.1.7.
The Plancherel algebra conjecture

Let notation be as in

7
; in particular,
we take
(G,M=T^{*}(X,\Psi))

and
(\check{G},\check{M})
a split hyperspherical pair
as in
5

defined over
\mathbb{F}
and
k
respectively. We will now spell out the consequence of the local conjecture for the Plancherel algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
:

Conjecture 8.1.8
.

(A consequence of
Conjecture
7.5.1
):

The Plancherel algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
is isomorphic as a
{\check{G}}
-equivariant algebra over
\mathcal{O}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
with the ring of functions on
\mathcal{O}(\check{M})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
:

(8.3)

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}\simeq\mathcal{O}(\check{M})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

(where the shearing on
\mathcal{O}(\check{M})
is through the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action, and the sheared moment map
\mathcal{O}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}(\check{M})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
corresponds to
the unital structure on
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
.)
Moreover, if
\mathbb{F}
is the algebraic closure of a finite field, this isomorphism is Frobenius-equivariant,
where the Frobenius action on the left hand side
arises from its natural action on
\mathcal{H}_{G}
and the trivial Frobenius structure on
\delta_{X}
; and
Frobenius is acting on the right hand side according
to the shear of the analytic action (§
6.8.3
).

In particular,
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
,
a priori
a differential graded algebra, is in fact formal
and commutative. On the level of cohomology, the commutativity follows
(again, bearing in mind the general caveats of §
7.2
) from the compatibility of the product with factorization, as in Section
16
, and convolution.
We also remark that the statement (
8.3
) is using
analytic normalization of
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
and the
analytic
shear on
\mathcal{O}_{\check{M}}
(§
6.8.1
).
The corresponding assertion with the arithmetic normalization of
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
, as in Remark
8.3.4
,
is that the normalized version of
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
is isomorphic to the
arithmetic
shear on
\mathcal{O}(\check{M})
, §
6.8.3
.

Remark 8.1.9
.

As a sanity check on signs let us compute the
case when
G={\mathbb{G}_{m}},X=\mathbb{A}^{1}
, so that
\check{M}=T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{1}

with scaling action of
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
.
Frobenius structures were discussed in
Example
6.8.2
.

In this case, we have (cf. (
7.9
))
that for a character
\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{j}

the corresponding isotypical component
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(j)}
,
the component by which
\check{G}
acts by
\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{j}
,
is identified with
H^{*}(B{\mathbb{G}_{m}})\langle-|j|\rangle
.
67
67

67

we emphasize that we have used the analytic normalization in this computation,
i.e., the Hecke operator
T_{j}
corresponding
to
\lambda\mapsto\lambda_{j}
is supported in valuation
j
and
\deg(T_{j})=j
, cf. Example
7.4.1
.

This is one-dimensional exactly in degrees
j,j+2,\dots
,
and the geometric Frobenius eigenvalue in degree
s
is given
by
q^{s/2}
.

On the other hand, writing
x,\xi
for the coordinates
on
\check{M}
, the isotypical space for
\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{j}

on
\mathcal{O}(\check{M})
is exactly

x^{j}(x\xi)^{m},m\geq 0
or
\xi^{-j}(x\xi)^{m},m\geq 0

depending on whether
j
is positive or negative.
Again, this is one-dimensional exactly in
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
degrees

-j,-j-2,\dots
, corresponding to cohomological degrees

(cf. Example

), thus matching the geometric computation.

Remark 8.1.10
.

(Rationality issues:)
We would also conjecture that Conjecture

8.1.8

remains valid
if
k
is not algebraically closed,
and even if
k
is not a field,
where
\check{M}
is taken to be the distinguished split form
that was postulated in §
5.3
.
In the case where
\Psi
is trivial we can even take
k
to equal
\mathbb{Z}
.
Indeed, in §
5.3
, we noted that compatibility
with this Plancherel algebra conjecture should be considered a defining property
of this split form.

Note that even in the group case that the predicted
\mathbb{Q}
-form
of
\check{M}
arising in the conjecture is not the “pinned” version;
that is to say,
\check{M}
is the cotangent bundle of
\check{G}
as
\check{G}\times\check{G}
-space,
but the action is twisted, on one factor, not by the Chevalley involution but rather by the duality
involution (§
2.3.2
) which does not preserve a pinning.

It is extremely interesting to study these issues when
k
has small characteristic. Work over
\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{C}
and consider, for example, the case when
X=G/H
is homogeneous; we will see that, in this case, the invariants

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{\check{G}}
are given simply by the cohomology
H^{*}(BH,k)
, the cohomology
of the classifying space of
H
with coefficients in
k
. Now, if the characteristic of
k
is a bad prime
for
H
, this cohomology can behave quite irregularly. On the other hand, the invariants
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{\check{G}}

can also behave badly: in finite characteristic, taking
\check{G}
-invariants is not exact, and one should use instead derived invariants.
It is plausible that these pathologies match up with one another. Again, this is not even
obvious in the group case, or in the case when
X=\mathrm{pt}
.

8.2.
The relative Grassmannian

The following object (known as the “variety of triples” in the Coulomb branch literature
[
BFN18
]
) will play a key role for us.
We use the term “relative Grassmannian” and
we have emphasized the intuition arising from the homogeneous case
X=H\backslash G
.
where it is essentially the affine Grassmannian of the stabilizer
H
.

Let
X
be a quasi-affine
G
-variety.
Informally, the relative Grassmannian
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
is the closed subscheme of
X_{O}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
classifying

pairs
x\in X_{O},g\in G_{F}/G_{O}
for which
xg\in X_{O}
.

where we identify
\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
with
G_{F}/G_{O}
.
In particular, it will come with a morphism

(8.4)

i^{\mathrm{Gr}}:\mathrm{Gr}^{X}\rightarrow X_{O}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{G}

Formally, we can define
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
as the pullback

(8.5)

\textstyle{\mathrm{Gr}^{X}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{b\hskip 16.38895pt}
\scriptstyle{a}
\textstyle{X_{O}\times_{G_{O}}G_{F}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{X_{O}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{i}
\textstyle{X_{F}}

of the action of
G_{F}
over the inclusion of the arc space.
This pullback is taken in the category of schemes,
68
68

68

where
G_{F}\times^{G_{O}}X_{O}

is the scheme that represents the functor assigning to a ring
R

the
G
-bundles on the formal disc
R[[t]]
which are trivialized on
R((t))

and moreover equipped with a section of the associated
X
-bundle.

see §
8.2.1
for further explication.

It should be noted that the top horizontal arrow
b
is not the same morphism
(indeed, does not even have the same codomain) as
i^{\mathrm{Gr}}
from (
8.4
).
Rather, the embedding
i^{\mathrm{Gr}}
of (
8.4
)
is given by
\iota=(a,b_{2}^{-1})
, where
b_{2}:\mathrm{Gr}^{X}\rightarrow G_{F}/G_{O}

is the second coordinate of
b
.
Said differently, the horizontal arrow
b
is represented,
in terms of pairs
(x,g)
with
xg\in X_{O}
,
by “
(x,g)\mapsto(xg,g^{-1})
.”

Next,
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
is equipped with an action of
G_{O}
.
If we consider
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
via (
8.4
) as classifying pairs
(x,g)
, the action
of
h\in G_{O}
sends this to
(xh,h^{-1}g)
; if we think in
terms of the pullback diagram (
8.5
)
G_{O}
acts both on
X_{O}
at the bottom left,
and acts by
X_{O}\times_{G_{O}}G_{F}
by right multiplication on
G_{F}
.

The quasi-affineness of
X
guarantees (see below) that
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
defines a locally closed subscheme of
X_{O}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
.
In the notation before (
8.4
), the maps
(x,g)\mapsto g,(x,g)\mapsto x,(x,g)\mapsto xg,

define

(8.6)

\Gamma:\mathrm{Gr}^{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Gr},p_{1}:\mathrm{Gr}^{X}\rightarrow X_{O},p_{2}:\mathrm{Gr}^{X}/G_{O}\rightarrow X_{O}/G_{O}

(note that
p_{2}
is only defined after quotienting by
G_{O}
).

8.2.1.
Explication as a (representable) functor

We will describe explicitly the functor represented by
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
, and why it is represented
by a locally closed subscheme of
X_{O}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
.

One can describe
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
as classifying a
G
-bundle
\mathcal{G}
on
\mathbb{P}^{1}
with a trivialization outside of
0
and an arc in
X
satisfying the condition that the arc, restricted to the punctured disc at
0
, extends to a section of the associated
X
-bundle of
\mathcal{G}
on the disc.

To say this symbolically,
X_{O}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
is the functor assigning to a test ring
R
the data of

(i)

a
G
-bundle
\mathcal{G}
on
\mathbb{P}^{1}_{R}

trivialized on
\mathbb{A}^{1}_{R}
;

(ii)

an element
x\in X(R[[t]])
.

Then,
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
is the subfunctor defined as follows:
Let
\mathcal{X}
be the
X
-bundle on
\mathbb{P}^{1}_{R}
associated to
\mathcal{G}
.
The trivialization of
\mathcal{G}
on
\mathbb{A}^{1}
gives
a corresponding trivialization of
\mathcal{X}
.
Therefore,
x
determines a section
x^{\mathcal{G}}
of
\mathcal{X}
over
R((t))
,
and
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
is determined by the condition that

x^{\mathcal{G}}
extend to an
R[[t]]
-point of
\mathcal{X}
.
Such an extension is unique for
X
affine since

R[[t]]\rightarrow R((t))
induces an injection on points,
and moreover the resulting functor is, in the case when
X
is affine, in fact representable by a (ind-)closed subscheme
of
X_{O}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
(in what follows, we will omit the “ind-”).

To verify closedness, we reduce this to the case where
G=\mathrm{GL}_{n}
and
X=\mathbb{A}^{n}

by choosing an equivariant embedding of
X
into a vector space;
and in that case
the
R
-points of
X_{O}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{G}

are pairs:

-

a locally free
R[[t]]
-submodule
M\subset R((t))^{n}

such that
M[t^{-1}]
is all of
R((t))^{n}
;

-

and
x\in R[[t]]^{n}
.

The condition defining
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
is then that
x\in M
, and this is readily verified to define a ind-closed subscheme.

If
X
is
quasi-affine
,
the functor noted above remains representable by a locally closed subscheme.
Indeed, as before, the above construction for the affine closure
X^{{\operatorname{aff}}}
of
X

yields a closed subscheme of
X^{\mathrm{aff}}_{O}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
;
we then impose the additional
open
condition that
x^{\mathcal{G}}

reduce at the special point
R[[t]]\rightarrow R

to a point of
X^{{\operatorname{aff}}}(R)
that in fact lies inside
X(R)
.

8.2.2.
The equivariant relative Grassmannian

In the homogeneous case
X=H\backslash G
, we have an equivalence

(8.7)

\mathrm{Gr}^{X}/G_{O}\simeq H_{O}\backslash H_{F}/H_{O},

i.e., considered equivariantly relative to
G_{O}
,
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}

recovers the
H_{O}
-equivariant affine Grassmannian of
H
.

69
69

69

This example perhaps motivates our name “relative Grassmannian.”

More generally the equivariant version
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}/G_{O}
can be described as the moduli stack of:

•

pairs of
G
-bundles on the disc, together with

•

sections on the associated
X
-bundles on the discs, and

•

an identification of the bundles and sections on the punctured disc.

Or, to put another way, it is the groupoid object
over
X_{O}/G_{O}
obtained by restricting the Hecke action
of the equivariant Grasmannian on
X_{F}/G_{O}
. This explains formally why the relative Grassmannian appears when studying the inner endomorphisms of the basic object (the constant sheaf on
X_{O}/G_{O}
) with respect to the spherical Hecke action.

8.2.3.
The twisted case

If
X
is equipped with an
\mathbb{A}^{1}
-torsor
\Psi\rightarrow X
then
we get a morphism

(8.8)

A:\mathrm{Gr}^{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1},

Given a point of
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
represented by
(x\in X_{O},g\in G_{F})
,
we lift
x
to
\tilde{x}\in\Psi_{O}
, and then consider
\tilde{x}g\in\Psi_{F}
;
since it lies above
xg\in X_{O}
it defines a canonical point
in
F/O
by comparison to an arbitrary lift
\widetilde{xg}\in\Psi_{O}
.
Using the “residue” morphism
F/O\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}

we get the desired map (
8.8
).
For later use we observe the cocycle property
of the map
A
from (
8.8
).

(8.9)

A(x,g_{1}g_{2})=A(x,g_{1})+A(xg_{1},g_{2})

8.2.4.
Essential finite-dimensionality

The relative Grassmannian is essentially a finite-dimensional construction, in the following sense.
Suppose we
replace the role of the affine Grassmannian above by some
sufficiently large stratum
\mathrm{Gr}_{\leq n}
.
We obtain a corresponding locally closed subscheme
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}_{\leq n}
.
The resulting

\mathrm{Gr}^{X}_{\leq n}\rightarrow X_{O}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{\leq n}
is pulled back from a
locally closed immersion of (finite dimensional!) varieties

(8.10)

i^{\mathrm{Gr},N}:\mathrm{Gr}^{X}_{\leq n;N}\rightarrow X_{N}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{\leq n}

(for some
N
; here
X_{N}=X_{O/t^{N}}
is the jet scheme of order
N
).
All this says is, if we fix the “denominators”
of
g
, the question of whether
xg\in X_{O}
is entirely
determined by the reduction of
x
modulo a fixed power of
t
. In all computations
where we use
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
its role can be replaced by one of these finite-dimensional truncations.

8.3.
Explication of the Plancherel algebra

We are ready to give our explicit and inherently “finite-dimensional” description of the Plancherel algebra.

We describe the Plancherel algebra as
a direct sum

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}=\bigoplus V\otimes{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}

of multiplicity spaces for irreducible representations
V
of
{\check{G}}
, which we will describe individually.

Let
V
be a representation of
\check{G}
, let
\mathcal{T}_{V}

be as in (
6.16
)
the associated perverse sheaf on
\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
.
Fix a sufficiently large closed
G_{O}
-invariant subset
\mathrm{Gr}_{\leq n}
on the affine
Grassmannian containing the support of
\mathcal{T}_{V}
.
We present the formula for the
analytically normalized
Hecke action (see Remark
8.3.4
below for modifications in the other case). Thus
\deg T_{V}
is defined as in §
7.4

in terms of the eigenmeasure on
X
, or equivalently
is the weight by which
\check{\eta}:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\rightarrow\check{G}

acts on
V
. Finally, recall from (
8.10
) that

\iota:\mathrm{Gr}^{X}\rightarrow X_{O}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
is pulled back from a finite type

\iota:\mathrm{Gr}^{X}_{\leq n;N}\hookrightarrow X_{N}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{\leq n},

where
X_{N}
is the mod
t^{N}
truncation of
X_{O}
and
\iota
a locally closed immersion.
Let
p:\mathrm{Gr}^{X}_{\leq n;N}\rightarrow X_{N}
be the second coordinate of this truncated map.

Proposition 8.3.1
.

(Multiplicity spaces of the Plancherel algebra):
With notation as above, we have

(8.11)

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}\langle-\deg T_{V}\rangle=\mathrm{Hom}_{G}(\mathcal{T}^{V}_{X},p^{!}k_{X_{N}})\simeq H^{*}_{G}(\mathbb{D}\mathcal{T}^{V}_{X})\langle-2\mathrm{dim}X_{N}\rangle

where we compute the
\mathrm{Hom}
- on the right
G
-equivariantly
70
70

70

More naturally, we would say
G_{O}
-equivariantly;
but since the map
G\rightarrow G_{O}
induces a homotopy equivalence it amounts to the same thing, and
this way the computation visibly only involves finite-dimensional data.
on the finite type scheme

\mathrm{Gr}^{X}_{\leq n;N}
;
\mathcal{T}^{X}_{V}
is the
*
-pullback of the Hecke operator

\mathcal{T}_{V}
to
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}_{\leq n;N}
, and
\mathbb{D}

is computed for ordinary (not equivariant) sheaves on
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}_{\leq n;N}
.

71

71

More properly, of course,

should be replaced by a chain-level model, since

is formally a chain complex,
well-defined up to homotopy.

We will give the proof in §
8.3.6
and examples in the

. At the moment we make several remarks.

Remark 8.3.2

(Comparison with
[

]
)
.

The above statement was written in a way that was evidently finite-dimensional, that is to say,

72

Recall that sheaf theory on infinite type schemes comes in two variants,

!
, according
to whether one takes, informally speaking, a system of sheaves on finite type truncations
that are compatible with respect to
*
-pullbacks or with respect to
!
-pullbacks. In the prior Section
we used by default
!
-sheaves; in the current situation they are equivalent
by the placidity of
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
, whch follows from (
8.10
).

In
[
BFN19
]
, it is shown that (a suitable shift of)
\mathfrak{A}:=\Gamma_{*}\omega_{\mathrm{Gr}^{X}}
has the structure of ring object in the spherical Hecke category, with
V
-isotypic components therefore given by (
8.12
). In fact
[
BFN19
]
discuss
only the case of
X
a vector space; their construction
applies, however, without change for
X
a smooth affine variety
(although not to the quasi-affine case).

It is natural to expect, and would be interesting to prove, that this ring structure agrees with the algebra structure that arises
via the definition of the Plancherel algebra as inner endomorphisms of the basic object (and such an identification should be completely formal, up to potential issues arising from
subtleties of sheaf theory in infinite type).

Remark 8.3.3
.

If
X
is equipped with a
\mathbb{A}^{1}
-bundle
\Psi\rightarrow X

and we work in either de Rham or étale sheaf theory,
the formulas (
8.12
) or (
8.11
) still make sense by twisting
p^{!}k_{X_{n}}
or
\omega^{\textrm{ren}}_{\mathrm{Gr}^{X}}
by
\mathcal{L}_{\psi}
,
the pull-back of an Artin-Schreier sheaf via (
8.8
).

This will, presumably, coincide with Definition
8.1.4
after it is extended
to cover the twisted setting. In the absence of this extension, let us
take (
8.12
) as the definition of
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}
in the twisted case.

We note that the direct construction of the product from
[
BFN19
]

does not apply in the case of twisted polarizations
because a certain map
fails to be proper in the quasi-affine case.
One expects that the twisting provided by
the Artin-Schreier sheaf makes it behave, from a cohomological standpoint, as if it were proper, but this remains to be worked out.

Remark 8.3.4
.

(Normalized versus unnormalized version:)
Note that (
8.12
) is an analytic normalization, in the sense
of §
2.7
. For the “unnormalized” or “arithmetic” Plancherel algebra
we use the same definition, but omit the shear
\langle\deg T_{V}\rangle
. By default, statements
that follow will use the analytic normalization except where otherwise noted.

Remark 8.3.5

(Trace of Frobenius)
.

Restricting to the case of
\mathbb{F}
the algebraic closure of a finite field
\mathbb{F}_{q}
,
let us compute the trace of geometric Frobenius
on the dual of
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}
using Lemma
2.6.1
.
The result of this computation will be used in the study of Plancherel measure.
As before, we work with the analytic normalization; for the arithmetic version one ignores the
\sqrt{\eta}
.

The trace-function associated to
\mathcal{T}^{X}_{V}

is the pullback of the usual Hecke function
T_{V}
associated to
\mathcal{T}_{V}

from the affine Grassmannian. The trace function
associated to the
\mathbb{D}p^{!}k_{X_{N}}=p^{*}\omega_{X_{N}}
is the pullback of the function
q^{-\mathrm{dim}X_{N}}

from
X_{N}
.

Applying Lemma
2.6.1
, the trace of Frobenius on the dual
of
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{V}
equals
the sum, over
(x,g)\in\mathrm{Gr}^{X}_{\leq n;N}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
,
of
q^{\mathrm{dim}(G)}\frac{T_{V}(g)\sqrt{\eta(g)}}{q^{\mathrm{dim}X_{N}}\#G(\mathbb{F}_{q})},

where the order of
G(\mathbb{F}_{q})
in the denominator arises from
the corresponding term in Lemma
2.6.1
,
and
q^{\mathrm{dim}(G)}
arises from the difference between
G
-equivariant
duality on
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}_{\leq n;N}
, which is what appears in Lemma
2.6.1
,
and ordinary non-equivariant duality which is what appears in the formula
(
8.11
).

Recall our notations
\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{f}

for
\mathbb{F}_{q}[[t]]
and
\mathbb{F}_{q}((t))
respectively.
Then
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}_{\leq n;N}
consists of pairs
(x,g)
,
where
x\in X(\mathfrak{o}/t^{N})
,

g\in(G_{\mathfrak{f}}/G_{\mathfrak{o}})^{\leq n}
,
and
xg
is integral.
Rewriting in terms of
\mathfrak{o}
-points, we get

(8.13)

\mbox{trace of Frobenius
on dual of ${\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}$}=\frac{q^{\mathrm{dim}(G)}}{\#G(\mathbb{F}_{q})}\cdot\int_{X_{\mathfrak{o}}\times G_{\mathfrak{f}}/G_{\mathfrak{o}}}\sqrt{\eta(g)}1_{X(\mathfrak{o})}(xg)T_{V}(g)dg,\

and the measure normalizations assign mass
1
to
G(\mathfrak{o})\subset G(\mathfrak{f})
,
and assign mass
\#X(\mathbb{F}_{q})/q^{\mathrm{dim}(X)}
to
X(\mathfrak{o})
.

In the case when
X
is equipped with an affine bundle
\Psi
,
the same formula holds when we modify the definition of
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}

according to Remark
8.3.3
, and including in the
integrand the twisting factor

\psi(A(x,g))
where
A(x,g):X_{\mathfrak{o}}\times G_{\mathfrak{f}}/G_{\mathfrak{o}}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}

is obtained from the
\mathbb{F}
-points of (
8.8
), and

\psi
is an additive character of
\mathbb{F}
.

8.4.
Some examples

The following examples are not given in the spirit of evidence,
but rather to illustrate that the objects appearing in the Conjecture
are interesting and computable.
Everywhere here we will, for the purpose of computing, work
at the level of cohomology, i.e.,
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{V}
refers to the cohomology
of the underlying chain complex.

Example 8.4.1
.

In the homogeneous case the discussion is particularly simple:
we have
for
X=H\backslash G
, with
H
reductive,
the eigenmeasure character is trivial, and after
(
8.7
) we have the equality

(8.15)

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}\simeq H^{*}_{H_{O}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{H},\mathbb{D}\mathcal{T}_{V}),

i.e., we take the Hecke operator on the
G
-affine Grassmannian,

*
-restrict to
\mathrm{Gr}_{H}
, dualize, and take equivariant cohomology.
“Duality” is normalized to preserve the basic object of
\mathrm{Gr}_{H}
,
and then no further shifts are required; thus, for example, when
V
is trivial,

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}
gives the
H_{O}
-equivariant cohomology of
\mathrm{Gr}_{H}
itself.

Here is a simple example where one can compute everything. Take
G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{3}
and
X=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{3}/\Delta\mathrm{PGL}_{2}
. Take

V=V_{a}\otimes V_{b}\otimes V_{c}

an arbitrary irreducible of the dual
\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{3}
.
Then

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}
is the cohomology of the
\mathrm{PGL}_{2}
-affine Grassmannian
with coefficients in the tensor product of the perverse sheaves associated by geometric Satake to
V_{a},V_{b},V_{c}
.
This tensor product is zero unless
a,b,c
all have the same parity;
and in that case it is the constant sheaf
k\langle a+b+c\rangle

on the
m
-dimensional stratum of
\mathrm{Gr}^{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}
indexed by
m=\min(a,b,c)
.
Geometric Satake here tells us that the cohomology of
k

on this stratum is identified with the cohomology of
\mathbb{P}^{\min(a,b,c)}
.
Dualizing and computing cohomology we find
a noncanonical isomorphism
of graded vector spaces (with Frobenius action when
\mathbb{F}
is of finite characteristic)

(8.16)

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}^{(V)}_{X}\simeq H^{*}(\mathbb{P}^{\min(a,b,c)})\otimes H^{*}(B\mathrm{PGL}_{2})\langle 2\min(a,b,c)-a-b-c\rangle,

– the noncanonicity arises from the fact that we used the degeneration of the pertinent spectral sequence.
Now let us check the
V_{a}\otimes V_{b}\otimes V_{c}
-isotypical component of
Conjecture
8.3
including the statement about Frobenius structures.
Here we have
\check{G}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{3}

and
\check{M}
the standard representation, i.e., the tensor product
of the three standard representations, and so

\eqref{chugchug}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{\simeq}}\mathrm{Hom}(V_{a}\otimes V_{b}\otimes V_{c},k[\mathbb{A}^{2}\otimes\mathbb{A}^{2}\otimes\mathbb{A}^{2}]),

On the right hand side, considering
k[\dots]

as polynomial on an
8
-dimensional vector space, the Frobenius action
on degree
d
polynomials is through a twist
\langle-d\rangle
, i.e.
by
q^{d/2}
(note that
d
is, by our conventions, negative to the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
grading).
To compute this we note that the
\mathrm{SL}_{2}
-action
on
\mathbb{A}^{8}
has a unique (up to scaling) quartic invariant.
This is well-known, particularly to those people who know it well.
The zero-locus of this semi-invariant has the form

U^{0}\backslash\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{3}

where
U^{0}
is the subgroup of upper triangular unipotent
matrices
u_{x,y,z}
satisfying
x+y+z=0
;
the action of scaling corresponds here to the left
action of the diagonal element
(1/t,t)
.
From this one can deduce an isomorphism
of graded vector spaces with
\mathrm{SL}_{2}
-action

k[\mathbb{A}^{8}]\simeq k[Q_{4}]\otimes k[U^{0}\backslash\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{3}],

where
\mathrm{SL}_{2}
acts trivially on
Q_{4}
in degree
4
. The factor
k[Q_{4}]
with its grading
matches with
H^{*}(B\mathrm{PGL}_{2})
above.
The
V_{a}\otimes V_{b}\otimes V_{c}
-isotypical component of

U^{0}\backslash\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{3}

is just the
U^{0}
-invariants on

V_{a}\otimes V_{b}\otimes V_{c}
,
which are readily computed
to be a
\min(a,b,c)+1
-dimensional
space, spanned by polynomials of degree

a+b+c-2j,0\leq j\leq\min(a,b,c),

which matches (
8.16
).

Example 8.4.2
.

We take the Whittaker case
X=U\backslash G
with its affine bundle
\Psi
.
In this case – taking (
8.12
) as the definition
as in Remark
8.3.3
,

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}=k,

i.e.,
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}
is one-dimensional for
V
trivial and zero otherwise.
The computation that
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}
is trivial for any nontrivial
V

representation is precisely the geometric version of the Casselman–Shalika formula
[
FGV01
]
.

Example 8.4.3
.

For
V=\mathbf{1}
, the trivial
representation, we have a distinguished morphism
k\rightarrow{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(\mathbf{1})}
.
This corresponds to the unit of the algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
.
With reference to (
8.3.1
),
it comes from the morphism
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{1}}^{X}\rightarrow p^{!}\delta_{X}

that comes from the identification

p_{!}\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{1}}^{X}\simeq\delta_{X}
.

There is always a map
from
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}/G_{O}}(\mathcal{T}_{V},\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{1}})

to
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}
(unnormalized version; for the normalized version add the shifts everywhere);
this encodes the
\mathcal{O}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
-module structure on
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
.
Again, from the point of view
of (
8.3.1
),
this arises as follows:
a homomorphism
f:\mathcal{T}_{V}\rightarrow\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{1}}

on
\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
gives
a map
\mathcal{T}_{V}^{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{1}}^{X}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle unit}}{{\rightarrow}}p^{!}\delta_{X}
,
i.e., a class in
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}
.

Example 8.4.4
.

(Product, in the homogeneous case):
Let us spell out what the product looks like in the homogeneous case
X=G/H

(again, explicating only at the level of cohomology).

By (
8.15
) we get

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}=H^{*}_{H_{O}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{H},\mathbb{D}\mathcal{T}_{V}),

where the dualization
\mathbb{D}
takes place on
\mathrm{Gr}_{H}

and is normalized to fix the basic object;
equivalently,
H_{O}
-equivariant homomorphisms from
\mathcal{T}_{V}

to the dualizing sheaf on
\mathrm{Gr}_{H}
.
Here there is a morphism

(8.17)

\mathcal{T}_{V}\star_{G}\mathcal{T}_{W}|_{\mathrm{Gr}_{H}}\rightarrow(\mathcal{T}_{V}|_{\mathrm{Gr}_{H}}\star_{H}\mathcal{T}_{W}|_{\mathrm{Gr}_{H}}),

arising from a restriction map in cohomology;
on the left,
\star_{G}
denotes convolution on the affine Grassmannian for
G
,
and on the right,
\star_{H}
denotes
the same on the affine Grassmannian for
H
.

Now we dualize on
\mathrm{Gr}_{H}
(thus reversing the arrow) and take
H_{O}
-equivariant cohomology on both sides.
On the left hand side we get
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V\otimes W)}
.
On the right hand side we first of all get the
H_{O}
-equivariant cohomology
of

(\mathbb{D}\mathcal{T}_{V})|_{\mathrm{Gr}_{H}}\star_{H}(\mathbb{D}\mathcal{T}_{W})|_{\mathrm{Gr}_{H}}

(because the convolution of sheaves involves only
descent along a smooth map and a proper pushforward and thus is compatible with
\mathbb{D}
);
and in turn we have a convolution product
in
H_{O}
-equivariant cohomology

H^{*}(A)\otimes H^{*}(B)\rightarrow H^{*}(A\star_{H}B)

which shows that this admits a map from
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}\otimes{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(W)}
.

For example, consider the case of
X=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/T
, and take
V_{n}

the
n+1
-dimensional irreducible representation of the dual group
\check{G}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}
; then

\mathcal{T}_{1}:=\mathcal{T}_{V_{1}}
is the constant sheaf
k\langle 1\rangle
on
\mathbb{P}^{1}\subset\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}
cf. §
6.5.1
.
Label the points of
\mathrm{Gr}_{T}
as
x_{n}
,
where
x_{n}
corresponds to the cocharacter
t\mapsto\mathrm{diag}(t^{n},1)
and
write e.g.
k_{n}
for the skyscraper on
\mathrm{Gr}_{T}
with value
k
at
x_{n}
.

First of all, the restriction of

\mathcal{T}_{V_{n}}
to
\mathrm{Gr}^{T}
is the sum

(k_{n}\oplus k_{n-2}\oplus\dots\oplus k_{-n})\langle n\rangle
,
from which we deduce that
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V_{n})}

is
n+1
-dimensional, with basis indexed by the points

x_{i}
with
|i|\leq n
and
i
having the same parity as
n
.
In particular, we get bases
d_{0}
for
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V_{0})}
,
e_{\pm 1}
for

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V_{1})}
, and
f_{-2},f_{0},f_{2}
for
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V_{2})}
,
where the index is the same as the indexing of points of
\mathrm{Gr}_{T}
,
We claim that the product
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V_{1})}\otimes{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V_{1})}\rightarrow{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V_{2})}
is given by

(8.18)

e_{1}^{2}=f_{2},e_{-1}^{2}=f_{-2},e_{1}e_{-1}=f_{0}+\xi d_{0}.

where
\xi
is a generator in
H^{2}(BT_{O})
.
To see this, we compute

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{1}|_{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(k_{1}\oplus k_{-1})\langle 1\rangle,

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{1}|_{T}\star\mathcal{T}_{1}|_{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(k_{2}\oplus k_{0}\oplus k_{0}\oplus k_{-2})\langle 2\rangle,

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{0}\oplus\mathcal{T}_{2}|_{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(k_{0})\oplus(k_{2}\oplus k_{0}\oplus k_{-2})\langle 2\rangle.

The morphism (
8.17
) here, for
V=W=V_{1}
, gives

(\mathcal{T}_{0}\oplus\mathcal{T}_{2})|_{T}\rightarrow\mathcal{T}_{1}|_{T}\star\mathcal{T}_{1}|_{T}
.
This gives a morphism of
\mathcal{T}_{O}
-equivariant sheaves on the points
\{x_{i}\}
,
and is an identity over
x_{\pm 2}
. Over
x_{0}
, the map comes from
the map of
\mathbb{C}^{\times}
-equivariant sheaves on a point:

(8.19)

k_{0}\oplus k_{0}\langle 2\rangle\rightarrow(k_{0}\oplus k_{0})\langle 2\rangle,

where all sheaves have trivial equivariant structure.
Explicitly, this is the the restriction map from
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant cohomology of
\mathbb{P}^{1}

to
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant cohomology of the poles
\pm\infty
,
where we consider both cohomology groups (via pushforward) as
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant sheaves on a point.
Thereore, in (
8.19
), the induced map on
k_{0}\langle 2\rangle
is the diagonal,
and the induced map on
k_{0}
is the map given by

(\xi,-\xi)
, where
\xi
is a generator of
H^{2}(B{\mathbb{G}_{m}})(1)
,
considered as a map
k_{0}\rightarrow k_{0}\langle 2\rangle
.
We recover (
8.18
) from this, after taking Verdier dual and passing to cohomology.

Now, let us sketch how (
8.18
) matches with the other side of Conjecture

8.1.8

In this case,
\check{G}=\mathrm{SL}_{2},\check{M}=M_{2}
,
the space of
2\times 2
-matrices with its natural
\check{G}
-action
by left multiplication, and with
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
acting by scaling, and the
conjecture says

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}=\mathrm{Hom}(V,k[M_{2}]),

where
M_{2}
is the space of
2\times 2
matrices,
with coordinates
(a,b;c,d)
say.
Taking
V=V_{1}
, the standard representation, the basis

e_{\pm 1}
for
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V_{1})}
corresponds to the
two embeddings
E_{\pm 1}

sending the coordinate vectors
u,v
of
V_{1}
to

(a,b)
and to
(c,d)
respectively.

Now, we may write
V_{1}\otimes V_{1}=V_{0}\oplus V_{2}
, where the factors
are spanned by
u\otimes v-v\otimes u

and
u\otimes u,v\otimes v,u\otimes v+v\otimes u

respectively.
We deduce that the
V_{0}
component of
E_{\pm 1}^{2}

equals zero, and the
V_{0}
component of
E_{1}E_{-1}

corresponds to the embedding of
V_{0}
to
k[M_{2}]
given by the determinant;
the determinant on
M_{2}
corresponds to
\xi
in the notation of (
8.18
).
On the other hand,
E_{1}^{2},E_{1}E_{-1},E_{-1}^{2}

give maps
V_{2}\rightarrow k[M_{2}]
that
correspond to
f_{2},f_{0},f_{-2}
in the notation of
(
8.18
).

Example 8.4.5
.

(The regular locus and the scheme of regular centralizers):
In our prior computations we can replace the role of
\mathcal{T}_{V}

with the constant sheaf on
\mathrm{Gr}_{G}
; this leads to the original definition of Coulomb branch in
[
BFN18
]
.
The corresponding object in the Satake category, by

[
BF08
]
, is the pushforward of the structure sheaf from the Kostant slice.

Specialize now to the case
X=G/H
.
The computation of (this analogue of, replacing
\mathcal{T}_{V}
by the constant sheaf)
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}

is well-known: it is the equivariant Borel–Moore homology
of the affine Grassmannian for
H
, which, as computated
by Bezrukavikov-Finkelberg, is precisely the ring of functions on
group scheme of regular centralizers
J_{H}
.
Working out the details
leads to the following consequence of the conjecture, which we will study
in later work:

\mbox{fiber of $\check{M}$ above the Kostant slice for $\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}$}\simeq J_{H}.

8.5.
Noncommutative deformations; the symplectic structure on
\check{M}

In Section
7.5.11
we discussed the canonical deformation of the automorphic category that arises from the structure of loop rotation, and which is required to relate to the Poisson structure on
{\check{M}}
. We now formulate a more precise form of this compatibility in terms of a noncommutative deformation of the Plancherel algebra.

Recall that we are considering the
H^{*}_{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}(\mbox{pt},k)\simeq k[u]
-linear category

\mathrm{SHV}_{u}(X_{F}/G_{O})=\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O})^{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}
of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant sheaves for the loop rotation action of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
on
\mathbb{F}((t))
.
The object is naturally
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant
for this action. We may thereby carry out the definition of
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
in
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant
cohomology.
This produces, in place of a
k
-algebra, a
k[u]
-algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{\hbar}
(with
u
in cohomological degree
2
), specializing to
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
when
u=0
.

The rigid structure of
{\check{M}}
provides a natural candidate for this algebra. Namely,
{\check{M}}
is built out of (twisted) cotangent bundles and symplectic vector spaces, which have canonical deformation quantizations. These deformation quantizations are
filtered
, i.e., their Rees algebras form
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant sheaves of algebras over
\mathbb{A}^{1}
, and hence may be sheared to define
k[u]
-algebras, which we propose to identify with the deformed Plancherel algebra:

Conjecture 8.5.1
.

Write, as per the construction (cf. §
4.1.2
),

\check{M}
as a Whittaker induction of the symplectic

\check{G}_{X}
-representation
S_{X}

along a morphism
\check{G}_{X}\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}\rightarrow\check{G}
,
and let
U
be the unipotent radical of the parabolic associated to the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\subset\mathrm{SL}_{2}
.

Then
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{\hbar}
is isomorphic to the sheared Rees algebra of the
quantum Hamitlonian reduction of

A:=\mbox{differential operators on $\check{G}$}\otimes\mbox{Weyl algebra of $S_{X}\oplus\mathfrak{u}/\mathfrak{u}_{+}$}

by the twisted action of
\check{G}_{X}U
; that is to say,
we first quotient by the ideal generated by the natural embedding

\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}\oplus\mathfrak{u}\rightarrow A
,
and then take invariants by
\check{G}_{X}U
.

As usual, a noncommutative deformation gives rise to a Poisson bracket,
i.e., a bilinear mapping satisfying the Leibniz rule, as follows:
If
A
is a
\mathbb{F}
-algebra, and
\tilde{A}
is a flat deformation of
A
over
\mathbb{F}[u]
,
then, for any
a,b\in A=\tilde{A}/u
, the commutator of any lifts
\tilde{a},\tilde{b}

to
\tilde{A}/u^{2}
is of the form

ux
, where the reduction
\bar{x}\in A
is independent of choices.
In particular, we formulate the following expectation, which
is a corollary to the above conjecture, and plays
for us a more important role:

Conjecture 8.5.2
.

(A consequence of Conjecture
8.5.1
.)

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{\hbar}
is flat over
\mathbb{F}[u]
;
the associated Poisson bracket, explained above,
is identified with the reference to (
8.3
) with the
Poisson bracket on
\mathcal{O}({\check{M}})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
induced by the given symplectic structure on
{\check{M}}
.

We will revisit this from the point of view of factorization in §
17
,
see in particular Remark
17.2.4
.

Example 8.5.3
.

(Noncommutative deformation in the Iwasawa–Tate case).
Let us compute in the caes of
G={\mathbb{G}_{m}},X=\mathbb{A}^{1}
,
already discussed in Example
7.3.5
;
we will sketch why the “Weyl algebra”
of Conjecture
8.5.2
appears.

74
74

74

This example presents a glorious number of confusing possibilities
for sign normalization, and
the reader should be sceptical of every single sign that follows.

First of all,

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}^{(triv),\hbar}=H^{*}(B(G_{O}\rtimes{\mathbb{G}_{m}}^{loop}))=k[\hbar,\tau].

where we understand the first coordinate
\tau\in H^{2}(BG)

and the second coordiante
\hbar\in H^{2}(B{\mathbb{G}_{m}}^{loop})
.
Above, and in what follows, we will be able to harmlessly replace
G_{O}\rtimes{\mathbb{G}_{m}}^{loop}

by its commutative subgroup
G\times{\mathbb{G}_{m}}^{loop}

because the inclusion of one into the other is a homotopy equivalence.

More generally, for any character
\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{n}

of the dual group, the associated isotypical component

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}^{(n),\hbar}
is free over this algebra, i.e.,

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}^{(n),\hbar}=k[\hbar,\tau]x_{n},

where
x_{n}
is in degree
n

and (viewed as internal endomorphisms of the basic object)
represents a generator for the degree
n
map
of sheaves

x_{n}:k_{O}\rightarrow k_{t^{n}O}\langle-n\rangle.

Then we have
x_{n}=x_{1}^{n},x_{-n}=x_{-1}^{n}
, and

(8.20)

x_{1}x_{-1}=\tau,x_{-1}x_{1}=\tau-\hbar.

From this we see we can identify the whole algebra with
k[x,y,\hbar]
with
xy-yx=\hbar

and
xy=\tau
;
x_{n}
corresponds to
x^{n}
and
x_{-n}
to
y^{n}
.

The key computation (
8.20
) follows from the following analysis in the finite dimensional model:

(i)

Given an inclusion
Y\rightarrow X

of a divisor into a variety
X
,
we have a restrction map
k_{X}\rightarrow k_{Y}

and also a map
k_{Y}\rightarrow k_{X}[2]

coming from the natural map
\iota_{!}\iota^{!}k_{X}\rightarrow k_{X}
.
The composites
k_{X}\rightarrow k_{X}[2],k_{Y}\rightarrow k_{Y}[2]
,
which represent classes in
H^{2}(X)
and
H^{2}(Y)
respectively,
are given by (respectively) by the fundamental class of
Y

inside
H^{2}(X)
, and its restriction to
Y
.

(ii)

The equivariant fundamental class of
\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}

inside
H^{2}_{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}(\mathbb{A}^{1})\simeq H^{2}(B{\mathbb{G}_{m}})=k[[t]]

is given by
nt
if
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
acts by
t\mapsto t^{n}
on
\mathbb{A}^{1}
.
In particular, the fundamental class of
t^{n+1}O
inside
t^{n}O
,
computed in
G_{O}\times{\mathbb{G}_{m}}^{loop}
-equivariant cohomology,
is given by
\tau+n\hbar
.

Example 8.5.4
.

(Multiplicity freeness):
We can readily compute the
\check{G}
-invariants on
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{\hbar}
:
they arise from the loop-equivariant
cohomology of
X_{O}/G_{O}
.
But the map
X_{O}/G_{O}\rightarrow X/G
induces a cohomology isomorphism
where
X/G
has trivial loop action.
That is to say,

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{\hbar}
is the trivial deformation of
H^{*}(X/G)
,
and (therefore, under Conjecture
8.5.2
)
all

\check{G}
-invariant functions Poisson-commute in
\check{M}
,
i.e.,
\check{M}
is a “multiplicity free” Hamiltonian
G
-space.
75
75

75

This Poisson commutativity can also be seen from the point of view of factorization. Namely for a closed embedding
i:Z\to X
the endomorphisms of the constructible complex
i_{*}k
have a natural commutative (
E_{\infty}
) algebra structure (the ring structure of cochains on
Z
). In our case it follows that the endomorphisms of the basic object form a
commutative
(
E_{\infty}
) algebra compatibly with factorization, i.e., a commutative factorization algebra, whence the induced
P_{3}
structure on cohomology is trivial.

This is precisely in line with our conjecture: it is condition

2
in our definition of hyperspherical (§
3.5
).
In the theory of automorphic forms, the central role
of multiplicity one is well-known on the automorphic side,
and on the spectral side has also been observed experimentally.

9.
The Plancherel algebra and the Plancherel formula for spherical functions

In this section we describe our primary evidence for Conjecture
7.5.1
– via its derivative Conjecture
8.1.8
– by explaining the relation to the numerical version.
Namely, working in the same setting as the previous section,
we will show that the Frobenius trace on Conjecture
8.1.8
recovers the
Plancherel formula
for spherical functions on
X(\mathfrak{f})
, where
\mathfrak{f}
is a nonarchimedean local field;
indeed (somewhat informally)

the Plancherel algebra categorifies the Plancherel measure.

More precisely, the Plancherel algebra is a
\check{G}
-representation, and we will
see that we obtain the Plancherel measure essentially by taking its character (in the sense of distributions,
and weighting by an element of
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
). The Plancherel measure encodes the inner products of all Hecke operators applied to the basic vector, while the Plancherel algebra encodes the Hom spaces between all Hecke functors applied to the basic object.
The Plancherel measure for spherical varieties has been explicitly computed in many cases by the second-named author, partly in collaboration with Jonathan Wang
[
Sak13
,
SW22
]
,
and we will see that this computation matches with the Frobenius trace of the local conjecture.

We will now outline what we prove, although deferring precise
issues of normalization to the later subsections.

In general, the Plancherel formula – for
\mathfrak{f}
a nonarchimedean local field,
\mathfrak{o}
its ring of integers,
and
(G,X)
defined over
\mathfrak{o}
with
G
, for simplicity, split reductive – gives the decomposition of
L^{2}(X(\mathfrak{f}))
as a
G(\mathfrak{f})
-representation, i.e.,

L^{2}(X(\mathfrak{f}))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}\int_{\lambda}\pi_{\lambda}
.
Restricting to
G(\mathfrak{o})
-invariants gives a corresponding direct integral representation over
spherical representations, i.e. representations with a
G(\mathfrak{o})
-fixed vector.
We fix the “basic vector”,

\mathbf{e}=\mbox{characteristic function of $X(\mathfrak{o})$},

and consider its Plancherel density
\mu
. This is a measure on the set of irreducible unitary, unramified representations of
G
(that we identify with a subset of
\check{A}/W
via the Satake isomorphism),
76
76

76

In this section, we take the dual group to be defined over
k=\mathbb{C}
, and use
\check{G},\check{A}
, etc., to denote the corresponding groups of
\mathbb{C}
-points.
characterized by the property – for Hecke operators
T_{V},T_{W}
indexed by representations
V,W\in\mathrm{Rep}(\check{G})
–

(9.1)

\langle T_{V}\mathbf{e},T_{W}\mathbf{e}\rangle_{L^{2}(X(\mathfrak{f}))}=\int_{t\in\check{A}/W}\chi_{V}(t)\overline{\chi_{W}(t)}\mu(t).

where
\chi_{V},\chi_{W}
are the characters of
V
and
W
respectively.

We have already seen the left hand side of (
9.1
) arise geometrically, in (
8.13
) –
at least for
W
trivial, which is all that is needed to characterize
\mu
. Namely, an application of Lemma
2.6.1
identifies it (see Proposition
9.2.1
below) with

(9.2)

[\mathrm{Hom}(T_{V}\star\delta_{X},\delta_{X})^{\vee}]=[\mathrm{Hom}(V,{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X})^{\vee}],

where we have used the “trace of Frobenius” notation as in the proof of Lemma
2.6.1
, the left side denotes homomorphisms in
\mathrm{Shv}(X_{F}/G_{O})
, and the right hand side denotes homomorphisms of
\check{G}
-modules;
here
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
is the Plancherel algebra introduced
in Definition
8.1.4
.

Since
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
corresponds, under Conjecture
8.1.8
, to
\mathcal{O}_{\check{M}}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}

under geometric Satake, a simple computation will extract
\mu

from the local conjecture.

The contents of this section, then, are as follows:

•

§
9.1
sets up notation.

•

§
9.2
we will prove Proposition
9.2.1
, which
computes the Plancherel density for
X(\mathfrak{f})/G(\mathfrak{o})
conditional on Conjecture
8.1.8
.

•

§
9.3
we will review the Plancherel formula for spherical functions on spherical varieties;
in Proposition
9.3.3
it is shown to agree, under conditions on
X
, with the prediction
of Proposition
9.2.1
.

•

§
9.4
goes in a slightly different direction and discusses the
algebraic

(rather than unitary) aspects of the Hecke module structure of functions on
X(\mathfrak{f})/G(\mathfrak{o})
.

9.1.
Setup:
X,S_{X}
and
V_{X}

We will work now in the following setup.

Let
\mathbb{F}_{q}
be the finite field with
q=p^{?}
elements,

\mathbb{Q}_{l}
(

In this section, we take

\check{G}

As in the prior sections, we will work with a dual pair

We already had a discussion of “distinguished split forms” for the dual of a spherical variety in §

77

77

cf. also

We make these assumptions, in order for the “simple” action of the Galois group of

We recall, again, in the notation of §

We recall that

9.2.
Categorical to numerical

In this section we will prove the following.

.

Then, with measures normalized as in §

(9.6)

\mu=\mbox{pushforward of $\mu_{0}$ by $\check{G}_{X}\times{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\operatorname{Id},2\rho_{L(X)}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\check{G}$},

Proof.

\mu
is uniquely characterized by (

),

Assuming Conjecture
8.1.8

,
