is thereby induced as an algebraic
\check{G}
-representation from the
\check{G}_{X}
-representation
\mathcal{O}_{V_{X}}^{\vee}=
the symmetric algebra on
V_{X}
.
Ignoring for a moment the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action (and the shear), we have isomorphisms of vector spaces

\mathrm{Hom}(V,\mathcal{O}_{{\check{M}}})^{\vee}=(V\otimes\mathcal{O}_{{\check{M}}}^{\vee})^{\check{G}}=(V\otimes\mathrm{Sym}V_{X})^{\check{G}_{X}}.

One can easily check that the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}={\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action on the right hand side corresponds to the combination of the action on
V
via the cocharacter
2\rho_{L(X)}
, and the action on
V_{X}
described in §
4.5
(where
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
is denoted by
\mathbb{G}_{gr}^{\prime}
).

A vector in degree
n
for this
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
action (i.e.,
\lambda\cdot v=\lambda^{n}v
) will
correspond to a vector in the sheared space with Frobenius eigenvalue
q^{-n/2}
.
Using the fixed isomorphism
k\simeq\mathbb{C}
, and taking
U_{X}=
a maximal compact subgroup of
\check{G}_{X}
, we can employ the Weyl character formula to compute invariants. This gives

\int\chi_{V}d\mu=\langle T_{V}\mathbf{e},\mathbf{e}\rangle=\int_{U_{X}}\chi_{V}(q^{-\rho_{L(X)}}g)\mathrm{tr}((g,q^{-\frac{1}{2}})|\mathrm{Sym}V_{X})dg

(with
q^{-\frac{1}{2}}
acting on
\mathrm{Sym}V_{X}
via
\mathbb{G}_{gr}^{\prime}
), which is
(
9.5
).

∎

9.3.
Known computations of the Plancherel density

In this section we explain the role of the
\check{G}_{X}
-representation
V_{X}
in
the unramified Plancherel formula for
X
over a nonarchimedean local field.

The density
\mu
was computed in many cases by the second-named author
[
Sak13
]
and extended
in joint work with J. Wang
[
SW22
]
. These papers are not restricted to the smooth case (indeed, the main objective of
[
SW22
]
was to study the “IC functions” of possibly singular spherical varieties), but in the smooth case we can summarize the findings as follows (still, with
G
split):

Suppose that
X
is a spherical affine
G
-variety such that
T^{*}X
is hypespherical. If
X
is homogeneous or
\check{G}_{X}=\check{G}
, and under some combinatorial assumptions that are true in every example that we know (see Proposition
9.3.3
),
the unramified Plancherel measure for
X
is given by (
9.5
); that is to say,
the “Frobenius trace of the local conjecture” is correct.

To see this, we must recall the setup of the quoted papers and translate it a form
where it can be readily compared with (
9.5
). As we shall
recall here, the papers
[
Sak13
,
SW22
]

prove (under assumptions on the spherical variety) that the Plancherel
measure is given as the pushforward, under
\check{A}_{X}^{(1)}\ni\chi\mapsto\chi q^{-\rho_{L(X)}}\in\check{A}\to\check{A}\sslash W
,
of a measure of the form

(9.7)

d\mu(t)=|W_{X}|^{-1}\frac{\det(I-t|{\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{a}}_{X}})}{\det(I-(t,q^{-\frac{1}{2}})|V_{X}^{\prime})}dt,

where
V_{X}^{\prime}
is a graded representation of
\check{A}_{X}
, equivalently, a representation of
\check{A}_{X}\times{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
. The multiset of weights of the representation
V_{X}^{\prime}
is
W_{X}
-invariant and will be described below.
It is not manifest
in the general situation of
[
Sak13
,
SW22
]

that this is the restriction of
\check{G}_{X}
-representation.
Hence, to compare with (
9.5
), we need to recall the conditions under which (
9.7
) is proven, and to compare the graded
\check{A}_{X}
-representations
V_{X}|_{\check{A}_{X}}
and
V_{X}^{\prime}
.

Let us first mention the conditions on
X
– in fact, also on twisted cases
(X,\Psi)
addressed in the aforementioned papers, in which case the assumptions below apply to the Whittaker induction datum:
X
is a spherical affine
G
-variety, or “Whittaker-induced,” in the sense of (
3.34
), from one satisfying the following assumptions:

•

M=T^{*}X
is hyperspherical. This, in particular, implies that
X
is smooth and affine and has no “roots of type
N
” (see Proposition
3.7.4
) – the latest being a necessary assumption for the validity of (
9.7
) in the aforementioned papers.

•

X
is either homogeneous, with the support of every spherical root having the type of a classical group, or
\check{G}_{X}=\check{G}
. Moreover, in the first case, there is a combinatorial condition
[
Sak13
, Statement 7.1.5]
on certain data that will be recalled in §
9.3.5
below; under this condition, (
9.7
) is
[
Sak13
, Theorem 9.0.1]
. In the second case, it is
[
SW22
, (1.11)]
. We expect the condition on the support of spherical roots to be removed, once a few more cases of simple spherical varieties are checked along the lines of
[
Sak13
, § 6]
, and the combinatorial condition
[
Sak13
, Conjecture 7.1.5]
to always be true.

For the remainder of this subsection, we assume the conditions above, and compare the

\check{A}_{X}
-representations
V_{X}|_{\check{A}_{X}}
and
V_{X}^{\prime}
.
The reader who is not familiar with the aforementioned papers is advised to read the statement of Proposition
9.3.3
, and skip its proof.

Remark 9.3.1
.

The conditions of
[
Sak13
, Theorem 9.0.1]
are a little bit more permissive than our current assumptions: they allow for spherical roots of even sphere type, where for the associated subquotient
\mathrm{SO}_{2n}\backslash\mathrm{SO}_{2n+1}
the subgroup
\mathrm{SO}_{2n}
is not split. The results from that paper motivated the painful definition of the “simple” Galois action that we provided for those cases in Definition
4.8.9
. However, we will leave it to the reader to compare with the results of
[
Sak13
]
for those cases.

9.3.2.
The space
V_{X}^{\prime}

For the proposition that follows, and for a given multiset
A
in a set
B
(i.e., function
B\to\mathbb{N}
), where
B
carries an action of a group
W
, we understand “the multiset of
W
-translates of
A
” to be the smallest multiset that is
W
-stable and contains
A
. In other words, its elements are the
W
-translates of elements of
A
, and the multiplicity of each element is the maximum multiplicity of a
W
-translate in
A
. Many natural questions about multiplicities, in the discussion that follows, are easily resolved by applying Lemma
4.4.1
to eliminate multiplicities, and we will not make further comments on those.

Proposition 9.3.3
.

Assume the conditions above for
X
, so that the Plancherel density is given by (
9.7
), for a graded
\check{A}_{X}
-representation
V_{X}^{\prime}
described in
[
Sak13
, Theorem 9.0.1]
or
[
SW22
, (1.11)]
. The space
V_{X}^{\prime}
admits a decomposition
V_{X}^{\prime}=S_{X}^{\prime}\oplus V_{X}^{\prime\prime}
, which compares to the decomposition
V_{X}=S_{X}\oplus[\mathfrak{g}_{X}^{\perp}\cap\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{e}]
of (
4.16
) as follows:

•

When
X
is affine homogeneous (or Whittaker-induced from such), the multiset of weights of the space
S_{X}^{\prime}
is the multiset of
W_{X}
-translates of valuations associated to colors of even sphere type, with grading 1; in particular,
S_{X}^{\prime}\subset S_{X}
. If those weights are minuscule, we have
S_{X}^{\prime}=S_{X}
.

•

When
X
is the affine closure of its open
G
-orbit, and
\check{G}_{X}=\check{G}
,
78
78

78

The first two cases intersect for affine homogeneous spherical varieties, with
\check{G}_{X}=\check{G}
. In those cases, the corrected version of
[
SW22
, Corollary 7.3.4]
implies that the weights of
S_{X}
and the
W_{X}
-translates of colors coincide (without counting multiplicities, except for the highest weights). Thus, our two statements about
S_{X}^{\prime}
agree in those cases.
the multiset of weights of the space
S_{X}^{\prime}
contains, with the same multiplicities and grading 1, the multiset of
W_{X}
-translates of valuations associated to colors of type
T
, and, ignoring multiplicities, coincides with the set of weights of
S_{X}
. Again, if those weights are minuscule, we have
S_{X}^{\prime}=S_{X}
.

•

In the general case (with
\check{G}_{X}=\check{G}
), both
S_{X}
and
S_{X}^{\prime}
are obtained from the corresponding spaces
S_{Y}
,
S_{Y}^{\prime}
associated to the affine closures of their open
G
-orbits by the recipe of Definition
4.4.3
.In particular, if
S_{Y}^{\prime}=S_{Y}
then
S_{X}^{\prime}=S_{X}
.

•

Finally, the graded
\check{A}_{X}
-representation
V_{X}^{\prime\prime}
can be identified with the smallest
W_{X}
-invariant subspace of
\mathfrak{g}_{X}^{\perp}\cap\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{e}
which contains its zero-weight subspace, as well as its intersection with the span of the support of every spherical root. (Here we identify
\check{\mathfrak{g}}
with
\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}
.)

We clarify the meaning of the last condition: Every (simple) spherical root
\gamma
can be written as a sum of simple roots of
G
; those appearing nontrivially in the sum form its
support
. The support of each spherical root defines a standard Levi subgroup of
\check{G}
, and since the dual group
\check{G}_{X}
is defined, as a subgroup of
\check{G}
, uniquely at least up to conjugation by
\check{A}
, its intersection with that Levi is well-defined up to conjugation by
\check{A}
. Choosing an invariant bilinear form to identify
\check{\mathfrak{g}}
with its dual, the image of that Levi subalgebra in
\check{\mathfrak{g}}
does not depend on the choice of form, and its intersection with
\mathfrak{g}_{X}^{\perp}\cap\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{e}
gives rise to a sub-
\check{A}_{X}
-representation of
\mathfrak{g}_{X}^{\perp}\cap\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{e}
. The smallest subspace invariant under the action of the normalizer, in
\check{G}_{X}
, of
\check{A}_{X}
is what is meant by “smallest
W_{X}
-invariant subspace” in the last item.

Remark 9.3.4
.

In all examples of smooth affine spherical varieties that we know, the weights associated to colors are minuscule (hence,
S_{X}^{\prime}=S_{X}
), and
V_{X}^{\prime\prime}=\mathfrak{g}_{X}^{\perp}\cap\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{e}
. Of course, we expect that
V_{X}=V_{X}^{\prime}
, always.

9.3.5.
Recollection of
[
Sak13
]
and proof of Proposition
9.3.3
in the homogeneous case.

We start with the unramified Plancherel formula of
[
Sak13
, Theorem 9.0.1]
, for the cases of homogeneous affine spherical varieties satisfying the conditions recalled in the beginning of §
9.3
.
To write the formula given in
[
Sak13
]
in the form (
9.7
), one needs to take a number of steps, which we detail here.

First of all, one needs to modify the measures; since we are talking about the case when
X=H\backslash G
with
H
reductive (or a Whittaker-induction of such), we will be working with
G
-invariant measures. The normalization (
9.3
) means that the measure on
X
is Tamagawa measure divided by the factor
q^{-\mathrm{dim}G}|G(\mathbb{F}_{q})|
, where by “Tamagawa measure” we mean the measure obtained by a
G
-invariant, residually nonvanishing, integral volume form on
X
(and the probability Haar measure on
\mathfrak{o}
).

Remark 9.3.6
.

For usage later in the proof, we will reformulate this volume when
X
is a point. In that case,
\mathrm{vol}(X(\mathfrak{o}))=\frac{q^{\mathrm{dim}(G)}}{|G(\mathbb{F}_{q})|}
, which is the reciprocal Tamagawa measure of
G(\mathfrak{o}
). The formula of Steinberg
[
Ste68
,
Gro97
]
states that this is equal to
\det(I-\mathrm{Fr}|V_{X})^{-1}
, where
\mathrm{Fr}
is the (geometric) Frobenius element, and
V_{X}
is the Galois representation

V_{X}=\bigoplus_{i}(T_{0}\mathfrak{c})_{i}(i),

where
\mathfrak{c}=\check{\mathfrak{t}}^{*}\sslash W
,
T_{0}
is the tangent space at the image of
0\in\check{\mathfrak{t}}^{*}
, the index
i
denotes its
i
-th graded piece by of the natural
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action descending from the action on
\mathfrak{t}
, and
(d)
denotes the
d
-th cyclotomic twist (multiplying the action of
\mathrm{Fr}
by
q^{-d}
).

In our setting,
\mathfrak{c}
is interpreted as the quotient
\check{M}/\check{G}
, where
\check{M}
is the Whittaker cotangent space for the dual group,
\check{M}=(f+\check{\mathfrak{u}}^{\perp})\times^{\check{N}}\check{G}
. By the Kostant section,
\mathfrak{c}
can also be identified with
\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{e}
, the centralizer of a principal nilpotent
e
, and the double of the above grading is obtained by the action of the element
h
of a corresponding principal
\mathfrak{sl}_{2}
-triple
plus 2
:

(9.8)

\mathrm{vol}(X(\mathfrak{o}))=\frac{q^{\mathrm{dim}(G)}}{|G(\mathbb{F}_{q})|}=\det(1-\mathrm{Fr}|\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{e})^{-1}.

We now return to our main concern.
On the other hand, the formula of
[
Sak13
, Theorem 9.0.1]
is using on
X

(1-q^{-1})^{-\mathrm{dim}A_{X}}
times the Tamagawa measure (see the remark at the end of Section 9 there). In particular, writing
\mathrm{vol}^{\prime}
for the volumes of that paper and
\mathrm{vol}
for our current normalization, and taking
\Phi=\mathbf{e}
, equation (9.2) of
[
Sak13
]
reads:

\mathrm{vol}^{\prime}(X(\mathfrak{o}))=\frac{1}{Q|W_{X}|}\int_{\check{A}_{X}^{1}}\mathrm{vol}^{\prime}(X(\mathfrak{o}))^{2}L_{X}(\chi)d\chi,

hence, in our current normalization,

\|\mathbf{e}\|^{2}=\mathrm{vol}(X(\mathfrak{o}))=\frac{1}{Q|W_{X}|}\int_{\check{A}_{X}^{1}}\mathrm{vol}^{\prime}(X(\mathfrak{o}))\mathrm{vol}(X(\mathfrak{o}))L_{X}(\chi)d\chi=

=q^{\mathrm{dim}G}\frac{(1-q^{-1})^{\mathrm{dim}A_{X}}}{|G(\mathbb{F}_{q})|}\frac{1}{Q|W_{X}|}\int_{\check{A}_{X}^{1}}\mathrm{vol}^{\prime}(X(\mathfrak{o}))^{2}L_{X}(\chi)d\chi,

Thus the Plancherel density of
\mathbf{e}
has the form

q^{\mathrm{dim}G}\frac{(1-q^{-1})^{\mathrm{dim}A_{X}}}{|G(\mathbb{F}_{q})|}\frac{1}{Q|W_{X}|}\mathrm{vol}^{\prime}(X(\mathfrak{o}))^{2}L_{X}(\chi),

(where we omit the implied probability Haar measure
d\chi
on
\check{A}_{X}^{1}
).
Now, we combine the definition of
L_{X}
given in
op. cit
. 7.2.3 with Theorem 9.0.3 which computes
\mathrm{vol}^{\prime}(X(\mathfrak{o}))
. The former has the form

L_{X}(\chi)=c^{2}\frac{\det(1-t|_{\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{a}}_{X}})}{\prod_{\theta\in\Theta}(1-q^{-r_{\theta}}e^{\theta})}

(we will comment on the set
\Theta
below, but we mention that the simplifying assumption that all colors are defined over
F
means that we can ignore the signs
\sigma_{\theta}
of
loc.cit.
), and the latter has the form

\mathrm{vol}^{\prime}(X(\mathfrak{o}))=Qc^{-1}.

This simplifies the Plancherel density of
\mathbf{e}
to

(9.9)

\frac{q^{\mathrm{dim}G}Q\cdot(1-q^{-1})^{\mathrm{dim}A_{X}}}{|G(\mathbb{F}_{q})|}\cdot\frac{\det(1-t|_{\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{a}}_{X}})}{|W_{X}|\prod_{\theta\in\Theta}(1-q^{-r_{\theta}}e^{\theta})}.

The constant
Q
depends on the parabolic
P(X)
, and is equal to

Q=\frac{\mathrm{vol}(G(\mathfrak{o}))}{\mathrm{vol}(P(X)^{-}(\mathfrak{o})P(X)(\mathfrak{o}))},

where
P(X)^{-}
is opposite to
P(X)
(and the volume appearing above explicated
e.g. in the statement of
op. cit.
9.0.3.)
One then computes the first factor (the first fraction) of (
9.9
) is equal to

\frac{(1-q^{-1})^{\mathrm{dim}A_{X}}}{\mathrm{vol}L(X)(\mathfrak{o})}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}\ker(L(X)\to A_{X})(\mathfrak{o})},

where the volumes are taken with respect to Plancherel measure.

Hence, we can write the Plancherel density of
\mathbf{e}
as

\frac{1}{|W_{X}|}\cdot\frac{\det(1-t|_{\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{a}}_{X}})}{\mathrm{vol}\ker(L(X)\to A_{X})(\mathfrak{o})\prod_{\theta\in\Theta}(1-q^{-r_{\theta}}e^{\theta})}.

Note that the kernel of the map
L(X)\to A_{X}
is connected (by condition
4
on hyperspherical varieties, §
3.5.1

and examining the proof of Proposition

3.7.4
) and its dual is the cokernel of the map
\check{A}_{X}\to\check{L}(X)

9.3.6
,
and in particular (

\mathrm{vol}\ker(L(X)\to A_{X})
is the (alternating) trace of
q^{-\frac{1}{2}}\in{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
acting on the exterior algebra of

\check{\mathfrak{l}}(X)^{e}/\check{\mathfrak{a}}_{X},

where

denotes the part of the Levi algebra

annihilated by the element

\mathfrak{sl}_{2}

This part is graded by the action of the element

Hence, we arrive at the following Plancherel density for

(9.10)

\frac{1}{|W_{X}|}\cdot\frac{\det(I-t|_{\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{a}}_{X}})}{\det(I-(q^{-\frac{1}{2}})|\check{\mathfrak{l}}(X)^{e}/\check{\mathfrak{a}}_{X})\cdot\prod_{\theta\in\Theta}(1-q^{-r_{\theta}}e^{\theta})}.

The denominator is what is denoted by

The set

The virtual colors are the smallest multiset

•

satisfies the statement of Proposition
9.3.3
. To prove the statement on
V_{X}^{\prime\prime}
, we check the zero- and nonzero-weight spaces for
\check{A}_{X}
separately. The zero weight space clearly coincides with the zero weight space of
\mathfrak{g}_{X}^{\perp}\cap\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{e}
, since
\check{\mathfrak{l}}(X)
is the centralizer of
\check{\mathfrak{a}}_{X}
in
\check{\mathfrak{g}}
.

For the nonzero-weight spaces, we have unfortunately been unable to identify them with those of
\mathfrak{g}_{X}^{\perp}\cap\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{e}
, but one can check the statement of Proposition
9.3.3
about the support of spherical roots, as follows: Let
\gamma
be a (simple) spherical root, and
P_{\gamma}
the parabolic defined by the support of its spherical roots. One can then consider the variety
X^{\circ}P_{\gamma}
, and its quotient
X_{\gamma}
by the unipotent radical of
P_{\gamma}
, which is a homogeneous spherical variety for the Levi
L_{\gamma}
. Colors of
X
contained in
X^{\circ}P_{\gamma}
are in bijection with colors of
X_{\gamma}
, and one can easily check by hand, for each of the cases of such simple roots (appearing in Section 6 of
[
Sak13
]
) that
V_{X_{\gamma}}=V_{X_{\gamma}}^{\prime}
. In particular,
V_{X_{\gamma}}^{\prime\prime}=\mathfrak{l}_{\gamma}\cap\mathfrak{g}_{X}^{\perp}\cap\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{e}
, and therefore
V_{X}^{\prime\prime}
can be identified with the smallest
W_{X}
-invariant
\check{A}_{X}
-subrepresentation of
\mathfrak{g}_{X}^{\perp}\cap\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{e}
which contains its intersections with
\mathfrak{l}_{\gamma}
, for every simple spherical root
\gamma
.

9.3.9.
Recollection of
[
SW22
]
and proof of Proposition
9.3.3
in the non-homogeneous case.

In the cases considered in
[
SW22
]
, we have
\check{G}=\check{G}_{X}
, and therefore (since this does not include twisted – i.e., Whittaker-induced – cases) every simple root is of “type
T
,” and
\check{M}=S_{X}
. In that case, the formula
[
SW22
, (1.11)]
on the Plancherel density of the basic function is of the form (
9.7
), with
V_{X}^{\prime}=S_{X}^{\prime}
described by a multiset
\mathfrak{B}_{X}
of weights – a crystal – with the following properties (see
[
SW22
, Theorem 7.1.9]
):

(1)

It is obtained from the corresponding crystal of the affine closure of the open
G
-orbit, according to the recipe of Definition
4.4.3
. We are employing, here, Proposition
4.4.9
, to identify the set
\mathcal{D}^{G}_{\text{sat}}(X)
of
op.cit
. with the set
\mathcal{D}^{G}(X)
of
G
-invariant divisors.

(2)

In the case of
X=\overline{X^{\bullet}}^{\operatorname{aff}}
, without counting multiplicities, the weights in
\mathfrak{B}_{X}
coincide with the weights of
S_{X}
; moreover,
W_{X}
-translates of colors appear in
\mathfrak{B}_{X}
with the same multiplicity as the corresponding colors. (This is unambiguous, because Lemma
4.4.1
reduces us to the case where all color multiplicities are
1
.)

The
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-grading of the space
S_{X}^{\prime}
is equal to
1
.

Remark 9.3.10
.

To compromise the recipes for the grading, here and in the previous case, we remark that the formulas (
9.11
) and (
9.12
), in the non-homogeneous case where there is an eigenmeasure with eigencharacter
\eta
, need to be shifted by the character
\eta
of (
3.8
); that is, (
9.11
) should become

(9.13)

2r_{D}=\left<\check{v}_{D},\eta+2\rho-2\rho_{L(X)}\right>,

and (
9.12
) should become

(9.14)

2r_{D^{\prime}}=\left<2\check{\rho},\gamma\right>-\left<\check{v}_{D},\eta+2\rho-2\rho_{L(X)}\right>.

Note that, by (
4.6
),
\eta+2\rho-2\rho_{L(X)}
is a character of
A_{X}
, hence these definitions make sense.
The fact that (
9.13
) gives
2r_{D}=1
when
\check{G}_{X}=\check{G}
follows, as in the homogeneous case, from (
4.10
) and (
4.18
).

9.4.
Questions about the Hecke module structure of spherical functions

The Plancherel formula describes the structure of
L^{2}(X_{\mathfrak{f}})^{G_{\mathfrak{o}}}
. One may also be interested in more algebraic versions of the same question:
in particular, the module structure of the space of functions
X_{\mathfrak{f}}\rightarrow k
(with
k
a coefficient ring)
that are invariant by
G_{\mathfrak{o}}
; this question becomes particularly interesting for
k
of finite characteristic.
We now sketch what our conjecture suggests about this, assuming throughout that
the residue characteristic should be invertible in
k
.

One hopes that a suitable “trace of Frobenius” on the category of sheavees,
recovers the vector space of
G_{\mathfrak{o}}
-invariant functions on
X_{\mathfrak{f}}
. This is studied in the group case in
[
Zhu18
]
;
we do not know it is true for
X_{\mathfrak{f}}/G_{\mathfrak{o}}
. Nonetheless, it is reasonable to believe it is so.

On the spectral side, the trace of an automorphism
F

on a category of coherent sheaves is the space of functions on the fixed locus of
F
;
or, more abstractly, the (derived) intersection of the diagonal and the graph of
F
.
In the case of an automorphism of
\check{M}
commuting with
\check{G}
,
the fixed locus of
F
on
\check{M}/\check{G}
is then
the twisted inertia stack:

\{(g\in\check{G},m\in\check{M}):gm=Fm\}/\check{G}
.
This reasoning suggests, then, that

(9.15)

C^{\infty}_{c}(X_{\mathfrak{f}};k)^{G_{\mathfrak{o}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\left(k\left[g\in\check{G},m\in\check{M}:(g,q^{-1/2})\cdot m=m\right]^{\check{G}}\right)^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

On both sides we take invariants in the
derived
sense – that is to say,
each
G_{\mathfrak{o}}
-orbit
G_{\mathfrak{o}}x\subset X_{\mathfrak{f}}
contributes not a copy of
k
,
but of the cohomology
H^{*}(G_{\mathfrak{o},x},k)
of the stabilizer.
The right hand side should also be interpreted in a derived sense.

If
k=\mathbb{C}
, these derived phenomena are irrelevant, and
we get simply the usual function space of
k
-valued
G_{\mathfrak{o}}
-invariant functions on
X_{\mathfrak{f}}
.
Then (
9.15
) follows from the work
[
Sak13
]
of the second-named author
in the situations to which that work is applicable.
Indeed, we can rewrite the right hand side as

k\left[g\in\check{G}_{X},v\in V_{X}:g\cdot v=q^{1/2}v\right]^{\check{G}_{X}}
.
Now for any
g\in\check{G}_{X}
the space of solutions to
gv=q^{1/2}v

corresponds to the
1/\sqrt{q}
-eigenspace for
g
, and a
g
-invariant function on this space
is clearly constant. Therefore, the ring on the right is simply the ring of class functions of
{{\check{G}}_{X}}
, and one can apply the results of
[
Sak13
]
to deduce
the desired isomorphism of Hecke modules (for
k=\mathbb{C}
)

C^{\infty}_{c}(X_{F}/G_{O})\simeq\mathbb{C}[{{\check{G}}_{X}}]^{{{\check{G}}_{X}}}

In particular, for
k=\mathbb{C}
, the module structure is insensitive to
V_{X}
, but this is presumably false for general
k
.
This is an interesting
point to study further.

To summarize parts of our previous discussion:
while, as we just noted,
V_{X}
is not reflected in the “mere” module structure of
C^{\infty}_{c}(X_{F}/G_{O})
,
it becomes visible if we consider also the basic function and inner product.
Indeed, our discussion implies
that, when
Proposition
9.2.1
applies,
there is an identification of Hecke modules equipped with distinguished vector and inner product:

(C^{\infty}_{c}(X_{\mathfrak{f}}/G_{\mathfrak{o}})\ni\mathbf{e},\langle-,-\rangle)\simeq(\mathbb{C}[{{\check{G}}_{X}}]^{{{\check{G}}_{X}}}\ni 1,\langle-,-\rangle_{L^{2}(\mu)})

where
\mu
is the Haar measure on a translate of the compact form of
{{\check{G}}_{X}}
, multiplied by a
q
-deformation of the character of the representation
V_{X}
.

Part III
Global theory

In this Part we study the global story – that is, starting from a
dual pair
(G,M)
and
(\check{G},\check{M})

of hyperspherical varieties, we examine
the matching of associated automorphic and spectral quantizations
in the setting of global Langlands – more specifically, for
a curve over either a finite field or the complex numbers.

We refer to page
1.4
for a summary of the contents of the various subsections.
To briefly reprise: we begin in §
10
by examining automorphic
quantization in global geometric Langlands,
giving “period sheaves” and “period functions.”
The spectral side of the story will be entirely parallel,
giving what we call the
L
-sheaf; it will
be treated in §
11
;
and in §
12
we will put the two together and formulate the geometric form of the conjecture, which asserts
that period and
L
-sheaves match under geometric Langlands.
After carrying out some sanity checks for the case of
\mathbb{P}^{1}

in §
13
, we then turn in §
14

to the arithmetic manifestation of the same phenomena – that is, the corresponding
statements concerning equalities of numerical periods with
L
-values.

10.
Period functions and period sheaves

According to the general picture explained in §
1.3
,
periods should give

objects
in the categories on the two sides (automorphic
and spectral) of the global geometric Langlands conjecture,
just as they give
vectors
in the vector space of automorphic functions
in global Langlands and
objects
of the category of local representations
in local Langlands.

In the current section we shall describe the global automorphic objects and the global automorphic vectors arising from a
polarized hyperspherical
G
-variety
M
- we will be more specific about the setting in a moment. These will be called “period sheaves” and “period functions.”
For example, when
M=T^{*}X
(that is to say, there is no twist in the polarization), we get a morphism

\pi:X/G\longrightarrow BG,

By taking maps from an algebraic curve
\Sigma
, and then pushing forward
the constant sheaf along the maps induced by
\pi
, we obtain
the “period sheaf” on the space of
G
-bundles.
Frobenius trace extracts the usual period function.

The contents of the present section are as follows:

•

§
10.1
sets up the considerable amount of notation needed.

•

§
10.2
introduces the space of bundles with an
X
-section, together
with the necessary twists needed for our conjecture.

•

§
10.3
defines the basic period sheaf and period function.

•

§
10.4
introduces a crucial “unitary” (analytic) normalization
of the period sheaf. The normalization process is a half-twisting that depends on the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action.

•

§
10.5
describes the modifications needed when
M
admits a twisted polarization (§
3.7
).

•

§
10.6
gives a number of examples, emphasizing
the roles of the various twists.

•

§
10.7
discusses how the statements
can be reformulated to be manifestly independent of spin structure.

•

§
10.8
explains the compatibility of period sheaves with Whittaker induction of Hamiltonian spaces, reducing their study to the vectorial case.

•

§
10.9

explains why the construction is independent of the choice of polarization –
an incarnation of the Fourier transform. (Therefore,
the period sheaf can indeed be viewed as attached to
M
, rather than
X
; we have however preferred
to denote it as
\mathcal{P}_{X}
rather than
\mathcal{P}_{M}
).

10.1.
Notation:
\Sigma
,
G
and
M

10.1.1.
Coefficient fields

We work over an algebraically closed base field
\mathbb{F}
, which is either
the algebraic closure of
\mathbb{F}_{q}
, or
\mathbb{C}
. We fix a smooth projective curve

\Sigma
over
\mathbb{F}
. For any statement that entails a Frobenius morphism (e.g., any mention of Weil structures on sheaves), or adeles, it is understood that
\Sigma
is defined over
\mathbb{F}_{q}
; in those cases “adeles” and “function field” of the curve will always mean over
\mathbb{F}_{q}
.

We also have a ring of coefficients
k
,
which we take to be
\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}}
or
\mathbb{C}
according
to whether
\mathbb{F}
is of finite characteristic or complex.
In the finite case, we fix a square root
\sqrt{q}\in k

of the cardinality of
\mathbb{F}_{q}
. As in the local case, we will present “normalized” or “analytic” versions of our conjectures, which make use of this choice, and arithmetic versions, which do not.

10.1.2.
Spin structure on the automorphic side

It will be convenient to choose a spin structure on
\Sigma
, i.e., a square root
\mathcal{K}^{1/2}
of its canonical bundle (though we will keep track of the dependence of our constructions on the choice and indicate how to formulate statements independent of it, see in particular §
10.7
.). For convenience, we will fix a rational section of this square root as well.
Squaring this gives rise to
a meromorphic differential form
\omega

whose zero divisor (the “different”)

(10.1)

\mathfrak{d}:=\sum n_{v}v,\ \ \sum n_{v}=(2g-2).

has all even multiplicities; we put
\mathfrak{d}^{1/2}=\sum\frac{n_{v}}{2}v
and
write
\mathcal{K}^{1/2}=\mathcal{O}(\mathfrak{d}^{1/2})
for the associated line bundle.
We also write
\partial
for an idèle associated to
\mathfrak{d}

so that
\partial=(\partial_{v})_{v}
with
\partial_{v}=\pi_{v}^{n_{v}}

and
\pi_{v}
a local uniformizer.

Let
F
be the function field of
\Sigma
,

\mathbb{A}_{F}
its ring of adeles, and
\widehat{\mathfrak{o}}\subset\mathbb{A}_{F}

its integral subring.
In the finite field setting,
\omega
gives rise to a homomorphism

(10.2)

\psi:\mathbb{A}_{F}/F\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{q},

whose restriction to the copy of
F_{v}
inside
\mathbb{A}_{F}

comes from the pairing
(f,\omega)\mapsto\mathrm{Res}_{v}(f\omega)
.
Fixing once
and for all an additive character
\psi
of
\mathbb{F}_{q}

valued in
k^{\times}
,
we get a character of
\mathbb{A}_{F}/F
, also to be denoted by
\psi
.
Notice that
varying the choice of rational section
while fixing the spin structure
\mathcal{K}^{1/2}
varies
\psi

by a
square
in
F^{\times}
.
From our definitions, the character
x\mapsto\psi(x)
of
\mathbb{A}_{F}

has the property that on each completion
F_{v}
it is trivial on
\partial_{v}^{-1}\mathfrak{o}_{v}

but not on
\varpi_{v}^{-1}\partial_{v}^{-1}\mathfrak{o}_{v}
;
thus
x_{v}\mapsto\psi(\partial_{v}^{-1}x_{v})
is an unramified character of
F_{v}
.

10.1.3.
G,M
, and polarizations

(G,M=T^{*}(X,\Psi))
will be a distinguished split
form over
\mathbb{F}
, in the sense of
Definition
3.9.9
81
81

81

The word “split” is relevant
here only in the context where
\mathbb{F}
has finite characteristic, and there because we did not
define a notion of hyperspherical in finite characteristic. For the purposes
of this chapter, the reader can ignore the word “split” entirely, and instead take the data of
(X,\Psi)_{/\mathbb{F}}

as a starting point, as in Remark
10.1.4
.
, of a hyperspherical variety admitting a distinguished polarization; where we recall
G
is to act on the right.
See §
10.9
for discussion of independence
of polarization as well as removing the assumption that
M
is polarized.

We will frequently allow ourselves to assume that
X
admits an eigenmeasure, see
§
3.8
.
This assumption is “harmless” for global applications, for reasons outlined in §
3.8.2
,
and
it should also be possible to formulate the discussion to avoid it entirely, see
preliminary discussion along these lines in Remark
12.6.5
. However,
we find it extremely helpful in thinking about how to normalize to maintain this assumption.

We will make use of
the quantity

(10.3)

\beta_{X}=(g-1)(\mathrm{dim}G+\gamma_{X}-\mathrm{dim}X).

where
\gamma_{X}
is, as in (
3.35
), the character through which
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
scales the eigenmeasure. This will appear as
a normalizing shift in our period sheaf;
a corresponding shift will also intervene on the spectral side.

Remark 10.1.4
.

Note that, while we make the hyperspherical assumption for global coherence of the paper,
all the considerations of this chapter can be applied to an arbitrary

G\times\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-space
X

with an eigenmeasure, or for that matter
the same situation allowing a
\mathbb{A}^{1}
-torsor
\Psi\rightarrow X
,
and there are certainly
examples where duality theory seems to work well that land outside our hyperspherical framework. A particularly important
example is the “Eisenstein case”
X=U\backslash G
considered as a
T\times G
space, which we will
at times consider by way of contrast.

10.1.5.
Context for the Langlands program and sheaf theory

We briefly recall the main outline of the geometric Langlands program and the underlying sheaf theory, see Appendices
B
and
C
for a more thorough overview.

Attached to
\Sigma
there are two basic spaces of interest for the geometric Langlands story:

•

The space
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
of coherent
G
-bundles
on
\Sigma
.

•

The space
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
of
\check{G}
-bundles on
\Sigma
.

We have used the word “space” loosely; more precisely,
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
is an algebraic stack over
\mathbb{F}

and
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
is a derived algebraic stack over
k
.
The dimensions of these spaces will often come up, and we abridge them
in the following way:

(10.4)

b_{G}=\mathrm{dim}\mathrm{Bun}_{G}=(g-1)\mathrm{dim}G,\;b_{H}=\mathrm{dim}\mathrm{Bun}_{H}=(g-1)\mathrm{dim}H,\dots

and so on, where
g
is the genus of the curve
\Sigma
;
the dimensions of the corresponding
\mathrm{Loc}
spaces are obtained by doubling these.

The geometric Langlands correspondence posits an equivalence
between a category of “constructible”-type sheaves on the former space,
and a category of “coherent” sheaves on the latter.
This general vision has
been formulated in at least three different contexts,
with varying specifics.

\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
is the space of algebraic
G
-bundles in all cases, but the
category of sheaves on it varies, and the definition of
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
also varies.
We give a résumé of these constructions in Appendix
C
;
for now we summarize sheaf theory on the automorphic side.

In all cases, we will write simply

(10.5)

\mathrm{Shv}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G})\supset\mathrm{Aut}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}),\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G})\supset\mathrm{AUT}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}),

for the “small” and “big” categories
\mathrm{Shv}
or
\mathrm{SHV}
of sheaves on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
, and, inside it, the “spectrally decomposable” subcategories
\mathrm{Aut}
or
\mathrm{AUT}
i.e.
the largest category on which it is reasonable to think about Hecke actions.
We describe
\mathrm{Shv}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G})
more explicitly in each case, but refer again to Appendix
C
for details.

•

Finite context:
\mathbb{F}=\overline{\mathbb{F}_{q}}
and
k=\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}}
.

\mathrm{Shv}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G})
consists of étale constructible sheaves on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
with coefficients in
k
.
This has a Frobenius action (when
\Sigma
is defined over
\mathbb{F}_{q}
); Frobenius-equivariant objects are
then Weil sheaves, and here we can talk about “Tate twists.”

•

Betti context:
\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{C}
, and
k=
an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.
82
82

82

Betti sheaves, actually, make sense over any coefficient ring

\mathrm{Shv}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G})
consists of (certain) sheaves on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
with coefficients in
k
and Lagrangian singular support. In many ways this is technically the simplest setup.

•

De Rham context:
\mathbb{F}=k=\mathbb{C}
. Objects of
\mathrm{Shv}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G})

are coherent
D
-modules on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
.

Remark 10.1.6
.

Still another context,
closely related to the “finite” setting, is to take
\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{C}
but to use constructible sheaves for the classical, instead of the étale, topology (and arbitrary coefficients), which also affects the definition of
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
on the spectral side. We will, somewhat abusively, use the “étale setting” to describe
either this setting or the finite setting, since many of the same conclusions will apply in both cases.

An important technical point is that we will work in all cases with the ind-finite or renormalized category of sheaves;
see §
B.6

and Appendix
C
for discussion;
while this is important in trying to get various categories to line up, the
reader unfamiliar with this notion will not lose a lot by ignoring these words
at a first reading (and this choice can be adjusted at the cost of adding “nilpotent singular support” requirements to the sheaf theory on the spectral side).

The constructions presented will have slightly different interpretations according to context.
We will explain most constructions in the Betti context, where they are particularly simple to describe.
When the translations to other contexts are not straightforward we will add a description of them.

In each context we will use the twist notation
\mathcal{F}\langle d\rangle

following §
2.5
,
and in particular (
2.6
). Recall
that this means three simultaneous twists (which may or may not apply, according to context):
a cohomological twist
[d]
, a Tate twist
(d/2)
,
using the fixed choice
\sqrt{q}
inside our field of coefficients
k
,
and a parity twist.

10.2.
The space
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
of bundles with an
X
-section

We discuss first the case of untwisted cotangent bundles,
M=T^{*}X
, with the twisted case to be discussed in §
10.5
. The space of primary interest
for defining the period sheaf is informally

\textrm{$\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}$}:=\mbox{``$G$-bundles with a section of the associated $X\otimes\mathcal{K}^{1/2}$-bundle.''}

For example, when
G=\mathrm{GL}_{n}
and
X
its standard representation with scaling
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
action, the fiber of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
over a vector bundle
V
is the space of sections of
V\otimes\mathcal{K}^{1/2}
; when

X=H\backslash G
with trivial
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
action
then
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
is identified with
\mathrm{Bun}_{H}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
.

Formally,

\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
– or
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}
when the group
G
is clear – is the algebraic stack defined as the pullback of mapping stacks

(10.6)

53.96324pt\raise-32.12279pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathrm{Bun}_{G\times\mathbb{G}_{gr}}}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces.

This is in fact an Artin stack, cf.
[
Ols06
, Theorem 1.1]
or see (a) below for a sketch.
Note that, for the considerations that follow, it does not matter whether we consider
these as classical or derived stacks.
The reason is as follows: Although one can meaningfully enrich
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}
to a derived stack, this will have no effect on
constructible sheaves – in particular the period sheaf – which are sensitive only to topology.

Remark 10.2.1
.

(a)

\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
and the geometry of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
is quite tame, as we now explain:

\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
is a union of open substacks, each of which
is a global quotient of a scheme; we exhibit the global quotient structure by “adding level structure,” i.e.
fixing a point on the curve and trivializing the bundle up to some order at that point, and then descending; the group involved
is thus a pro-unipotent extension of
G
. Upon pullback to each such open substack, the morphism
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}

is a global quotient of a morphism of schemes, as we can see by choosing a
G
-equivariant embedding of
X
into a vector space
and thus reducing to the case when
G=\mathrm{GL}_{n},X=\mathbb{A}^{n}
.

(b)

For
X
homogeneous,
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
is smooth (although its morphism to
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
need not be smooth). This is true more generally
for
X
smooth on the locus of maps
which generically land in the open
G
-orbit on
X
. For an example of nonsmoothness see §
10.6.2
.

10.3.
The period sheaf and the period function.

The compactly supported (i.e.,
!
-) pushforward of the constant sheaf along
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}

will be called the
unnormalized period sheaf

\mathcal{P}_{X}
.

\mathcal{P}_{X}=\mbox{compactly supported pushforward of constants along $\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}$.}

We emphasize that this is a
!
pushforward; a
dual
*
pushforward
will appear on some rare and interesting occasions e.g. Remark
10.3.1
and §
14.8
; and in that case we will use
*
explicitly in the notation.

In the finite context
\mathcal{P}_{X}
is considered as a Weil sheaf, i.e.,
with a Frobenius equivariant structure. We take the trivial Frobenius action on the constant sheaf here, to be “corrected” later, when we introduce the normalized period sheaf.

Let us compute the function associated to this Weil sheaf.

Recall that we can uniformize
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
as the quotient
G(F)\backslash G(\mathbb{A})/G(\widehat{\mathfrak{o}})
; the sections of the bundle parameterized
by
g\in G(\mathbb{A})
are identified with the elements of
x\in G(F)
with the property that
xg\in G(\widehat{\mathfrak{o}})
. Thus, for example in the case
G={\mathbb{G}_{m}}
,
the element of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}(\mathbb{A})
that is given by the uniformizer
\varpi_{x}
at a single
point
x
of the curve
\Sigma
parameterizes the line bundle
\mathcal{O}(x)
(we spell this out to avoid possible sign confusion).
With reference to these adelic uniformizations the chosen spin structure of §
10.1
can be identified with the class of
\partial^{1/2}=\prod_{v}\varpi_{v}^{n_{v}/2}
in
F^{\times}\backslash\mathbb{A}_{F}^{\times}/\prod_{v}\mathfrak{o}_{v}^{\times}=\mathrm{Bun}_{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
,
and the set of
\mathbb{F}_{q}
-points in the fiber of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
over
the
G
-bundle represented by
g\in G(\mathbb{A}_{F})

is identified with

(10.7)

X(F)\cap\prod_{v}X(\mathfrak{o}_{v})\cdot(g^{-1},\partial^{-1/2}).

The Frobenius trace on the period sheaf recovers the
period function
(or theta series)
associated to
X
, to be denoted by regular font,

P_{X}:\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\rightarrow k,

which sends
a
G
-bundle to the number of sections of the associated
X\otimes\mathcal{K}^{1/2}
-bundle, equivalently:

(10.8)

P_{X}(x):g\in G(\mathbb{A})\mapsto\sum_{x\in X(F)}(g,\partial^{1/2})\cdot\Phi(x).

Here,
\Phi

is the characteristic function of
X(\widehat{\mathfrak{o}})

inside the adelic points of
X
, and the action of
G\times\mathbb{G}_{gr}

on such functions
is understood as
(g,\lambda)\Phi(x)=\Phi(x(g,\lambda))
(i.e., it is an
unnormalized
action, as opposed the normalized action that we will introduce in (
10.11
) below).

As is often the case (see §
2.7
),
it will be convenient to also have a version of
P_{X}

that incorporates half-twists, because it will relate
more clearly to unitary structures in the theory of automorphic forms.
We turn to this next, in §
10.4
.

Remark 10.3.1
.

(The star period)
There is a second variant of the period sheaf, which is of great interest, although
it will not play such a role in this paper. This is the
*
-variant
\mathcal{P}_{X}^{*}
–
understood as the *-push-forward of the dualizing sheaf from
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
. Equivalently, this is the “naive Verdier dual” of
\mathcal{P}_{X}
; that is to say,
a sheaf on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
being a compatible system of sheaves on a system
of open truncations, we apply usual Verdier duality at each level; note however
that
[
DG15
]
(cf. §
B.8
, §
C.5
) this naive Verdier duality is not an equivalence of categories.
The classical meaning of this sheaf is not so easy to understand,
and its existence is an interesting puzzle in the classical theory. See §
14.8
.

Remark 10.3.2
.

Let us discuss technical issues in the de Rham context. As we have seen (§
10.2.1
),
the map
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
has a very simple nature.
In particular, there is no difficulty in defining either
!
or
*
pushforward of the constant sheaf
along these maps in any of our sheaf-theoretic contexts.

Indeed (by definition, cf. §
B.6
) a sheaf on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
is a compatible system of sheaves
on open quasicompact substacks of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
; and in turn, on each open quasicompact substack,
sheaves are defined as the ind-completion of
the category obtained by taking the limit of small sheaf categories over
maps of an affine
Y
into that open quasicompact substack.
When pulled back to such
Y
, the map
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}

becomes a morphism of schemes.

Therefore,
\mathcal{P}_{X}
and
\mathcal{P}_{X}^{*}
are, locally on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
, even compact objects
of the automorphic category, i.e., objects of the small category of sheaves, though they are not compact themselves since they don’t have quasicompact support.
By means of the functor (
B.3
) from the ind-finite to the usual category, they can also
be considered elements of the latter.

10.4.
Normalized periods and normalized period sheaves

\mathcal{P}_{X}
has an important variant.
This is the
normalized period sheaf
, which corresponds
to formula (
10.8
) using the
unitarily normalized
action of
G
.
To define a normalized period sheaf we
assume the existence of an eigen-volume form as in (
3.8
)
with eigencharacter
\eta:G\rightarrow{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
.

The normalized version of (
10.8
)
is

(10.9)

P_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}:g\in G(\mathbb{A})\mapsto q^{-\beta_{X}/2}\sum_{x\in X(F)}g\star(\partial^{1/2}\cdot\Phi(x)),

(10.10)

=q^{\frac{g-1}{2}(\mathrm{dim}X-\mathrm{dim}G)}\sum_{x\in X(F)}(g,\partial^{1/2})\star\Phi(x).

where
\star
denotes normalized actions, defined thus:

(10.11)

g\star\Psi=|\eta(g)|^{1/2}(g\cdot\Psi),(g,\lambda)\star\Psi=|\eta(g)|^{1/2}|\lambda|^{\gamma_{X}/2}(g,\lambda)\cdot\Psi

are the unitary

\beta_{X}
is as in (
10.3
),
and
\gamma_{X}
is as in (
3.35
). That is to say, (
10.9
) uses only unitary normalization of
G
, whereas (
10.10
)
uses unitary normalization of both
G
and
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
; to deduce (
10.10
) from (
10.9
) we use

|\mathfrak{d}^{1/2}|=q^{1-g}
and the definition (
10.3
)
of
\beta_{X}
.

To make the sheaf version
note that
\eta:G\rightarrow{\mathbb{G}_{m}}

induces
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}

and in particular a degree function
\deg:\mathrm{Bun}_{G}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}
.
We put

(10.12)

\mathcal{P}_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}:=\mathcal{P}_{X}\langle\deg+\beta_{X}\rangle.

Note that
\mathcal{P}_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}
is not, in general, a global twist of
\mathcal{P}_{X}

because of the non-constant function
\deg
. The star period sheaf of Remark
10.3.1
also has a normalized variant, obtained by taking naive Verdier duality, or equivalently
\mathcal{P}_{X}^{*\mathrm{norm}}=\mathcal{P}_{X}^{*}\langle-\deg-\beta_{X}\rangle
.

Let us try to describe the origin of the two twists in (
10.12
), by degree and by
\beta_{X}
.
83
83

83

A better, but notationally cumbersome, way to separate the twists is to split off the term
(g-1)\gamma_{X}
from
\beta_{X}
; this term plays exactly the same role for
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
as the degree plays for
G
– remember from (
10.6
) that
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
is defined as a fiber over
\mathcal{K}^{\frac{1}{2}}\in\mathrm{Bun}_{\mathbb{G}_{gr}}
. In the discussion that follows, references to
\beta_{X}
really are meant for the remaining terms
(g-1)(\mathrm{dim}G-\mathrm{dim}X)
.

-

The twist by
\langle\beta_{X}\rangle
appears already in the homogeneous case
X=H\backslash G
, in which case
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}=\mathrm{Bun}_{H}
, and splits the difference between the constant and the dualizing sheaf of
\mathrm{Bun}_{H}
; in this case,
the period sheaf can be thought of as the push-forward of the intersection complex of
\mathrm{Bun}_{H}
, but we emphasize that our definition does
not
agree with the intersection complex of
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}
in general.
The numerical explanation of the
\beta_{X}
twist is that the factor
q^{-\beta_{X}/2}
is an attempt to render
P_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}
approximately
L^{2}
-normalized

(10.13)

\|P_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}\|_{L^{2}}\approx 1.

-

On the other hand, the degree twist
\langle\deg\rangle
has to do with the linear fiber
S^{+}
, and is a standard twist in the geometrization of the Weil representation
[
Lys06
]
. If
S^{+}
is nontrivial, this twist cannot be interpreted through the intersection complex of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
(which is, in general, singular), but can be thought of as the sheaf-theoretic analog of half-densities in the
Schrödinger model of the Weil representation.

Remark 10.4.1

(The degree sheaf)
.

It will be convenient to represent the degree shift
\mathcal{F}\mapsto\mathcal{F}\langle\deg\rangle
as tensor product with a sheaf. Namely, this is achieved
(in any of our contexts) by the (
\eta
-pullback of the) locally constant sheaf

\underline{\deg}\in\mathrm{Shv}(\mathrm{Bun}_{\mathbb{G}_{m}}),

which is given by
k\langle d\rangle
on
\mathrm{Pic}^{d}
;
in the language of §
6
,
\underline{\deg}
is the shear of the constant sheaf by the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action on
\mathrm{Shv}(\mathrm{Bun}_{\mathbb{G}_{m}})
corresponding to the
\mathbb{Z}
-grading by degree.
Under the sheaf-function correspondence (see §
2.5
)
this corresponds to the function
\mathcal{L}\mapsto q^{-\mathrm{deg}\mathcal{L}/2}
.
If we uniformize line bundles adèlically
via (
11.5
) this matches with
x\in\mathbb{A}^{\times}\mapsto|x|^{1/2}_{\mathbb{A}}
. In other words,
\underline{\deg}
is an automorphic avatar of the square root of the cyclotomic character
\varpi^{1/2}
under class field theory.

Remark 10.4.2
.

It is worth noting that there are three shifting processes appearing implicitly in the above discussion.

(a)

the shift by
\mathcal{K}^{1/2}
embedded in the definition of
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}
, which reflects the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
action;

(b)

the twist by
\langle\deg\rangle
in (
10.12
); this reflects the failure of
X
to be unimodular;

(c)

the twist by
\langle\beta_{X}\rangle
.

Roughly speaking, the first twist is related to a translation on the automorphic side,
whereas the second twist is related to a translation on the spectral side – see Remark
11.5.2
.
As such, these twists do not commute with one another: as is usual in Fourier analysis,
spectral and automorphic translations do not commute.
In physics automorphic and spectral translations correspond to shifts of magnetic and electric flux, respectively, and the lack of commutativity is an aspect of the “uncertainty of fluxes” studied in
[
FMS07b
,
FMS07a
]
; see also Remark
C.3.8
.

10.4.3.
Changing the grading

The following remarks are not essential to understanding the main conjecture but
will be used later in analysis of parity issues.
Given a central cocharacter
\lambda:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to Z(G)
we denote by
X[\lambda]
the
G\times\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-space
X
with
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action twisted by
\lambda
.
The effect of passing from
X
to
X[\lambda]
is to translate the unnormalized period function/sheaf by the translation action of the
Z(G)
-torsor
\lambda(\mathcal{K}^{1/2})
(or numerically by the central element
\lambda(\mathfrak{d}^{1/2})
of
G
):

\mathcal{P}_{X[\lambda]}=\lambda(\mathcal{K}^{1/2})\ast\mathcal{P}_{X}.

Here,
to normalize signs, “translation by
\lambda(\mathcal{K}^{1/2})
” means that the delta function at a point would be sent to the delta function at its translate by
\lambda(\mathcal{K}^{-1/2})
. We will prove that the normalized period sheaf is transformed similarly:

Lemma 10.4.4
.

The operation
X\mapsto X[\lambda]
affects the normalized period sheaf as follows:

\mathcal{P}_{X[\lambda]}^{\mathrm{norm}}\simeq\lambda(\mathcal{K}^{1/2})\ast\mathcal{P}_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}.

Proof.

Observe first of all that, see (
10.3
),

(10.14)

\beta_{X[\lambda]}=\beta_{X}+(g-1)\langle\lambda,\eta\rangle.

If we translate the sheaf
\langle\deg\rangle
on
\mathrm{Bun}_{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}
by
\mathcal{K}^{1/2}

we get
\langle\deg+(g-1)\rangle
. Correspondingly, since we understand
\langle\deg\rangle
on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}

as the pullback of the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
sheaf via
\eta:G\rightarrow{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
,

(10.15)

\mathrm{T}(\mathcal{F}\langle\deg\rangle)=(\mathrm{T}\mathcal{F})\langle\deg+(g-1)\langle\eta,\lambda\rangle\rangle.

where
\mathrm{T}
refers to a translation by
\lambda(\mathcal{K}^{1/2})
. Thus, from the definition (
10.12
),

\mathcal{P}_{X[\lambda]}^{\mathrm{norm}}=(\mathrm{T}\mathcal{P}_{X})\langle\deg+\beta_{X[\lambda]}\rangle,\mathrm{T}\mathcal{P}_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}=\mathrm{T}\mathcal{P}_{X}\langle\deg+\beta_{X}+(g-1)\langle\eta,\lambda\rangle\rangle.

and comparing with (
10.14
) we deduce the lemma.
∎

10.5.
Modification for the twisted case

We are now going to explain how to define the period sheaf
and its variants in the case of twisted polarizations
(X,\Psi)
(see §
3.2.1
).
At a high level, the modification is simply

twist by a rank one “Artin–Schreier” local system on
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}
.

Here, the Artin–Schreier sheaf is pulled back from a sheaf on
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}

in the finite and de Rham context, and a slight modification in the Betti context.
We start by defining it on
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
, and then explain how it is to be pulled back to
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}
.

Definition 10.5.1
.

We understand the “Artin–Schreier sheaf” on thus:

(a)

In the finite context, it is the étale sheaf of rank one
k
-modules on
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
whose trace function is the fixed additive character
\mathbb{F}_{q}\to k^{\times}
, obtained, in the usual way, from the covering
x^{q}-x
, see e.g.
[
Del77
, Sommes. trig.]
.

(b)

In the de Rham context, it is the exponential
D
-module on
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
, i.e.,
the sheaf associated to the differential equation
f^{\prime}=2\pi if
.

(c)

In the Betti context we understand the “Artin–Schreier sheaf”
to be a locally constant sheaf in the analytic topology on
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
, where
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}

acts by squaring on
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
, defined as

\left(j_{!}k^{-}\oplus j_{*}k\right)[-1]

where

j:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
,
and
k,k^{-}
are respectively the trivial
and nontrivial one-dimensional local systems on
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\simeq B\mu_{2}
.

The point in (c) is that although we cannot
make sense of a Artin–Schreier sheaf on
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
itself, its pushforward to
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}

makes sense (cf.
[
NY19a
, Section 2.5.2]
),
and this will be sufficient for our purposes. To compare with
[
NY19a
]
, note that in our case
the action of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
on
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
is the squaring action; computing
the pushforward of the sheaf used in op.cit. leads to the formula above.

Now, in our current situation,
M=T^{*}(X,\Psi)
with
\Psi
a
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
-bundle over
X
,
and the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
action scales
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
via squaring.
Recall from §
10.2
that we define
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
as the fiber of
\mathrm{Map}(\Sigma,\frac{X}{G\times{\mathbb{G}_{m}}})
over
\mathcal{K}^{\frac{1}{2}}
.
An affine bundle
\Psi\rightarrow X
as in §
3.7
defines a map

X\rightarrow B{\mathbb{G}_{a}}

equivariant for the action of
G\times\mathbb{G}_{gr}
where the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action scales
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}

by the square character, and
G
acts trivially. In particular, we have a map

\mathrm{Map}(\Sigma,\frac{X}{G\times{\mathbb{G}_{m}}})\to\mathrm{Map}(\Sigma,\frac{\mbox{pt}}{{\mathbb{G}_{a}}\rtimes{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}),

wherein the action of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
on
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
is by squaring.

Correspondingly,

\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}
maps to the stack of
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}\rtimes{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
torsors reducing to
\mathcal{K}^{1/2}
;
said differently,
this is the stack of torsors for
\mathcal{K}=(\mathcal{K}^{1/2})^{\otimes 2}
considered as a vector bundle;
this stack is identified with
the quotient of
H^{1}(\Sigma,\Omega^{1})\simeq\mathbb{G}_{a}
by the trivial action of
H^{0}(\Sigma,\Omega^{1})
, and in particular maps to the affine line
\mathbb{G}_{a}
. This gives us a (non-schematic)
morphism:

(10.16)

\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}\longrightarrow\mathbb{G}_{a}

which measures the obstruction of lifting the
X
-section to a
\Psi
-section.
This already suffices to define the Artin–Schreier sheaf on
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}
in the de Rham and finite contexts as the pullback of the corresponding sheaf on
\mathbb{G}_{a}
,
84
84

84

Or, to only use a schematic morphism, one first notes that the Artin–Schreier sheaf on
\mathbb{G}_{a}

descends to its quotient by the trivial action of
H^{0}(\Sigma,\Omega^{1})
, and then pulls back to
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}
.

and we define
\mathcal{P}_{X}
as the compactly supported pushforward of this sheaf:

\mathcal{P}_{X}=\mbox{$!$-pushforward of the Artin--Schreier sheaf along $\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}$.}

We also define the
*
-period sheaf
\mathcal{P}_{X}^{*}
as the ordinary pushforward of the Verdier dual of the Artin–Schreier sheaf.

In the Betti context we note that we get also

\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\rightarrow\mathbb{G}_{a}/\mathbb{G}_{m}

where the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
action on the left arises from that on
X
; and on the right it is squaring.
We can correspondingly define the Artin–Schreier sheaf on
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
by pullback. Since
the morphism
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
factors through the quotient

\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
we then define
\mathcal{P}_{X}
by pushing
forward this Artin–Schreier sheaf via
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
.

We introduce normalized versions of these sheaves according to precisely
the same shift
\langle\deg+\beta_{X}\rangle
that occurred previously in (
10.12
).

Remark 10.5.2
.

Note that, in the twisted case, the definition of the period sheaf depends on the choice of an Artin–Schreier sheaf,
which we fixed in
Definition
10.5.1
; recall that in the finite case, this depends on the choice of an additive character of
\mathbb{F}_{q}
.
We consider this choice fixed throughout the paper.

10.5.3.
Period function

We will now describe explicitly the associated period function, i.e., trace of Frobenius, which
recovers well-known “Fourier–Whittaker periods” in the theory of automorphic forms.

Let
\psi^{\prime}
be the character of
\mathbb{A}
given by
\psi^{\prime}(x)=\psi(\partial^{-1}x)
. This need not be trivial on
F
;
as we have seen however it is “unramified” on each
F_{v}
.
Recall that
\Psi
is the total space of a
\mathbb{A}^{1}
-bundle over
X
.
Consider then the induced space of functions

(10.17)

\Phi:\Psi(\mathbb{A}_{F})\rightarrow k,\ \ \Psi(\tilde{x}\cdot t)=\Psi(\tilde{x})\psi^{\prime}(t)\ \ (\tilde{x}\in\Psi(\mathbb{A}_{F}),t\in\mathbb{G}_{a}(\mathbb{A}_{F})),

and inside it consider the “basic function” which is characterized
by satisfying (
10.17
), being supported on the preimage of
X(\widehat{\mathfrak{o}})
,
and being identically
1
on
\Psi(\widehat{\mathfrak{o}})
.

For such a function
\Phi
the translate
\partial^{1/2}\cdot\Phi:\Psi(\mathbb{A}_{F})\rightarrow k

satisfies

(\partial^{1/2}\cdot\Phi)(\tilde{x}t)=\psi^{\prime}((\partial^{1/2})^{2}t)\Phi(\tilde{x}\partial)=\psi(t)(\partial^{1/2}\cdot\Phi)(\tilde{x})\ \ (\tilde{x}\in\Psi(\mathbb{A}),t\in\mathbb{G}_{a}(\mathbb{A})),

and therefore equalling
\partial^{1/2}\cdot\Phi(x)
if
t\in F
.
In particular, for
x\in X(F)
, the value of
\partial^{1/2}\cdot\Phi
on any lift
\tilde{x}\in\Psi(F)

is independent of choice of
\tilde{x}
; let us call this simply
\partial^{1/2}\cdot\Phi(x)
.
With these conventions (
10.8
) still holds.

Example 10.5.4
.

For later usage, we will write out a formula in the Whittaker case, i.e.,
X=U\backslash G

with the
\mathbb{G}_{a}
-torsor defined by the sum
U\rightarrow\mathbb{G}_{a}
of identifications of the simple root spaces with
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
. There is nothing
novel here, but it will be useful to have explicit formulas for the various shifts and constants.
Let
f
be a function on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
. We will compute

(10.18)

\sum_{\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\mathbb{F}_{q})}P_{X}(g)f(g)=\int_{G(F)\backslash G(\mathbb{A})}P_{X}(g)f(g),

where the sum is taken over
G
-bundles weighted by inverse size of their automorphism group (i.e., the sum over
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
considered as a groupoid),
and the latter integral is taken with respect to the measure with
\mathrm{vol}(G(\hat{\mathfrak{o}}))=1
.

Unfolding via (
10.8
), taking into account the prior discussion, the above equals

\int_{U(F)\backslash G(\mathbb{A})}f(g)(g,\partial^{1/2})\cdot\Phi(g).

Now,
\partial^{1/2}
is acting on
X=U\backslash G
by means of (see §
3.4.5
) left translation through the element

a_{0}^{-1}
, where

(10.19)

a_{0}:=e^{-2\check{\rho}}(\partial^{1/2})\in T(\mathbb{A}_{F})

and correspondingly
\partial^{1/2}\cdot\Phi
is
is supported on
U(\mathbb{A})a_{0}\cdot G(\widehat{\mathfrak{o}})
.
Write
du
for the measure on
U(\mathbb{A})

where
U(\mathfrak{o})
has measure
1
;
it assigns to
U(\mathbb{A})/U(F)
the measure
q^{(g-1)\mathrm{dim}U}
.
The measure
d(a_{0}^{-1}ua_{0})

assigns to
a_{0}U(\mathfrak{o})a_{0}^{-1}
the mass
1
,
and equals
du
multiplied by
|e^{2\rho}(a_{0}^{-1})|=q^{-(g-1)\langle 2\rho,2\check{\rho}\rangle}
.
Thus (
10.18
) equals

q^{-(g-1)\langle 2\rho,2\check{\rho}\rangle}\int_{U_{F}\backslash U_{\mathbb{A}}}\psi(u)f(ua_{0})du=q^{(g-1)(\mathrm{dim}U-\langle 2\rho,2\check{\rho}\rangle)}\int_{U_{F}\backslash U_{\mathbb{A}}}\psi(u)f(ua_{0})d^{\prime}u.

where in the latter integral we use the Haar probability measure. Observe
that the exponent of
q
is simply
\beta_{X}=(g-1)(\mathrm{dim}U-\langle 2\rho,2\check{\rho}\rangle)

(compute via (
10.3
) and (
3.36
)),
so we get

(10.20)

\sum_{\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\mathbb{F}_{q})}P_{X}(g)f(g)=q^{\beta_{X}}\int_{U_{F}\backslash U_{\mathbb{A}}}\psi(u)f(ua_{0})d^{\prime}u,

and the analog for the normalized period where we replace
\beta_{X}
by
\beta_{X}/2
,
see (
10.9
). In the last formula,
d^{\prime}u
is again the invariant measure with total mass
1
.

10.6.
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
and the period sheaf : examples

The following collection of examples are intended to give some indication
of the geometry involved with both period sheaves and the spaces
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
.
Note that we will sometimes consider examples of
X
with non-neutral
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action,
i.e., with a
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action that differs from that specified in §
3.7
;
the point to note here is that the choice of
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action really affects
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
!

10.6.1.
Homogeneous spaces:

We consider the case of
X
with trivial vectorial and
\mathrm{SL}_{2}
component, i.e.,

X=H\backslash G
for
H
reductive.
Here we will use the neutral
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
action, as specified in §
3.7
;
what makes this case particularly easy think about is that

the neutral
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
action is
trivial
.

Also, in this case, there exists a
G
-invariant volume form on
X
with
\eta
and
\gamma
both trivial.

The map

\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
is simply identified with the natural map
\mathrm{Bun}_{H}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
;
the period sheaf
\mathcal{P}_{X}
assigns to a
G
-bundle the compactly supported cohomology
of the space of reductions to an
H
-torsor, and the period function
P_{X}
counts
the number of such reductions (i.e., the size of the fibers of
\mathrm{Bun}_{H}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
).
The normalized period sheaf twists by
\langle b_{H}\rangle
, and
the normalized period function takes the value

(10.21)

P_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}(x)=P_{X}(x)\cdot q^{-b_{H}/2}.

10.6.2.
The Iwasawa–Tate period.

Take
X=\mathbb{A}^{1}
as a
G={\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-space, and let us start
by considering the
trivial

\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action. The unnormalized period function is equal to

P_{X}:\mathcal{L}\rightarrow q^{h^{0}(\mathcal{L})}\ (\textrm{trivial $\mathbb{G}_{gr}$-action})

(for
\mathcal{L}
a line bundle on
\Sigma
).
The star period
P_{X}^{*}
is more interesting and is described in §
14.8.3
.

Let us describe the geometry of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
and the period
sheaf
in this case.
There is a tautological map

\pi_{r}:\mathrm{Sym}^{r}\Sigma\rightarrow\mathrm{\mathrm{Bun}}_{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}},\ \ (Q_{1},\dots,Q_{r})\mapsto\mathcal{O}(\sum Q_{i}).

The fiber of
\pi_{r}

above a line bundle
\mathcal{L}
is the space of such effective divisors
\{Q_{i}\}
together with an isomorphism
\mathcal{O}(\sum Q_{i})\simeq\mathcal{L}
, which is the same as the
space of nonzero global sections of
\mathcal{L}
; that is to say, the fibers of
\pi_{r}
are punctured affine spaces.
Note here that we are really regarding
\mathrm{Bun}_{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}
as a stack; if, in our discussion,
we were to replace its role by the Picard
scheme
, the analogous fibers would be projective spaces.

With this in hand, we can describe

\{\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}\}=\mbox{partial compactification of $\pi_{r}$}

where we allow the zero sections of line bundles, i.e., omitting the phrase “nonzero” in the above description.
Note that, unlike §
10.6.1
,
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
is not smooth.

Now let us switch to the
scaling

\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action, i.e., the “neutral” action.
Now

\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
parametrizes line bundles
{\mathcal{L}}
with a section of
{\mathcal{L}}\otimes\mathcal{K}^{1/2}
(and its geometric description
is exactly parallel to that given in the previous paragraph). The normalized period function is

(10.22)

P_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}\mbox{ with scaling $\mathbb{G}_{gr}$}:\mathcal{L}\mapsto q^{h^{0}(\mathcal{L}\otimes\mathcal{K}^{1/2})-\frac{1}{2}\deg(\mathcal{L}\otimes\mathcal{K}^{1/2})}.

Observe this now has a pleasing symmetry
\mathcal{L}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{L}^{-1}
.

Let us spell out the twists.
Here,
\beta_{X}
as in (
10.3
) is given by
(g-1)

and the factor
q^{-\beta_{X}/2}
of (
10.9
), coincides with
q^{-\frac{1}{2}\deg(\mathcal{K}^{1/2})}
; also,

|\eta(g)|^{1/2}
contributes
q^{-1/2\deg(\mathcal{L})}
. Geometrically,
the normalized period sheaf twists the period sheaf
by
\langle d+g-1\rangle

on the component where
\deg(\mathcal{L})=d
, categorifying the factor
q^{-\frac{1}{2}(d+g-1)}
. We can think of
g-1
as the dimension of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
and

d
as the Euler characteristic of
\mathcal{L}\otimes\mathcal{K}^{1/2}
, i.e.
the expected dimension of fibers of
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
, so that all in all
this is the analog of the twist by
b_{H}
appearing in the case §
10.6.1
.

10.6.3.
The Eisenstein case
U\backslash G

For
G
arbitrary take

X=U\backslash G

as a
G\times T
-space i.e.,
(g,t):Ux\mapsto Ut^{-1}xg
.
This case does not fall in our general setup, for
X
is not affine, but nonetheless our definitions
of period sheaf and period function make sense, and it will be valuable for us to examine them.

There are two
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-actions we shall consider in this paper; one is trivial,
and the other, which we shall examine here, is
where
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
acts via the restriction of the
G\times T
-action
via
(1,e^{-2\rho})
. (A discussion of the relation between these two actions is given, in a more general context,
in §
12.6
).
Explicitly in the latter action
\lambda\in\mathbb{G}_{gr}

acts through left multiplication on
U\backslash G
by
\lambda^{2\rho}\in G
.

For example, in the case
G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}
, this
X
is the
punctured affine plane via
g\in\mathrm{SL}_{2}\mapsto(0,1)g
;
if we take the nontrivial action of
\mathbb{G}_{gr}

it amounts to inverse scaling on this punctured plane.
Then the fiber
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
over a rank
2
unimodular vector bundle
V
is
the space of
everywhere injective maps
\mathcal{K}^{1/2}\rightarrow V
, equivalently,
the space of extensions

\mathcal{K}^{1/2}\rightarrow V\rightarrow\mathcal{K}^{-1/2}.

The total space of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
can thereby
identified with the affine space
H^{1}(\Sigma,\mathcal{K})\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}

modulo automorphisms
H^{0}(\Sigma,\mathcal{K})
.

More generally, if the base curve has genus
\geq 2
, and we take
X=U\backslash G

with the nontrivial
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
action just described, we may identify

(10.23)

\mathrm{\mathrm{Bun}}^{X}_{G}=\mathbb{A}^{r}/\mathcal{U}

as the quotient of
the affine space
\mathbb{A}^{r}
(where
r=
the semisimple rank, and the coordinates are indexed by simple roots for
G
)
by a
trivial action
of a certain unipotent group scheme
\mathcal{U}
.
The map
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{\mathrm{Bun}}_{G}

is not a closed immersion, but rather factors
through the quotient of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
by
the action of a torus in
G
; as a result, at the level of points over an algebraically closed field,
the image of
\mathbb{G}_{m}^{r}\subset(\mathbb{A}^{1})^{r}
is a single
point of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
.

10.6.4.
The Whittaker case.

The Whittaker case was already discussed in Example
10.5.4

and we just make a couple of minor additional remarks.
With reference
to the presentation (
10.23
), the period function is given by pushing forward
\psi(\sum_{i=1}^{r}x_{i})
on
\mathbb{A}^{r}

to
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
, and the period sheaf
the geometrization of that construction via Artin–Schreier sheaves.
By definition and (
3.37
),
the normalized period function is related to the unnormalized one by

(10.24)

P_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}=q^{-\beta_{X}/2}P_{X},\beta_{X}=(g-1)[-\langle 2\rho,2\rho^{\vee}\rangle+\mathrm{dim}U].

Remark 10.6.5
.

The quantity
\beta_{X}
is closely related to dimension of
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}
;
this is easy to see in the homogeneous case
H\backslash G
,
but also remains true in the twisted case.
For example the Whittaker case just described, the dimension of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
, i.e., the space of (
10.23
), is the sum of negated Euler characteristics
of bundles
\langle\alpha,\rho\rangle\cdot\mathcal{K}

over positive roots
\alpha
, with
\mathcal{K}
the canonical divisor;

(10.25)

\mathrm{dim}\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}=(g-1)\sum_{\alpha}\left[1-2\langle\alpha,\rho\rangle\right]=(g-1)[-\langle 2\rho,2\rho^{\vee}\rangle+\mathrm{dim}U]=\beta_{X}.

10.7.
Dependence on spin structure

As mentioned, we have felt free to choose a spin structure.
However, it is sometimes desirable to have a formulation
which is manifestly independent of spin structure.
We will discuss such a formulation now, which will use
the extended dual group (§
2.8
, §
C.7
).
Note, however, we will make little use of this formulation and include it for completeness.

For the discussion that follows, we assume that
M
satisfies the parity condition discussed
in (
5.8
). Namely, we assume that we specify a

central involution
z\in G

whose action on
M
coincides with
-1\in\mathbb{G}_{gr}
.

As we observed in the discussion surrounding (
5.8
),
if
M
admits a dual hyperspherical pair
(\check{G},\check{M})

with
\check{M}
polarized, then
z
is the product of
e^{2\rho}

with the dual of the character by which
\check{G}

acts on an eigenmeasure on
\check{X}
.

Assuming (
10.7
), the action of
G\times\mathbb{G}_{gr}
then factors through its quotient by
(z,-1)
, which
is precisely the extended group
{}^{C}G_{z}
, (§
2.8
,
C.7
).
Now define

{}_{z}\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
as
the fiber of
\mathrm{Bun}_{{}^{C}G_{z}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Bun}_{{\mathbb{G}_{m}}}
above the
canonical bundle. Equivalently we can write

{}_{z}\mathrm{Bun}_{G}\simeq\mathrm{Bun}_{G}\times^{\mathrm{Bun}_{\mathbb{Z}/2}}\mathrm{Spin}_{\Sigma},

where
\mathrm{Spin}_{\Sigma}
denotes the stack of spin structures (square roots of
\mathcal{K}
) on
\Sigma
, and the group stack
\mathrm{Bun}_{\mathbb{Z}/2}
of
\mathbb{Z}/2
-torsors on
\Sigma
acts both on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
via the central embedding
z:\mathbb{Z}/2\to Z(G)
, and simply transitively on the

\mathrm{Spin}_{\Sigma}
.
The choice of a spin structure
\mathcal{K}^{1/2}
gives rise to an identification

(10.26)

{}_{z}\mathrm{Bun}_{G}\simeq\mathrm{Bun}_{G}

and changing this choice
\mathcal{K}^{1/2}\mapsto\mathcal{K}^{1/2}\otimes\mathcal{L}
by a 2-torsion line bundle changes the identification by the translation action of

\mathcal{L}
on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
.

Next we define a period sheaf on
{}_{z}\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
by replacing pushforward along
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
by pushforward along its twisted version
that renders the following square Cartesian:

\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 18.20215pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-18.20215pt\raise Our above definition of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}
is obtained from this one by transporting via (
10.26
)
after fixing a spin structure.
An equivalent way of formulating this is that the
period sheaf is (independently of the choice of spin structure) defined as an object in a twisted version of sheaves on

\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
:

(10.27)

\mathcal{P}_{X}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Bun}_{\mathbb{Z}/2}}(\mathrm{Spin}_{\Sigma},\mathrm{Shv}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}))

where

\mathrm{Bun}_{\mathbb{Z}/2}
acts on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
via the central homomorphism

\{\pm 1\}\rightarrow Z(G)
sending the nontrivial element to
z
.

10.8.
Reduction to the vectorial case

Hyperspherical varieties are built (as in Theorem
3.6.1
)
by a process of Whittaker-induction from the special case of
M
a vector space.
This gives rise to a corresponding structure for period sheaves:

the period sheaf for general
M
is a Whittaker induction for the period sheaf in the case of
M
a vector space.

We will make this explicit.
This explication is completely straightforward, and can be referred to only as necessary;
we note it mainly for reference and as a comparison point for a similar (but less straightforward) discussion in the spectral case.
For simplicity we restrict ourselves to unnormalized period sheaves in this section.

Recall that, in the case
\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{C}
, a polarized hyperspherical variety
M

has the structure (see Theorem
3.6.1
) of a
Whittaker-induction
along
H\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}\rightarrow G
of a polarized symplectic
H
-representation

T^{*}S
, with associated twisted polarization
X=S\times^{HU}G
with
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
-bundle
\Psi\rightarrow X
.
In what follows, the fact that
M
is hyperspherical will not matter;
all that matters is the homomorphism
H\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}\rightarrow G

and the
H
-space
S
. Let us review the notation in more detail.

We fix a homomorphism
H\times SL_{2}\to G
with underlying cocharacter
\varpi:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to G
.
We will also restrict to the situation (automatic in the polarized case
by Definition
3.7.1
)
where all the
\varpi
-weights on the Lie algebra are even.
85
85

85

There is
an analogue of the construction that follows without this requirement, but now involving a geometric
version of a Jacobi
\theta
function. To simplify our life, we simply exclude this situation.

Let
U=U_{+}\subset G
be the unipotent subgroup defined by the positive part of the grading.
To this data we can associate
the
\mathbb{A}^{1}
-bundle
(\Psi\longrightarrow U\backslash G)

where
\Psi=U_{0}\backslash G
,

U_{0}
being the kernel of
U\rightarrow\mathbb{G}_{a}
.

These are
G\times H
-spaces:
G\times H
acts on compatibly on
\Psi
and
U\backslash G
by the rule
(g,h):U_{0}x\mapsto U_{0}h^{-1}xg
.
Correspondingly, the twisted cotangent bundle
T^{*}_{\Psi}(U\backslash G)

(see §
3.2.1
for definition) is a graded Hamiltonian
G\times H
-space, cf.
Example
3.4.10
; it can be regarded as the Whittaker induction along
H\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}\rightarrow G

of
T^{*}H
.

Associated to the
G\times H
-space
U\backslash G
, endowed with the affine bundle
\Psi
, we obtain
the Whittaker period sheaf
\mathcal{P}_{U\backslash G,\Psi}\in\mathrm{Shv}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}\times\mathrm{Bun}_{H})
following §
10.5
, explicitly,
the pushforward under

\mathrm{Bun}_{HU}\to\mathrm{Bun}_{G}\times\mathrm{Bun}_{H}
of the corresponding pulled-back Artin–Schreier sheaf;
this can be regarded as the quantization of
T^{*}_{\Psi}(U\backslash G)
.
We use this sheaf as an integral transform to define automorphic Whittaker functoriality.
To avoid difficulties with *-pullback and !-pushforward in the de Rham setting, we
restrict to étale or Betti settings, although it would be interesting to give a uniform treatment along the lines
of §
12.3.2
.

Definition 10.8.1
.

The automorphic Whittaker induction functor

\mathsf{WI}:\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}_{H})\longrightarrow\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G})

is the integral transform given by the Whittaker period sheaf
\mathcal{P}_{U\backslash G,\Psi}
:

\mathsf{WI}(\mathcal{F})=\pi_{1!}(\pi_{2}^{*}\mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{P}_{U\backslash G,\Psi}).

By the projection formula, Whittaker induction is equivalently described as the integral transform given by the Artin–Schreier sheaf on

\mathrm{Bun}_{HU}
(as a correspondence between
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
and
\mathrm{Bun}_{H}
).
It follows that the Whittaker induction of the constant sheaf on
\mathrm{Bun}_{H}
recovers the period sheaf associated to the
G
-space
(X=HU\backslash G,\Psi)
. More generally, using base change and the projection formula one checks that Whittaker induction commutes with the formation of period sheaves:

Lemma 10.8.2
.

Given a homomorphism
H\times SL_{2}\to G
, where
\mathbb{G}_{m}\subset\mathrm{SL}_{2}

has only even weights in its action on the Lie algebra of
G
, and
S=T^{*}Y
a polarized Hamiltonian
H
-space, the period sheaf of the Whittaker induction
(X=Y\times^{HU}G,\Psi)
of
S
is naturally identified with the Whittaker induction of the period sheaf of
S
:

\mathsf{WI}(\mathcal{P}_{Y})\simeq\mathcal{P}_{X,\Psi}.

This Lemma allows us to reduce certain questions
about period sheaves
to the case of symplectic representations,
see for example the next section §
10.9
.

Remark 10.8.3

(Whittaker reduction)
.

We can also use the Whittaker period sheaf
\mathcal{P}_{U\backslash G,\Psi}
as an integral transform in the opposite direction
to define a Whittaker restriction (or “Whittaker-Jacquet”) functor

\mathsf{WJ}:\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G})\longrightarrow\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}_{H}).

An analogous argument shows that
\mathsf{WJ}
performs Whittaker reduction on period sheaves, i.e., takes the period sheaf for a polarized
G
-space
M
to that of the (twisted-polarized) Hamiltonian
H
-space given by its reduction
M{/\!/}_{\psi}U
.
It would be interesting to verify if
\mathsf{WJ}
is identified with the left adjoint of
\mathsf{WI}
– this seems technically nontrivial
because of the absence of smoothness or properness above.

10.9.
Independence of polarization.

We have described the construction of period sheaves for polarized hyperspherical varieties
M
. This leaves two natural questions: show that the period sheaf is independent of the polarization, i.e., depends only on
(G\times\mathbb{G}_{gr},M)
– and extend the definition to
M
which don’t admit a polarization. We address the sheaf-theoretic question in the finite setting; probably a version works in the other contexts too, but we did not check.

Proposition 10.9.1
.

Let
M=T^{*}(X_{1},\Psi_{1})=T^{*}(X_{2},\Psi_{2})
be two distinguished polarizations (§
3.7
, §
3.9
) of an
\mathbb{F}
-hyperspherical variety
M
,
defined by a completely reducible datum
\mathcal{D}_{\mathbb{F}}
over
\mathbb{F}
(see discussion below).

There is a isomorphism
\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{norm}}_{X_{1}}\simeq\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{norm}}_{X_{2}}
between their normalized period sheaves, in the finite setting.
When the hyperspherical data specifying
M
and the polarizations are defined over a finite field
\mathbb{F}_{q}\subset\mathbb{F}
, the corresponding normalized period functions
P^{\mathrm{norm}}_{X_{1}}
and
P^{\mathrm{norm}}_{X_{2}}
are equal.

Note that this independence is asserted
having fixed an Artin–Schreier sheaf
, which affects the definitions in the twisted case (see Remark
10.5.2
). Recall that hyperspherical varieties (and polarizations) over
\mathbb{F}
have been defined in Definition

using the notion of a hyperspherical datum
\mathcal{D}_{\mathbb{F}}
which includes a symplectic or usual representation of a reductive subgroup
H
of
G
(over
\mathbb{F}
). We say that the datum is completely reducible if this is the case for that representation of
H
.
86
86

86

This complete reducibility is, as usual, automatic in characteristic
that is large relative to the weights of
\rho
or
\rho^{+}
;
this can deduced from
[
Jan03
, Part II, Chapter 6]
.

Proof.

The only difference between two polarizations of
M
arises from
the possibility of two different
\rho^{+}
