138.07832pt\raise-27.72476pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-0.8264pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{q_{x}}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 157.26567pt\raise-32.91226pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 157.26567pt\raise-32.91226pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma)}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces.

Note that the unramified morphism
q
is locally of finite type, and
!
-pushforward along it was used to define the period sheaf. Its ramified variant
q_{x}
is of
ind-
finite type – i.e., if we bound the poles at
x
of the twisted map to
X
we obtain finite type morphisms. As a result, the functor

q_{x!}:\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}(\Sigma,\Sigma\setminus x))\longrightarrow\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))

is well defined, independently of the theory of sheaves in infinite type. (In fact it agrees with the colimit preserving extension of the
!
-pushforward along the finite type closed substacks with bounded poles.)
We may then compose with the (Hecke-linear) spectral projection (§
C.4
, §
12.4
) to land in the “automorphic” global category:

Definition 15.1.4
.

The unramified
\Theta
-series at
x
is the composition

\textstyle{\Theta_{X,x}:{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X,\mathcal{K}^{1/2}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\pi_{x}^{*}}
\textstyle{\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}(\Sigma,\Sigma\setminus x))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(q_{x!})^{spec}}
\textstyle{\mathrm{AUT}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))}

By base change on the pullback square above there is a natural identification

(15.2)

\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{X}

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle q_{!}\underline{k}

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle q_{!}\pi^{*}\underline{k}

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle q_{x!}i_{x!}\pi^{*}\underline{k}

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle q_{x!}\pi_{x}^{*}i_{!}\pi^{*}\underline{k}

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\Theta_{X,x}(\delta_{X})

between the period sheaf and the
\Theta
-series of the basic object
\delta_{X}\in{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X,\mathcal{K}^{1/2}}
.
Moreover,
\Theta_{X,x}
admits a natural
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
-linear structure,
for it “arises from
G(O)
invariants on a
G(F)
-equivariant diagram.”

The functor
\Theta_{X,x}
has a normalized version

(15.3)

\Theta_{X,x}^{\mathrm{norm}}=\Theta_{X,x}\langle\deg+\beta_{X}\rangle

obtained by post-composing wuth the shift
\langle\beta_{X}\rangle
as well as the
\deg
-shear as in (
10.12
). The constant shift by
\beta_{X}
commutes with Hecke actions, and the
\deg
shift has the effect of making
\Theta_{X,x}^{\mathrm{norm}}
Hecke-linear for the standard action on the target and
normalized
(
\deg
-shifted) action on
\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O})
of §
7.4
. There is a similar identification of the image of the basic sheaf by
\Theta_{X,x}^{\mathrm{norm}}
and the normalized spectrally-projected period sheaf
(\mathcal{P}_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}})^{spec}
.

The
\Theta
-series description of the period sheaf provides it with an action of the Plancherel algebra:

Proposition 15.1.5
.

The identification
(\mathcal{P}_{X})^{spec}\simeq\Theta_{X,x}^{\mathrm{norm}}(\delta_{X})
endows the spectrally projected period sheaf
(\mathcal{P}_{X})^{spec}
, as an object in the
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{G}
-module category
\mathrm{AUT}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))
with the structure of module for the Plancherel algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}\in Alg(\overline{{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{G}})
, the inner automorphisms of the basic object.

Note a similar assertion holds before spectral projection, but we focus on the spectrally projected version for comparison with the spectral side.

Remark 15.1.6
.

(Twisting by spin structures.)
We can remove the dependence of the local category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X,\mathcal{K}^{1/2}}
and the
\Theta
-series on the choice of spin structure following the model of §
10.7
(whose conventions we follow). Namely we consider the stacks
{}_{z}\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}(D)\hookrightarrow{}_{z}\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}(D,D^{*})
of
{}^{C}G
-bundles on the disc with associated
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-bundle
K
and sections (on
D
or
D^{*}
) of the associated
X
-bundle. The
\Theta
-series construction defines a functor

\mathrm{SHV}({}_{z}\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(D,D^{*}))\longrightarrow\mathrm{SHV}({}_{z}\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))

sending the basic object to the period sheaf, which is identified with the version defined above for any choice of
\mathcal{K}^{1/2}
, and any two identifications differ by the translation action of
\mathrm{Bun}_{\mathbb{Z}/2}
on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma)
.

15.2.
Spectral
\Theta
-series and local-global compatibility

We now discuss the spectral counterpart of the one-point
\Theta
-series construction of Section
15.1
.

Fix a smooth affine
\check{G}\times\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-variety
\check{X}
. Rather than working with the symplectic space
{\check{M}}/{\check{G}}
with its shearing, i.e., morally on the shifted cotangent
T^{*}[2]{\check{X}}/{\check{G}}
, we work with a Koszul dual form. Namely consider the stack

(L{\check{X}})/{\check{G}}\simeq(T[-1]{\check{X}})/{\check{G}}

which classifies
{\check{G}}
-local systems on the disc with a flat section of the associated
{\check{X}}
-bundle on the punctured disc (here
L{\check{X}}=Map(S^{1},{\check{X}})\simeq T[-1]{\check{X}}
is the derived loop space of
{\check{X}}
). This is the natural spectral counterpart of the stack
X_{F}/G_{O}
of
G
-bundles on the disc with a section of the associated
X
-bundle on the punctured disc (as in Section
15.1
).

The spectral category
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})
has a Koszul dual description:
we identify [ind-]coherent sheaves on
T[-1]{\check{X}}/{\check{G}}
, sheared to take into account the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action on
{\check{X}}
,
with sheared quasicoherent sheaves on
T^{*}{\check{X}}
by the shear of Koszul duality

(15.4)

{\mathbb{K}}_{\check{X}}=\mathrm{Hom}(i_{*}\omega_{X},-):\mathrm{QC}^{!}(T[-1]{\check{X}}/{\check{G}})\longrightarrow\mathrm{QC}(T^{*}[2]{\check{X}}/{\check{G}})

{\mathbb{K}}_{\check{X}}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}:\mathrm{QC}^{!}(T[-1]{\check{X}}/{\check{G}})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\longrightarrow\mathrm{QC}(T^{*}{\check{X}}/{\check{G}})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}.

On the right of the first equation,
\mathrm{QC}(T^{*}[2]{\check{X}}/{\check{G}})
really
means that we shear
\mathrm{QC}(T^{*}{\check{X}}/{\check{G}})
by the rescaling action on the cotangent bundle.
The shearing in the second equation additionally involves the correction from the action on the base. Koszul duality has been normalized here to identify the pushforward
i_{*}\omega_{\check{X}}
under the zero-section with the ring of functions
\mathcal{O}_{T^{*}[2]{\check{X}}}
.

The spectral category, in either Koszul dual form, carries an action of the (spectral) spherical Hecke category. Starting from Section
7.1
we have been using the description of this action as the action of
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})
on
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})
given by pullback along the moment map. On the other hand the spectral Hecke category has a Koszul dual description (discussed in Section
13.2
) as the category ind-coherent sheaves on the stack
\mathfrak{\check{g}}[-1]/{\check{G}}\simeq(0\times_{\mathfrak{\check{g}}}0)/{\check{G}}
of pairs of local systems on the disc equipped with an identification of the punctured disc. This category is monoidal under convolution, and acts on sheaves on
L{\check{X}}/{\check{G}}
by modifications of local systems at the origin.

15.2.1.
The spectral
\Theta
-series

We define a functor of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
-modules, the (one-point unramified) spectral
\Theta
-series

(15.5)

{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}},x}:{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\mathbb{K}}_{\check{X}}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}}{{\rightarrow}}QC^{!}(L{\check{X}}/{\check{G}})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\longrightarrow QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}),

where in the middle we have the category of ind-coherent sheaves on
L{\check{X}}
,
but
sheared through the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
action
and
{\mathbb{K}}_{\check{X}}
is the Koszul duality functor
of (
15.4
).

The functor
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}},x}
is defined using the spectral counterpart of

\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}(\Sigma,\Sigma\setminus x)
from Section
15.1
, namely the stack
\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma,\Sigma\setminus x)
of
{\check{G}}
-local systems with a flat section of the associated
{\check{X}}
bundle
away from
x\in\Sigma
, via the resulting correspondence

\textstyle{\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}_{\check{G}}(D)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{i}
\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\pi}
\scriptstyle{i_{x}}
\scriptstyle{q}
\textstyle{\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}_{\check{G}}(D,D^{*})}
\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma,\Sigma\setminus x)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\pi_{x}}
\scriptstyle{q_{x}}
\textstyle{\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}}

where we recall that
\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}_{\check{G}}(D)\simeq{\check{X}}/{\check{G}}
and
\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}_{\check{G}}(D,D^{*})\simeq T[-1]{\check{X}}/{\check{G}}
.

We define the spectral
\Theta
-series as
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}},x}={\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatbslash}}\circ q_{x*}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\pi_{x}^{!{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

(in notation similar to (
11.29
); in particular,
{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatbslash}}
is the identification of

QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{G}}})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
with
QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{G}}})
from the trivialization of the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
action).
This admits a natural
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
-linearity from identifying the groupoid of Hecke modifications at
x
on
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
as the pullback from the groupoid
\mathrm{pt}/{\check{G}}\times_{{\check{G}}/{\check{G}}}\mathrm{pt}/{\check{G}}
on local systems on the disc. Again, there is a normalized version
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}},x}^{\mathrm{norm}}
by incorporating the same
\varepsilon
and
\beta
twists as in (
11.20
).

Just as in (
15.2
)
there is a natural identification

{\mathcal{L}}_{\check{X}}\simeq{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}},x}(\left[i_{*}\omega_{X}\right]^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}})

between the
L
-sheaf of
{\check{X}}
and the
\Theta
-series applied to the basic object
i_{*}\omega_{X}
(the base change calculation is identical to the identification of the period and
\Theta
-series in Section
15.1
, with the roles of
*
and
!
exchanged).
Here the notation
[\dots]^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
means the following:
i_{*}\omega

a priori
belongs to the unsheared category, but we may regard it in the sheared
category because the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant objects are identified between usual and sheared categories, as in (
6.6
).

The Hecke-linearity of the
L
-functor implies that the image of the basic object
i_{*}\omega_{X}
carries an action of the enriched (or inner) endomorphisms of the basic object, which is just the algebra of functions
\mathbb{O}_{\check{M}}:=\mathcal{O}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})\in{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})
:

Corollary 15.2.2
.

Fix
x\in\Sigma
and consider
QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})
as a module category for the Hecke category
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})
through modification of local systems at
x
. Then the
L
-sheaf
{\mathcal{L}}_{\check{X}}\in QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})
carries the structure of module over the algebra
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}}\in{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})
.

We are ready, now, to state the one-point form of local-global compatibility in the case when both sides are polarized.
Thus we assume given a dual hyperspherical pair
(G,M=T^{*}X)
and
(\check{G},\check{M}=T^{*}\check{X})
.
We further assume that the spectral eigencharacter
\check{\eta}:{\check{G}}\to{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
is trivial (see however Remark
15.2.4
). In this case we do not need to introduce spectral epsilon factors to normalize the spectral side;
the normalization is simply a shift

{{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}},x}^{\mathrm{norm}}:={\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}},x}\langle-\beta_{\check{X}}\rangle}
:

Conjecture 15.2.3

(Local-Global Conjecture, 1-point version)
.

The equivalence
\mathbb{L}_{X}
of the local conjecture (Conjecture
7.5.1
) and the geometric Langlands correspondence are intertwined by the normalized spectral and automorphic
\Theta
-series:

\textstyle{\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}(D,D^{*}))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\Theta_{X,x}^{\mathrm{norm}}}
\scriptstyle{\mathbb{L}_{X}}
\textstyle{\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}^{{\check{X}}}(D,D^{*}))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}},x}^{\mathrm{norm}}}
\textstyle{\mathrm{AUT}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{GL}}
\textstyle{\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma))}

Moreover applied to basic objects this identification recovers the identification of period and L-sheaves given by the global conjecture (Conjecture
12.1.1
).

Equivalently, the conjecture asserts that the identification of period and
L
-sheaves is linear with respect to the identification
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}\simeq\mathbb{O}_{\check{M}}
of Conjecture
8.1.8
and the actions
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}\circlearrowright\mathcal{P}_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}
of Proposition
15.1.5
and
\mathbb{O}_{\check{M}}\circlearrowright{\mathcal{L}}_{\check{X}}^{\mathrm{norm}}
of Corollary
15.2.2
. (Again note that in our special case with trivial eigencharacter normalization does not affect the local spectral category at all.)

Remark 15.2.4

(Epsilon factors and normalized local-global compatibility)
.

In the general case when we are given a nontrivial eigencharacter
\check{\eta}:{\check{G}}\to{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
, we need to define the normalized form

{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})^{\mathrm{norm}}={QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})\otimes_{\text{Rep}({\check{G}})}\varepsilon_{1/2,D}^{\vee}({\check{G}})

of the local spectral category by tensoring with a half-epsilon gerbe, as we briefly sketch. The half-epsilon gerbe on
D^{*}
, an invertible sheaf of categories over
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(D^{*})
, is pulled back from a half-epsilon gerbe for
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
via
\check{\eta}:\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(D^{*})\to\mathrm{Loc}_{\mathbb{G}_{m}}(D^{*})
. The abelian half-epsilon gerbe in turn is constructed (by analogy with §
11.2.6
) out of the skyscraper sheaf of categories at
\{\mathcal{K}^{1/2}\}\in\mathrm{Pic}(D^{*})
by applying local geometric class field theory. The local and global half-epsilon factors are related by a functor

\varepsilon_{1/2,\Sigma\setminus x}^{\vee}:\varepsilon_{1/2,D}^{\vee}\longrightarrow\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma))

much as the local category and
L
-sheaf are related by the
\Theta
-series, and this functor allows us to twist the spectral
\Theta
-series to its normalized form

{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}},x}^{\mathrm{norm}}:{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})^{\mathrm{norm}}\longrightarrow QC^{!}(\mathrm{\mathrm{Loc}}_{\check{G}}).

16.
Automorphic factorization

The theory of factorization algebras is an algebraic counterpart of the theory of
E_{2}
-algebras in topology first introduced by Beilinson and Drinfeld
[
BD
,
BD04
]
to capture the commutativity of unramified Hecke operators through a mechanism of colliding points on a curve. (We refer to §
D.3
and §
D.4
for a brief overview of
E_{n}
-algebras, factorization algebras and factorization homology.)

In particular, the spherical Hecke category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{G}
has not only the structure of monoidal category but that of monoidal
factorization category
. In the constructible setting this results
[
Noc20
]
in an
E_{3}
-monoidal structure on
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{G}
–a derived weakening of the notion of symmetric monoidal category.
The spectral form of the spherical Hecke category
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})

correspondingly has a well-understood
E_{3}
-structure in the constructible setting; however, the de Rham form and the factorizable geometric Satake correspondence are unavailable at the time of writing (but expected in upcoming work
[
CR23
]
).

In this section we discuss, in the de Rham and étale settings, the construction of a factorizable form of the local category
\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O})
and of the Plancherel algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
of §
8
. In particular, we explain that the structure on
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
of associative algebra object of the Hecke category can be enhanced to a locally constant factorization associative algebra object of the factorizable Hecke category on any smooth curve
\Sigma
. In the étale setting over
\mathbb{C}
this makes
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
into an
SO(2)
-fixed
E_{3}
-algebra object in
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{G}
, also known as an associative oriented disc algebra.

These constructions are largely variants of familiar constructions in the literature, in particular the factorization structure of loop spaces of Kapranov and Vasserot
[
KV04
]
and the relative Coulomb branch construction (ring object) of Braverman-Finkelberg-Nakajima
[
BFN19
]
, as seen through the formalism of factorization (or chiral) categories as developed by Raskin and Gaitsgory (see
[
Ras17a
]
and
[
Ras17b
]
as well as
[
Gai11b
]
, which is closely related to the construction of this section in the Eisenstein case).

A crucial output of the theory of factorization is the mechanism of
factorization homology
(see §
D.4.7
) which “integrates” or globalizes factorization algebras over
\Sigma
.
Factorization homology appears to play a role in geometric settings analogous to the construction of Euler products (as suggested for example in
[
Gai15a
]
and private communications by J. Francis and C. Barwick). This notion is much better behaved and understood in the topological setting of
E_{n}
-algebras, hence in the Betti spectral setting, to which §
17
and §
18
are restricted, but we continue to provide an overview on both sides.

The factorization homology of the Hecke category (in both automorphic and spectral forms) produces the
global Hecke category

\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
through which the actions of spherical Hecke functors on the global category factors. Likewise we can “globalize” the Plancherel algebra to produce an object that we call the
RTF algebra

{\mathbb{R}\mathbb{T}\mathbb{F}}_{X,\Sigma}
, which is an associative algebra object in the global Hecke category.

We sketch the idea behind a factorizable form of the
\Theta
-series construction, conditionally on the further development of sheaf theory in infinite type.
The existence of this factorizable
\Theta
-series implies that
the one-point action of the Plancherel algebra on the period sheaf descends to the RTF algebra.
Just as the Plancherel algebra encodes maps between Hecke transforms of the basic object in the local setting, the structure on
{\mathbb{R}\mathbb{T}\mathbb{F}}_{X,\Sigma}
of algebra in the global Hecke category produces maps between arbitrary Hecke functors applied to the period sheaf.
Thus the RTF algebra plays the role of a geometric counterpart (categorification) of the Relative Trace Formula, the self-pairing of the period functional with arbitrary insertions of Hecke operators, as we discuss in §
16.3.5
. We leave as an open problem the detailed study of the RTF algebra and its relation to the more familiar forms of the relative trace formula.
This chapter is included as motivation and for the benefit of a more complete conjectural picture that ties in the local and global conjectures.
We explain the main ideas but do not verify all the technical details; we hope these
can be examined in a more thorough treatment of the topic.
In the next section we present the spectral counterpart of this story in the Betti setting, which is not plagued by the same technical difficulties.

The contents are as follows:

-

§
16.1
presents the setup of factorizable loop spaces, factorization categories and factorization homology.

-

§
16.2

discusses factorizable forms of the spherical Hecke category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
, the
X
-spherical category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X}
and the Plancherel algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
.

-

§
16.3

introduces the RTF algebra, the factorization homology of the Plancherel algebra, and sketches the idea of the factorizable
\Theta
-series, which endows the period sheaf with an action of the RTF algebra.

We will make use of some notions concerning sheaves of categories, ULA objects and rigid tensor categories which are collected in Appendix
§
B.9
.
In Appendix
D
we explain how the structures discussed in this chapter arise naturally from the algebraic formalization of boundary conditions in topological quantum field theory.
The constructions of this section work in the de Rham and constructible (in particular étale) sheaf-theoretic settings as described in Appendix
B
.

16.1.
Factorization Categories

16.1.1.
Factorization algebras from loop spaces

We first discuss the basic geometric source of factorization relevant to us, the factorizable version of arc and loop spaces as introduced in
[
KV04
]
– see
[
Ras17b
, Section 2]
for an excellent overview.
We defer to Appendix
D
for background material including generalities on factorization and the Ran space.

For the purpose of this section,
X
can be an arbitrary smooth affine
G
-variety.
Of course, when we discuss the global conjecture, we need to make the further restrictions on
X
used by that conjecture.

For a point
x\in\Sigma
let
O_{x}\subset F_{x}
denote the complete local ring of
\Sigma
at
x
and its field of fractions. Given an affine scheme
X
we have an ind-scheme of loops and a subscheme of arcs

LX_{x}=X(F_{x})\supset LX_{+,x}=X(O_{x})

both of infinite type over
k
.
As
x
varies, these spaces assemble to ind-schemes
LX_{\Sigma}\to\Sigma
(and likewise for arcs).

More generally, by
[
KV04
, Proposition 3.5.2]
, given any finite set
I
the arc and loop constructions, applied to the formal completions of finite subsets of
\Sigma
, are representable by ind-schemes (of ind-finite, respectively ind-infinite type)
LX_{+,\Sigma^{I}}\subset LX_{\Sigma^{I}}
over
\Sigma^{I}
. Moreover, for
X
smooth these multipoint arc spaces are “pro-smooth”:
LX_{+,\Sigma^{I}}\to\Sigma^{I}
can be represented
as the filtered inverse limit of smooth schemes under smooth affine morphisms over
\Sigma^{I}
, see
[
KV04
, Example 4.2.5]
and
[
Ras17b
, Lemma 2.5.1]
.

We also need a hybrid of the loop and arc constructions: given a map
I\to J
and a
J
-tuple
\{x_{j}\}_{j\in J}
of points in
\Sigma
, we may consider the ind-scheme of loops into
X
at the points
x_{j}
which are required to be arcs (i.e., integral) at the
\{x_{j}\}_{j\in J\setminus I}
(where
J\setminus I
denotes the complement of the image). This defines an ind-scheme
LX_{\Sigma^{J},+:\Sigma^{J\setminus I}}
over
\Sigma^{J}
(see also
[
Ras17b
, Section 2.10]
).
As discussed in §
D.4.3
, it’s convenient to extend these assignments over the category of possibly empty finite sets.

These objects carry three additional structures, which make
\{LX_{\Sigma^{I}}\}
(and its arc subscheme) into a factorization algebra over
\Sigma
in the correspondence category of ind-schemes:

\bullet

Ran’s Condition:
For every surjection
I\twoheadrightarrow J
we have an isomorphism

LX_{\Sigma^{I}}\times_{\Sigma^{I}}\Sigma^{J}\simeq LX_{\Sigma^{J}}.

\bullet

Factorization:
For every decomposition
I\simeq I_{1}\coprod I_{2}
we have an isomorphism

LX_{\Sigma^{I}}|_{U_{I_{1},I_{2}}}\simeq[LX_{\Sigma^{I_{1}}}\times LX_{\Sigma^{I_{2}}}]|_{U_{I_{1},I_{2}}}

of the restrictions to the locus
{U_{I_{1},I_{2}}}\subset\Sigma^{I}
of disjoint
I_{1}
- and
I_{2}
-tuples.

\bullet

Unitality:
For every injection
I\hookrightarrow J
we have a correspondence

\textstyle{LX_{\Sigma^{J},+:\Sigma^{J\setminus I}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\Sigma^{J}\times_{\Sigma^{I}}LX_{\Sigma^{I}}}
\textstyle{LX_{\Sigma^{J}}}

compatible with factorization data.

We can summarize the conditions as saying we have an ind-scheme
LX^{fact}
over
\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma}
which is multiplicative, as well as an extension of this structure over the unital Ran space (i.e., replacing surjections of finite sets by arbitrary maps of possibly empty finite sets).

Replacing
X
by an affine group-scheme
G
over
k
, we have corresponding versions of the loop group
LG_{x},LG_{\Sigma^{I}}
and
LG^{fact}
which are group ind-schemes over
k
,
\Sigma^{I}
and
\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma}
respectively, and the subgroups
LG_{+}
of arcs. If
X\circlearrowleft G
is a
G
-variety, we obtain factorizable versions of the actions on the loop spaces
LG\circlearrowright LX
compatible with factorization structures.

16.1.2.
Factorization Categories

We now pass from spaces to categories of sheaves. Factorization categories are generalizations of
E_{2}
-monoidal categories, which themselves are derived versions of braided tensor categories. The theory of factorization categories is developed in
[
Ras17a
,
Gai10
]
in the de Rham setting (see also
[
But20b
]
for a useful overview and applications in a context very close to ours and
[
Noc20
]
for the factorizable Hecke category).
We do not present the fully structured
\infty
-categorical definition here, for which we refer to the above references, but only a practical snapshot thereof.
The discussion below applies equally well in constructible sheaf theories but not in the Betti setting – we crucially use the
!
-tensor product.

Definition 16.1.3
.

A faithful unital factorization category over
\Sigma
consists of the following data

\bullet

For every finite set
I
, we are given a sheaf of categories
\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I}}
over
\Sigma^{I}
.

\bullet

Ran’s Condition:
For every surjection
\alpha:I\twoheadrightarrow J
we have an isomorphism

\Delta_{\alpha}^{!}\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I}}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{J}}.

\bullet

Factorization:
For every decomposition
I\simeq I_{1}\coprod I_{2}
we have a full embedding

[\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I_{1}}}\boxtimes\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I_{2}}}]|_{U_{I_{1},I_{2}}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I}}|_{U_{I_{1},I_{2}}}

of the restrictions to the locus
{U_{I_{1},I_{2}}}\subset\Sigma^{I}
of disjoint
I_{1}
- and
I_{2}
-tuples.

\bullet

Unitality:
For every injection
I\hookrightarrow J
we have a morphism

SHV(\Sigma^{J})\otimes_{SHV(\Sigma^{I})}\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I}}\longrightarrow\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{J}}

of sheaves of categories compatible with factorization data.

The unital structure on
\mathcal{C}
is said to be ULA if the unit morphism

u_{\Sigma^{I}}:SHV(\Sigma^{I})\to\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I}},

defined by the injection of the empty set to
I
, is ULA over
\Sigma^{I}
for all
I
(i.e., has a
\mathrm{SHV}(\Sigma^{I})
-linear continuous right adjoint).

Again as noted the full unital factorization structure is best expressed as an assignment
I\to\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I}}
over the category of possibly empty finite sets, or a multiplicative sheaf over the unital Ran space.

Define
\omega_{\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I}}}=u_{\Sigma^{I}}(\omega_{\Sigma^{I}})
. Thanks to the ULA property of the unital structure we can consider its inner endomorphisms

\mathcal{A}_{\Sigma^{I}}=\underline{\mathrm{End}}(\omega_{\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I}}})=u_{\Sigma^{I}}^{R}u_{\Sigma^{I}}(\omega_{\Sigma^{I}}),

where
u^{R}
and
u
are linear over sheaves on
\Sigma^{I}
(so in particular the construction is compatible with restriction maps) This guarantees that the
\mathcal{A}_{\Sigma^{I}}
form a factorizable sheaf valued in associative algebras, and in the constructible setting we may further apply Lurie’s results summarized in Corollary
D.4.6
:

Proposition 16.1.4
.

Let
\mathcal{F}
denote a faithful unital factorization category over
\Sigma
, with a ULA unit.

•

The internal endomorphisms of the unit object

\mathcal{A}_{\Sigma^{I}}=\underline{End}(\omega_{\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I}}})\in SHV(\Sigma^{I})

form a factorization associative algebra on
\Sigma
.

•

In the constructible setting over
\mathbb{C}
, if we further assume that
\mathcal{A}
is locally constant, then the
!
-fibers
\mathcal{A}_{x}

(x\in\Sigma)
form an associative
E_{\Sigma}
-algebra, or (for
\Sigma=\mathbb{A}^{1}
) an
SO(2)
-fixed
E_{3}
-algebra.

Recall from §
D.4.4
that local constancy is the property of a factorization algebra (as a
!
-sheaf on
\mathrm{Ran}(\Sigma)
) that its
!
-restriction to the strata of
\mathrm{Ran}(\Sigma)
(configurations of
I
distinct points) are locally constant, together with a hypercompleteness assumption (which is automatically satisfied for bounded below cochain complexes such as we will encounter).

16.1.5.
Factorization homology

The first two items in Definition
16.1.3
give the definition of a (!-)
sheaf of categories
over the Ran space
\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma}
(as in
[
Gai10
]
), and we let

\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma}}:=\lim_{\leftarrow,\Delta_{\alpha}^{!}}\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I}}

denote its global sections. However, since we are using
!
-sheaves,
\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma}}
behaves like a
homology
theory for
\Sigma
with coefficients in
\mathcal{C}
: indeed by passing to left adjoints we can rewrite this limit as a colimit over
!
-pushforwards, which we consider the
factorization homology
of
\mathcal{C}
:

\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{C}:=\lim_{\rightarrow,\Delta_{\alpha,!}}\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma^{I}}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma}}.

This is parallel to the definition of
factorization algebras in topology (see §
D.4
, especially Remark
D.4.1
) as factorizable
cosheaves
on the Ran space of a manifold, and their factorization homology is defined as the cosheaf homology.

The Ran space
Ran(\Sigma)
is homologically contractible
[
BD
,
Lura
]
, so that
C_{*}\mathrm{Ran}(\Sigma)\simeq k
. However the Ran space of course still carries a large category of constructible sheaves or
D
-modules
\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma})=\lim_{\rightarrow}\mathrm{SHV}(\Sigma^{I})
, which is itself the factorization homology of the unit factorization category. As a result the notion
\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{C}
of factorization homology for a factorization category is too large: a unital structure on
\mathcal{C}
defines a functor
u:\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma})\to\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{C}
, so rather than a single unit (a pointing by
\mathrm{Vect}
) we have a
\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma})
-worth thereof. In particular the images of skyscrapers at distinct points of
\Sigma
will not typically be isomorphic.

Therefore it is useful to refine the notion of factorization homology for unital factorization categories to a unital or “independent” version
[
Gai10
]
by erasing the contribution of
\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma})
. Namely the unital structure on
\mathcal{C}
endows
\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{C}
with the structure of module for the monoidal category
(\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma}),\ast)
of sheaves on
Ran(\Sigma)
with the convolution monoidal structure (arising from the algebra structure on the Ran space in the correspondence category).
This monoidal category is augmented to
\mathrm{Vect}
, and the unital factorization homology

\int_{\Sigma}^{u}\mathcal{C}=\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{C}\otimes_{(\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma}),\ast)}\mathrm{Vect}

is defined as the coinvariants of the naive factorization homology. This construction takes the place for factorization categories of the (Betti) factorization homology of
E_{n}
-algebras, though is not as well behaved (see e.g.
[
Ber19b
]
).
By construction
\int_{\Sigma}^{u}\mathcal{C}
is pointed by
\mathrm{Vect}
, in particular the image of skyscrapers at distinct points of
\Sigma
have been identified.

16.2.
The Factorizable Plancherel Algebra

In this section we present the factorization categories associated to loop spaces and the factorization algebras extracted from them, leading to the factorizable form of the Plancherel algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
.

16.2.1.
Sheaves on loop spaces

Consider the factorization space
LX
over
\Sigma
. Applying the functor
\mathrm{SHV}
to the cosheaf
LX_{\Sigma^{I}}
over
\Sigma^{I}
we obtain a sheaf of categories
\underline{\mathrm{SHV}}(LX)_{\Sigma^{I}}
over
\Sigma^{I}
. Varying
I

we have an assignment

I\mapsto\underline{\mathrm{SHV}}(LX)_{\Sigma^{I}}

from finite sets to sheaves of categories, which assemble to a sheaf of categories
\underline{\mathrm{SHV}}(LX)^{fact}
over the Ran space of
\Sigma
.
This assignment further satisfies the faithful form of the factorization axiom above. In the
D
-module setting, these maps are equivalences by the symmetric monoidal property of the assignment
X\mapsto\mathcal{D}(X)
, producing the strong notion of factorization category as it appears in
[
Ras17a
]
.

Proposition 16.2.2
.

[
Ras17b
, 2.10]
,
[
Ras17c
, 6.3]

The categories
\{\underline{\mathrm{SHV}}(LX_{\Sigma^{I}})\}
define a unital factorization category
\mathrm{SHV}(LX)^{fact}
over
\Sigma
. The unital structure is given by the factorizable basic objects
\Phi_{X,\Sigma^{I}}=i_{*}\omega_{LX_{+,\Sigma^{I}}}\in\mathrm{SHV}(LX_{\Sigma^{I}})
for varying
I
, which are ULA over
\Sigma^{I}
.

Note the ULA property of the unit follows from the pro-smoothness of the arc space and the preservation of the ULA condition under smooth pullback and proper pushforward.

It follows from the proposition that in the constructible setting, the internal endomorphisms
\underline{\mathrm{End}}(\Phi_{X,\Sigma})^{fact}=\{\underline{\mathrm{End}}(\Phi_{X,\Sigma^{I}})\in\mathrm{SHV}(\Sigma^{I})\}
form a locally constant factorization associative algebra on
\Sigma
. (Hypercompleteness is automatic since the sheaf is bounded below, and constructibility for the stratification by diagonals is evident).
Therefore we may apply Lurie’s results from §
D.4.4
. The corresponding
E_{3}
algebra over
\mathbb{C}
is the simply the commutative algebra of cochains on
L_{+}X
(equivalently on
X
). To get a more interesting algebra we need to invoke equivariance.

16.2.3.
Factorizable spherical category

In order to incorporate equivariance we first recall the factorizable spherical category (see
[
Noc20
]
). See
[
Noc20
]
and
[
But20b
]
in particular for the notion of factorization monoidal category (associative algebra object in factorization categories).

Definition 16.2.4
.

The factorizable spherical category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{fact}
is the unital factorization monoidal category defined by the assignment

I\mapsto{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Sigma^{I}}=(\mathrm{SHV}(LG_{+,\Sigma^{I}}\backslash LG_{\Sigma^{I}}/LG_{+,\Sigma^{I}}),\ast)\in Alg(\mathrm{SHV}(\Sigma^{I}))

of the convolution category of
LG_{+}
-equivariant sheaves on the Beilinson-Drinfeld affine Grassmannian, with its natural unital factorization structure.

Note that (as discussed in §
6.6
,§
B.6
) we use the ind-finite (or “renormalized”) form of the spherical category
[
AG15
]
.

The factorization structure on the spherical category is naturally compatible with the action of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
on
SHV(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))
by Hecke modifications over varying points – in other words, these actions assemble to an action of
\int_{\Sigma}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
on
SHV(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))
(which is compatible in a suitable sense with the unital structure).

Remark 16.2.5
.

The factorizable spherical category satisfies a nontrivial local constancy property
[
Noc20
]
, which results in
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
carrying an
E_{3}
(or in general associative
E_{\Sigma}
) monoidal structure in the constructible setting. This local constancy uses the ind-properness of the affine Grassmannian in a fundamental way. See
17.1
for the spectral origin of this
E_{3}
structure.

Lemma 16.2.6
.

The monoidal category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Sigma^{I}}
is rigid over
\Sigma^{I}
.

Proof.

The rigidity over
\Sigma^{I}
follows, as for the standard rigidity of the spherical category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
over a point, from the ind-properness of the affine Grassmannian, which results in the ind-proper convolution map having a continuous right adjoint. Note that the compactness of the unit in the spherical category is a feature of working with ind-finite (renormalized) sheaves, and fails eg in
\mathcal{D}(LG_{+}\backslash LG/LG_{+})
.
∎

16.2.7.
Equivariant version.

We now consider the factorizable version of the local category
\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F}/G_{O})
, by passing to the Hecke-module category of
LG_{+,\Sigma^{I}}
-equivariant sheaves on
LX_{\Sigma^{I}}
. The rigidity of the factorizable Hecke category guarantees (through Proposition
B.9.7
) that the ULA property of the unit (the basic sheaf
\Phi_{X,\Sigma^{I}}
) upgrades to the Hecke-linear setting as well, and the following proposition is a formal consequence of the setup
(though again we do not present the details here):

Proposition 16.2.8
.

Let
X
be a smooth affine
G
-variety.

\bullet

The assignment

I\mapsto{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{X,\Sigma^{I}}:=\mathrm{SHV}(LG_{+,\Sigma^{I}}\backslash LX_{\Sigma^{I}})

extends to define a
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{fact}
-module in faithful unital factorization categories
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X,fact}
over
\Sigma
, with ULA unit given by the equivariant basic object
\Phi_{X}
.

\bullet

The internal endomorphisms

\{{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X,\Sigma^{I}}=\underline{\mathrm{End}}(\Phi_{X,\Sigma^{I}})\in{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Sigma^{I}}\}

form a locally constant factorization associative algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{fact}\in Alg({\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{fact})
in the factorizable spherical category, the factorizable Plancherel algebra.

\bullet

In the constructible setting over
\mathbb{C}
, this endows the Plancherel algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X,x}
with the structure of associative
E_{\Sigma}
-algebra object in the Hecke category, or for
\Sigma=\mathbb{A}^{1}
with an
SO(2)
-fixed
E_{3}
-algebra structure.

Remark 16.2.9

(Normalized version)
.

Just as in the one-point case explained in §
15.1
,
the construction of Proposition
16.2.8
has a natural “normalized” modification in our setting of spherical varieties. Namely we use the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action on
X
to twist the stacks
LX_{\Sigma^{I}}
of maps of punctured discs on
\Sigma
into
X
by
\mathcal{K}^{1/2}
, and also shift the Hecke action by the degree
\deg_{\eta}
as in §
7.4
.

Remark 16.2.10
.

The local constancy of the factorizable Plancherel algebra here is not a subtle geometric property, like the local constancy of the Hecke category itself
[
Noc20
]
, but rather a formal consequence of the same local constancy: any section of the factorizable Hecke category over powers of the curve is automatically locally constant on the strata. We view a factorization algebra in
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
as a (lax monoidal) functor of factorization categories from the unit
\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma})
. The former is not itself locally constant but the inclusion of locally constant categories into sheaves of categories admits a left adjoint (as in
[
AGK+20b
, Lemma G.1.6]
) through which any morphism to a locally constant category factors. In particular stratum by stratum a factorization algebra in
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
is given by a functor from local systems on the stratum.

Problem 16.2.11
.

For
X
a smooth affine spherical variety, and working in the constructible setting over
\mathbb{C}
, is the factorizable form of the
X
-spherical category locally constant? In particular this would endow
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X}
with an
SO(2)
-fixed
E_{2}
structure (i.e., upgrade it to a balanced braided tensor category).

Note that as discussed in §
7.5.3
,
7.5.11
this local constancy is in fact implied by the local conjecture, since by the affineness of the spectral category (§
7.1.3
) the entire Hecke category is given by modules for the Plancherel algebra, hence inherits its locally constant factorization structure.

As discussed in §
7.6
, there is substantial recent progress in understanding the categories
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X}
in many examples. In particular the work on the Gaiotto conjecture (
[
BFGT21
]
,
[
BFT22a
]
,
[
BFT22b
]
,
[
TY23b
]
and
[
TY23a
]
) provides an explicit understanding of how to construct and describe monoidal structures on
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X}
in a series of examples, which one hopes will lead to an understanding of the factorization structures on the automorphic category in general.

Remark 16.2.12
.

(The factorizable relative Grassmannian and the product on the Plancherel algebra:)
Let us sketch the factorization structure on the Plancherel algebra
in a more explicit way, in particular again making clear its essentially finite-dimensional content.
We also indicate explicitly how it recovers a product structure on
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
, which we anticipate (but don’t check) agrees with the one from
[
BFN18
]
.

In §
8.2
we introduced the relative Grassmannian

\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
as the subvariety of
\mathrm{Gr}\times X_{O}

consisting, informally, of pairs
(x,g)
with
xg\in X_{O}
.
Now, both
X_{O}
and
\mathrm{Gr}
extend to factorization spaces;
and the relative Grassmannian extends to a factorization subspace of
the product space.

Let us explicate this in the case
\Sigma=\mathbb{P}^{1},G=\mathrm{GL}_{n},X=\mathbb{A}^{n}
; the same discussion applies
to the general case with only notational changes.

The fiber of
X_{O}

and
\mathrm{Gr}
over the point
(z_{1},z_{2})\in\Sigma^{2}
are given, respectively,
are defined as the projective and direct limits over
N
of:

•

Points
\mathbf{x}
of
\mathbb{A}^{n}
valued in the ring

\mathbb{C}[t]/f^{N}
, with
f=f_{z_{1},z_{2}}=(t-z_{1})(t-z_{2})
;

•

projective
\mathbb{C}[t]
-submodules
\Lambda
of
\left(\frac{f^{-N}\mathbb{C}[t]}{f^{N}\mathbb{C}[t]}\right)^{n}
.

Clearly, along the diagonal
z_{1}=z_{2}
, the fiber reduces to a similarly
defined family over
\Sigma
itself.
Moreover, the factorization subspace corresponding to
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}

is defined by the condition that
\mathbf{x}\in\Lambda
;
this is clearly compatible with specialization to the diagonal.

Now let us spell out how this constructs the product on
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
.
Recall that
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}
denotes the
V
-multiplicity space of the Plancherel algebra. In what follows, the role of the factorizable spaces
can be replaced by the finite dimensional versions sketched above.

There exists
sheaves
\mathcal{T}_{V,W}
on the factorizable
affine Grassmannian over
\Sigma\times\Sigma

whose fibers are
T_{V}\boxtimes T_{W}
away from the diagonal
and
T_{V\otimes W}
at the diagonal.
Working still over
\Sigma\times\Sigma
, take the
!
-pullback of this sheaf to the factorization version of
\mathrm{Gr}^{X}
,
and then the
*
-pushforward to
\Sigma\times\Sigma
.
Recalling the computation (
8.11
) of the multiplicity spaces of the Plancherel algebra,
the resulting sheaf on
\Sigma\times\Sigma
comes with canonical identifications:

\mbox{off diagonal $!$-stalks}\simeq{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}\otimes{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(W)},\mbox{diagonal $!$-stalks}\simeq{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V\otimes W)}.

Then a specialization map – which, for
!
-stalks, goes from the “nearby” stalk to the “special” stalk –
gives rise to the product

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V)}\otimes{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(W)}\rightarrow{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{(V\otimes W)}

16.3.
Factorizable
\Theta
-series and the RTF algebra

Proposition
16.2.8
defines a factorizable version
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{fact}
of the Plancherel algebra, an algebra object in the factorizable Hecke category. We now pass to factorization homology, i.e., compactly supported sections of
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{fact}
over
\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma}
,
an algebra object in the monoidal category
\mathbb{H}_{G,\Sigma}=\int_{\Sigma}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{fact}
given by the colimit of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Sigma^{I}}
over
!
-pushforwards (see
[
Gai10
]
for a discussion of monoidal structure on factorization homology):

Definition 16.3.1
.

We define the RTF algebra to be the factorization homology of the
factorization associative algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{fact}
,

(16.1)

{\mathbb{R}\mathbb{T}\mathbb{F}}_{X,\Sigma}=\int_{\Sigma}{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}^{fact}\in Alg(\mathbb{H}_{G,\Sigma})

The constructions of the previous sections show the way to assemble the one-point
\Theta
-series
\Theta_{X,x}:{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X}\to SHV(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))
as the point
x
varies into an “adèlic geometric” object, the Ran version of the
\Theta
-series. However to do so one must face the following difficulty: the
\Theta
-series is defined by
*
-pullback on
*
-sheaves, while the factorization structure was defined using
!
-pullbacks on sheaves of categories defined using
!
-tensor products. Thus in order to carry out this construction we must assume that

•

the categories of
*
and
!
sheaves on
LG_{+,\Sigma^{I}}\backslash LX_{\Sigma^{I}}
are identified for all
I
, compatibly with
!
-pushforward along diagonal maps, and

•

the
!
-pushforwards along diagonal maps satisfy base change with
*
-pullbacks of
*
-sheaves.

This is beyond the scope of the current work, and we leave the following as an open problem:

Problem 16.3.2
.

Fix
X
a smooth affine spherical
G
-variety. Show the following:

(1)

The one-point
\Theta

\scriptstyle{\int_{\Sigma}\Theta_{X}}

(2)

The period sheaf
\mathcal{P}_{X}
admits the structure of module for the RTF algebra

extending the action of

The
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}

Remark 16.3.4
.

The spherical Hecke action on
\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))
is unital, in the sense that it factors the action of
\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma})
on
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
through the functor
\Gamma_{c}:\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma})\to\mathrm{Vect}
. Likewise one can ask for the factorizable
\Theta
-series to be naturally unital, i.e., to factor coinvariants of
\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Ran}_{\Sigma})
to define a
\int_{\Sigma}^{u}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
-linear functor

\Theta_{X}:\int_{\Sigma}^{u}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X}\longrightarrow SHV(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))

sending the unit (
\mathrm{Vect}
-pointing) to the period sheaf.

Discussion.

We sketch the main idea behind factorizable
\Theta
-series, contingent on the sheaf-theoretic hypotheses above. Let
\mathrm{Bun}^{X}_{G}(\Sigma^{I})\to\Sigma^{I}
denote the moduli stack of
G
-bundles on
\Sigma
with a section of the associated
X
-bundle on the complement of the universal

-tuple of points of
\Sigma
. This stack sits in a correspondence

and the
\Theta

By our sheaf-theoretic hypothesis, the

. Moreover this structure extends over the unital Ran space by inserting arc spaces (and the corresponding objects, the basic sheaves

\textstyle{LG_{+,\Sigma^{J}}\backslash LX_{\Sigma^{J},+:\Sigma^{J\setminus I}}.\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

.

In the second part, the functor

16.3.5.
Relation to the Relative Trace Formula

We briefly comment on the reasoning behind the nomenclature for the RTF algebra. We refer to
[
Yun18
]
for an overview of the geometric interpretation of relative trace formulas in the function field setting, and to
[
FN11
]
(see a review in
[
Fre13b
]
) for a study of a geometric version of the Arthur and Kuznetsov trace formulas very close in spirit to our current work.
In particular see
op.cit.
for the interpretation of the spectral side of these trace formulas in terms of the spectral side of geometric Langlands; the spectral analog of the RTF algebra, the L-observables, is studied in §
18
.

The relative trace formula expresses the inner product of
\Theta
-series, i.e., the inner products of Hecke operators applied to period functionals. Let us approach this problem in our unramified geometric setting, replacing the inner product by a Hom pairing (cf. Lemma
2.6.1
).

Given two spherical
G
-varieties
X,Y
we can consider the Hom space
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))}(\mathcal{P}_{X},\mathcal{P}_{Y})
between the corresponding period sheaves
\mathcal{P}_{X}
and
\mathcal{P}_{Y}
;
a geometric incarnation of this is the fiber product
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{X}\times_{\mathrm{Bun}_{G}}\mathrm{Bun}_{G}^{Y}
. More generally we can insert Hecke functors
H_{V_{i}}
at finitely many points
\{x_{i}\}
of
\Sigma
and evaluate
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SHV}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))}(\bigotimes H_{V_{i},x_{i}}\ast\mathcal{P}_{X},\mathcal{P}_{Y})
. This Hom space is related to the stack of pairs of
G
-bundles related by a Hecke modification of prescribed type and sections of associated
X
- and
Y
-bundles (whose point count is related to the relative trace formula as explained in
[
Yun18
, 2.2.4]
).

As explained in §
12.8
(in the discussion of the closely related
L^{2}
version of the global conjecture), and in parallel with the characterization of the Plancherel algebra in Remark
8.1.2
, these twisted Hom spaces for varying Hecke functors assemble into a single object, the inner Hom
between the period sheaves taking values in the global Hecke category.
(Here we should first pass from
\mathcal{P}_{X},\mathcal{P}_{Y}
to their spectral projection to make the
action of Hecke functors vary nicely; for simplicity we will not explicitly keep track of this in the notation.)
This is, in other words, an enrichment of the usual
\mathrm{Hom}
– one recovers the usual
\mathrm{Hom}

by taking morphisms from the identity object of the global Hecke category;
we will denote it by
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}}(\mathcal{P}_{X},\mathcal{P}_{Y})

and call it the “RTF space.”

The RTF algebra
{\mathbb{R}\mathbb{T}\mathbb{F}}_{X,\Sigma}

comes with a morphism, in the global Hecke category,

{\mathbb{R}\mathbb{T}\mathbb{F}}_{X,\Sigma}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}}(\mathcal{P}_{X},\mathcal{P}_{X}).

We regard the left-hand side as an approximation to the RTF space in the case
X=Y
.
More precisely,
{\mathbb{R}\mathbb{T}\mathbb{F}}_{X,\Sigma}
can be considered the part of the RTF space which is “of local origin”, i.e., comes from integrating the local version of the RTF provided by the Plancherel algebra

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathrm{Hom}_{{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}}(\Phi_{X},\Phi_{X}).

Based on the spectral description studied in §
18
, we propose the following heuristic picture: when
we localize the story at a Langlands parameter with a unique fixed point on
{\check{X}}
, then the RTF algebra and full RTF space should agree. This is closely related to the assertion of Conjecture
12.8.1
.
In general, the former provides the “
{\check{X}}
-local part” of the later: on one hand, the RTF decomposes as a sum over automorphic representations of periods squared. On the other hand, the RTF algebra geometrizes the part of this sum which is supported on the diagonal of
{\check{X}}
– the sum of squares of contributions associated to individual fixed points on
{\check{X}}
, rather than the square of the sum.

Remark 16.3.6

(More general RTF)
.

To put this construction in context, it is useful to consider the following perspective: the RTF algebra is associated not just to the pair
(X,X)
of
G
-spherical varieties but to the identity map between them. More generally, given two spherical varieties
X,Y
together with a
G
-equivariant correspondence
X\leftarrow Z\rightarrow Y
we can ask to quantize
Z
to an intertwiner, a
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{G}
-linear functor between the categories
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X}
and
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{Y}
compatible with factorization. The “inner endomorphisms” construction then produces a
({\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X},{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{Y})
-bimodule
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{Z}
. Passing to factorization homology we find a
({\mathbb{R}\mathbb{T}\mathbb{F}}_{X,\Sigma},{\mathbb{R}\mathbb{T}\mathbb{F}}_{Y,\Sigma})
-bimodule
{\mathbb{R}\mathbb{T}\mathbb{F}}_{Z,\Sigma}
together with a map

{\mathbb{R}\mathbb{T}\mathbb{F}}_{Z,\Sigma}\longrightarrow RTF_{X,Y}(\Sigma)=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}}(\mathcal{P}_{X},\mathcal{P}_{Y})

to the global RTF space, which can be considered a contribution to the RTF from the intertwiner
Z
. This is part of the richer story of the higher category of periods suggested by the interpretation as boundary conditions, which we explore in forthcoming work.

17.
Local Spectral Quantization

In this section and the next we adopt the point of view that the construction of
L
-sheaves for a hyperspherical variety
{\check{M}}
is a problem of quantization, relative to the stack
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma)
of Langlands parameters on a curve.

Namely, for each local system
\rho
, we aim to produce an associative algebra (“observables”) and a module for this algebra (“states”).
The states are the fiber
{\mathcal{L}}_{\check{M}}|_{\rho}
of the
L
-sheaf at
\rho
, while the observables are the fiber at
\rho
of a sheaf of algebras we introduce, the algebra of “
L
-observables”
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}},\Sigma}
, which provides the spectral counterpart of the RTF algebra
{\mathbb{R}\mathbb{T}\mathbb{F}}_{M,\Sigma}
from the previous chapter. We view the
L
-observables and
L
-sheaf at
\rho
as the output of deformation quantization and geometric quantization, respectively, applied to a symplectic variety, which for
{\check{M}}=T^{*}{\check{X}}
polarized is simply the cotangent bundle of the stack of
\rho
-twisted maps from
\Sigma
to
{\check{X}}
, i.e., the (homotopy) fixed points of the Galois group or fundamental group of
\Sigma
, acting on
{\check{X}}
through
\rho
.

From the perspective of number theory, the
L
-observables and its action as endomorphisms of the
L
-function provide a geometric counterpart of the
L
-function of the symplectic variety
{\check{M}}
and its square-root provided by the
L
-function on
{\check{X}}
.
See also Remark
18.0.2
for a discussion from the perspective of shifted symplectic geometry,
and Appendix
D
where this problem is placed in the context of the problem of quantizing hamiltonian
{\check{G}}
-varieties to boundary conditions for a 4d TQFT
\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}
.

We restrict ourselves entirely to the topological setting over
\mathbb{C}
, so that local systems are always meant in the Betti sense, and factorization algebras are meant in the locally constant sense as
E_{n}
-algebras, see Appendix
D.4
. For the local considerations of §
17
there is no distinction between the Betti and étale settings over
\mathbb{C}
; the global considerations of §
18
are confined to the Betti setting.

In this section we focus on the
local
and factorizable origin of this deformation quantization problem, which we encode by introducing the notion of a
spectral deformation quantization
of
{\check{M}}
: a rotation-invariant
E_{3}
(or factorization associative) algebra
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}}
in the spectral Hecke category, the “
L
-algebra”, which deforms the
\mathcal{O}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star})
-algebra of functions
\mathcal{O}({\check{M}})
. This notion recovers in particular a deformation quantization in the usual sense of
\mathcal{O}({\check{M}})
as a Poisson algebra.

We shall then describe explicit spectral deformation quantizations in the polarized and twisted polarized cases.
We can combine this discussion with the factorizable Plancherel algebra of the previous section to give a factorizable form of the local conjecture (contingent on a factorizable form of the Satake correspondence, cf.
[
CR23
]
):
namely, there should exist a
a factorizable identification

{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{\simeq}}\mathbb{O}_{\check{M}}.

In §
18
we will use the factorization structure (via the mechanism of factorization homology) to describe the global deformation quantization obtained as the factorization homology of the
L
-algebra,
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}},\Sigma}=\int_{\Sigma}\mathbb{O}_{\check{M}}
and its relation to geometric quantization, namely its action on the
L
-sheaf. From the arithmetic perspective, the structure described in this section can be viewed as a subtle extra structure on the
{\check{G}}
-representation
\mathcal{O}({\check{M}})
needed to construct a geometric form of the Euler product.

In more detail:

•

§
17.1
discusses the factorizable form of the spectral Hecke category;

•

§
17.2
gives the formal definition of a spectral deformation quantization for a given
(\check{G},\check{M})

and discuss its relationship to the deformation of
\check{M}
arising from loop rotation;

•

§
17.3
constructs spectral deformation quantizations for polarized hamiltonian varieties
{\check{M}}=T^{*}{\check{X}}
, while

•

§
17.4
extends that construction to the twisted polarized setting
{\check{M}}=T^{*}_{\Psi}{\check{X}}
, and

•

§
17.5
explains how the spectral quantization of twisted cotangent bundles produces an Arthur (or spectral Whittaker) induction functor on quantized Hamiltonian spaces.

17.1.
The factorizable spectral Hecke category

As mentioned we will work in the simpler Betti setting over
\mathbb{C}
, where the tools of topological field theory (specifically factorization homology and
E_{n}
-algebras) allow us to give a precise and tight relation between the local and global conjectures. We refer the reader to Appendix
D
, specifically Section
D.3
, for a brief review of
E_{n}
-algebras and their relation to Poisson geometry. In particular we take advantage of Lurie’s identification of
E_{n}
-algebras with locally constant factorization algebras on
\mathbb{R}^{n}
(see Section
D.4.4
) to go back and forth between the two perspectives.

Terminology 17.1.1
.

For the rest of this chapter, we will often use the term factorization algebra to denote

an
\mathrm{SO}(2)
-equivariant
locally constant factorization algebra
\mathcal{A}
on
\mathbb{R}^{2}
,

where a factorization algebra is understood in the topological sense (§
D.4.4
),
i.e., a cosheaf on the Ran space of
\mathbb{R}^{2}
with multiplicative structure, or equivalently as an
E_{2}
-algebra.

Such
\mathcal{A}
then gives rise to a locally constant factorization algebra on any oriented surface
\Sigma
,
in a fashion that is compatible with pullback under morphisms of such. In practice this is how we shall think of them, i.e.,
a “
\mathrm{SO}(2)
-equivariant factorization algebra” is a compatible collection of locally constant factorization algebras on all oriented surfaces.
From the
E_{n}
perspective, an
SO(2)
-equivariant factorization algebra is an
E_{2}
-algebra that is invariant (in the derived sense)
for the natural action of the rotation group on
E_{2}
-algebras. These are identified with the notion of “framed
E_{2}
-algebra,” i.e., an algebra over the operad of framed little discs, and give rise to algebras over the colored operad of discs in
\Sigma
for any oriented surface
\Sigma
(see Section
D.4.4
).

We can also speak of “factorization categories,” which
are factorization algebras, in the sense above, now taken to be valued in
\mathsf{DGCAT}_{k}
.
Symmetric monoidal categories give rise to factorization categories, see e.g.
[
Ras17b
]
.
A natural example is the abelian Hecke category of equivariant perverse sheaves on the Grassmannian,
which can be understood as a factorization category in the sense above
whose stalk at any point of
\mathbb{R}^{2}
is identified with the “usual” abelian Hecke category.
Crucially for us, the factorization picture extends to the entire derived Hecke category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
, as has been carried out in detail by Nocera
[
Noc20
]
. Here
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
is as in §
6.6
but we drop explicit mention of the group
G
.
This gives the Hecke category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
an
SO(2)
-fixed
E_{3}
structure, as we now discuss:

17.1.2.
The
E_{3}
structure on the Hecke category

The convolution structure on the Hecke category is compatible with the factorization
E_{2}
structure (as first observed by Lurie), making
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
into a monoidal factorization category, or equivalently an
E_{3}
-category. It is important to note that unlike its abelian version this is truly a noncommutative object, i.e., is not given by a symmetric monoidal (i.e.,
E_{\infty}
) structure.

This gives us the ability to talk about, e.g., a “factorization associative
algebra” inside
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
.
Just as
we can think of an associative algebra as (the image of the unit under) a lax monoidal functor from
\mathrm{Vect}_{k}
,
we can define a factorization associative algebra object as a a lax monoidal functor of monoidal factorization categories from
\mathrm{Vect}_{k}

to the factorizable Hecke category.
Passing to a stalk at a given point, we get an algebra object of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
in the usual sense,
and via derived Satake we also get a
{\check{G}}
-equivariant algebra
over
\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}[2]
. By an abuse of notation we will say “
A\in{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
is a factorization associative algebra in
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
”
in this situation, i.e., we will use the same notation
for the factorization object and its stalk.

On the spectral side, the
E_{3}
structure on the Hecke category just described is visible in
the description of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
(see
[
AG15
]
),
which already arose in §
13.2.2
, as ind-coherent sheaves on the stack

\textrm{Map}(S^{2},B{\check{G}})\simeq\mathfrak{\check{g}}[-1]/{\check{G}}\simeq B{\check{G}}\times_{\mathfrak{\check{g}}/{\check{G}}}B{\check{G}}

of local systems on
S^{2}
.
Here the fiber product description comes from the decomposition of
S^{2}
into hemispheres.
This mapping stack description makes
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(S^{2})
into an
SO(3)
-fixed
E_{3}
-algebra in the correspondence category, whence a corresponding monoidal structure on ind-coherent sheaves thanks to the formalism of
[
GR17
]
, as explained in
[
Toe13
]
.

There is not to our knowledge a published proof that
the “automorphic” and “spectral”
E_{3}
structures match. We will however not be making formal use of this.

Remark 17.1.3
.

A crucial point in
[
Noc20
]
is the local constancy.
This arises from the following fact: if we let
\mathcal{G}r

be the affine Grassmannian – i.e., the space of modifications of a
G
-bundle at a point –
and define similarly
\mathcal{G}r(D)
to be the space of modifications of a
G
-bundle
supported inside a disc, the map

\mathcal{G}r\rightarrow\mathcal{G}r(D)

is a stratified homotopy equivalence with respect to natural stratifications on both sides.
As we have noted in Problem

16.2.11
, it’s an important
question to clarify when the corresponding
local constancy holds for the
X
-spherical category.

Remark 17.1.4
.

Note that we can regard
stack
\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}[2]/{\check{G}}
as the shifted cotangent bundle
T^{*}[3]B{\check{G}}
, which carries a natural 3-shifted symplectic structure. The
E_{3}
-monoidal structure on the Hecke category provides a deformation quantization
[
CPT+17
]
of this structure on
T^{*}[3]B{\check{G}}
(see also
[
BBZB+20
]
for a discussion).

17.2.
Spectral Deformation Quantization.

We define the notion of “spectral deformation quantization.”

17.2.1.

Recall that the cohomology of an
E_{3}
-algebra forms a graded Poisson algebra of degree
-2
(graded
P_{3}
-algebra).
Now the sheared algebra
\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}({{\check{M}}})
has a graded Poisson bracket of degree
-2
, i.e., is a graded
P_{3}
algebra, and we would like to deform it into an
E_{3}
algebra, or equivalently a locally constant factorization associative algebra on the Euclidean plane
\mathbb{R}^{2}
. Moreover we would like to do this compatibly with two key structures:

\bullet

action of changes of coordinates (
SO(2)
-action on the plane): we would like an associative factorization algebra defined on any oriented surface
\Sigma
, and

\bullet

the Hamiltonian
{\check{G}}
-action: we would like to quantize
{{\check{M}}}
compatibly with the
E_{3}
-structure on the spherical category via the sheared moment map
\mu:{{\check{M}}}\to\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}}
.

These desiderata are captured in the following definition:

Definition 17.2.2
.

A spectral deformation quantization of the Hamiltonian
{\check{G}}
-variety
{{\check{M}}}
consists of the following:

\bullet

a locally constant factorization associative algebra object
\mathbb{O}_{{{\check{M}}}}
in the factorizable Hecke category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
(see
§
17.1
)
and

\bullet

an identification of the cohomology of
\mathbb{O}_{{{\check{M}}}}
with sheared functions on
{\check{M}}
,

H^{\ast}(\mathbb{O}_{{{\check{M}}}})\simeq\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}({{\check{M}}})

as Poisson algebras in
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})
.

In this situation, the
{{\check{M}}}
-Hecke category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{{\check{M}}}=\mathbb{O}_{{{\check{M}}}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}_{{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}}
denotes the corresponding quantum Hamiltonian
{\check{G}}
-space, by which we connote a factorization
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
-module category.

Note that we can pass between the deformation
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}}
and the deformation

{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{{\check{M}}}
of its module category: to pass from the latter to the former, we take
endomorphisms of the unit object.

Example 17.2.3
.

(Spectral deformation quantization in the presence of the local conjecture):
We already saw in §
8
that, in the context of the local unramified conjecture,
\mathcal{O}(\check{M})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
– considered
as an algebra object in the Hecke category – arises as the Plancherel algebra
{\mathbb{P}\mathbb{L}}_{X}
,
the endomorphisms of the unit object in the
X
-spherical category. The discussion of Section
16
upgrades this construction to a locally constant associative factorization algebra. Hence the Plancherel algebra is naturally an
SO(2)
-invariant
E_{3}
algebra, and gives (assuming the local conjecture) a spectral deformation quantization of
\mathcal{O}(\check{M})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
.

Remark 17.2.4

(Comparing two forms of quantization)
.

A spectral deformation quantization of
\check{M}
gives rise in particular to a deformation of the commutative algebra
\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}({\check{M}})
to an
E_{3}
-algebra
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}}
:

This is a special case of a general construction that can be used to degenerate an object to its cohomology: the Postnikov tower construction (i.e., the t-structure on the dg category
\mathrm{Vect}
of chain complexes) upgrades
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}}
to a filtered object in
\mathrm{Vect}
(cf.
[
Lura
]
). We then apply the Rees construction (as in
[
Mou21
]
) to obtain a
{\mathbb{A}}^{1}/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-object, with fiber at zero (the associated graded) given by the cohomology, namely
\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}({\check{M}})
.

On the other hand, there is another deformation of
\mathcal{O}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}({\check{M}})
of interest.
Namely,
SO(2)
-equivariance gives rise to a deformation of
\mathcal{O}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}({\check{M}})
over
k[[u]]=H^{*}(B\mathrm{SO}(2),k)
,
by considering derived
\mathrm{SO}(2)
-invariants (i.e.,
\mathrm{SO}(2)
-equivariant cohomology). This deformation moreover acquires the structure of associative
k[[u]]
-algebra. This can be seen (after passing to cohomology) by considering the
SO(2)
-invariants of the
E_{3}
-algebra
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}}
, which has one associative multiplication preserved by
SO(2)
.

There is a strong compatibility between these two deformations of
\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}({\check{M}})
, namely they give rise to the same 2-shifted Poisson bracket:

Claim: the
SO(2)
-equivariant deformation defines a deformation quantization of
\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}({\check{M}})
, i.e., the associated Poisson bracket is identified with the Poisson bracket arising from the symplectic structure.

This justifies, in other words, the definition of the Poisson bracket given in
§
8.5
.
The quoted can be proved by an argument of Ben-Zvi and Neitzke (a version appears in
[
BBZB+20
, Section 6]
, see
[
But20a
, Proposition 25.1.1]
for a more precise general version) and amounts to
a computation in the
\mathrm{SO}(2)
-equivariant homology of
S^{2}
,
which is indexing binary operations on the cohomology.
We briefly explain the relevant identity there.
Consider the cohomology of
B\mathrm{SO}(2)
with
coefficients in the homology of
S^{2}
. This is supported in degrees
-2,0,2,\dots
;
and as a
k[u]
module (where
u
is a generator for
H^{2}(B\mathrm{SO}(2))
) is given by
taking a free module on generators
L,R
in degree
0
(corresponding
to the inclusion of the two fixed points) and adjoining
the class
P
arising from the fundamental class of
S^{2}

satisfying
Pu=L-R
.
This identity
Pu=L-R
corresponds, after translating, to the desired identity
u\{x,y\}=xy-yx
.

Return now to Definition
17.2.2
.
For a general (shifted) symplectic variety (or Hamiltonian
{\check{G}}
-variety)
the question of constructing a spectral deformation quantization
poses a problem of shifted deformation quantization, as studied (and solved using formality) in
[
CPT+17
]
– or more rigidly, invoking the grading, a problem of
filtered
deformation quantization (as in
[
Los22
]
).
In the coming sections (§
17.3
, §
17.4
) we explicitly
construct a spectral deformation quantization in all polarized and twisted polarized cases.
The general case of our hyperspherical varieties is thereby reduced to the vectorial case, i.e., to the spectral form of the Weil representation,
much as automorphic quantization can be achieved using the theory of the Weil representation
(§
10.9.2
).

17.3.
Spectral quantization for cotangents

We describe explicitly how to give a spectral deformation quantization when
M=T^{*}X
is a cotangent bundle
and the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
action on
X
is trivial:

Let
i:{\check{X}}\to{\mathcal{L}}{\check{X}}\simeq T[-1]{\check{X}}
denote the inclusion of constant loops (zero section). Thanks to the Koszul resolution we find an algebra isomorphism
\mathrm{End}(i_{*}\omega_{\check{X}})\simeq\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}({{\check{M}}})
, and we use the resulting Koszul duality equivalence

(17.1)

Hom(i_{*}\omega_{\check{X}},-):QC^{!}({\mathcal{L}}{\check{X}})\longrightarrow{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({{\check{M}}}),

which naturally upgrades to a monoidal equivalence with respect to convolution on the source and tensor product on the target.

On the other hand, the monoidal category
QC^{!}({\mathcal{L}}{\check{X}})
naturally upgrades to a factorization category, since
{\mathcal{L}}{\check{X}}=Map(S^{1},{\check{X}})
carries a framed
E_{2}
-structure in the correspondence category of stacks, by considering maps from complements of little discs into
{\check{X}}
.

This discussion can be upgraded to be
{\check{G}}
-equivariant. The action of Hecke modifications on
{\check{G}}
-local systems on the disc induces an action on the stack
{\mathcal{L}}{\check{X}}/{\check{G}}
of local systems with a section of the
{\check{X}}
-bundle on the punctured disc, i.e., the basechange of the descent groupoid in the following diagram:

\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 21.4591pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&&\cr&&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-3.0pt\raise Hence
QC^{!}({\mathcal{L}}{\check{X}}/{\check{G}})
forms a factorization algebra object in modules for the factorization monoidal category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}
.

From this we can formally deduce that the internal endomorphisms of the unit in
QC^{!}(\mathcal{L}\check{X}/{\check{G}})
defines a factorization associative algebra object
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}}
in
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}
.
It is easy to describe the underlying associative algebra object, since as a mere module category for a monoidal category we can identify
the
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}
-module
QC^{!}({\mathcal{L}}{\check{X}}/{\check{G}})
with the
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})
-module

{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({{\check{M}}}/{\check{G}})
. The internal endomorphisms of the unit
\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}({\check{M}})\in{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({{\check{M}}}/{\check{G}})
are identified with the image
of
\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}({\check{M}})
under the moment map
\mu:{{\check{M}}}\to\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}
, so it follows that we have an equivalence
\mathbb{O}_{{{\check{M}}}}\simeq\mu_{*}\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}({{\check{M}}})

of algebra objects in the Hecke category.

17.4.
Spectral quantization for twisted cotangents

Next we show how to spectrally deformation quantize twisted cotangent bundles. The construction is closely related to our calculation of spectral Whittaker
L
-sheaves on
\mathbb{P}^{1}
in §
13.6
, in particular the calculation of Equation
13.12
.

Let
{\check{G}}\circlearrowright({\check{X}},\Psi)
be as in Section
11.6
.
The twisted cotangent bundle
T^{*}_{\Psi}{\check{X}}
is obtained by Hamiltonian reduction by
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
from the cotangent
T^{*}\Psi
of the total space of
\Psi
, i.e., we have a
{\check{G}}
-equivariant identification

T^{*}_{\Psi}{\check{X}}\simeq T^{*}\Psi\times_{{\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}}^{{\mathbb{G}_{a}}}\mathrm{pt}_{1}.

We thus will start from the spectral quantization of
T^{*}\Psi
as constructed above and apply a quantized form of Hamiltonian reduction, by quantizing
\mathrm{pt}_{1}
.

To do so it will be important to keep track of gradings. First recall that
\mathbb{G}_{gr}\circlearrowright{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
with weight 2. Thus the category

{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathbb{G}_{a}}={QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}/{\mathbb{G}_{a}})\simeq QC({\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}})\otimes QC({\mathbb{G}_{a}}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}})

has a factor given by
unsheared
sheaves on the affine line, and in particular contains a skyscraper object
\mathcal{O}_{1}
at
1\in{\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}
.

We would like to endow
\mathcal{O}_{1}\in{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
with the structure of factorization associative algebra quantizing its evident commutative algebra structure with respect to the symmetric monoidal structure on
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}/{\mathbb{G}_{a}})
. For this we note that for any group
H
the category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{H}
is linear over the
SO(2)
-fixed
E_{4}
-algebra
135
135

135

This is in fact commutative, and is
physically the ring of local operators in the field theory, i.e., functions on the Coulomb branch
(\mathfrak{h}^{*}/H)^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
.

\mathrm{End}(1_{{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{H}})\simeq\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}(\mathfrak{h}^{*})^{H}

Thus we may specialize the entire Hecke category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
over
1\in{\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}
, and recover
\mathcal{O}_{1}
as the unit in the specialized category, whence its factorization associative algebra (
SO(2)
-fixed
E_{3}
) structure.

Now we suppose
\Psi\to{\check{X}}
is a
{\check{G}}\times\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-equivariant affine bundle, where
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
acts on
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
as above. It follows that the category
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(T^{*}\Psi/{\check{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}_{a}})
has the structure of quantum Hamiltonian
{\check{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
-space. We now need to impose the moment map condition for
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
in a factorizable fashion.

Proposition 17.4.1
.

The category
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})
associated to a twisted cotangent bundle
{\check{M}}=T^{*}_{\Psi}{\check{X}}
carries a canonical structure of factorization
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}
-module through its identification with the category

{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})\simeq\mathcal{O}_{1}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}(QC^{!}({\mathcal{L}}\Psi/{\check{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}_{a}}))

of modules for the factorization associative algebra
\mathcal{O}_{1}\in{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\mathbb{G}_{a}}}
in the factorization
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\check{G}}}\otimes{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
-module category

{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(T^{*}\Psi/{\check{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}_{a}})\simeq QC^{!}({\mathcal{L}}\Psi/{\check{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}_{a}})).

The category
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})
is pointed by the sheared structure sheaf of
{\check{M}}/{\check{G}}
. This corresponds under Koszul duality (compare with the calculation in §
13.6
) to the unit in the factorization category
\mathcal{O}_{1}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}(QC^{!}({\mathcal{L}}\Psi/{\check{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}_{a}}))
. This unit is given by
\mathcal{O}_{1}\ast i_{*}\omega_{{\check{X}}/{\check{G}}}
, the action of
\mathcal{O}_{1}\in{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
on the unit of
QC^{!}({\mathcal{L}}\Psi/{\check{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}_{a}})
, itself given as the pushforward of the dualizing sheaf under the inclusion of constant loops

i:{\check{X}}/{\check{G}}\simeq\Psi/{\check{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}_{a}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}\Psi/{\check{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}_{a}}.

17.5.
Arthur Induction: Local Case

We now explain another perspective on the quantization of twisted cotangent bundles: it provides the local counterpart for the Arthur induction of
L
-sheaves and local, spectral counterpart of the Whittaker induction for hamiltonian actions (Sections

,
11.6
, and

As a warm-up let us consider the case when

{\check{H}}\subset{\check{G}}
–

for

and

Equivalently (taking the point of view of Hamiltonian spaces mentioned

\textstyle{\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\textstyle{{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

Remark 17.5.1
.

The factorization bimodule
