18.
Global Spectral Quantization

In this section we study the global spectral quantization of hyperspherical varieties
{\check{M}}
.
This consists of three ingredients
136
136

136

We are indebted to Pavel Safronov for teaching us this tripartite point of view on quantization in general and specifically of shifted symplectic geometry, cf.
[
Saf23
]
.
, which can all be explicitly constructed in the polarized and twisted polarized cases
{\check{M}}=T^{*}_{\Psi}{\check{X}}
:

\bullet

geometric quantization: the
L
-sheaf
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}}}
, an object of
\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma))
;

\bullet

deformation quantization: the algebra of
L
-observables
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}},\Sigma}
, an algebra in the
global Hecke category

\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}=\int_{\Sigma}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
which acts on
\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma))
;

\bullet

compatibility: the action
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}},\Sigma}\circlearrowright{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}}}
encoded in the spectral
\Theta
-series, a functor of
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
-modules

\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}_{\Sigma}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\longrightarrow\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma)).

To carry this out, we shall review and apply the theory developed by Beraldo (building on work of Arinkin and Gaitsgory), which describes the global Hecke category on the spectral side explicitly as a refinement of
QC(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})
which captures not only support on
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
(Langlands parameters) but also
singular support
(expected to be related to Arthur parameters).
We conclude with a foray into the geometric study of Arthur parameters, whose construction is closely related to the theory of
L
-sheaves for twisted polarizations.

The material of this chapter relates in particular to three prior sections of the paper:

(a)

In §
11.10
, and in particular §
11.10.4
, we discussed (in the case
\check{X}=\mbox{ a vector space}
) how the
L
-sheaf
in the vectorial case could be seen as a representation of a certain algebra
deforming the
L
-sheaf not of
\check{X}
but of
\check{M}
.

(b)

In §
12.8
we examined the algebra
of (a) in more detail over the locus
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}^{\circ}\subset\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
where
there is a unique fixed point on
\check{M}
and
saw that the deformation of (a) is simply a Clifford algebra
deforming an exterior algebra.
In our current terminology,
this Clifford algebra is (an incarnation of)
the algebra of
L
-observables, i.e.,
a deformation quantization;
and the existence of
geometric quantization is the question of Morita trivialization of the family of Clifford algebras,
which, we anticipate, is controlled by the anomaly (Remark
12.8.2
).

(c)

The corresponding phenomenon in number theory is expressed by
(
14.9
): the endomorphisms of the period sheaf
corresponds to the square of the period, and at the numerical level,
there is no distinction between
\mathbb{O}_{\check{M}}
and its
undeformed version
L_{\check{M}}
.

However, the discussion here refines all of these prior discussions in an important way,
as we now explain – for

\mathbb{O}_{\check{M},\Sigma}
has
a structure finer than “sheaf of algebras over
\mathrm{Loc}
,”
and we will now seek to construct it together with this finer structure.
Indeed,
the global Hecke category provides a quantization of the
1
-shifted cotangent bundle
T^{*}[1]\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
, a higher analog of the sheaf of differential operators,
and thus
\mathbb{O}_{\check{M},\Sigma}

will be equipped with a structure loosely analogous to a
D
-module and the
L
-sheaf with that of a solution.
See §
18.1.1
for an informal discussion.

Remark 18.0.1

(Beyond the polarized case)
.

In general quantization problems are very hard without the data of a polarization. However as in several other points in this paper we can apply the rigid structure theory of hyperspherical varieties. We describe Arthur induction functors for both the local (§
17.5
) and global (§
18.5
) quantization problems, which reduce the three quantization problems above to the linear case of a symplectic representation, i.e., to the spectral analog of the theory of the Weil representation.
We will discuss this case in more detail elsewhere.

•

§
18.1
reviews the notions (relative flat connections, shifted differential operators and microlocalization
of coherent sheaves) needed for global spectral quantization, mainly following Beraldo;

•

§
18.2
shows that a spectral deformation quantization gives a sheaf of algebras – the
L
-observables

\mathbb{O}_{\check{M},\Sigma}
– over
\mathrm{Loc}
, and
as alluded to above,
something more
microlocal
– an algebra over the Hochschild cohomology of
\mathrm{Loc}
. This generalizes the
Clifford algebra encountered in §
11.10
, and should be considered the
global
spectral deformation quantization. The compatibility with global geometric quantization is expressed by the condition that the
L
-sheaf be a module for
L
-observables, which we interpret as a solution to a “categorified holonomic differential equation”.

•

§
18.3
verifies the compatibility between our global spectral deformation and geometric quantizations in the polarized case. We apply a result of
[
HL22a
]
to identify the
L
-observables in this case with “relative differential operators” along
\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}\to\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
.

•

§
18.4
describes the modifications needed to describe
L
-observables and spectral
\Theta
-series in the twisted polarized case.

•

§
18.5
introduces the notion of Geometric Arthur Parameters: we study global Arthur functoriality, a geometric construction of nontempered Langlands parameters parallel to Arthur functoriality (§
14.9
) which combines the singular support theory of
[
AG15
]
with an eigenproperty for Hecke operators that is sheared by an Arthur
SL_{2}
.

Remark 18.0.2

(Shifted Symplectic Geometry Perspective)
.

The constructions in this section and the previous fit very naturally into the framework of shifted symplectic geometry
[
PTVV13
]
and its origin as the semiclassical phase space geometry of the BV-AKSZ construction of quantum field theories
[
AKSZ97
]
, see
[
CHS22
]
.
We refer to
[
PV18
,
Saf23
]
for discussions of shifted deformation and geometric quantization, respectively.

As discussed in Remark
3.1.3
,
3.3.2
the equivariant moment map

\mu:{\check{M}}/{\check{G}}\to\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}}

gives the symplectic variety
{\check{M}}
the structure of 1-shifted Lagrangian in
\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}}=T^{*}[1]B{\check{G}}
. We instead want to consider the sheared version
{\check{M}}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
which is a 2-shifted symplectic stack in the sense of
[

]
; for example, in the polarized case when
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
acts trivially on
{\check{X}}

As we have noted elsewhere (see e.g. Remark

6.4.1
,
11.4.1
) it is troublesome to work with
{\check{M}}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
directly as a geometric object, and in this text we have generally
“simulated” it by carrying out constructions on
{\check{M}}
and shearing them.

Ignoring this issue for this discussion, the sheared moment map
\mu^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}:{\check{M}}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}/{\check{G}}\to\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}[2]/{\check{G}}
defines a shifted Lagrangian in the 3-shifted symplectic stack
\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}[2]/{\check{G}}=T^{*}[3]B{\check{G}}
.
In the AKSZ formalism, quantizing spaces of maps into
{\check{M}}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
defines a 3d TQFT (Rozansky-Witten theory), while quantizing spaces of maps into
{\check{M}}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}/{\check{G}}\to\mathrm{pt}/{\check{G}}
(coupling maps to
{\check{M}}
to
{\check{G}}
-local systems) defines a boundary condition for a 4d TQFT (the 4d B-model
\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}
). The AKSZ description of Kapustin-Witten theory in terms of

is due to Elliott and Yoo
[
EY18
]
and is the basis of recent work
[
HY
]
on S-duality for boundary theories and the analysis
[
EGW24
]
of associated factorization algebras of observables.

The quantization of

is the
E_{3}
-monoidal spectral Hecke category, while the quantization of
\mu^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
is given by the spectral deformation quantization

constructed in this section (and its category of modules, the factorizable local category
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})
), an
E_{3}
-algebra object in (and
E_{2}
-module category for) the Hecke category.

Now we evaluate these constructions on an oriented compact surface
\Sigma
. The mapping stack

, this construction recovers the cotangent bundle of the space of maps into

. More generally, the moment map defines a shifted Lagrangian

, and a relative symplectic variety

(18.1)

\textstyle{\mathrm{Map}(\Sigma,\check{M}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}/\check{G})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

Given a local system

18.1.
Relative flat connections and coherent microlocalization

In this section, to provide technical background for what follows
we review the theory of relative flat connections, shifted differential operators and microlocalization of coherent sheaves following Beraldo
[
Ber19a
,
Ber21a
]
.
This theory provides a categorified or
shifted
137
137

137

Categorification and shifting are meant to be roughly synonymous –
n
-shifted symplectic spaces are the classical phase spaces of
(n+1)
-dimensional quantum field theories, whose topological aspects are captured by
n
-categories.
analog of the quantization of the cotangent bundle by differential operators and the corresponding theory of singular support and wave front sets of distributions.

18.1.1.
Coherent microlocalization and “shifted” differential operators

Now, on any variety
Y
, the endomorphisms of any sheaf
{\mathcal{L}}
are of course an
\mathcal{O}_{Y}
-algebra,
but they also have a finer structure: There is a morphism of sheaves of algebras

(18.2)

HH^{*}(Y)\rightarrow\mathrm{Ext}^{*}({\mathcal{L}},{\mathcal{L}}),

from Hochschild cohomology of
Y
to the derived endomorphisms of
{\mathcal{L}}
.
For
Y
smooth this arises from a canonical action (the “Atiyah class”) of the tangent bundle
\mathcal{T}_{Y}

by degree
1
endomorphisms

\mathcal{T}_{Y}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ext}^{1}({\mathcal{L}},{\mathcal{L}})

arising by associating to a vector field
X
the
self-extension of
\mathcal{L}
arising by
infinitesimally displacing
\mathcal{L}
along
X
.

Said differently, the self-ext algebra on the right
can be regarded as the pushforward of a sheaf on the shifted cotangent bundle
T^{*}Y[1]
.
This describes a microlocal geometry for the coherent sheaf
\mathcal{L}

138
138

138

This is an analogue
of the following process in real analysis: for a function on a smooth manifold
M
,
there is a standard way (the “Wigner distribution”) to lift

|f|^{2}

to a distribution on the classical phase space
T^{*}M
.
This distribution expresses how the
mass of
f
is distributed microlocally, and bears a close relation to the action of quantum observables on
f
, in particular the module over the algebra of differential operators on
M
generated by
f
.

and is indeed a shifted version of the usual versions of microlocalization, e.g. the ring of functions on
T^{*}Y[1]
,
carries a Poisson structure with bracket of degree
-2
, which is the Gerstenhaber bracket
when identified with
HH^{\ast}(Y)
.

When developed in a derived setting – replacing the graded algebra
HH^{*}(Y)
by the algebra of Hochschild cochains – it yields quite a fine invariant: endomorphisms of a sheaf that commute with the Hochschild action are automatically locally constant. For example, if
{\mathcal{L}}_{1},{\mathcal{L}}_{2}
are line bundles, so that
\mathrm{End}({\mathcal{L}}_{i})=\mathcal{O}
, coincidence of the associated morphisms (
18.2
) at the derived level is equivalent to
{\mathcal{L}}_{1}\otimes{\mathcal{L}}_{2}^{-1}

admitting a flat structure. See Remark
18.1.11
for a more precise formulation.

Return now to the general concern of this paper. Suppose that
\check{M}
is polarized. In §
12.8

we have constructed a certain sheaf of algebras
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}},\Sigma}
over the “nonpolar locus”
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}^{\circ}
—
essentially a deformation of the
L
-sheaf of
\check{M}
itself –
acting on the
L
-sheaf,
i.e., with a morphism

\mathbb{O}_{\check{M},\Sigma}\longrightarrow\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{L}_{\check{X}}).

Now, according to our discussion above, we can seek to construct

\mathbb{O}_{\check{M},\Sigma}

not merely as an
\mathcal{O}
-algebra, but as an algebra equipped with a morphism from
HH^{*}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})
, compatibly with its action on the
L
-sheaf.

In the remainder of this section we will do this (in fact over the entire stack of local systems), if
\check{M}
has a spectral deformation quantization.
But the technical implementatiom of all this is difficult
because
\mathrm{Loc}
is not a variety. We will now recall the work of Beraldo
[
Ber19a
,
Ber21a
]
, which constructs a suitable version
of “the category of
HH^{*}(\mathrm{Loc})
-modules.”

18.1.2.
Relative flat connections

Let
f:Y\to Z
be a morphism. Then we can speak of the “completion
\hat{Z}_{Y}
of
Z
along
f
.”
This is represented by the functor sending a scheme
U

to morphisms
U\rightarrow Z
together with a lift
U_{\mathrm{red}}\rightarrow Y

of the induced morphism from the reduced subscheme of
U
.
This has a hybrid behavior: if
f
is a closed immersion, this will recover
the formal completion of
Z
along
Y
; if
Z
is a point, it will
recover the de Rham stack of
Y
. In general the completion
\widehat{Z}_{Y}
is
the fiber product
\widehat{Z}_{Y}=Y_{dR}\times_{Z_{dR}}Z
of
Z
with the de Rham space of
Y
.

The category of
relative flat connections

\mathrm{Flat}(Y/Z)=\mathrm{Flat}(f:Y\to Z)
was introduced by Arinkin-Gaitsgory and Beraldo
[
AG18
,
Ber21a
]

with the notation
\mathrm{IndCoh}_{0}(\widehat{Z}_{Y})
and is a modification of ind-coherent sheaves on the completion of
Z
at
Y
.
139
139

139

We only consider representable morphisms of
bounded
, locally of finite presentation, perfect stacks, avoiding many of the key technicalities of
[
Ber21a
]
and
[
Ber19a
]
. It is defined as the pullback

\textstyle{\mathrm{Flat}(Y/Z)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{QC(Y)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\Upsilon_{Y}}
\textstyle{QC^{!}(\widehat{Z}_{Y})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\widehat{f}^{!}}
\textstyle{QC^{!}(Y)}

where
\widehat{f}:Y\to\widehat{Z}_{Y}
is the completion of
Z
along
Y
.
In other words, relative flat connections on
f
are ind-coherent sheaves on the completion of
f
which are quasicoherent
140
140

140

Our use of the term relative flat connections instead of relative
D
-modules is meant to evoke this regularity condition – or to emphasize the role of
\mathrm{Flat}(Y/Z)
as relative
left

D
-modules, cf.
[
Ber21a
]
.
, i.e., in the image of the symmetric monoidal functor

\Upsilon_{Y}=-\otimes\omega_{Y}:QC(Y)\to QC^{!}(Y),

when pulled back to
Y
.

Let us first illustrate two extreme instances of this notion: if
Z
is a point we recover
D
-modules on
Y
, while if
Y
is smooth and
f
a closed embedding we recover (ind-coherent) sheaves on the completion of
Z
along
Y
.

18.1.3.
Relative flat connections as modules for relative differential operators

In general
[
Ber21a
, 0.3.8]
relative flat connections
\mathrm{Flat}(Y/Z)
are identified with quasi-coherent sheaves on
Y
equipped with a “compatible” action of the relative tangent complex
T_{Y/Z}
,
i.e., the fiber of
T_{Y}\rightarrow f^{*}T_{Z}
.
Here
T_{Y/Z}
is identified with
\mathcal{O}_{Z}
-linear derivations of
\mathcal{O}_{Y}
and as such
can be regarded as a sheaf of differential graded Lie algebras on
Y
, acting nontrivially on the structure sheaf of
Y
.

Equivalently, then, we can regard
\mathrm{Flat}(Y/Z)
as modules in
QC(Y)
for
the
relative differential operators
for
Y/Z
:

(18.3)

\mathcal{D}(f):=\mbox{
the universal enveloping algebra of the Lie algebroid $T_{Y/Z}$.}

Just as with the ordinary sheaf of differential operators this is not an algebra in
QC(Y)
but a monad, i.e., an algebra object in endofunctors of
\mathrm{QC}(Y)
, representable (via the mechanism of integral transforms) by a sheaf on
Y\times Y
supported near the diagonal. We regard
\mathcal{D}(f)
(or rather its pushforward to
Z
) as a deformation quantization of the relative cotangent complex
T^{*}_{Y/Z}
, as a relative symplectic variety over
Z
.

Remark 18.1.4

(Enveloping algebras)
.

A general definition of universal enveloping algebra in the
QC^{!}
setting is given in
[
GR17
, Volume 2, Chapter 8, Section
4.2]
, as the groupoid algebra of a formal groupoid. Namely given a Lie algebroid
T
on
Y

one has an adjoint pair
(\operatorname{Ind},\mathrm{For})

of functors, induction and the forgetful functor,
between
\mathrm{QC}^{!}(Y)
and
T
-modules in
QC^{!}(Y)
.
We then define
{\mathcal{U}}T:=\mathrm{For}\circ\operatorname{Ind}

to be the resulting monad, i.e., an algebra object in endofunctors of
\mathrm{QC}^{!}(Y)
. One can think of
{\mathcal{U}}T
geometrically as
\pi^{!}\pi_{*}
where
\pi:Y\to Y/\exp(T)
is the quotient by the formal groupoid corresponding to
T
.

In our setting (cf.
[
Ber21a
, 0.3.8]
)
there is again an adjunction
(\operatorname{Ind},\mathrm{For})
between
QC(Y)
and
\mathrm{Flat}(Y/Z)
, and the quasicoherent sheaf underlying the algebra of relative differential operators is
\mathcal{D}(f)=\mathrm{For}(\operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal{O}_{Y}))
. For example:

-

For
Z=\mathrm{pt}
and
Y
smooth this recovers the usual induction / forgetful adjunction between
\mathcal{O}
-modules and
D
-modules, i.e., the description of
\mathcal{D}
as the underlying
\mathcal{O}
-module of the induced
D
-module
\operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal{O})
.

-

For
Y\rightarrow Z
a closed embedding, again with
Y
smooth, the functor
\mathrm{For}

!
-restricts a sheaf on a formal neighborhood of
Y

to a sheaf on
Y
, whereas
\operatorname{Ind}
is the pushforward. Correspondingly,
\mathrm{For}(\operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal{O}))
recovers
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{Z}}(\mathcal{O}_{Y},\mathcal{O}_{Y})
.

Note that since we are taking the enveloping algebra of the relative tangent complex of
Y/Z
, the algebra
\mathcal{D}(f)
is naturally
\mathrm{QC}(Z)
-linear, i.e., its pushforward to
Z
defines an algebra object in
QC(Z)
– a quasicoherent sheaf of algebras – rather than just a monad.

We note for future reference that there is a “de Rham pushforward” functor
f_{*,dR}:\mathrm{Flat}(Y/Z)\to QC^{!}(Z)
(again we’re assuming
f
representable), such that the composition
f_{*,dR}\circ\operatorname{Ind}\simeq f_{*}\circ\Upsilon
is the ind-coherent pushforward.

A little more on the two basic examples:

•

When
f:Y\rightarrow Z
is a smooth morphism of smooth varieties,
\mathcal{D}(f)

consists of differential operators on
Y
that are “along the fibers,” which is to say, they commute
with multiplication by functions on
Z
; this quantizes the usual relative cotangent bundle of
f
.

•

When
f:Y\rightarrow Z
is an LCI immersion, then
\mathcal{D}(f)
consists, as noted above,
Z
-linear endomorphisms of
\mathcal{O}_{Y}
. This can also be seen from the Koszul dual description of sheaves on the formal completion in terms of the monad
i^{!}i_{*}
.
In this case the relative cotangent bundle
T^{*}(Y/Z)
has fibers (when considered as a sheaf on
Z
) given by odd symplectic vector spaces
N[1]\oplus N^{*}[-1]
where
N
is the normal bundle to
Y\hookrightarrow Z
, and its quantization
\mathcal{D}(f)
should be considered as its Clifford algebra quantization.

18.1.5.
Shifted
\mathcal{D}
-modules

Beraldo defines the category
\mathbb{H}(Y)
of shifted differential operators as (suitably regular) integral transforms for ind-coherent sheaves supported near the diagonal:

Definition 18.1.6
.

[
Ber19a
,
Ber21a
]

The monoidal category
\mathbb{H}(Y)
of shifted differential operators on a quasi-smooth stack
Y
is the convolution category of sheaves on the formal neighborhood of the diagonal of
Y
,

\mathbb{H}(Y):=\mathrm{Flat}(\Delta:Y\to Y\times Y)

By
[
Ber21a
, Corollary 3.5.3]

\mathbb{H}(Y)
is in fact a
rigid
monoidal category for
Y
a perfect stack (such as all the stacks arising in this chapter).
Locally (for
Y
affine) the category
\mathbb{H}(Y)
can be identified Koszul dually with the category of modules for the algebra of Hochschild cochains
HC^{\ast}(Y)
on
Y
, the self-Ext of the structure sheaf of the diagonal, i.e., with integral transforms generated by the identity. Its monoidal structure comes in this realization from the
E_{2}
-algebra structure on Hochschild cochains. On the level of cohomology, this
E_{2}
structure recovers the shifted Poisson (
P_{2}
) algebra of polyvector fields, i.e., functions on
T^{*}[1]Y
. Thus the algebra
HC^{\ast}(Y)
and its module category
\mathbb{H}(Y)
define deformation quantizations of the shifted symplectic stack
T^{*}[1]Y
.

Remark 18.1.7
.

Note the close parallel with Grothendieck’s definition of differential operators as integral transforms for functions supported set-theoretically on the diagonal.
Indeed, for
Y
smooth, the subtleties of
QC^{!}
disappear and
\mathbb{H}(Y)
-modules are precisely crystals of categories on
Y
, which are sheaves of categories with a flat connection (sheaves of categories on the de Rham space
Y_{dR}
) or equivalently
\mathcal{D}(Y)
-module categories. In general, to illustrate the rigidity of
\mathbb{H}(Y)
-actions, observe that a
\mathbb{H}(Y)
-linear functor
F:QC(Y)\to QC(Y)
is determined by the object
F(\mathcal{O})
, which acquires the structure of
D
-module, and thus if
F
is proper (preserves compact objects)
F(\mathcal{O})
is in fact a local system.
For
Y
quasi-smooth,
\mathbb{H}(Y)
-modules are singular generalizations of crystals of categories and admit a theory of singular support in
T^{*}[1]Y
just as
D
-modules have singular support in
T^{*}Y
. From this perspective crystals of categories play the role of local systems – they are characterized by having zero singular support.

The two natural
\mathbb{H}(Y)
-modules
QC(Y)
and
QC^{!}(Y)
play the role of smooth functions and distributions, and in the latter case Beraldo’s theory recovers the notion of singular support of (ind-)coherent sheaves
[
AG15
]
, which is zero for quasicoherent sheaves.
Namely given a coherent sheaf
\mathcal{F}\in QC^{!}(Y)
we may consider its internal endomorphisms
\underline{\mathrm{End}}_{\mathbb{H}(Y)}(\mathcal{F})
as an algebra object in
\mathbb{H}(Y)
,
which we regard as a “chain-level microlocalization” of
\mathcal{F}
, or as the system of differential equations satisfied by
\mathcal{F}
. Passing to cohomology we find its classical limit, the classical (or cohomological) microlocalization, an algebra on
T^{*}[1]Y
as before whose support recovers the singular support of
\mathcal{F}
.
There is a monoidal functor
QC(Y)\to\mathbb{H}(Y)
with a continuous and lax-monoidal right adjoint
\mathbb{H}(Y)\to QC(Y)

(see
[
Ber20a
, 0.3.4]
), which means that we can “forget” an algebra object in
\mathbb{H}(Y)
to a quasicoherent sheaf of algebras – in particular the algebra
\underline{\mathrm{End}}_{\mathbb{H}(Y)}(\mathcal{F})
refines the usual sheaf inner hom
\underline{\mathrm{End}}_{QC(Y)}(\mathcal{F})
, lifting it to a microlocal object.

18.1.8.
Enhanced relative differential operators

The algebra of relative differential operators
\mathcal{D}(f)
was defined above
– after pushforward to
Z
– is a sheaf of algebras on
Z
.
However this pushforward has a richer microlocal structure – it naturally defines an algebra in
\mathbb{H}(Z)
, as we now describe.

For a morphism
f:Y\to Z
, the category
\mathrm{Flat}(Y\to Z)
of relative flat connections is itself a
shifted
D
-module
on
Z
, i.e., it has the structure of module for shifted differential operators
\mathbb{H}(Z)
. In Lie algebra language this action is given by the map of Lie algebras
f^{*}T_{Z}[-1]\to T_{Y/Z}
coming from the relative tangent sequence of
f
. More formally, it is a consequence of applying the functoriality of
QC^{!}
to the action of the formal groupoid given by the completion of the diagonal
\Delta:Z\to Z\times Z
on that given by the completion of
f:Y\to Z
, see also Remark
18.1.10
.) We can use this to define an “enhanced” algebra of relative differential operators,
an algebra object in
\mathbb{H}(Z)
whose underlying quasicoherent sheaf is the pushforward to
Z
of
\mathcal{D}(f)
:

Definition 18.1.9
.

The enhanced relative differential operators along
f:Y\to Z
(for
Z
perfect) are the algebra object
\underline{D}(f)\in Alg(\mathbb{H}(Z))
given by internal endomorphisms of
\operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal{O}_{Y})\in\mathrm{Flat}(Y/Z)
.

Remark 18.1.10
.

The shifted
D
-module structure
\mathbb{H}(Z)\circlearrowright\mathrm{Flat}(Y/Z)
is part of the rich functoriality of the theory of shifted
\mathcal{D}
-modules developed in
[
Ber19a
]
(see
[
Ber20a
, 0.3.4]
for a useful summary). Namely
\mathrm{Flat}(Y/Z)=\mathbb{H}(\mathrm{pt}\leftarrow Y\to Z)
is identified as the “Gauss-Manin” sheaf of categories on
Z
, the pushforward of the structure sheaf of categories
QC(Y)
to
Z
in the world of categories with flat connection,

\mathrm{Flat}(Y/Z)\simeq QC(Y)\otimes_{\mathbb{H}(Y)}\mathbb{H}(Y\to Z)\circlearrowright\mathbb{H}(Z).

Remark 18.1.11

(The center of
\mathbb{H}
and microlocalization)
.

To continue the metaphor of coherent microlocalization from §
18.1.1
, we would like to understand the greater rigidity imposed by enhancing a
QC(Z)
-module to an
\mathbb{H}(Z)
-module. One way to measure this is to look at the functorial endomorphisms of modules for the two monoidal categories, i.e., their centers. The center of
QC(Z)
is identified
[
BZFN10
]
with sheaves
QC({\mathcal{L}}Z)
on the derived inertia, which contains
QC(Z)
itself. On the other hand the main theorem of
[
Ber21a
]
identifies the center of
\mathbb{H}(Z)
with [a subtle derived version of]
\mathcal{D}
-modules on the inertia
{\mathcal{L}}Z
. In particular if
Z
is a scheme this is identified with
\mathcal{D}
-modules on
Z
itself, and the only coherent objects in the center are flat vector bundles (local systems).
Compare with the distinction between center of
\mathcal{O}(Z)
for
Z
affine, which are
(classically) functions
\mathcal{O}(Z)
or (derivedly) distributions on
{\mathcal{L}}Z
, and the center of
\mathcal{D}(Z)

which is (classically)
locally constant functions or (derivedly) the de Rham cohomology of
Z
. We interpret this loosely as limiting the ambiguity in prescribing a coherent sheaf by the
\mathbb{H}
-module it generates to tensoring with flat vector bundles.

18.2.
L-observables and Hecke constraints

Having recalled the necessary technical preliminaries,
will now define the algebra of
L
-observables. Recall that in §
12.8
we defined a quasicoherent sheaf of algebras
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}}^{\circ}
on an open
\mathrm{Loc}^{\circ}\subset\mathrm{Loc}
in the vectorial case. In that setting the relative symplectic variety of (
18.1
)
is a symplectic odd vector bundle, equivalently the data of a quadratic vector bundle and
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}}^{\circ}
is its deformation quantization to a Clifford algebra.
Moreover Conjecture
12.8.1
(combined with the global period conjecture) identifies this algebra with the inner endomorphisms of the L-sheaf, in the cases where it has been defined. The construction of this section, which depends on being given a spectral deformation quantization, defines a sheaf of algebras on all of
\mathrm{Loc}
, together with a microlocal refinement (algebra in
\mathbb{H}(\mathrm{Loc})
). As we will see, it still acts on the
L
-sheaf, though in general we do not expect it to give the full inner endomorphism algebra.

Fix now a smooth projective curve
\Sigma
over
\mathbb{C}
, which we consider in its Betti realization as an oriented topological surface, and
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}=\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma)
the associated stack of Langlands parameters, a quasi-smooth algebraic stack.

Recall (§
D.4.7
) that given a locally constant factorization category
\mathcal{C}
on a surface
\Sigma
, the
factorization homology

[
AF15
]
, or topological chiral homology in the terminology of
[
Lura
]
, is the universal category equipped
\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{C}
with functors
i_{x}:\mathcal{C}_{x}\to\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{C}
for
x\in\Sigma
compatible with the unital factorization structure. If
\mathcal{C}=QC(Z)
is the symmetric monoidal category of sheaves on a perfect stack, then
\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{C}\simeq QC(\mathrm{Map}(\Sigma,Z))
calculates sheaves on the mapping stack.

We can apply this to globalize the Hecke action.
The global spectral category
QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})
carries an action
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{x}\circlearrowright QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})
of the spherical Hecke category for every
x\in\Sigma
. These actions
assemble together into the action of the
global Hecke category

\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}:=\int_{\Sigma}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}},

which was identified by Beraldo
[
Ber19b
]
with shifted differential operators on
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
:

Theorem 18.2.1
.

[
Ber19b
]

There is an equivalence of monoidal categories between the global Hecke category
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
, i.e., the factorization homology of the spherical category, and shifted differential operators on
\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{G}}}
,

\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}\simeq\mathbb{H}(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{G}}}).

In particular
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
is rigid, and the local Hecke actions factor through the global action

\textstyle{\bigotimes_{x\in\Sigma}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\mathrm{End}(QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}))}
\textstyle{\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

18.2.2.
L-observables

We are now in a position to define the “algebra of
L
-observables,”
and to define abstractly a notion of
L
-sheaf in terms of it:

Definition 18.2.3
.

Suppose given a spectral deformation quantization
\mathbb{O}_{\check{M}}
.
The L-observables sheaf

\mathbb{O}_{{{\check{M}}},\Sigma}=\int_{\Sigma}\mathbb{O}_{\check{M}}\in Alg(\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma})

is the algebra object of the global Hecke category
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
that is defined by factorization homology of the factorization associative algebra
\mathbb{O}_{\check{M}}
in the Hecke category.

That the
L
-observables sheaf is indeed an algebra object follows from the lax monoidal functoriality of factorization homology
[
AF15
]

applied to the functor from
\mathrm{Vect}
associated to
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}}
.
As noted in §
18.1.5
that we may consider such an algebra object in
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}=\mathbb{H}(\mathrm{Loc})
as a “microlocal refinement” of an underlying quasicoherent sheaf of algebras on
\mathrm{Loc}
.

Remark 18.2.4
.

One way of taking a semiclassical limit here
is by replacing the factorization structures by “naive” commutative multiplications:

Above we use the “sophisticated” factorization structure on the spherical Hecke category.
If we instead endow it with its naive symmetric monoidal structure
({QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}}),\otimes)
coming
from tensor product of coherent sheaves,
the factorization homology recovers the shear of
QC(\mathrm{Map}(\Sigma,\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}}))
(since shearing commutes with factorization homology).
The latter category – the semiclassical limit of the global Hecke category – is a decompleted form of the category of sheaves on the shifted
cotangent bundle
T^{*}[1]\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
, where the shift comes from the orientation class of
\Sigma
.

Similarly, the “semiclassical limit” of the algebra of
L
-observables
can be obtained by using
the naive structure of
\mathcal{O}_{{\check{M}}}
as a commutative algebra over
\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}}

in place of the spectral deformation quantization.
In this limit,
the
L
-observable sheaf degenerates to the structure sheaf of the “spectral Gaiotto Lagrangian” from Remark
18.0.2
, i.e., the
pushforward of the sheared structure sheaf under the integrated moment map
\mu_{\Sigma}
of
18.1
. The underlying quasicoherent sheaf on
\mathrm{Loc}
, i.e., the pushforward
q_{{\check{M}},*}\mathcal{O}
, is a variant of the
L
-sheaf of
{\check{M}}
.

18.2.5.
L
-eigensheaves and shifted differential equations

The rigid monoidal category
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
acts on the spectral category
QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})
– an action we can interpret as either by Hecke functors or by shifted differential operators. Therefore, for an algebra object
A\in\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
,
we can consider
A
-module objects
L
in
\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc})
. This notion can be expressed equivalently as giving an algebra map

A\to\underline{\mathrm{End}}_{\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}}(L)
to internal endomorphisms of
L
, or as a pointed
\mathbb{H}
-linear functor

A{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}_{\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}}\longrightarrow\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}),\hskip 21.68121ptA\mapsto L,

and refines the more familiar notion of module for the underlying quasicoherent sheaf of algebras.

Definition 18.2.6
.

An L-eigensheaf for
{{\check{M}}}
is a module object
in
\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{G}}})
under the
L
-observables
\mathbb{O}_{{{\check{M}}},\Sigma}
.
Equivalently, an
L
-eigensheaf is given by an the data of
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
-linear morphism

{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{M}},\Sigma}:\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}},\Sigma}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\longrightarrow QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}).

We call such a functor a spectral
\Theta
-series for
{\check{M}}
and the category
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}^{\check{M}}:=\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}},\Sigma}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
the category of
L
-observables for
{\check{M}}
.

We are going to verify in §
18.3
that this notion of
L
-eigensheaf is compatible with the
constructions appearing earlier in the paper (i.e., “an
L
-sheaf is an
L
-eigensheaf.”)
The terminology “
L
-eigensheaf” is meant to suggest, roughly speaking, that it satisfies all Hecke constraints encoded by the L-observables. This is a less flabby notion than it might appear, or than the notion of module for the underyling quasicoherent sheaf of algebras might suggest:
the ambiguity in an
L
-eigensheaf
is, roughly speaking, that of twisting by a flat bundle.
Recall that by Theorem
18.2.1
the global Hecke category
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
recovers the shifted differential operators on the stack of Langlands parameters. Thus the pointed
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
-module
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}^{\check{M}}
is prescribing a categorified system of differential equations, and an
L
-eigensheaf is precisely a solution of this system inside
QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})
. This is a categorified analog of the problem of finding a distributional solution of an algebraic system of differential equations as a map from a cyclic
D
-module. Our expectation (cf. Remark
18.1.11
) is that the eigensheaf condition loosely speaking determines the
L
-sheaf up to tensoring with flat vector bundles; it would be useful to formulate this more precisely.

Remark 18.2.7

(Holonomicity)
.

In fact the
L
-eigensheaf condition is the shifted analog of a holonomic
\mathcal{D}
-module, in the following sense: the semiclassical limit of the
L
-observables form a shifted Lagrangian
\mu_{\Sigma}
(
18.1
) of Remark
18.2.4
in
T^{*}[1]\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
. It is a very interesting problem to
establish analogues of the strong finiteness properties of holonomic differential equations.

Remark 18.2.8

(Numerical analogue)
.

The analogue of the
L
-eigensheaf property in the numerical relative Langlands program is that the period function transforms
under each local Hecke algebra as the basic function on
X_{F}
does. This is not a trivial constraint; for example,
it is frequently enough to force the period function only to pair nontrivially with forms that are functorially lifted from another group.
However, it is nonetheless a much less rigid property than the categorified version that appears above. One key reason for this
is that the above notion keeps track of the derived Hecke and factorization structure.

18.2.9.
Affineness and categorical factorization homology

We spell out a more abstract perspective we will need in §
18.3
to interface with results of
[
HL22a
]
. Namely, the given definition of
\mathbb{H}^{\check{M}}_{\Sigma}
is a “shortcut” made possible by the affineness of
{\check{M}}
: the module category

\mathbb{H}^{\check{M}}_{\Sigma}=\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}},\Sigma}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}(\mathbb{H}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}))\in\mathbb{H}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}

is the global counterpart to the local Hecke-module category

{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{\check{M}}=\mathbb{O}_{\check{M}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}({\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}})\in{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}.

Specifically,
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{\check{M}}
is a factorization algebra object in
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}
-modules, hence its factorization homology defines a global module
\int_{\Sigma}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{{{\check{M}}}}\in\mathbb{H}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
.

Lemma 18.2.10
.

The
L
-observable category
\mathbb{H}^{\check{M}}_{\Sigma}
is identified as
\mathbb{H}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})
-module category with the factorization homology
\int_{\Sigma}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{{{\check{M}}}}
.

Proof.

The factorization homology is defined a colimit over disc embeddings of the
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}
-module categories
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{\check{M}}
. This is calculated as a colimit of the induced
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}=\int_{\Sigma}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}
-module categories
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{M}}\otimes_{{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}}\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
. Thus we are reduced to calculating a colimit of categories of modules for algebra objects in a fixed monoidal category. But the functor
R\mapsto R{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
taking algebras to their pointed categories of modules preserves colimits (it is the left adjoint of taking inner endomorphisms of the pointing), so the colimit category is identified with modules for the colimit algebra.
∎

18.3.
L-sheaves and L-observables in the polarized case

We now examine the polarized case
{\check{M}}=T^{*}{\check{X}}
for a
{\check{G}}
-variety
{\check{X}}
,
and, in particular, the compatibility of the constructions of this section with
the rest of the paper.

Specifically we shall verify that the
L
-sheaf as constructed previously –
i.e.,
the push-forward
L_{{\check{X}}}(\Sigma)=q_{*}\omega_{\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}}
of the dualizing sheaf
under

(18.4)

q:\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{G}}}

–
is in fact a
L
-eigensheaf, with respect to the spectral deformation quantization constructed in §
17.2
. In fact we interpret the results of
[
HL22a
]
in our case as giving a complete description of the
L
-observables and the spectral
\Theta
-series construction in terms of the theory of relative flat connection and relative differential operators from §
18.1
.

This is all in accordance with the semiclassical picture described in the introduction to the section.
In the case at hand,
the “relative” symplectic variety over
\mathrm{Loc}_{G}
described in (
18.1
)
is the relative cotangent bundle of
\mathrm{Loc}^{{\check{X}}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Loc}_{G}
;
as we discussed, the algebra of
L
-observables is a “relative” deformation quantization
of this, and it is therefore reasonable to expect that it is described by relative differential operators.

18.3.1.
Spectral
\Theta
-series in the polarized case

We first give a direct argument for the eigensheaf property of the
L
-sheaf in the polarized case by exhibiting it as the image of a spectral
\Theta
-series functor (as in Definition
18.2.6
). In other words, we present the spectral counterpart of the argument we explained for Problem
16.3.2
(without the accompanying technical difficulties in the automorphic setting).

Proposition 18.3.2

(Polarized L-sheaf)
.

The L-sheaf
L_{{\check{X}}}(\Sigma)\in QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})
, as defined in Section
11
,
carries the structure of
L
-eigensheaf attached to
\check{M}
,
given the spectral deformation quantization described in §
17.2
.
That is to say, the
L
-sheaf carries the structure of module for the L-observables
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}},\Sigma}\in Alg(\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma})
.

Prop.
18.3.2
.

In Section
15.2
(and more specifically (
15.5
)) we enhanced the L-sheaf to the image of the unit under the one-point
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
-linear spectral
\Theta
-series

L_{{\check{X}},x}:QC^{!}({\mathcal{L}}{\check{X}}/{\check{G}})\to QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}).

The construction is easily seen to extend to a factorizable morphism of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
-module, which automatically gives a global spectral
\Theta
-series, hence an
L
-eigensheaf.

More precisely, given an arbitrary collection of embedded discs
\iota_{I}:\coprod_{I}D_{I}\hookrightarrow\Sigma
with boundary circles
\partial\iota_{I}:\coprod\partial D_{I}\hookrightarrow\Sigma
we consider
{\check{G}}
-local systems on
\Sigma
with sections of the associated
{\check{X}}
-bundle on the complement of the discs, with its natural action of Hecke modifications of local systems and forgetful map to
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
:

\textstyle{({\check{X}}/{\check{G}})^{I}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{i}
\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\pi}
\scriptstyle{i_{\iota_{I}}}
\scriptstyle{q}
\textstyle{\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(\iota_{I},{\check{X}}\mbox{ on }\partial\iota_{I})}
\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma,{\check{X}}\mbox{ on }\Sigma\setminus\iota_{I})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\pi_{\iota_{I}}}
\scriptstyle{q_{\iota_{I}}}
\textstyle{\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}}

This correspondence defines the
I
-fold version of the
\Theta
-series, and is easily seen to be unital, sending the pushforward of the dualizing sheaf on the closed locus
\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}
to the L-sheaf, and compatible with the factorizable
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
-action.

It follows from the universal property of factorization homology (its construction as a colimit) that these multipoint
\Theta
-series descend to the factorization homology. In particular this endows the L-sheaf with a factorizable action of the local L-observables, hence an action of
\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}},\Sigma}
.
∎

18.3.3.
L
-observables and relative differential operators

We now turn to the identification of

.
This identification will be deduced from (a special case of) a recent result of Ho and Li

]
, which calculates factorization homology (and more generally associated topological field theory structure) of a wide class of Hecke categories generalizing Beraldo’s description of the global Hecke category

First recall that Lemma

allows us to identify the category

Theorem 18.3.4

[

Let

The category of

Moreover to an open embedding

\textstyle{{\mathcal{Y}}^{N}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

We specialize this construction to our setting

•

For

\textstyle{({\check{X}}/{\check{G}})^{I}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

When specialized to our setting, we find:

In particular we highlight the following additional consequences of the general construction of

18.4.

We briefly discuss the modifications necessary to carry out the construction of one-point and factorizable spectral

18.5.
Geometric Arthur Parameters

In this section we discuss the geometric counterpart of the theory of Arthur parameters and its relation to the process of Arthur functoriality on the automorphic side, as discussed in §
14.9
on the numerical level.
While Arthur’s conjectures propose the parametrization of nontempered automorphic forms, the geometric counterpart proposes the parametrization of automorphic sheaves with a
sheared
Hecke eigenproperty and nontrivial singular support. The shearing and singular support are both captured by the datum of an
SL_{2}
homomorphism. Thus the
basic situation for this section (as in §
3.4
and §
11.9
) is that we are given
a subgroup
\check{H}\subset\check{G}
and a commuting
SL_{2}
:

\iota:\check{H}\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}\rightarrow\check{G}.

We restrict ourselves to even
SL_{2}
’s, i.e., we demand that the corresponding cocharacter
\varpi
acts on
\mathfrak{\check{g}}
with only even weights (see Remark
18.5.1
for a discussion of the odd case).
Recall from §
14.3
that in the setting of Arthur’s conjectures
[
Art89
]

one considers Arthur parameters

\phi_{A}:\Gamma_{F}\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}\rightarrow\check{G}(k),

where
\phi_{A}|\Gamma_{F}
is a Langlands parameter into the centralizer
{\check{H}}
of the
\mathrm{SL}_{2}
which is pure of weight zero, as defining Langlands parameters

\phi_{L}=\phi_{A}\circ\left(\mathrm{id}\times\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\varpi^{1/2}&0\\
0&\varpi^{-1/2}\end{array}\right]\right):\Gamma_{F}\rightarrow\check{G}(k),

into
{\check{G}}
(where
\varpi
is the cyclotomic character).

The geometric counterpart of this is the construction of
sheared local systems
for
{\check{G}}
out of (usual)
{\check{H}}
-local systems and the commuting
SL_{2}
;
informally, these will be
{\check{G}}
-local systems whose associated vector bundles are given cohomological gradings (and weights) by the associated cocharacter
\iota|_{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
.

In §
11.9
we constructed an Arthur (or spectral Whittaker) induction functor from sheaves on
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}}

to sheaves on
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
, while in §
17.5
we constructed a local counterpart from
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{H}}
-modules to
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}
-modules. We now establish local-global compatibility and use it to check that Arthur induction satisfies a Hecke eigenproperty with eigenvalues given by sheared local systems. In other words, this process constructs objects with Hecke eigenvalues given by a derived local system, cohomologically regraded by the diagonal part
\iota|_{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
of the Arthur
SL_{2}
, and with singular support given by the Arthur nilpotent. This is a global counterpart of the “Arthur” properties of the Hecke module
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})
described in Section
7.5.9
.

Remark 18.5.1
.

[Odd
SL_{2}
’s]
The case of odd
SL_{2}
triples is not covered by our current construction. The essential issue is that of defining the global spectral geometric quantization – i.e.,
L
-sheaf – of a non-polarized symplectic representation, in this case the action of the
SL_{2}
centralizer
{\check{H}}
on
W=\mathfrak{u}/\mathfrak{u}_{+}
. Again, this question reduces to the case of the spectral Weil representation §
11.10.4
, which we intend to discuss in more detail elsewhere.

Remark 18.5.2

(Functoriality and domain walls)
.

More broadly, Arthur functoriality is expected to have the structure of a domain wall or interface (§
D.1.4
)
between the arithmetic TQFTs

\mathsf{AI}:\mathcal{B}_{\check{H}}\longrightarrow\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}

describing the theory of Langlands parameters for the groups
{\check{H}}
and
{\check{G}}
. Such a domain wall encodes in particular maps
\mathcal{B}_{\check{H}}(\Xi)\to\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}(\Xi)
for arbitrary input geometries
\Xi
, compatible with all the relations and structures of the field theory. (Indeed such a domain wall structure is to be expected for the spectral quantization of any hyperspherical
{\check{G}}\times{\check{H}}
-variety; see §
12.3
for a related discussion of periods vs. functoriality.)

This domain wall, in the physics context of supersymmetric gauge theory, was constructed in the work of Gaiotto and Witten
[
GW09b
,
GW09a
,
Gai18
]
(see also Remark
1.2.1
). Namely to an
SL_{2}
homomorphism into a group
{\check{G}}
they attach a maximally supersymmetric (1/2 BPS) boundary condition for
{\mathcal{N}=4}
super-Yang-Mills theory for (the compact form of)
{\check{G}}
, the Nahm pole boundary condition associated to the
SL_{2}
data
\iota
. The Nahm pole boundary condition has flavor symmetry given by the (compact form of) the centralizer
{\check{H}}
of the
SL_{2}
, which enables it to be coupled to the
{\check{H}}
super-Yang-Mills theory and thereby upgraded to a domain wall between the theories, which may further be topologically twisted to define a domain wall between the TQFTs
\mathcal{B}_{\check{H}}
and
\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}
.

18.5.3.
Sheared local systems

In Example
6.4.3
we discussed
the equivalence
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})^{\varpi{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\simeq\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
, which does not respect the standard fiber functor.
As a result, the tensor category
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
has many nonisomorphic fiber functors

(-)^{\varpi{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}:\text{Rep}({\check{G}})\to\mathrm{Vect},\hskip 21.68121ptV\mapsto\underline{V}^{\varpi{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

taking a representation to the shear of the underlying vector space by the given cocharacter

\varpi:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to{\check{G}}
. Geometrically, a cocharacter defines a map
B\varpi:B{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to B{\check{G}}
and such a map defines a sheared fiber functor

\textstyle{\text{Rep}({\check{G}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(-)^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
\textstyle{\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
forget
\textstyle{\mathrm{Vect}.}

We will be interested in these functors primarily as defining
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
-module category structures on
\mathrm{Vect}
– i.e., potential “eigenvalues” for
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
-actions. We denote
\mathrm{Vect}
with this
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
-module structure as
\mathrm{Vect}^{\varpi{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
(or
\mathrm{Vect}_{\rho}^{\varpi{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
if we keep track of twisting by a
{\check{G}}
-torsor).

This is a remarkable feature of Tannakian formalism in the derived setting that diverges from classical experience:
seemingly Tannakian categories like
\text{Rep}(\check{G})
have infinitely many non-isomorphic fiber functors due to the phenomenon of shearing. Indeed Tannakian reconstruction in the derived setting
[
Lurb
,
BHL17
,
Ste23b
]
requires that one impose a connectivity (or t-exactness) hypothesis to circumvent such phenomena. In our current setting this bug is a crucial feature:
the sheared actions of
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
on
\mathrm{Vect}
arise naturally as the Hecke eigenvalues for Arthur parameters (see e.g.
[
FN11
,
LL09
]
).
Recently S. Slaoui and G. Stefanich have shown that for a large class of geometric stacks
X
shearing is the
only
obstruction to Tannakian reconstruction, in that isomorphism classes of tensor functors
QC(X)\to\mathrm{Vect}
are parametrized not just by points of
X
but by points and inertial cocharacters
\underline{x}:\mathrm{pt}/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to X
via the shearing construction
\mathcal{F}\mapsto(\underline{x}^{*}\mathcal{F})^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
.

Recall that
{\check{G}}
-local systems
\rho
on a curve
\Sigma
are identified with connective tensor functors
\underline{\rho}:\text{Rep}({\check{G}})\to\mathrm{Loc}(\Sigma)
to the tensor category of local systems on
\Sigma
, through the assignment of the associated local system to a representation
V\in\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
,
\underline{\rho}(V)=\rho\times^{\check{G}}V
.
If
\rho
is endowed with a
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
of automorphisms
\varpi:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(\rho)
,
then so is the symmetric monoidal functor
\underline{\rho}
(i.e., each of the associated local systems
\underline{\rho}(V)
is functorially and multiplicatively assigned a
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
symmetry). Hence

\underline{\rho}
can be sheared to
give a new functor
\underline{\rho}^{\varpi{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}:\text{Rep}({\check{G}})\to\mathrm{Loc}(\Sigma)
, a
sheared
{\check{G}}
-local system
, whose associated
local systems
\underline{\rho}^{\varpi{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}(V)
carry nontrivial cohomological gradings.

From another point of view, we can fix a cocharacter
\varpi:{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to{\check{G}}
and consider
{\check{G}}
-local systems
\rho
endowed with a reduction to the centralizer
{\check{G}}^{\varpi}
of
\varpi
. We may then shear
\rho
by the induced
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-symmetry. The associated local systems
\underline{\rho}^{\varpi{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}(V)
are given by giving the local systems
\underline{\rho}(V)
(for
{\check{G}}
-representations
V
) a cohomological grading determined by the
\varpi
-grading of
V
.

These sheared local systems are not
points of
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
in the usual sense, but rather “Tannakian points”, in that they give non-connective tensor functors from
QC(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})

to
\mathrm{Vect}
. Namely, the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-symmetry of the local system
\rho
defines a morphism
i_{\rho}:\mathrm{pt}/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}\to\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
, and hence a tensor functor

\textstyle{QC(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{i_{\rho}^{*}}
\textstyle{\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(-)^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
\textstyle{\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
forget
\textstyle{\mathrm{Vect}.}

Sheared local systems are the geometric avatars of the Langlands parameters associated to Arthur parameters.
Given an
{\check{H}}
-local system
\rho_{\check{H}}
and a homomorphism
\iota:{\check{H}}\times SL_{2}\to{\check{G}}
, the induced local system
\rho=\rho_{\check{H}}\times^{{\check{H}}}{\check{G}}
has in particular a reduction to the centralizer of the induced cocharacter
\varpi=\iota|_{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
of
{\check{G}}

and we can form the sheared local system
\rho^{\varpi{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
,
which will play an important role in what follows.

18.5.4.
Arthur induction

Recall that in §
11.9
we used the
L
-sheaf for the Whittaker space
{\check{M}}=T^{*}_{\Psi}{\check{G}}/U
as the kernel for a spectral Whittaker induction functor

\mathsf{AI}:QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}})\longrightarrow QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})

from sheaves on
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}}

to sheaves on
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
. On the other hand in §
17.5
the local spectral quantization of
{\check{M}}
provided the kernel
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\check{G}}\leftarrow{\check{H}}\times SL_{2}}
for a local counterpart, taking
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{H}}
-modules to
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}
-modules. We now establish local-global compatibility by applying the Whittaker version of spectral
\Theta
-series from §
18.4
:

Proposition 18.5.5
.

Local and global forms of Arthur functoriality are compatible:

•

(One-point) Fixing a point
x\in\Sigma
,

\mathsf{AI}
lifts to a natural map
\mathsf{AI}_{{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}}
of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}
-modules

\textstyle{QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{AI}}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes id}
\textstyle{QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})}
\textstyle{{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\check{G}}\leftarrow{\check{H}}\times SL_{2}}\otimes_{{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{H}}}QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{AI}_{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}}

•

(Factorizable) More generally,
\mathsf{AI}
lifts to a map
\mathsf{AI}_{\mathbb{H}}
of
\mathbb{H}_{{\check{G}}}
-modules

\mathbb{H}_{{\check{G}}\leftarrow{\check{H}}\times SL_{2}}\otimes_{\mathbb{H}_{\check{H}}}QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}})\longrightarrow QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})

where
\mathbb{H}_{{\check{G}}\leftarrow{\check{H}}\times SL_{2}}
is the factorization homology
of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\check{G}}\leftarrow{\check{H}}\times SL_{2}}
.

Proof.

Using the self-duality of
\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}})
and the tensor product identification

\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}})\otimes\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})\simeq\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{H}}\times{\check{G}}})

the desired functors are represented by integral transform constructions

{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\check{G}}\leftarrow{\check{H}}\times SL_{2}}\longrightarrow QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{H}}\times{\check{G}}})

and

\mathbb{H}_{{\check{G}}\leftarrow{\check{H}}\times SL_{2}}\longrightarrow QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{H}}\times{\check{G}}})

linear for the one-point and global Hecke categories for
{\check{H}}\times{\check{G}}
, respectively.
Now observe that the source of these functors as the (one-point and factorizable) spectral quantizations of the hyperspherical
{\check{G}}\times{\check{H}}
-space

{\check{M}}=T^{*}_{\Psi}{\check{G}}/U
. Thus the desired functors are provided by the (one-point and factorizable) spectral
\Theta
-series construction of §
18.4
.
∎

We will now apply Proposition
18.5.5
to establish properties of the Arthur induction functor which are global analogues of the local Arthur properties from §
7.5.9
. To do so we analyze
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\check{G}}\leftarrow{\check{H}}\times SL_{2}}
, a factorization algebra in
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}\otimes{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{H}}
-modules. Recall from Proposition
17.4.1
that ignoring its factorization structure (fixing a point
x\in\Sigma
), i.e., as a plain module category for the monoidal category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{G}}\otimes{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{H}}\simeq{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})\otimes{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{h}}^{\star}/{\check{H}})
, we have an equivalence

{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\check{G}}\leftarrow{\check{H}}\times SL_{2}}\simeq{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(T^{*}_{\Psi}({\check{G}}/U)/{\check{G}}\times{\check{H}})

where the module structure comes from applying
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}
to the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-equivaraint diagram

\textstyle{T^{*}_{\Psi}({\check{G}}/U)/{\check{G}}\times{\check{H}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}}}
\textstyle{\mathfrak{\check{h}}^{\star}/{\check{H}}.}

This identification does not respect factorization structures but it does respect the
SO(2)
-action of changes of coordinates, so gives an equivalence that is locally constant on
\Sigma
.

The Slodowy slice description of Example
3.4.10
,
provides an identification of
{\check{H}}\times{\check{G}}\times\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-spaces

T^{*}_{\Psi}{\check{G}}/U\simeq\mathfrak{\check{g}}_{e}\times{\check{G}},
where
{\check{H}}\circlearrowright\mathfrak{\check{g}}_{e}
via the coadjoint action, compatibly with the moment map to
\mathfrak{\check{h}}^{\star}
, though not with the moment map to
\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}
.
Thus we have an isomorphism

(18.6)

{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\check{G}}\leftarrow{\check{H}}\times SL_{2}}\simeq{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}_{e}/{\check{H}})

as plain
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})\otimes{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\check{H}}
-modules. Explicitly the
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
action is given by

(18.7)

\text{Rep}({\check{G}})\simeq QC(\mathrm{pt}/{\check{G}})^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\rightarrow QC(\mathrm{pt}/{\check{H}})\rightarrow QC(\mathfrak{\check{g}}_{e}/H)^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}

where the first isomorphism comes from the inner structure of the
\varpi
-action on
{\check{G}}

(see Example
6.4.3
and §
18.5.3
).

From this one can deduce the following

Corollary 18.5.6
.

Arthur induction takes Langlands parameters to Arthur parameters:

(1)

The functor
\mathsf{AI}
is naturally
\varpi
-sheared: for any
x\in\Sigma
it intertwines the
\text{Rep}({\check{H}})
and
\text{Rep}({\check{G}})
-actions
via the sheared forgetful functor
(-)^{\varpi{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}:Rep({\check{G}})\to Rep({\check{H}})
. Moreover the identification is locally constant in
\Sigma
.

(2)

The functor
\mathsf{AI}
produces
f
-antitempered sheaves

\mathsf{AI}:QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}})\longrightarrow QC^{!}_{f-anti}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})\subset QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}),

i.e., sheaves annihilated by the local Hecke action at any
x\in\Sigma
of the sheared structure sheaf
\mathcal{O}^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}_{\mathcal{N}_{<f}}\in{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}})
.

(3)

Furthermore, when restricted to
QC(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}})
the functor
\mathsf{AI}
produces sheaves which are also
f
-tempered,
i.e., with singular support contained in
\mathcal{N}_{<f}
.

In particular for any smooth point
\{\rho_{\check{H}}\}\in\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}}
, the Whittaker induction of the skyscraper
\mathsf{AI}(k_{\rho_{\check{H}}})
is an
f
-tempered and
f
-antitempered sheared Hecke eigensheaf with eigenvalue the shear
(\rho_{\check{G}})^{\varpi{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
of the induced
{\check{G}}
-local system (cf. Section
18.5.3
).

This construction of geometric Arthur parameters suggests an explicit description of the graded pieces of the “Arthur filtration” of the spectral category
\mathrm{QC}^{!}_{\mathcal{N}}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}})
by
f
-tempered sheaves for nilpotent orbits
f
(as discussed for example in
[
Lys23
]
), whose numerical counterpart is discussed in §
14.9
. Namely we conjecture

Conjecture 18.5.7
.

The functor
\mathsf{AI}
, restricted to quasicoherent sheaves on
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{H}}
, generates the
f
-tempered graded piece of the Arthur filtration.

If the Arthur restriction is identified with the adjoint of Arthur induction (see Remark §
11.9.3
) this would then produce a monadic descripition of the pieces of the Arthur filtration in terms of the bi-Whittaker reduction
U{}_{\psi}\backslash\!\backslash T^{*}{\check{G}}{/\!/}_{\psi}U
.

Part V
Appendices

Appendix A
Koszul Duality.

We discuss some examples of shearing in relation to Koszul duality and the construction of a spectral analog of the exponential sheaf.

A.1.
Koszul duality and sheaves on lines.

We now examine in some detail various categories of modules for symmetric and exterior algebras, which arise throughout this work in many guises. As elsewhere, we work with coefficients of characteristic zero, and all constructions are derived, i.e., take place in the relevant dg or
\infty
-categories. (We recommend
[
GKM98
]
for a thorough discussion of the basic issues of Koszul duality in the language of triangulated categories, and
[
DG13
]
for the
\infty
-categorical setting.)

The essential features are all visible in the case of the symmetric algebra
S=k[x_{0}]
in a single variable of cohomological degree
0
, which we give
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-weight
-2
, and the Koszul dual exterior algebra
\Lambda=k[y_{-1}]
on a generator in cohomological degree
-1
, which we give
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-weight
2
. (We keep track of cohomological degrees with subscripts and have
x,y
denote dual coordinates, indicating
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-weights. All algebras appearing in this section will be formal, so we will
often identify a dg algebra with its cohomology ring.)

Remark A.1.1

(Even shearings)
.

Note that the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-weights appearing in this section – and hence the associated shearings – are all even, so that we do not encounter changes of parity and all vector spaces are considered even.

A.1.2.
S
-modules

The basic category we start from is the usual module category for
S
, i.e., quasicoherent sheaves on the affine line
\mathbb{A}^{1}=\mathrm{Spec}(S)
,

S{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\simeq QC(\mathbb{A}^{1}).

We will keep track of four basic
S
-modules:

(a)

the structure sheaf
k[x_{0}]
;

(b)

the skyscraper
k_{0}
at
0
, arising from
S\rightarrow k
sending
x_{0}
to
0
;

(c)

the skyscraper
k_{1}
at
1
,arising from
S\rightarrow k
sending
x_{0}
to
1
.

(d)

the structure sheaf of the punctured line
k[x_{0},x_{0}{}^{-1}]
.

The first three objects are represented by perfect complexes of
S
-modules, which categorically speaking form the small category of compact objects
in the big category of arbitrary unbounded complexes of
S
-modules

\mathrm{Perf}(S)=(S{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod})^{c}\hookrightarrow S{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\mathrm{Perf}(S)).

A.1.3.
S^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
-modules

Now let us shear, according to the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
-action: we have
S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\simeq k[x_{2}]
where
u=x_{2}
has cohomological degree
2
, which we identify with the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant cohomology ring
H^{\ast}(B{\mathbb{G}_{m}})
.
Passing to categories of modules, we have

S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\simeq{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathbb{A}^{1}).

As discussed in §
6.3
,
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathbb{A}^{1})
is not equivalent to
QC(\mathbb{A}^{1})
itself, though the corresponding categories of
graded
modules are equivalent,
i.e., quasi-coherent sheaves on
\mathbb{A}^{1}/{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
is equivalent to its shear.
The category
S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
has a topological interpretation as a form of the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant category of a point. More precisely it is the ind-finite’ or “renormalized” form of
\mathrm{Shv}_{\mathbb{G}_{m}}(\mathrm{pt})
, defined as the ind-category of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant constructible sheaves on a point.

We note three basic objects in
{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathbb{A}^{1})
:

(a)

the regular module
S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}=H^{\ast}_{\mathbb{G}_{m}}(\mathrm{pt})
itself;

(b)

the augmentation
k_{0}^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}=k=H^{\ast}_{\mathbb{G}_{m}}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
;

(d)

the periodic module
k[x_{2},x_{2}{}^{-1}]
(the structure sheaf of the sheared punctured line, or
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-Tate cohomology of a point).

The first two are compact objects, i.e., objects of the small category
\mathrm{Perf}(S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}})={QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathbb{A}^{1})^{c}
. These objects
(endowed with evident
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant structures) are
the shears of the correspondingly labelled objects (a), (b), (d)
inside
S
-modules. However,
the ungraded
S
-module
k_{1}
does not have an analogue in the sheared category.

A.1.4.
\Lambda
-modules

Let us consider the Koszul dual setting. Let

\Lambda=k[y_{-1}]\simeq\mathrm{Hom}_{S^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(k,k)

be the Koszul dual (homological) exterior algebra,
which is naturally identified with the homology
H_{\ast}({\mathbb{G}_{m}})
with its Pontrjagin product (i.e., the “topological group algebra” of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
).
We can also consider
\Lambda
as the ring of functions on the affine derived scheme
\mathrm{Spec}(\Lambda)\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1]
, the shifted version of the
dual
affine line, so that
\Lambda{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\simeq QC(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])
. Topologically,
\Lambda
-modules realize locally constant actions of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
, i.e.,
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant sheaves on a point;
indeed
\Lambda
-modules recover the standard notion of equivariant
D
-modules on a point,

\Lambda{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\simeq\mathcal{D}(B{\mathbb{G}_{m}}).

We note two basic bounded coherent (finite dimensional) objects in
\Lambda{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
:

(a)

the augmentation
k
, and

(b)

the regular module
\Lambda
.

Again the small category of compact objects here is given by perfect complexes of
\Lambda
-modules.
The first object is not perfect (=compact), while the latter is.
In the realization
\Lambda{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\simeq QC(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])
,
k
corresponds to the skyscraper sheaf at the origin, a singular point.

We have functors switching the augmentation and regular modules for
S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
and
\Lambda

(A.1)

-\otimes_{S^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}k:S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\longleftrightarrow\Lambda{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}:Hom_{\Lambda}(k,-)

k\longleftrightarrow\Lambda[-1]

S^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}\longleftrightarrow k.

i.e., they exchange equivariant and ordinary cohomology of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-spaces
[
GKM98
]
;

\Lambda[-1]
can be thought of as the dualizing sheaf of
\Lambda
, or as the cohomology of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
.

In particular the functors can not be inverse equivalences on the full (unbounded) categories of modules, since the noncompact augmentation of
\Lambda
is taken to the regular module for
S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
,
and the latter is compact inside the category of
S^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
-modules. In other words, they don’t restrict to equivalences of the categories of perfect modules for
S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
and
\Lambda
, though they do identify perfect
S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
-modules with bounded coherent
\Lambda
-modules.

Another way to see the failure of (
A.1
) to be an equivalence is that the periodic module
k[x_{2},x_{2}^{-1}]\in S^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
vanishes under (
A.1
), for it is sent to the acyclic complex

(A.2)

\underline{\mathsf{Per}}:\cdots\rightarrow k[y_{-1}]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle y_{-1}}}{{\rightarrow}}k[y_{-1}]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle y_{-1}}}{{\rightarrow}}k[y_{-1}]\rightarrow\cdots

In this equation, the various copies of
k[y_{-1}]
are placed in degrees that differ by
2
from each other.

A.1.5.
Ind-coherent modules for
\Lambda

We can make Koszul duality (
A.1
) an equivalence by “correcting” either side.

The solution we will adopt is to correct the side of
\Lambda
-modules: we enlarge
\Lambda{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}=QC(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])
to the
ind-coherent category
of
\Lambda
,
i.e., the ind-category of the category of
\Lambda
-modules
with finite-dimensional cohomology. We will denote this category by
QC^{!}(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])
.
This enlarged category of
\Lambda
-modules consists of formal colimits of finite dimensional (coherent)
\Lambda
-modules.
If we replace
\Lambda
by a usual ring (rather than a dg-ring) the
ind-coherent category can be equivalently
described as the (dg-enhanced) homotopy category of injective complexes of
\Lambda
-modules
[
Kra05
]
;
in such a category acyclic complexes of the general form (
A.2
) need not be trivial.

Since the category of
\Lambda
modules is the ind-completion
of the category of perfect complexes, extending the inclusion of perfect
into coherent complexes gives

(A.3)

\Xi:QC\rightarrow QC^{!}.

We warn that
\Xi
does not agree, when restricted to coherent sheaves,
to the tautological inclusion of coherent sheaves into
QC^{!}
–
see examples (b), (b)’ below.

Remark A.1.6
.

We note that there is also a functor

\Psi:QC^{!}\rightarrow QC

in the opposite direction (we follow the lettering of
[
Gai11a
]
),
which is right adjoint to
\Xi
, and
arises from the ind-completion of the inclusion of coherent sheaves into
QC
.
This functor is not fully faithful. (In the case when
\Lambda
is a usual Noetherian ring,
this
\Psi
is just the tautological functor from injective complexes to the derived category and is denoted
Q
by Krause.)

The passage from usual modules to the ind-coherent category has
the effect of (in fact is designed for) forcing the augmentation of
\Lambda
to be a compact object (in fact a compact generator) like
S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\in(S^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}){\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
, and indeed Koszul duality now extends to an equivalence

S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}={QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}(\mathbb{A}^{1})\longleftrightarrow QC^{!}(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])=\operatorname{Ind}(\Lambda^{\cdot}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}_{f.d.}).

Some examples:

(b)

k
as a
\Lambda
-module is coherent and thus
gives an object of the ind-coherent category (via the inclusion
of the coherent category to the ind-coherent).
It will be convenient, for comparison with what follows
to represent
k
by the coherent complex of free modules

(A.4)

k:\qquad\cdots\rightarrow 0\rightarrow 0\rightarrow k[y_{-1}]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle y_{-1}}}{{\rightarrow}}k[y_{-1}]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle y_{-1}}}{{\rightarrow}}\cdots

(where the various copies of
k[y_{-1}]
are generated in degrees
1,3,5,\dots
) and under Koszul duality corresponds to
S^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
.

(b)’

The image of
k
under the functor
\Xi
of (
A.3
)
can be thought of as the
bounded above
complex of free
\Lambda
-modules:

(A.5)

\Xi(k):\qquad\cdots\rightarrow k[y_{-1}]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle y_{-1}}}{{\rightarrow}}k[y_{-1}]\rightarrow 0\rightarrow 0\rightarrow\cdots

where the various copies of
k[y_{-1}]
are generated in degrees
0,-2,-4,\dots
, and
which we regard as being in the ind-coherent category
by taking only finitely many terms of the above, and then taking a direct limit.

\Xi(k)[1]
corresponds under Koszul duality to
S^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}[x_{2}^{-1}]/S^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
,
which is a direct limit of torsion modules.

(c)

The infinite acyclic complex encountered in
A.2
,
understood as the colimit of bounded-below truncations as above,
now yields a nonzero object
\underline{\mathsf{Per}}
of the ind-coherent category,
which fits now into a sequence

k\rightarrow\underline{\mathsf{Per}}\rightarrow\Xi(k)[1]
.
This
\underline{\mathsf{Per}}
is the image of
S^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}[x_{2}^{-1}]
under Koszul duality. Under
the functor
\Psi
of Remark
A.1.6
it is carried to the trivial object.

A.1.7.
Singular support

The distinction between the categories

\Lambda{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\simeq QC(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1]),S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}\simeq QC^{!}(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])

can also be captured by the theory of singular support of (ind-)coherent sheaves
[
BIK08
,
AG15
]
.

Namely, the singular support of an object of
QC^{!}(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])

is a closed conical subset of
\mathbb{A}^{1}
– i.e., either
\{0\}
or all of
\mathbb{A}^{1}
!
Explicitly
the singular support is zero if and only if
the Koszul dual module is torsion. “Quasicoherent sheaves are ind-coherent sheaves with trivial singular support,” in the sense that

\Xi:QC(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])\rightarrow QC^{!}(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])

is fully faithful with essential image those objects with zero singular support.

Remark A.1.8
.

Care is needed with these notions! As we saw above, the augmentation object
k
in
\Lambda
-modules
can be considered in
QC^{!}
in two different ways, giving
the objects called
k
and
\Xi(k)
above.

-

The singular support of
k
is
\mathbb{A}^{1}
, but

-

The singular support of
\Xi(k)
is
\{0\}
.

A.2.
The spectral exponential sheaf

We now define an exotic object on the affine line which plays the role of the exponential
D
-module or Artin-Schreier sheaf in the coherent setting. It can be considered a spectrally quantized form of the Hamiltonian
{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
-space

\mathrm{pt}_{1}:=\mbox{ a point with moment map value $1\in{\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}$}.

In other words, we are seeking an algebraic
avatar of the exponential function, which defines a character of the Lie algebra

\exp:{\mathfrak{g}_{a}}:=\mathrm{Lie}({\mathbb{G}_{a}})\to k

of the additive group – but not of the additive group itself.
Correspondingly, we are going to construct this spectral exponential not
as a quasicoherent sheaf on
B{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
, but rather inside a sheared version of that category.
Indeed, the category
QC(B{\mathbb{G}_{a}})=\text{Rep}({\mathbb{G}_{a}})
of representations of the additive group is identified by Cartier duality with sheaves on the dual additive formal group, i.e., the formal completion of the dual Lie algebra
{\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}
at
0
, and thus doesn’t have an object corresponding to the skyscraper
k_{1}
. However, we can perform the decompletion formally using Koszul duality and shearing.

To formalize this, we use the same setting as the previous section, with Koszul dual symmetric and exterior algebras
S=k[x_{0}]
(where
x_{0}
has
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
weight
-2
) and
\Lambda=k[y_{-1}]
(where
y_{1}
has
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
weight
2
). To make the link
with what we just said, we adopt the following point of view:

-

We view the
y
-line
\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1]\simeq\Omega{\mathbb{G}_{a}}
as the based loops in the additive group.
141
141

141

Equivalently, the shift by 2 of the classifying stack
B{\mathbb{G}_{a}}\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}[1]
(a coaffine stack, cf.Remark
6.4.1
).

-

We view the
x
-line
\mathrm{Spec}(S)\simeq{\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}
as the dual Lie algebra of the additive group.

As discussed above,
Koszul duality identifies ind-coherent sheaves on the
y
-line

QC^{!}(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])\simeq QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}({\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}})

with the shear of ordinary quasicoherent sheaves on
x
-line.
This is an equivalence of
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-categories, where, writing out the actions:

•

the shearing
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
is acting on
\mathbb{A}^{1}
by the inverse square character, and
on the coordinate
y
on
\mathbb{A}^{1}
by the square character;

•

dually, the shearing
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
acts on
{\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}
by the square character, and on the coordinate
x
on
{\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}
by the inverse square character.

Now observe that since the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-weights of
x
and
y
are opposite, we find a sheared Koszul duality equivalenc

QC^{!}(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}},\textrm{negated action}}\simeq QC({\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}).

On the left,
we are now shearing by the the
inverse
of the action just described, i.e.
the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-action on
\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1]
is through squaring. We are led to the following definition:

Definition A.2.1
.

Let
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
act on
\mathbb{A}^{1}
through squaring.
The spectral exponential sheaf

\exp\in QC^{!}(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}

is the image of the skyscraper
k_{1}
at 1 (evaluation module at
1\in{\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}}
) by the sheared Koszul duality equivalence
QC({\mathfrak{g}_{a}^{\ast}})\simeq QC^{!}(\mathbb{A}^{1}[-1])^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
.

Here are a couple of different ways to think about this construction:

•

Recall that by definition, the shear of a category has the same
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant objects as the original category, but with the enriched graded Hom-spaces modified by a shear, and from this data one formally reconstructs the whole category.
Thus we start with the
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
-equivariant skyscraper, the augmentation object
k\in QC^{!}(\mathbb{A}[-1])
, which corresponds to
S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}\in S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
.
Thus its endomorphism algebra is the symmetric algebra
S^{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}
. Now, the sheared category
\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathbb{A}[-1])^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
is built so that (i) it has an object by name
k^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
