to descend to the moduli of the Betti spaces of curves, i.e., the classifying spaces of diffeomorphism groups or homotopy type of the moduli of curves. Thus a Betti TFT amounts to (a small amount of the structure of) a topological field theory in the traditional sense, a functor of (oriented) topological manifolds, with invariants
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)
forming local systems over the moduli of curves and carry actions of mapping class groups.

A de Rham field theory is a higher analog of the structure of topological conformal field theory
[
Get94
]
,
[
Seg99
]
, i.e., a CFT with a homotopic trivialization of the stress tensor. Indeed this is a general feature of “topological twists” of supersymmetric quantum field theories, explored in
[
ES19
]
, in which the action of changes of coordinates (and deformations of metrics) is made exact in a structured way (through the action of the supersymmetry algebra). This gives a weak form of topological invariance – in particular the categories
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)
attached to curves carry a flat connection over the moduli of curves which is not integrable in general (i.e., parallel transport is not defined) and do not inherit actions of mapping class groups. (This is a major difference with the classical setting of rational CFT or 3d TFT as in
[
BFM91
,
BK01
]
.)

Likewise in the étale version for
\mathbb{F}={\overline{\mathbb{F}}}_{q}
, we might ask an étale field theory to be
functorial for isomorphisms of the étale site of
\Sigma
. Let us point out one important feature of this. For a curve
\Sigma
defined over
\mathbb{F}_{q}
, the étale site of
\Sigma/{\overline{\mathbb{F}}}_{q}
carries a canonical Frobenius automorphism. Hence the invariant
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)
carries a Frobenius automorphism (the action of an “arithmetic mapping class group element”), and if it is dualizable, we may evaluate its Frobenius trace and consider it as the invariant attached to the corresponding “arithmetic 3-manifold”, the mapping torus of Frobenius.

D.5.5.
Global states

We now spell out the key data encoded in Definition
D.5.2
, and in particular the motivating case where objects of
\mathcal{C}=k{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}^{3}
are dg 2-categories, of
{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}=k{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}^{2}
are dg categories and of
{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ\circ}}=k{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}
are vector spaces (following our Terminology
D.0.1
).

The most basic data associated to an algebraic quantum field theory is the “space of states”:

\bullet
the states on
\Sigma
define an invariant
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)=\langle 1_{\mathcal{Z}_{\Sigma}}\rangle_{\mathcal{Z},\Sigma}\in{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}
, i.e., a dg category.

Explicitly, the unital structure of
\mathcal{Z}
in particular endows the factorization homology on any curve
\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{Z}
with a pointing
1_{\mathcal{Z},\Sigma}
(morphism from
1_{\mathcal{C}}
), and
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)
is the value of the state
\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{Z},\Sigma}
on the pointing.

If we assume
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)
is dualizable then we further get that

\bullet
any automorphism
F\in Aut(\Sigma)
defines an invariant
Tr(F,\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma))\in{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ\circ}}
, i.e., a dg vector space, which we think of as the states
\mathcal{Z}(M_{F,\Sigma})
of the theory on the mapping torus of
F
(a 3-manifold).

D.5.6.
Factorization algebra of observables / local data

The local data of
\mathcal{Z}
on a fixed curve
\Sigma
includes:

\bullet
an invariant
\mathcal{Z}_{x}=\mathcal{Z}(D^{*}_{x})\in\mathcal{C}
(i.e., a 2-category) to every point
x\in\Sigma
, which we think of as the states of the field theory on the “1-manifold”
D^{*}_{x}
, the punctured disc at
x
.

\bullet
The invariant extends multiplicatively to finite subsets
S\subset\Sigma
:

\mathcal{Z}_{S}\simeq\bigotimes_{x\in S}\mathcal{Z}_{x}.

\bullet
We are given a unit: an object
1_{\mathcal{Z}_{x}}=\mathcal{Z}(D_{x})\in\mathcal{Z}_{x}
(
x\in\Sigma
), the “vacuum state” at
x
, and

\bullet
we insert units to extend
\mathcal{Z}_{S}
to be functorial under all maps of finite sets over
\Sigma
.

The structure of factorization algebra glues together the objects
\mathcal{Z}_{x}
for varying
x
, and most importantly encodes the “operator product expansion” (OPE), i.e., behavior when points collide: namely the invariants
\mathcal{Z}_{S}
assemble to a factorizable cosheaf over the [unital version of the] Ran space
Ran(\Sigma)
of all finite subsets of
\Sigma
.

D.5.7.
States / correlation functions

The global aspect of
\mathcal{Z}
is given by spaces of correlation functions:

\bullet
for every finite subset
S\subset\Sigma
we are given a functional

\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{Z},S}:\mathcal{Z}_{S}\to 1_{\mathcal{C}}.

Concretely, applying this morphism to objects
\mathcal{M}_{i}\in\mathcal{Z}_{x_{i}}
(i.e., composing with morphisms
\mathcal{M}_{i}:1_{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathcal{Z}_{x_{i}}
) we obtain an invariant

\langle\bigotimes\mathcal{M}_{i}\rangle_{\mathcal{Z},S}\in\overline{\mathcal{C}}.

These assignments are asked to be invariant under maps of finite sets, in particular insertion of the unit at new points. Thus if we insert the unit everywhere we obtain the global states
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)
.

We require that all of the assignments
\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{Z},S}
to assemble to a single state on
\mathcal{Z}
, i.e., a morphism out of the global observables
\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{Z}
, i.e., the homology of the Ran space with coefficients in the cosheaf defined by
\mathcal{Z}
.
This guarantees that the assignment of correlation functions respects the factorization structure on the
\mathcal{Z}_{S}
, in particular varies well with
x
and is compatible with collisions of points.

D.5.8.
Defects in algebraic quantum field theories

Algebraic field theories following Definition
D.5.2
afford defect operators of various dimensions. We continue to think of an algebraic quantum field theory as the
[1,2]
-dimensional part of a 4d TFT, and our terminology reflects this choice: as common in physics we label defects by their dimension in space-time (although emphasizing
co
dimension is more natural when thinking of an abstract
[1,2]
-dimensional field theory).

\bullet
Surface defects: the assignment
x\mapsto\mathcal{Z}(D_{x}^{*})
itself plays the role of the 2-category of surface defects in a 4d TFT, while its factorization structure captures the operator product expansion (
E_{2}
-structure) on surface defects. They play the role of possible codimension 2 singularities (ramification data) on
\Sigma
.

\bullet
Line defects: the “unramified Hecke category”
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{Z}}
of
\mathcal{Z}
plays the role of the category
\mathcal{Z}(S^{2})
of line defects. These are by definition endomorphisms of the unit observable

1_{\mathcal{Z}_{x}}=\mathcal{Z}(D_{x})\in\mathcal{Z}_{x}=\mathcal{Z}(D^{*}_{x}),

i.e.,

{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{Z}}:=End(1_{\mathcal{Z}_{x}})\in{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}.

(The algebraic avatar of the 2-sphere here being two discs joined along the punctured disc.)
The factorization algebra structure on
\mathcal{Z}_{x}
, with
1_{\mathcal{Z}_{x}}
as its unit, provides the Hecke category with the structure of an factorization associative algebra on
\Sigma
valued in
{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}
– in the Betti setting this amounts to the structure of
E_{3}
-algebra in
{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}
, as expected from line defects in 4d TFT.

\bullet
Observables from line defects: for any choice of point
x\in\Sigma
we have an action of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{Z}}
on
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)
by Hecke modifications. This is a consequence of the unitality: we identify
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)
with correlation functions with the unit inserted at
x
, whence an action of endomorphisms of the unit. More generally
\langle\bigotimes\mathcal{M}_{i}\rangle_{\mathcal{Z},S}
carries an action of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{Z}}
at all points away from the ramification set
S
. This action descends to the global Hecke category, given by the factorization homology

(D.2)

\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{Z},\Sigma\setminus\{x_{i}\}}:=\int_{\Sigma\setminus\{x_{i}\}}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{Z}}\hskip 7.22743pt\circlearrowright\hskip 7.22743pt\langle\bigotimes\mathcal{M}_{i}\rangle_{\mathcal{Z},S}

In particular for
S
empty we obtain an action of
\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{Z},\Sigma}
on
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)
.

\bullet
Local operators: the point defects in a 4d TFT are captured in the algebraic quantum field theory setting by endomorphisms of the unit line defect, i.e., endomorphisms of the unit in
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{Z}}
. These endomorphisms form an
E_{2}
factorization algebra on
\Sigma
, i.e., the algebraic counterpart of the
E_{4}
structure on local operators in four dimensions.

\bullet
Domain walls and boundary theories: we postpone to Section
D.7
the discussion of the algebraic avatars of the richest class of defects in 4d TFT.

D.6.
Langlands correspondence via field theory

We now outline how the structure of algebraic quantum field theory is meant to apply in the setting of the Langlands correspondence, in parallel to the discussion of the previous section (see
[
BZN18
]
for a more limited discussion along similar lines). Namely, we explain how the geometric Langlands correspondence on a smooth projective curve
\Sigma
over an algebraically closed field might be understood as an equivalence
\mathcal{A}_{G}\simeq\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}
between algebraic quantum field theories, valued in
k
-linear 2-categories
\mathcal{C}=k{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}^{3}
. Moreover in the étale setting when
\Sigma
is defined over a finite field, we discuss how passing to Frobenius traces following
[
AGK+21
]
– and assuming that we have available the structure described in
Remark
D.5.4
– would recover a form of the Langlands conjecture for function fields.

Remark D.6.1

(Categorical difficulties)
.

The full structure of
\mathcal{A}_{G}
and
\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}
as algebraic quantum field theories is far from being precisely formulated. For example we can ask: what is the precise target category
\mathcal{C}
and the associated sheaf theory
SHV_{\mathcal{C}}
? This is part of the problem of formulating the local geometric Langlands conjecture (being developed by D. Arinkin, D. Gaitsgory, S. Raskin and others): what kind of objects are the “local 2-categories
\mathcal{A}_{G}(D^{*}_{x})
and
\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}(D^{*}_{x})
”?
Just as ind-coherent sheaves are not sheaves in a naive sense (projecting to
QC
kills some objects) it is not clear we should consider them as actual 2-categories (i.e., objects of
k{\hbox{-}}\mathrm{mod}^{3}
) or as more sophisticated objects constructed by a higher sheaf theory
2IndCoh
and valued in the 3-category
3IndCoh(pt)
(these objects are defined in forthcoming work of Stefanich
[
Ste23a
]
). However their unramified parts form a “sub-field theory” that is fairly well understood and already contains a great amount of structure (in particular all that is directly relevant to this paper), and we hope our schematic overview of the general expectations is useful regardless.

Remark D.6.2

(Topological invariance)
.

The field theories
\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}
on the spectral side (and hence, by the Langlands conjectures, the automorphic theories
\mathcal{A}_{G}
) in the Betti, de Rham and étale settings satisfy a strong “topological invariance” property: they are
built from the
corresponding stacks
\mathrm{Loc}^{?}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma)
of (
?=
B, dR or et) local systems, which are themselves functors of
\Sigma_{?}
. In other words, they form algebraic TFTs as in Remark
D.5.4
. In the Betti setting, this means we are in the traditional setting of topological field theory (which was precisely the motivation for the Betti Langlands conjecture
[
BZN18
]
).
In the étale setting, we only note again that this form of topological invariance implies that the value of the theory on curves defined over finite fields inherit Frobenius automorphisms.

\bullet
[Global geometric] The global unramified automorphic invariants
\mathcal{A}_{G}(\Sigma)=\mathrm{AUT}^{?}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))
are given by the [étale, de Rham or Betti form of the] dg category of automorphic sheaves on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma)
(as in §
C
).
On the spectral side,
\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}(\Sigma)=\mathrm{QC}^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}^{?}(\Sigma))
is given by ind-coherent sheaves on the [étale, de Rham or Betti] stack of local systems on
\Sigma
. Thus the conjectured equivalence
\mathcal{A}_{G}\simeq\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}
on
\Sigma
thus realizes the geometric Langlands conjecture.

\bullet
[Global arithmetic] If we assume a form of “étale topological invariance” as in Remarks
D.5.4
and
D.6.2
, we can see some of the structure of the arithmetic Langlands correspondence for function fields. The categories
\mathcal{A}_{G}(\Sigma),\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma)
are dualizable, hence one can evaluate the trace of any automorphism of
\Sigma
. For
\Sigma
defined over
\mathbb{F}_{q}
we may consider the categorical trace of Frobenius, which defines the values of the field theories
\mathcal{A}_{G}
and
\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}
(in the étale setting of
[
AGK+20b
]
) on the “arithmetic 3-manifold”
M_{F,\Sigma}
corresponding to
\Sigma
, the mapping torus of Frobenius.

The trace
Tr(F,\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma))
is identified with volume forms on the stack
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}^{arith}(\Sigma)
of
arithmetic
restricted local systems (Frobenius fixed points on
Loc_{\check{G}}
) (see
[
AGK+20b
, Section 24]
). On the other hand, the Trace Theorem
[
AGK+21
]
recovers the space of unramified automorphic forms – compactly supported functions on
Bun_{G}(\Sigma)(\mathbb{F}_{q})
as the categorical trace of Frobenius on
\mathrm{AUT}^{res}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G}(\Sigma))
.
Thus the conjectural isomorphism of vector spaces
\mathcal{A}_{G}(M_{F,\Sigma})\simeq\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}(M_{F,\Sigma})
recovers the unramified Langlands conjecture for function fields, as formulated in
[
AGK+20b
]
following the work of V. Lafforgue
[
Laf18b
]
.

\bullet
[Local geometric]
The local automorphic 2-category
\mathcal{A}_{G}(D^{*})
is expected to be given by categorical representations of the algebraic loop group
G_{F}
, i.e., by a suitable version of module categories for the convolution monoidal category
SHV(G_{F})
.

The local spectral 2-category
\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}(D^{*})
in the de Rham setting is expected to be Stefanich’s
2IndCoh(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(D^{*}))
, a modification (in the spirit of the modification
QC\leadsto QC^{!}
) of the 2-category of quasicoherent sheaves of categories on the stack of local systems on
D^{*}
.
The conjectured equivalence
\mathcal{A}_{G}\simeq\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}
on
D^{*}
is the local geometric Langlands conjecture.

\bullet
[Local unramified] While these 2-categories are poorly understood, their
unramified
parts are quite familiar. The unit object (or vacuum)

\mathcal{A}_{G}(D)\in\mathcal{A}_{G}(D^{*})

is given by the
G_{F}
-category of sheaves on the affine Grassmannian
Gr=G_{F}/G_{O}
.
Its endomorphisms, the Hecke category of (’t Hooft) line operators
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{G}}
, form the spherical Hecke category
SHV(G_{O}\backslash G_{F}/G_{O})
. The (factorization) 2-category of modules for
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{G}}
defines the well-understood unramified part of the local 2-category.

On the spectral side
\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}(D)
is given by the category
Rep({\check{G}})\simeq QC(pt/{\check{G}})
of representations of the dual group thought of as sheaves on the substack
pt/{\check{G}}\to Loc_{{\check{G}}}(D^{*})
of trivial local systems on the punctured disc.
Its endomorphisms, the (Wilson) line operators
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}}
recover the derived spherical category
QC^{!}(Loc_{{\check{G}}}(S^{2}))
, and the Langlands duality of field theories on the (factorization) monoidal categories of line operators
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{G}}\simeq{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}}
predicts the derived Satake correspondence
[
BF08
]
(and its factorizable form
[
CR23
]
).

We may also pass to the Frobenius trace on the geometric Satake correspondence and recover the classical Satake correspondence (as in
[
Zhu18
]
). Namely, the Frobenius trace on
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{G}}=SHV(G_{O}\backslash G_{F}/G_{O})
produces the spherical Hecke algebra, endomorphisms of the unramified representation
k[Gr]
while the Frobenius trace on
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}}
produces functions on Frobenius-twisted conjugacy classes in
{\check{G}}
.

\bullet
[Unramified Hecke action and shtukas] The Hecke categories
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{G}}\simeq{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}}
act on the global states
\mathcal{A}_{G}(\Sigma)\simeq\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma)
by modifications at any point
x\in\Sigma
(
D.2
). Thus the duality of field theories predicts the Hecke-linearity of the geometric Langlands correspondence. Moreover this equivalence respects the factorization monoidal structure of the Hecke categories, so that we may integrate over
x\in\Sigma
to obtain an equivalence as modules for the unramified global Hecke categories
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}=\int_{\Sigma}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}
.
In the Betti setting, the global Hecke category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Sigma,\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}}
is Beraldo’s global Hecke category
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
with its action on
\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}(\Sigma)=QC^{!}(Loc_{{\check{G}}}(\Sigma))
.
In general the global Hecke action detects singular support of coherent sheaves on
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma)
(the “sheafification” of the automorphic category over
T^{*}[1]\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma)
).

In the global arithmetic setting, we obtain likewise the action of the spherical Hecke algebra on unramified automorphic forms.
More significantly, for any unramified Hecke functor
H_{S}
acting at
S\subset\Sigma
we can take the categorical trace of Frobenius composed with
H
,

Tr(F\circ H,\mathcal{A}_{G}(\Sigma)\simeq\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}(\Sigma))

– in other words consider the value of the field theory on the arithmetic 3-manifold
M_{F,\Sigma}
with insertions of line defects along
S
. As explained in
[
AGK+20b
,
AGK+21
]
this categorical trace recovers the Langlands conjecture for the cohomology of moduli of unramified shtukas on
\Sigma
with prescribed legs at
S
.

\bullet
[Local operators and singular support]
The local operators, i.e., endomorphisms of the unit in
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{Z}}
, are identified on the automorphic side with the equivariant cohomology ring
H^{*}(BG)
and spectrally with the shifted invariant polynomials
\mathcal{O}(\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}[2])^{\check{G}}
. The vanishing of these operators measures the difference between ind-finite and ind-safe (renormalized and unrenormalized) categories of sheaves on
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
on the automorphic side (cf. §
B.6
), and the difference between ind-coherent sheaves with or without nilpotent singular support on the spectral side §
C.2
.

\bullet
[Ramified global]
The local Langlands 2-categories of surface defects
\mathcal{A}_{G}(D^{*})
and
\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}(D^{*})
control ramification: one may view the action of a surface defect at
x\in\Sigma
as modifying the ramification data considered at
x
.

Namely, given objects
\mathcal{M}_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{G}(D^{*})
we can consider the
correlation functions
, the automorphic categories
\langle\mathcal{M}_{i}\rangle_{\mathcal{A}_{G},\Sigma}\in DGCat_{k}
. These give the categories of sheaves on the stacks of
G
-bundles on
\Sigma
with given ramification data at points
x_{i}\in\Sigma
– for example taking
\mathcal{M}_{i}=SHV(G_{F}/H)
for a congruence subgroup
H
corresponds to imposing
H
-level structure at
x
.
On the other hand inserting the unit surface defect, i.e., the unramified
G
-category,
captures the imposition of no ramification at
x
.

The colimit of all these assignments, the factorization homology
\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{A}_{G}
(i.e., the global observables on
\Sigma
), is a version of a “restricted tensor product” of the local automorphic 2-categories

\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{A}_{G}\sim\bigotimes_{x\in\Sigma}^{\prime}G_{F}\mbox{-cat},

and the “correlation function functional”

\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{A}_{G},\Sigma}:\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{A}_{G}\to{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}},

plays the role of the functor of
G_{F}
-coinvariants, or its representing object, the geometric counterpart of the space of all adèlic automorphic forms.

Spectrally, for local ramification data
\check{\mathcal{M}}_{i}\in\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}(D^{*})
, the correlation functions
\langle\mathcal{M}_{i}\rangle_{\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}},\Sigma}
give the dg categories of ind-coherent sheaves on moduli of local systems with prescribed ramification. The duality
\mathcal{A}_{G}\simeq\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}
on correlation functions gives the ramified geometric Langlands conjecture.

Thus the equivalence of algebraic quantum field theory encodes a very general and flexible form of the ramified Langlands conjecture in the setting of curves.
On the one hand, we recover the action of unramified Hecke modifications as the action
D.2
of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{G},\Sigma\setminus S}=\int_{\Sigma\setminus S}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{G}}
on spaces of correlation functions
\langle\mathcal{M}_{i}\rangle_{\mathcal{A}_{G},\Sigma}
. On the other hand,
passing to Frobenius traces is then expected to give the ramified Langlands conjecture for function fields.

\bullet
[Local arithmetic] Finally, we note that the Frobenius trace on the local geometric Langlands conjecture is expected to realize the categorical local Langlands conjecture in the spirit of
[
Zhu18
,
FS21
]
(see also
[
BZCHN24
]
for a discussion).
Namely, the trace of Frobenius on
\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}(D^{*})=2IndCoh(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(D^{*}))
formally produces the category
QC^{!}(Loc_{\check{G}}^{arith}(D^{*})
of ind-coherent sheaves on the stack of local arithmetic Langlands parameters.
Much more speculatively, as suggested in
[
Gai16a
]
, the trace of Frobenius on the 2-category
\mathcal{A}_{G}(D^{*})
is expected to produce the category of sheaves on the Kottwitz space of
G
-isocrystals
G_{F}/_{\sigma}G_{F}
. In particular it should contain as a full subcategory the local Langlands category of smooth representations of
G_{F}
.

Thus the duality
\mathcal{A}_{G}\simeq\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}
on the “arithmetic 2-manifold”
F
is meant to produce a full embedding

Rep^{sm}(G_{F})\hookrightarrow QC^{!}(Loc^{arith}_{\check{G}}(D^{*}))

of smooth representations of
G_{F}
into ind-coherent sheaves on the stack of local Langlands parameters.

D.7.
Boundaries in algebraic quantum field theory

We now discuss the formulation of interfaces (or domain walls) and boundary theories in the setting of algebraic quantum field theory.

Definition D.7.1
.

Let
(\mathcal{W},\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{W}})
and
(\mathcal{Z},\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{Z}})
be algebraic quantum field theories on curves valued in
\mathcal{C}
, as in Definition
D.5.2
.

(1)

A morphism or interface
\mathcal{D}:\mathcal{W}\to\mathcal{Z}
between field theories is a lax morphism of unital factorization algebras on curves
\mathcal{W}\to\mathcal{Z}
together with a specified natural transformation

\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{D},\Sigma}:\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{Z},\Sigma}\circ{\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{D}}\longrightarrow\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{W},\Sigma}

making the following diagram commute:

\textstyle{\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{W}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{W},\Sigma}}
\scriptstyle{\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{D}}
\textstyle{\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{Z}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{Z},\Sigma}}
\textstyle{1_{\mathcal{C}}}

(2)

A boundary theory
\Theta\in\mathcal{Z}
for the field theory
\mathcal{Z}
is a morphism from the trivial theory

\Theta:1_{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathcal{Z}.

Remark D.7.2

(Lax structures)
.

The structure of boundary theory we describe here is [an algebraic version of] a fragment of the notion of lax boundary TFT from
[
JFS17
]
. The laxness is evident in two places: first, we ask for a morphism of field theories only to commute with correlation functions up to specified natural transformation rather than natural isomorphism.

Second, we ask for the map of factorization algebras itself to be lax. It’s useful to recall one role of lax monoidal functors. If we think of an object
M\in C
in a
k
-linear monoidal category
C
as the image of the unit
k\in Vect_{k}
under a functor from the unit category
\underline{M}:Vect_{k}\to C
with
M=\underline{M}(k)
, then the structure of associative algebra object on
M
(in particular the map
M\otimes M\to M
) corresponds to a lax monoidal structure on the functor
\underline{M}
(so that we have a morphism
M(k)\otimes M(k)\to M(k\otimes k)=M(k)
which is not required to be an isomorphism).

Let us spell out the notion of boundary field theory
\Theta\in\mathcal{Z}
. It is very helpful to refer back to the case when
\mathcal{Z}
is trivial:

Lemma D.7.3
.

A boundary theory
\mathcal{D}:1_{\mathcal{C}}\to 1_{\mathcal{C}}
for the trivial theory is equivalent to the data of a field theory
\mathcal{D}
valued in
{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}
.

In general we find
relative
versions of all the structures of a field theory, valued in the “bulk theory”
\mathcal{Z}
rather than in
{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}
.
Alternatively, it is useful to refer to the next section where we identify these structures with (relatively) familiar objects in the relative Langlands program.

D.7.4.
Global state

The unital structure of
\Theta:1_{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathcal{Z}
applied to correlation functions produces

\bullet
the states on
\Sigma
define a “
\Theta
-series” functional
\Theta(\Sigma):\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)\to 1_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}
,
i.e., a [representing] object in the dg category
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)
.

Given sufficient dualizability we can then pass to trace of any automorphism
F
of
\Sigma
to obtain

\Theta(M_{F,\Sigma}):\mathcal{Z}(M_{F,\Sigma})\to 1_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ\circ}},

i.e., a linear functional on the vector space
cZ(M_{F,\Sigma})
.

D.7.5.
Local observables

Considering the morphism
\Theta
at points
x\in\Sigma
produces the following algebraic structures:

\bullet
a unital
factorization algebra object

\{\Theta_{x}\in\mathcal{Z}_{x}\}_{x\in\Sigma}
of
\mathcal{Z}
– i.e., a section of the factorization algebra compatible with factorization
[
Ras17a
]
, and equipped with a unit morphism
\Phi:\mathcal{Z}(D)\to\Theta
from the unit of
\mathcal{Z}
.

\bullet
a unital
factorization associative algebra object

{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Theta}\in{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{Z}}
in the Hecke category of
\mathcal{Z}
.

(The latter, viewed as a lax morphism
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Theta}:1_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}\to{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}\mathcal{Z}
of unital factorization associative algebras, comes by applying the lax morphism of unital factorization algebras
\Theta:1_{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathcal{Z}
to the endomorphisms of the unit.)

How should we understand these structures? Recall that from the point of view of 4d TFT, the [factorization or
E_{2}
] 2-category
\mathcal{Z}
encodes surface – i.e., codimension 2 – defects, while its [factorization associative or
E_{3}
] Hecke category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{Z}}
encodes line – i.e., codimension 3 defects.
The relative versions
\Theta
and
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Theta}
describe codimension 2 (line) and 3 (point) defects in the boundary theory (and reduce to line and point defects, respectively in the
{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}
-valued theory or “3d TFT”
\Theta
in the case when
\mathcal{Z}
is trivial). In this language,
\Theta
is the value of the 4d TFT on a cylinder
S^{1}\times I
with one end marked by the boundary condition
\Theta
, while
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Theta}
is the value on
S^{2}\times I
with a similiarly marked boundary.

D.7.6.
Unramified local observables

We may also consider the unramified part of
\Theta
,

\Theta^{unr}:=Hom_{\mathcal{Z}}(\mathcal{Z}(D),\Theta).

This forms a unital factorization algebra in
{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}
. Keeping track of linearity over endomorphisms of the vacuum
\mathcal{Z}(D)
we can further consider
\Theta^{unr}
as a unital factiorization algebra in modules for the line operators (Hecke category)
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{Z}}
. Topologically this is the value of the theory on a 2-disc ending on the boundary, i.e., the link of a line in the boundary. Physically these operators form the codimension 2 defects in the boundary theory. The unit of
\Theta^{unr}
is provided by the basic object
\Phi
, i.e., the unit of
\Theta
.
(In the presence of sufficient dualizability assumptions to recover the ULA and rigidity conditions as in §
16
we recover

{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Theta}\simeq\underline{End}_{{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{Z}}}(\Phi)

as its internal endomorphisms.)

D.7.7.
Boundary correlation functions

We now consider the global data produced by a boundary condition. We can evaluate factorization homology of the factorization algebra object
\Theta\in\mathcal{Z}
to obtain an object
\int_{\Sigma}\Theta\in\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{Z}
, and then apply correlation functions
\langle-\rangle_{\mathcal{Z}}
:

\bullet
a functional on correlation functions with values in
\Theta
, i.e., a morphism

\langle-\rangle_{\Theta,\Sigma}:\langle\int_{\Sigma}\Theta\rangle_{\mathcal{Z},\Sigma}\to 1_{{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}}.

This amounts to a compatible family of morphisms

\langle\bigotimes_{S}\Theta_{x_{i}}\rangle\longrightarrow 1_{{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}},

which for
S
empty reproduces the “
\Theta
-series” functional

\Theta(\Sigma):\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)\to 1_{{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}}.

Again if
\mathcal{Z}
is trivial this amounts to the data of correlation functions in the
{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}
-valued theory
\Theta
.

Finally we observe that boundary observables on
\Sigma\setminus S
act on boundary correlation functions, in the boundary version of
D.2
(for simplicity we formulate this only in the everywhere unramified case):

\bullet
The boundary observable algebra
\mathbb{H}_{\Theta,\Sigma}:=\int_{\Sigma}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Theta}
, an algebra object in
\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{Z},\Sigma}
, acts on the functional
\Theta(\Sigma)
on the
\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{Z},\Sigma}
-modules
\mathcal{Z}(\Sigma)
.

D.8.
Relative Langlands duality via field theory

We now explain how to match the structures underlying relative Langlands duality with those of boundary conditions in field theory.
To a hyperspherical
G
-variety
M
we would like to attach its
automorphic quantization
, a boundary theory
\Theta_{M}\in\mathcal{A}_{G}
for the automorphic field theory. Likewise to a hyperspherical
{\check{G}}
-variety
{\check{M}}
we would like to attach its
spectral quantization
, a boundary theory

{\mathcal{L}}_{\check{M}}\in\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}
for the spectral field theory (see Definition
17.2.2
for a weaker notion of spectral deformation quantization). We recount below some of the expected values of these boundary theories. The relative Langlands duality studied in this paper is organized by the following principle:

Conjecture D.8.1

(Meta-conjecture)
.

The automorphic and spectral quantizations of dual hyperspherical varieties are identified under the conjectural Langlands correspondence of algebraic quantum field theories
\mathbf{L}:\mathcal{A}_{G}\simeq\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}
: i.e., there is a commutative diagram

\textstyle{1_{\mathcal{C}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\Theta_{M}}
\scriptstyle{\sim}
\textstyle{1_{\mathcal{C}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{M}}}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{A}_{G}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{L}}
\scriptstyle{\sim}
\textstyle{\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}}

Let us spell out how this meta-conjecture encodes various structures that we have encountered throughout the main text.

\bullet
[Local geometric]
The local object
\Theta_{M}\in\mathcal{A}_{G}(D^{*})
is given in the polarized case
M=T^{*}X
by the category of sheaves
\mathrm{SHV}(X_{F})
with its
G_{F}
-action. Its unramified part
\Theta_{M}^{unr}
is the unramified local category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}^{X}_{G}=SHV(X_{F}/G_{O})
, a factorization algebra in
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{G}}
-module categories. The unit, i.e., the basic sheaf
\Phi\in\Theta_{M}^{unr}
, is the constant sheaf on
X_{O}
.

The local object
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{M}}}\in\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}(D^{*})
is given in the polarized case
{\check{M}}=T^{*}{\check{X}}
by the category
QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}^{\check{X}}(D^{*}))
of ind-coherent sheaves on the stack of locally constant maps into
{\check{X}}/{\check{G}}
, considered relative to the stack
\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}(D^{*})
of Langlands parameters.
Its unramified form
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{M}}}^{unr}
is identified with
QC^{!}({\mathcal{L}}{\check{X}}/{\check{G}})\simeq{QC^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}}({\check{M}}/{\check{G}})
, the unramified local spectral category.

Conjecture
7.5.1
identifies
\Theta_{M}
and
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{M}}}
as module categories for the line operators (Hecke category)
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{G}}\simeq{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}}
, and is expected to upgrade to an equivalence of factorization algebras in Hecke modules.

The ramified local geometric duality is the (currently imprecisely formulated) expectation that
\Theta_{M}
and
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{M}}}
are identified under the conjectural local geometric Langlands correspondence (in fact compatibly with factorization).

\bullet
[Local observables] The boundary observables, the factorization associative algebra
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Theta_{M}}\in{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{A}_{G}}
, recover the
Plancherel algebra
or relative Coulomb branch algebra of §
8
. Indeed the description of
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Theta}
in terms of the theory on
S^{2}\times I
amounts to the description of the Plancherel algebra as homology of the relative Grassmannian, while the description as internal endomorphisms of the basic sheaf (the unit)
\Phi\in\Theta_{M}^{unr}
in the Hecke category recovers the definition of the Plancherel algebra.

On the spectral side we find the local
{\mathcal{L}}
-observables

{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{M}}}}\simeq\mathbb{O}_{\check{M}},

the spectral deformation quantization of functions on the Hamiltonian
{\check{G}}
-space
{\check{M}}
(Definition
17.2.2
). This is a factorization associative algebra in the Hecke Category
{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}}
, quantizing the shear of the moment map
{\check{M}}/{\check{G}}\to\mathfrak{\check{g}}^{\star}/{\check{G}}
. In other words, we recover
{\check{M}}
and its Hamiltonian
{\check{G}}
-action directly out of its spectral quantization
{\mathcal{L}}_{\check{M}}
by passing to cohomology of local observables.

\bullet
[Global geometric, unramified]
The boundary condition
\Theta_{M}\in\mathcal{A}_{G}
defines a “
\Theta
-series” functional

\Theta_{M}(\Sigma):\mathcal{A}_{G}(\Sigma)=\mathrm{AUT}^{?}(\Sigma)\to 1_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}},

which is representable by an object in the automorphic category: the
M
-period sheaf
\mathcal{P}_{M}
. Likewise
{\mathcal{L}}_{\check{M}}\in\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}}
determines an object

{\mathcal{L}}_{\check{M}}(\Sigma)\in QC^{!}(\mathrm{Loc}^{?}_{\check{G}}(\Sigma)),

the
L
-sheaf of
{\check{M}}
. The duality between these recovers the global period conjecture.

\bullet
[Global observables, unramified] The global observables
\mathbb{H}_{\Theta,\Sigma}=\int_{\Sigma}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Theta}\in\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{A}_{G},\Sigma}
recover the RTF algebra, an associative algebra object in the global Hecke category
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
. The RTF algebra acts by endomorphisms of the period sheaf
\Theta_{M}(\Sigma)\in\mathcal{A}_{G}(\Sigma)
, compatibly with the
\mathbb{H}_{\Sigma}
-action.

Likewise the factorization homology
\mathbb{H}_{{\mathcal{L}},\Sigma}\in\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}},\Sigma}
of the local
{\mathcal{L}}
-observables gives the algebra object of
{\mathcal{L}}
-observables studied in §
17
, which acts as endomorphisms of the
{\mathcal{L}}
-sheaf
{\mathcal{L}}_{\check{M}}(\Sigma)\in\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}(\Sigma)
.

\bullet
[Correlation functions and
\Theta
-series]

For a finite subset
S\subset\Sigma
, we may consider the “
M
-ramified” global category
\langle\bigotimes_{S}\Theta_{M,x_{i}}\rangle_{\mathcal{A}_{G},\Sigma},
a module for the global Hecke category away from
S

\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{A}_{G},\Sigma\setminus S}
.
In the polarized case
M=T^{*}X
this is the category of sheaves on the stack of
G
-bundles with
X
-level structure along
S
(i.e., with a section of the associated
X
-bundle on the punctured neighborhood of
S
).
The boundary state
\langle-\rangle_{\Theta,S}
is then [represented by] an object of this category, preserved by the S-RTF algebra

\mathbb{H}_{\Theta_{M},\Sigma\setminus S}=\int_{\Sigma\setminus S}{\overline{\mathcal{H}}}_{\Theta_{M}}.

(In the case where
S
is empty, we recover [the functor represented by] the
X
-period sheaf.)

This object
\langle-\rangle_{\Theta,S}
is an avatar of the
\Theta
-series operation: assuming sufficient dualizability, such an object is equivalent to the data of a functor

\bigotimes_{x_{i}\in S}\Theta_{M,x_{i}}\to\mathrm{SHV}(Bun_{G}(\Sigma,S))

respecting
\prod_{S}G(F_{x_{i}})
-actions
from the local
X
-category on
S
to sheaves on the stack of bundles with full level structure along
S
.
(See §
16
for the unramified version of
\Theta
-series.)
In the colimit over
S
, the factorization homology

\int_{\Sigma}\Theta_{M}\in\int_{\Sigma}\mathcal{A}_{G}

is a geometric analog of the
G(\mathbb{A}_{\Sigma})
-representation
L^{2}(X(\mathbb{A}))
, and the state
\langle-\rangle_{\Theta}
plays the role of the adèlic
\Theta
-series.

We have a parallel story on the spectral side: the category
\langle\bigotimes_{S}{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{M}},x_{i}}\rangle_{\mathcal{B}_{\check{G}},S}
is given in the polarized case
{\check{M}}=T^{*}{\check{X}}
by ind-coherent sheaves on the stack of local systems with
{\check{X}}
-fixed points structure along
S
(i.e., with a flat section of the associated
{\check{X}}
-bundle around
S
). The state
\langle-\rangle_{{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{M}},x_{i}},S}
is represented by an object of this category – a ramified generalization of the
{\mathcal{L}}
-sheaf – preserved by the action of the
{\mathcal{L}}
-observables away from
S

\mathbb{H}_{{\mathcal{L}}_{\check{M}},\Sigma\setminus S}=\int_{\Sigma\setminus S}\mathbb{O}_{{\check{M}}}.

The unramified part of this construction
recovers the
{\mathcal{L}}
-functor construction discussed in §
17
, while for
S
empty we recover the
{\mathcal{L}}
-sheaf
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\check{X}}}\in QC^{!}(Loc_{\check{G}}(\Sigma))
.

\bullet
[Arithmetic] We leave to future work to spell out the form of these conjectures obtained by taking Frobenius traces everywhere.
At the top level, taking Frobenius trace of the period sheaves we obtain the period, as a linear functional on the global space of automorphic forms, and taking Frobenius trace of the
L
-sheaves we obtain a geometric avatar of the L-function, realized as a derived volume form on the stack of arithmetic local systems. However the necessary dualizability conditions to perform these trace only hold if we localize (on the automorphic side via the Hecke action) to the open locus
\mathrm{Loc}^{\circ}
, away from the poles of the L-function, where the map
\mathrm{Loc}^{\check{X}}\to\mathrm{Loc}_{\check{G}}
is proper.

.

Remark D.8.2

(Interfaces and functoriality)
.

More generally, it is an interesting problem to understand Langlands functoriality and its generalizations in terms of interfaces of field theory. For example, a group homomorphism
{\check{H}}\to{\check{G}}
induces natural morphisms on moduli of local systems and hence a natural interface
\mathcal{B}_{{\check{H}}}\to\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}
. Applying the Langlands corresponds produces a mysterious conjectural morphism
\mathcal{A}_{H}\to\mathcal{A}_{G}
of automorphic theories. But there are many more interfaces
\mathcal{B}_{{\check{H}}}\to\mathcal{B}_{{\check{G}}}
– in particular, those coming from spectral quantization of hamiltonian
{\check{H}}\times{\check{G}}
-spaces. In other words, we might think of the assignment
{\check{G}}\to\mathcal{B}_{\check{H}}
as a “quantization” functor out of a higher category of reductive groups and bihamiltonian actions, or equivalently (in the language of Remark
3.1.3
) shifted Lagrangian correspondences between the 3-shifted symplectic stacks
T^{*}[3]pt/{\check{G}}=\mathfrak{g}^{\star}[2]/{\check{G}}
. As remarked in §
12.3
, in a formal sense, i.e., ignoring problems with duality, and suppressing the structure of composition, the study of functoriality can be subsumed in the study of boundary theories. For example the theta correspondence can be viewed either as an operation on spaces of automorphic forms or as the study of a particular period for a product group.

Appendix E
Some miscellaneous computations

We gather here various computations that were postponed from the main body of the
text, to avoid disturbing too far the flow of proof.

E.1.
Unnormalized Eisenstein periods

We carry out the computation of the numerical period in the case of of minimal unramified Eisenstein series.
The computation is in fact completely straightforward, but it is delicate in the matter
of signs and shifts. The shift is interesting, and this is why we explicate it, although
we will be quite terse. This computation
has been alluded to in the main text at various points (§
12.3.5
, §
14.5.4
).

After setup, we derive in Lemma
E.1.4
the usual formula for the constant term of the Eisenstein series,
adapted to our notation. In §
E.1.5
we then pass from
this to the computation of the numerical period.

E.1.1.
Notation

Let
X^{*}
be the cocharacter group of the torus quotient
A
of a Borel subgroup
B\subset G
, and let

(E.1)

\lambda\in X^{*}\otimes(\mbox{everywhere unramified characters of id{\`{e}}le class group})

(tensor product of abelian groups).
Such a
\lambda
defines a character
A(\mathbb{A})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{\times}
.
For such
\lambda
, and
\alpha
a root of
G
, we can form

\lambda_{\alpha}:=\langle\lambda,\alpha^{\vee}\rangle,

which is now an everywhere unramified character of the idele class group.

In what follows we regard
2\rho
both as an element of
X^{*}
but also
as an element of the above group (
E.1
) via tensoring with the
norm
|\cdot|
on the idele class group which sends
each uniformizer
\varpi_{v}
to
q_{v}^{-1}
.
Let
\partial
be an idele representing the diiferent, as in (
10.1
), i.e.
an idele of everywhere even local valuation equal to
n_{v}
, where the
n_{v}

are the vanishing orders of a
1
-form. As in (
10.2
) this normalizes
an additive character
\psi:\mathbb{A}/F\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{\times}
,
which is locally trivial on
\partial_{v}^{-1}
but nontrivial on any larger open compact subgroup of
F_{v}
.
As an example of our notation
\langle 2\rho,\alpha^{\vee}\rangle(\partial)=|\partial|=q^{-(2g-2)}
;
In what follows we write

D=|\partial|^{-1}=q^{2g-2}

for the “discriminant.”

E.1.2.
Notation concerning completed zeta functions

Let
\xi(-)
be the completed
L
-function of the global field; we have the functional equation

\xi(0,\chi)=\chi(\partial)q^{g-1}\xi(1,\chi^{-1})
.
As in (
11.9
) we put

\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(s,\chi)=\epsilon(s,\chi)^{-1/2}\xi(s,\chi)=\chi(\partial)^{-1/2}q^{(s-1/2)(g-1)}\xi(s,\chi).

so that

(E.2)

\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(0,\chi)=\chi(\partial)^{-1/2}q^{(1-g)/2}\xi(0,\chi),\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(1,\chi)=\chi(\partial)^{-1/2}q^{(g-1)/2}\xi(1,\chi).

If we omit
s
it means that we take
s=0
. Thus
\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(\chi^{\prime})=\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(\chi)
, with
\chi^{\prime}:=|\cdot|\chi^{-1}
.
Suppose now that
\mathfrak{s}
is any
T
-stable subspace
of
\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{t}
; then we write

(E.3)

\xi(s,\mathfrak{s})=\prod\xi(\lambda_{\alpha},s)

where the product is taken over roots
\alpha
occuring
in
\mathfrak{s}
. Similarly for
\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}
etc.

E.1.3.
The Eisenstein series

We briefly summarize the construction of Eisenstein series
and compute the constant term after Whittaker normalization in Lemma
E.1.4
.

We use the standard adelic uniformization of the rational points of
\mathrm{Bun}_{G}
.
For
\lambda
in (
E.1
) we let

(E.4)

\varphi_{\lambda}:G(\mathbb{A})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}

be the unique left
N(\mathbb{A})
-invariant and right
K=G(\widehat{\mathfrak{o}})
-invariant
function whose value on
A(\mathbb{A})
is given by
\lambda+\rho

(here, we interpret
\rho
as
2\rho\otimes|\cdot|^{1/2}

inside the group (
E.1
)).
The standard Eisenstein series is obtained by summing this over the
F
-points of
G/B
;
this is convergent for
\lambda
sufficiently “positive,” e.g.
\lambda=t\rho
for
t
positive
and extends by meromorphic continuation to other
\lambda
.

Let us normalize Haar measure on
U(\mathbb{A})
so that the mass of
U(F)\backslash U(\mathbb{A})
is trivial.
This measure equals
D^{-\mathrm{dim}(U)/2}
multiplied by the measure which assigns to each
U(\mathfrak{o}_{v})
the mass
1
.

The constant term of
E_{\lambda}

may be computed as usual using the Bruhat decomposition
of
B_{F}\backslash G_{F}
into
U_{F}
-orbits of the form
wU_{F}

with stabilizer
U^{w}_{F}=\mathrm{Ad}(w)U_{F}\cap U_{F}
. This gives:

(E.5)

\int_{[U]}E_{\lambda}(ug)=\sum_{w}\int_{U^{w}_{F}\backslash U(\mathbb{A})}\varphi_{\lambda}(wug)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle GK}}{{=}}\sum_{w\in W}\prod_{\alpha>0,w\alpha<0}\frac{D^{-1/2}\xi(0,\lambda_{\alpha})}{\xi(1,\lambda_{\alpha})}\varphi_{w\lambda}

(here the
D^{-1/2}
arises from normalization of measure, as explained above, and “GK” stands for Gindinkin and Karpilevic).
The Whittaker coefficient has a similar formula with only the long Weyl element contributing; we obtain

E_{\lambda}^{\psi}(g):=\int_{[U]}E_{\lambda}(ug)\psi(u)du=\prod_{\alpha}D^{-1/2}\frac{1}{\xi(1,\lambda_{\alpha})}W_{\lambda},

with
W_{\lambda}=\prod W_{\lambda,v}
, and

W_{\lambda,v}
is given by
\xi_{v}(1,\lambda_{\alpha})\cdot\int\varphi(wug)\psi(u)du
,
where the integral is taken over
U(F_{v})
with respect to the measure assigning mass one to

U(\mathfrak{o}_{v})
.

We write

\psi(u)=\psi_{0}(a_{0,v}^{-1}ua_{0,v})

with (cf. (
10.19
)):

a_{0,v}=e^{2\rho^{\vee}}(\pi_{v}^{-n_{v}/2}),a_{0}=(a_{0,v})_{v}=e^{2\rho^{\vee}}(\partial^{-1/2}).

so that
\psi_{0}
is “unramified,” i.e.
equal to one on
U(\mathfrak{o}_{v})
but not on larger compact subgroups;
then

(E.6)

\displaystyle W_{\lambda,v}(g_{v})=\xi_{v}(1,\lambda_{\alpha})\int\varphi(wa_{0,v}ua_{0,v}^{-1}g)\psi_{0}(u)d(\mathrm{Ad}(a_{0,v})u)

(E.7)

\displaystyle=|\langle\lambda+\rho-2\rho,\rho^{\vee}\rangle(\pi_{v}^{n_{v}})|W^{0}(a_{0,v}^{-1}g),

where
W^{0}
is the unramified local Whittaker function with
W^{0}(1)=1
,
explicitly given as
\int_{U_{v}}\varphi(wug)\psi_{0}(u)du
.
Globally we get

E_{\lambda}^{\psi}(g)=\left(\prod_{\alpha}D^{-1/2}\xi(1,\lambda_{\alpha})^{-1}\right)\langle\lambda-\rho,\rho^{\vee}\rangle(\partial)W^{0}(a_{0}^{-1}g).

By Example

10.5.4
the
normalized period

\langle P_{\mathrm{Whit}}^{\mathrm{norm}},E_{\lambda}\rangle
thereby equals
the value of this at
g=a_{0}
,
multiplied by
q^{\beta/2}

where

\beta=(g-1)[\mathrm{dim}U-\langle 2\rho,2\rho^{\vee}\rangle]
.
Since
\langle\rho,\rho^{\vee}\rangle(\partial)=q^{-2(g-1)\langle\rho,\rho^{\vee}\rangle}
we get

\langle P_{\mathrm{Whit}}^{\mathrm{norm}},E_{\lambda}\rangle=q^{b_{U}/2}\left(\prod_{\alpha}D^{-1/2}\xi(1,\lambda_{\alpha})^{-1}\right)\langle\lambda,\rho^{\vee}\rangle(\partial)

with
b_{U}=(g-1)\mathrm{dim}U
, as usual.
Taking into account that
D^{-\mathrm{dim}U/2}=q^{-(g-1)\mathrm{dim}U}=q^{-b_{U}}
we get, in the shorthand of
(
E.3
):

(E.8)

\langle P_{\mathrm{Whit}}^{\mathrm{norm}},E_{\lambda}\rangle=q^{-b_{U}/2}\xi(1,\mathfrak{n})^{-1}\langle\lambda,\rho^{\vee}\rangle(\partial)

Lemma E.1.4
.

Write

\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}:=\frac{E_{\lambda}}{\langle P_{\mathrm{Whit}}^{\mathrm{norm}},E_{\lambda}\rangle}
.
Then the constant term of
\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}
, for the Haar probability measure on
U(\mathbb{A})/U(F)
, is given by

(E.9)

\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}^{U}=\sum_{w\in W}\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(0,w^{-1}\overline{\mathfrak{n}}).\varphi_{w\lambda},

where on the right we again use the shorthand of (
E.3
).

Proof.

Dividing (
E.5
) by (
E.8
) we get

(E.10)

\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}^{U}=q^{b_{U}/2}\sum_{w\in W}\langle-\lambda,\rho^{\vee}\rangle(\partial)\cdot c_{w}\varphi_{w\lambda},\mbox{ where }c_{w}=\prod_{\alpha>0}\begin{cases}D^{-1/2}\xi(0,\lambda_{\alpha}),&w\alpha<0\\
\xi(1,\lambda_{\alpha}),&w\alpha>0\end{cases}.

We must check that

(E.11)

\langle-\lambda,\rho^{\vee}\rangle(\partial)\cdot c_{w}=q^{-b_{U}/2}\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(0,w^{-1}\overline{\mathfrak{n}}).

for which we rewrite
the definition (
E.10
) via (
E.2
) and the functional equation.

c_{w}=\prod_{\alpha>0}D^{-1/4}\begin{cases}\lambda_{\alpha}(\partial)^{1/2}\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(0,\lambda_{\alpha}),&w\alpha<0\\
\lambda_{\alpha}(\partial)^{1/2}\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(0,-\lambda_{\alpha}),&w\alpha>0\end{cases}.

Our result follows after observing that the set
\{\alpha:\alpha>0,w\alpha<0\}\cup\{-\alpha:\alpha>0,w\alpha>0\}

is precisely the set of roots of the form
\{w^{-1}\beta:\beta<0\}
, and that
D^{\mathrm{dim}(U)/4}=q^{b_{U}/2}
.

∎

E.1.5.
The numerical Eisenstein period

The space of interest is
X=U\backslash G
as a
G\times T

space (i.e., via the right action
(g,t):Ux\mapsto Ut^{-1}xg
);
the point stabilizer is
T^{\Delta}U\hookrightarrow G\times T

with
T^{\Delta}
the diagonal copy of
T
:

(E.12)

X\simeq(T^{\Delta}U)\backslash G\times T.

The putative dual space is

\check{X}=\check{G}/\check{U}

with action (expressed on the left given by
(\check{g},\check{t}):x\check{U}\mapsto gxt\check{U}
,
that is to say
\check{X}=G/T^{-\Delta}U
in evident notation).

We take the
\mathbb{G}_{gr}
action on both
X
and
\check{X}
to be trivial.
The modular characters
are given by
\eta_{\mathrm{aut}}:(g,t)\mapsto e^{2\rho}(t)

and the same for
\check{X}
.

Example E.1.6
.

Here is an example, to help with figuring signs. In the case
G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}
, we have
X=\mathbb{A}^{2}-\{0\}

where
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
, identified with
T
via the positive coroot, acts by scaling
and
\mathrm{SL}_{2}
acts by right multiplication, and
\check{X}=\mathbb{A}^{2}-\{0\}/\mu_{2}
,
where
{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
, identified with
\check{T}
via the posiitve root,
acts via scaling and
\mathrm{PGL}_{2}
acts by left multiplication.

Now consider the automorphic form on
G\times T
given by

\varphi=\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}\boxtimes(w\lambda)^{-1}
,
for
\lambda
as in (
E.1
), and some
w\in W
, the Weyl group for
G
.
We now compute the ratio of periods

(E.13)

\frac{\langle P^{\mathrm{norm}}_{X},\varphi\rangle}{\langle P^{\mathrm{norm}}_{\mathrm{Whit}},\varphi\rangle}

The denominator equals one by choice of
\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}
as in Lemma
E.1.4
, for the normalized Whittaker period is the same computed on
G
or on
G\times T
. For
the numerator we use (
E.12
) as well as (
10.10
);
im the notation of the latter we have

\langle P^{\mathrm{norm}}_{G/U},\varphi\rangle=q^{-(b_{T}+b_{U})/2}\int_{U_{F}T_{F}^{\Delta}\backslash(T\times G)_{\mathbb{A}}}\Phi^{0}(g)|\eta_{\mathrm{aut}}(g)|^{1/2}\varphi(g)

where
\Phi^{0}
is the characteristic function of
U_{\mathbb{A}}T_{\mathbb{A}}^{\Delta}(G\times T)(\widehat{\mathfrak{o}})
and the measure on
T\times G

assigns mass
1
to the maximal compact.
The modular character here is given by
\eta:(t,t)\mapsto e^{2\rho}(t)
,
cf. discussion of §
3.8.1
:
the right adjoint action of
T^{\Delta}
on the tangent space at the identity coset of

(T^{\Delta}U)\backslash(T\times G)
is given by

\mathrm{Ad}(t^{-1})
on
\mathfrak{b}^{-}
.
Using Iwasawa decomposition and noting
that the integrally normalized meausre
du
is
q^{b_{U}}
multiplied by
the probability measure, we rewrite the above as:

q^{(b_{U}-b_{T})/2}\int_{T_{F}\backslash T_{\mathbb{A}}}\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}^{U}(t)(w\lambda)^{-1}(t)|e^{-\rho}(t)|

where
dt
is now the Haar measure on
T
corresponding to the standard measure on
\mathrm{Bun}_{T}

where each bundle is weighted by inverse-automorphism;
the factor
e^{-\rho}
arises from
e^{-2\rho}
from the measure in Iwasawa decomposition,
combined with the square root of the modular character.

In fact, the right hand side of (
E.13
) will diverge, since it involves (in effect) integrating a character over
T
.
We treat this purely formally: we regard it as nonzero only when the character is trivial,
in which cae it will be given by the
\zeta
-value computing the volume of
[T]
,
which we shall formally understand to
q^{(g-1)r}\xi(1)^{r}=q^{b_{T}}\xi(1)^{r}
with
r=\mathrm{dim}(T)

(this is only a formal expression, for
\xi
has a pole at
1
).

Computing formally thus, (
E.13
) equals

(E.14)

q^{b_{U}/2}q^{b_{T}/2}\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(0,w^{-1}\overline{\mathfrak{n}})\cdot\xi(1)^{\mathrm{rank}}=q^{b_{U}/2}\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(0,w^{-1}\overline{\mathfrak{b}}).

We compare this with what we would expect starting from (
14.7
)
(which is of course formulated only for cusp forms). The dual space is

\check{X}=\check{G}/\check{U}
with left action given by
(\check{g},\check{t}):x\check{U}\mapsto\check{g}x\check{t}\check{U}
;
the parameter of
\varphi

is given by
(\lambda,(w\lambda)^{-1})
, and fixes precisely
\check{x}=w^{-1}\check{U}
.
The adjoint action of
\pi_{1}
on the tangent space
T_{\check{x}}\check{X}

corresponds to the adjoint action of
\lambda
on
w^{-1}\overline{\mathfrak{b}}
.
Therefore, taking the ratio of (
14.7
) for both
G/U
and the Whittaker period
we would be led instead to a prediction of
\xi^{\mathrm{norm}}(0,w^{-1}\overline{\mathfrak{b}})
;
that is to say,
(
E.13
) is in line with (
14.7
)
except for the factor
q^{b_{U}/2}
.
This discrepancy – which, geometrically, would manifest itself as a shift
\langle b_{U}\rangle
–
was already mentioned in the text, and would be interesting to understand.
The paper
[
CV24
]
contains other examples which exhibit similar discrepancies.

E.2.
Numerical derivation of the effect of twisting

Example E.2.1
.

We revisit Lemma
12.6.4
from a numerical standpoin, examining the effect of twisting the choice of
K^{1/2}
. This computation serves solely as a sign-check on that Lemma.
We put ourselves in the situation of Conjecture
14.2.1
.
Returning to (
10.9
)

(E.15)

P_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}:g\in G(\mathbb{A})\mapsto q^{-\beta_{X}/2}|\eta_{\mathrm{aut}}(g)|^{1/2}\sum_{x\in X(F)}g\cdot(\partial^{1/2}\cdot\Phi(x)),.

and replace
X
by
X^{\prime}=X[\eta_{\mathrm{spec}}^{\vee,-1}]
. Then
\beta_{X^{\prime}}=\beta_{X}+\tau
with
\tau=(g-1)\langle\eta_{\mathrm{aut}},\eta_{\mathrm{spec}}\rangle
we get
the result is

P_{X^{\prime}}=\sum_{x}(g,\partial^{1/2})\cdot^{\prime}\Phi(x)=\eta_{\mathrm{spec}}^{\vee}(\partial^{-1/2})\left[q^{\beta_{X}/2}|\eta_{\mathrm{aut}}(g)|^{-1/2}P_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}\right].

Pairing this against
f
with central character
\omega_{f}
gives
can be computed in terms of the same pairing for the normalized period:

P_{X^{\prime}}(f)=q^{\beta_{X}/2}\omega_{f}(\eta_{\mathrm{spec}}^{\vee}(\partial^{1/2}))P_{X}^{\mathrm{norm}}(f^{\prime})

where
f^{\prime}
is
f
twisted by
|\eta_{\mathrm{aut}}|^{-1/2}
.
This has the effect of twisting the Galois parameter of
f
through the composite

\textrm{cyclotomic}^{1/2}\circ\eta_{\mathrm{aut}}^{\vee,-1}
.
Applying Conjecture
14.2.1
we find

P_{X^{\prime}}(f)=q^{(\beta_{X}-b_{G})/2}\omega_{f}(\eta_{\mathrm{spec}}^{\vee}(\partial^{1/2}))L^{\mathrm{norm}}(0,T^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}},^{\prime}})

where
T^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}}}
is the tangent space
sheared by the twisted action for
\check{X}^{\prime}=\check{X}[\eta_{\mathrm{aut}}^{\vee,-1}]
.

Now
\omega_{f}(\eta_{\mathrm{spec}}^{\vee}(\partial^{1/2}))

is the square root of the central
\epsilon
-factor for the Galois parameter
of
f
acting on
\det(T)
. We apply (
11.43
) which says

\epsilon(0,T^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}},^{\prime}})=\varepsilon(1/2,T)q^{b_{G}-\beta_{\check{X}^{\prime}}}

to rewrite

P_{X^{\prime}}(f)=q^{\beta_{X}/2+\beta_{\check{X}^{\prime}}/2-b_{G}}\ L^{\mathrm{norm}}(0,T^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}},^{\prime}})

and using
\beta_{\check{X}^{\prime}}=\beta_{\check{X}}-\tau
this becomes

P_{X^{\prime}}(f)=q^{-b_{G}}q^{\beta_{X}/2+\beta_{\check{X}^{\prime}}/2-\tau/2}L^{\mathrm{norm}}(0,T^{{\mathbin{\mkern-6.0mu\fatslash}},^{\prime}})

which can be compared with (
11.35
), i.e.
the conclusion is that
X^{\prime}
and
\check{X}^{\prime}
are dual,
but one has to twist the period sheaf by
\beta_{X}+\beta_{\check{X}}-\tau
.

∎

E.3.
Proof of Proposition
5.1.1

Proof.

(sketch)
Soulé’s etale Chern class
[
Sou79
, II]
defines a morphism

(E.16)

c_{22}:H_{2}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2r}(F),\mathbb{Z}/2)\rightarrow H^{2}(F,\mathbb{Z}/2)

which can be verified (comparing with the discussion of
[
Del96
]
and
[
Pra04
]
)
to define the metaplectic extension of
\mathrm{Sp}_{2r}(F)
, that is to say,
the unique topological double cover thereof.

Now consider the two representations of
H
defined by

H\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}_{2r}\mbox{ and }H\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\theta}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathbb{G}_{m}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{SL}_{2},

where the last map is the inclusion
of a maximal torus. It follows from (
5.1
) that these two representations of
H
have the
same second Chern class. Therefore the two maps

H_{2}(H(F),\mathbb{Z}/2)\rightarrow H^{2}(F,\mathbb{Z}/2)

arising from pulling back (
E.16
) via
H\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}_{V}

or
H\rightarrow\mathrm{SL}_{2}
must coincide.

We claim that the latter pullback of
c_{22}
, via
H\rightarrow\mathrm{SL}_{2}
is trivial.
Indeed, this factors through
\mathbb{G}_{m}(F)
, and our claim follows
from the fact that
the metaplectic cover of
\mathrm{SL}_{2}(F)
splits over
\mathbb{G}_{m}(F)=F^{\times}
.
159
159

159

At the level of cocycles, this amounts to fact
that the Hilbert symbol
F^{\times}\times F^{\times}\rightarrow\pm 1

is trivialized as
2
-cocycle by
the
1
-cocycle

\eta:u\varpi^{n}\mapsto\bar{u}^{n}\cdot(-1,-1)^{n\choose 2}

where we write, for short,
\bar{u}=\pm 1
according to whether
u
is residually a square or not.

Therefore, the pullback of the metaplectic cover under
H\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}_{2r}(F)
does too.

∎

The construction above globalizes:
if
F
is a global function field, then the metaplectic cover of
\mathrm{Sp}(\mathbb{A}_{F})

splits upon pullback to
H(\mathbb{A}_{F})
compatibly with its standard splitting on
\mathrm{Sp}(F)
.
Moreover, if we push out the metaplectic cover by
\pm 1\rightarrow S^{1}
, the result
above remains valid for

F=\mathbb{R}
or an extension of
\mathbb{Q}_{2}
.
In relation to rationality issues we note at least the following:

Lemma E.3.1
.

Suppose
\rho:H\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}

is a homomorphism of split
\mathbb{Z}
-groups,
and that after base change to
\mathbb{C}
the Chern class condition of Proposition
5.1.1

is satisfied (for some character
\theta:H\rightarrow{\mathbb{G}_{m}}
, which
we may as well suppose defined over
\mathbb{Z}
).

Then the metaplectic cover pulled back to
H(F)
splits over any field
F

in which
\pm 2
are both squares.

A similar assertion holds for
\mathbb{Z}[1/N]
, with identical proof, but now additionally requiring prime divisors of
N
to be squares.

Proof.

We are going to verify that the condition of Proposition
5.1.1
, i.e.

c_{2}(\rho)=c_{1}(\theta)^{2}

in absolute étale cohomology
over
F
.

To do so we will first compute in étale cohomolgy over
\mathbb{Z}[1/2]
and first show that
there the difference is decomposable:

(E.17)

c_{2}(\rho)-c_{1}(\theta)^{2}\in H^{1}\cup H^{3},

from which we will readily deduce the result in the final paragraph.

Let
P
be a Borel subgroup of
H
over
\mathbb{Z}
.
Note that
c_{2}(\rho)-c_{1}(\theta)^{2}

dies in the mod
2
étale cohomology of
BP_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]}

(i.e., the classifying space of
P
as a group scheme over
\mathbb{Z}[1/2]
,
which can be constructed as a simplicial
\mathbb{Z}[1/2]
-scheme).
To see this, we note that
P
can be replaced by a maximal torus,
and the cohomology
BT_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]}
is a polynomial
ring over
H^{*}(\mathbb{Z}[1/2])
generated by the Chern classes
of a basis of
\mathrm{Hom}(T,{\mathbb{G}_{m}})
. Both
c_{2}(\rho)
and
c_{1}(\theta)

can be expressed as polynomials in these Chern classes
(with coefficients in
\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}
); the subring of such classes in
H^{*}(BT_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]})

maps isomorphically to
H^{*}(BT_{\mathbb{C}})
, and therefore
the coincidence of
c_{2}(\rho)
and
c_{1}(\theta)^{2}
in
BT_{\mathbb{C}}

implies the same over
\mathbb{Z}[1/2]
.

Now consider the map in étale cohomology
induced by
BP_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]}\rightarrow BH_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]}
.
We will show its kernel is decomposable, and in fact belongs
to the right hand side of (
E.17
), concluding the proof.
By the Serre spectral sequence
(applied in
H
-equivariant cohomology with mod
2
coefficients for the fibration
\pi:H/P\rightarrow\mathrm{Spec}\mathbb{Z}[1/2]
)
we get a spectral sequence converging to the étale cohomology of
BP_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]}

and whose
E_{2}^{pq}
term is given by

H^{p}(BH_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]},R^{q}\pi_{*}\mathbb{Z}/2).

The
R^{q}\pi_{*}
terms are vanishing only for
q
even;
we will repeatedly use this without comment. The only possible obstruction
to the injectivity of the edge map
H^{4}(BH)\rightarrow H^{4}(BP)

comes from the differential
d_{3}:E_{3}^{12}\rightarrow E_{3}^{40}
.
But
E_{3}^{12}=E_{2}^{12}=H^{1}(BH_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]},R^{2}\pi_{*}\mathbb{Z}/2)

and the action of
\pi_{1}(BH_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]})=\pi_{1}(\mathbb{Z}[1/2])
on
R^{2}\pi_{*}\mathbb{Z}/2

is trivial (in fact, this is the mod
2
reduction of
R^{2}\pi_{*}\mathbb{Z}_{2}

which is a sum of copies of
\mathbb{Z}_{2}(1)
, indexed by Schubert cells of codimension
1
).

Consequently, each class in
E_{2}^{12}
is a product
of a class in
E_{2}^{10}=E_{3}^{10}
and
E_{2}^{02}=E_{3}^{02}
.
Since the differential
d_{3}
is a derivation,
we conclude that the image of such a class under
d_{3}

has the form
E_{3}^{10}\cup E_{3}^{30}
.
However,
E_{3}^{10}=E_{2}^{10}=H^{1}(BH_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]},\mathbb{Z}/2)
and
E_{2}^{30}=E_{3}^{30}=H^{3}(BH_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]},\mathbb{Z}/2)
,
so the image of such a class under
d_{3}
corresponds
to a class in
H^{4}(BH)
that decomposes as
H^{1}\cup H^{3}
,
i.e.
is decomposable as in (
E.17
).
The kernel of

H^{4}(BH)\rightarrow H^{4}(BP)
consists entirely of such classes, and so we are done with the proof of (
E.17
).

Finally, the claimed result follows from (
E.17
), because
the natural map
H^{1}(\mathbb{Z}[1/2],\mathbb{Z}/2)\rightarrow H^{1}(BH_{\mathbb{Z}[1/2]})
is an isomorphism; the source group
coincides with the group of square classes in
\mathbb{Z}[1/2]^{\times}
, and this is killed
by passage to any
F
as in the statement.
∎

E.4.
Proof of Proposition
E.4.1

In the main text, we used the following perhaps intuitively obvious
manifestation of the rigidity of homomorphisms between reductive groups:

Proposition E.4.1
.

Suppose
that
G_{1},G_{2}
are split groups over
\mathbb{Z}
and

\mathcal{F}

a conjugacy class of complex homomorphism
(G_{1})_{\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow(G_{2})_{\mathbb{C}}

containing a homomorphism defined over
\mathbb{Q}
.
For any sufficiently large
p
, the following is valid:

There exists, up to conjugacy, only one homomorphism
f_{q}:(G_{1})_{\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}}\rightarrow(G_{2})_{\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}}

of the associated reductive groups over
\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}

which fits into a diagram

\mathcal{F}\ni f_{\mathbb{C}}\leftarrow f_{\mathbb{Q}}\rightarrow f_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}\leftarrow f_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\rightarrow f_{\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}}

Here the
f_{R}:(G_{1})_{R}\rightarrow(G_{2})_{R}
denote homomorphisms of
group schemes over
R
, and arrows
f_{R}\rightarrow f_{R^{\prime}}

denote base change by a ring homomorphism
R\rightarrow R^{\prime}
.

Proof.

By assumption there is a
\mathbb{Q}
-homomorphism
f_{\mathbb{Q}}^{0}
in the conjugacy class of
f
.
We will fix such an
f_{\mathbb{Q}}^{0}
once and for all.
The constants
p_{0},N
coming out of the argument are going to depend on the choice of
f_{\mathbb{Q}}^{0}
.

Suppose given diagrams

(E.18)

f_{\mathbb{C}}\leftarrow f_{\mathbb{Q}}\rightarrow f_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}},f^{\prime}_{\mathbb{C}}\leftarrow f_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\prime}\rightarrow f^{\prime}_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}

where
f^{\prime}_{\mathbb{C}},f_{\mathbb{C}}
are conjugate.
Let
f_{\bar{p}},f^{\prime}_{\bar{p}}
be the base-changes of
f_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}},f^{\prime}_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}

along

\mathbb{Z}_{p}\rightarrow\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}
. We will
first of all show that
f_{\bar{p}},f^{\prime}_{\bar{p}}
are conjugate to one another so long as
p\geq p_{0}
.

We will need a version of “the scheme of homomorphisms from
G_{1}
to
G_{2}
.”
We fix
a
G_{2}\times G_{2}
-stable subspace
subspace
W_{2}\subset\mathbb{C}[G_{2}]
such that
W_{2}\cap\mathbb{Z}[G_{2}]

(integral lattice defined by the Chevalley form) generates
\mathbb{Z}[G_{2}]
.
Let us fix a similarly stable
W_{1}\subset\mathbb{C}[G_{1}]

with the property that
f_{0,\mathbb{Q}}^{*}W_{1}\subset W_{2}
. The same inclusion is then holds
true for both
f_{\mathbb{Q}}
and
f_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\prime}
:
both
f_{\mathbb{Q}}
and
f_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\prime}
send
W_{2}\cap\mathbb{Q}[G_{2}]

to
W_{1}\cap\mathbb{Q}[G_{1}]
.

The functor that sends a ring
A

to homomorphisms of
A
-group schemes

\theta:G_{1,A}\rightarrow G_{2,A}
with the property that

\theta^{*}W_{2,A}\subset W_{1,A}
is representable by a finite type
\mathbb{Z}
-scheme that we will call
Y
.
160
160

160

In SGA3,
[
DG70
, Corollaire 7.2.3,XXIV]
there is a more systematic treatment of the
\mathrm{Hom}
-scheme.
However, the “full”
\mathrm{Hom}
-scheme is much bigger, because it includes, e.g., Frobenius morphisms in characteristic
p
. By imposing
the condition that
\theta^{*}
map
W_{2}
to
W_{1}
, we eliminate the Frobenius morphism in almost all characteristics
thereby producing a finite type scheme.

Indeed,
\theta^{*}
defines an element of the affine space
\mathrm{Hom}(W_{2,A},W_{1,A})
,
thus realizing the functor as a subfunctor of this affine space.
The condition that
\theta
define a homomorphism of group schemes amounts
to imposing the condition that it extend to a Hopf algebra homomorphism,
which is seen to be the
A
-points of a
\mathbb{Z}
-subscheme.
Moreover, there is an evident action of
G_{2}
on
Y

by post-composing a homomorphism with conjugation on
G_{2}
.

Now,

f_{\mathbb{Q}},f_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\prime}
both define
\mathbb{Q}
-points of
Y
.
They lie in the same irreducible component of
Y_{\mathbb{C}}
,
comprising the
(G_{2})_{\mathbb{C}}
-orbit of either one.
Let
Y_{0}
denote its Zariski closure of this irreducible component inside
Y

(that is to say, the Zariski closure of the corresponding set of closed points in the underlying scheme
Y
).
We equip
Y_{0}
,
a priori
a closed subset, with
the reduced scheme structure.

By general principles, our “reference” morphism
f^{0}_{\mathbb{Q}}

extends to a
\mathbb{Z}[1/N]
-point of
Y
for some
N
;
necessarily, the resulting morphism
\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{Z}[1/N]\rightarrow Y

factors uniquely through
Y_{0}
.
To simplify typography write
\mathbb{Z}^{\prime}:=\mathbb{Z}[1/N]
.
thus,
f^{0}_{\mathbb{Q}}
extends to a
\mathbb{Z}^{\prime}
-point
f^{0}_{\mathbb{Z}^{\prime}}
of
Y_{0}
.
Acting on this
f^{0}_{\mathbb{Z}^{\prime}}
we get a morphism of schemes
over
\mathbb{Z}^{\prime}

(E.19)

(G_{2})_{\mathbb{Z}^{\prime}}\rightarrow(Y_{0})_{\mathbb{Z}^{\prime}}

whose image is, by Chevalley’s theorem, a constructible subset,
and it contains all points on the generic fiber
(Y_{0})_{\mathbb{Q}}
.
The complement of this constructible
set is itself constructible, and so has constructible image
in
\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{Z}^{\prime}
,
disjoint from the generic point of
\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{Z}^{\prime}
. Therefore, enlarging
N
,
we can suppose that this orbit map (
E.19
) is surjective at the pointwise level.
This implies, in particular, that
each fiber
Y_{0}\times\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}

is a single orbit of
(G_{2})_{\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}}

for sufficiently large
p
.

Return now to (
E.18
).
Observe that
f_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}
and
f_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}^{\prime}

correspond to maps
\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{Z}_{p}\rightarrow Y
; the condition
that
f_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}^{*}W_{2,\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\subset W_{1,\mathbb{Z}_{p}}
and its analogue for
f^{\prime}
follow from the statement over
\mathbb{Q}
.
The image of these maps
\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{Z}_{p}\rightarrow Y
lie inside
Y_{0}
,
and therefore the maps themselves factor uniquely through
Y_{0}\hookrightarrow Y
.
In particular, so long as
p
does not divide
N
, the maps
\mathrm{Spec}\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}\rightarrow Y
classifying
f_{\bar{p}},f^{\prime}_{\bar{p}}

have images belonging to the same
G_{2}
-orbit, i.e.

f_{\bar{p}},f^{\prime}_{\bar{p}}
are conjugate to one another by
G_{2}(\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}})
.

∎
